article.title: The Faceless Slideshow Format Behind 17M Organic Study Views
article.content:
An AI study app is achieving serious recognition with one of the cheapest (and polarizing) content formats on TikTok: faceless slideshows.

ScrollToStudy turns notes and study materials into flashcards, quizzes, summaries, and a personalized study feed. The product is built around a scrolling interface, making it feel closer to social media than a traditional flashcard app.

Last month, it reached 10K downloads.

Its growth so far has come almost entirely from faceless slideshow content.

Across five TikTok accounts, the app has generated 17M views. Every account follows the same basic setup: study slideshows, generic advice, and a soft app mention built into the sequence.

The strongest format right now is built around one hook:

“Toxic exam advice my professor gave us… and I hate that it actually works”

Same format, same hook, same advice, and it worked three different times.

The slideshow itself is simple. It runs through numbered study tips, with one slide used to mention the app directly:

“I started using ScrollToStudy every time instead of scrolling on TikTok”

The best-performing version was posted on March 17, 2026, and reached 5M views with nearly 300K bookmarks.

Then there is the second conversion layer.

The top comment says, “Wow scroll to study sounds genius!” and has almost 6K likes. Whether planted or not, it works as a secondary CTA by making the product feel noticed and validated inside the comment section.

The app skipped overproduced UGC, heavy edits, and big creator networks. Instead, it shows you can hit millions of views with a simple faceless slideshow, a curiosity-driven hook, and one product mention right in the middle.

Low risk, high reward for study apps. But will it last?

article.title: The New AI Assistant Marketing ALL Niches on TikTok (& Winning)
article.content:
Poke is not really an app in the typical sense.

It is an AI assistant that lives in SMS, where each role (called “recipe”) feels like its own product.

One can act like a fitness tracker. Another can turn into an AI photo tool. Another can work like a productivity assistant.

Instead of one app, think of a sort of mini App Store of AI tools, all running right inside your texts.

Got the picture? Good, because this product structure is exactly where their growth strategy starts.

Instead of trying to market one broad assistant to everyone, Poke can promote each of these recipes like it is its own standalone app, using the hooks and formats that already work in that niche.

And that is exactly what they are doing.

Some ambassadors promote Poke Fit like a fitness app. Others push Poke Pics through prank-style AI content. So the real distribution story is not one product going viral, but one backend being split into multiple category-specific growth tracks.

That gives the team way more room to experiment and ultimately crack virality.

A fitness creator does not need to explain the full product. They only need to sell the fitness version. A photo creator can do the same with the photo recipe. The backend stays the same, but the content changes depending on the niche.

One creator, Christina, uses the handle @journalwithchristina and mainly promotes Poke Fit through nutrition and fitness hooks.

Another ambassador, @journalwithbritain, uses the same “journalwith” identity system but promotes Poke Pics instead, with faceless prank videos.

The ambassadors are not locked into selling one broad brand message. They can pick the recipe that fits their content best, even if the underlying product is the same.

So far, the most aggressively pushed recipes seem to be Poke Fit and Poke Pics.

The UGC campaign only started in February 2026, but the first promising videos are already coming in.

On April 3, 2026, creator @kate.ventsssss hit 250K views promoting Poke Pics with a faceless prank video.

A couple of weeks earlier, on March 20, 2026, creator @sadie.ventsssss hit 214K views promoting Poke Fit through a long-hook storyline tied directly to the product name.

Most AI assistants have a positioning problem. They can do too many things, which makes them harder to market clearly. Poke’s team solved that by turning one broad product into multiple niche-specific entry points. That makes the content much easier to understand and much easier to distribute.

The campaign is still early, with 1.5M total views so far, but the structure is smart: one backend, multiple use cases, multiple creator lanes. If one of those lanes finally breaks out, the product gets a repeatable way to market the same assistant like a portfolio of different apps.

article.content:
This sound is back, and now it is being used as a soft-launching hate format.

People use it to test an opinion before fully saying it out loud. Most videos are about dislike, annoyance, or quiet frustration, then the joke lands when everyone else agrees.

How to use: this works well for social, dating, work, or study apps. Start with a small complaint your audience will instantly recognize, then use the trend to show that other people feel the same way.

This hook is built around one simple idea: you remember you have free will, then do something impulsive because of it.

The setup is broad, but it can go in a lot of directions, from chaotic jokes to very clear product actions.

How to use: this is a strong fit for utility apps. Start with the “practice your free will” line, then show the action your product makes possible. Book the trip, build the site, send the message, buy the thing.

Read the full trend here.

This is a faceless guessing format built around one very simple interaction.

The creator shares two true details and one lie, usually using their birthday where the month and day are real but the year is fake. The whole point is to guess before the reveal.

How to use: this works well for faceless apps because the format does not need much. One screen recording, one short hook, and one reveal is enough. You can adapt it anywhere your audience likes testing themselves, guessing, or interacting before the answer is shown.

Another version is already at 3.6M views. See the format here.

This trend is about showing how one phrase can mean two completely different things.

Creators write a line like “trying to explain I mean this, not that,” then show the version they mean and the version people assume, usually through images, emojis, or visual contrasts.

How to use: this fits apps that live inside a specific lifestyle, identity, or habit. Use it to clarify the version of the behavior your audience actually relates to, then connect your app to that side.

This audio is being used for small heartwarming moments that feel almost too cute to handle.

Most videos keep it very simple: soft face-cam, one line of text starting with “when…”, then a small wholesome moment.

How to use: this works best for apps tied to couples, nostalgia, friendships. A couple app can use it for a sweet ritual. A photo or memory app can use it for old pictures or family moments. The goal is to make the app feel personal, not just useful.

article.title: Do AI Pranks Always Go Viral?
article.content:
CelebGen is an AI app for iPhone and iPad that creates ultra‑realistic selfies with celebrities or iconic locations.

You probably remember that classic TikTok format where people used an edited AI photo to prank someone. A bunch of apps pulled in millions of views with that kind of content.

CelebGen tried to tap into that same angle, but the results shown here weren’t fully organic.

“I pranked my bestie telling her I met her celeb crush” → 1.8M views

The rest of their content follows a single pattern-> creator slideshows featuring selfies with celebrities.

However, the only truly organic hit came from @alexa.paparazzi, four months ago:

“Friendsmas with my two best friends!” → 4.7M views

Since prank-based AI image apps perform best, CelebGen could get better results by leaning more into that format.

Below are four practical tips on how to execute this format in a way that actually drives organic views.

article.title: One Sound Format Took This App Past 50M Views
article.content:
Omnira is a focus and sleep app built around sound.

It combines a variety of things such as 8D audio, binaural beats, white noise, nature sounds, and guided meditations into one product, with a clear positioning around attention support, stress relief, and better sleep.

Released in May 2025, it reached 10K downloads last month.

Across its main TikTok and Instagram accounts, plus a smaller ambassador wave, the app recently crossed 50M views. Most of that came from the official @omnira_app pages alone, which generated around 21M views on Instagram and 20M on TikTok by reposting the same founder-led videos across both platforms.

The founder appears on screen, usually lip-syncing to a popular song, while the actual hook is the sound itself. The audio is presented as an 8D or bilateral-stimulation experience, and the CTA asks viewers to try it in a specific way.

On TikTok, the best-performing video hit 1.8M views & 18.4K bookmarks with:

“This is called bilateral stimulation. It activates both sides of your Hemispheres and can be Extremely soothing for those With an overloaded brain.”

On Instagram, the biggest video hit 4M views with nearly the same structure:

“FACT: bilateral stimulation is extremely soothing for those with an overloaded mind”

After realizing this winning strategy was going viral multiple times, they started creating new accounts to replicate it.

One of them was @evelyngonzalez90, which appears to be the founder’s partner. She hit two 1M+ views videos by doing the same strategy but reacting to it, with the founder alongside her. The hook was always the same:

“Just put your phone under your chin and listen to this”

Most apps need to explain why the product matters. Omnira’s format skips that step by turning the video itself into the demo. The viewer is testing the “feature” in real time, which makes the CTA feel much more natural.

That is especially important for a product like this, where the value is sensory. You cannot really sell it with screenshots alone. You need people to hear what you want them to feel.

article.title: They Copied Viral App Videos and Turned Them Into 500K Downloads
article.content:
A ChatGPT-wrapper app just hit 500K downloads in the last 30 days with a French-led TikTok playbook that looks rough, low-cost, and surprisingly effective.

Macaron AI is an AI app that lets users create their own mini-tools inside a chat-style interface instead of downloading a different app for every need. Someone can use it to build a meal tracker, habit logger, planner, or other simple utility just by describing what they want.

The app is currently ranked #11 in Utilities in France.

On TikTok, Macaron AI has generated around 163M views across eight accounts, although some videos appear to have been partially boosted.

From January 15 to March 25, 2026, Macaron ran three faceless TikTok accounts that went extremely viral.

@macaronai1 reached 88M views.@macaronai2 reached 44M views.@macaronai00 reached 23M views.

Each account only posted 28 videos.

That is what makes the strategy interesting.

Instead of trying to invent original concepts for TikTok, Macaron seems to have taken viral videos already proven for other apps and swapped in a Macaron-made mini-app as the demo.

That works because the product is broad enough to fit almost any consumer-app use case. If the original ad is selling a budgeting tool, a planner, a couple feature, or a niche utility, Macaron can position itself as the app that can generate something similar inside its own interface.

One of the clearest examples came on March 25, 2026, when @macaronai1 hit 18.2M views with:

“I surprised my boyfriend with a cute couples photo shoot”

The structure looks borrowed from an existing paid partnership for another app. But instead of keeping the original CTA, the video swaps in an AI-generated voice telling viewers to download Macaron. At the end, it adds the app name, icon, and a direct install button.

That is the core idea behind the playbook.

Take a format that already proved it can sell an app, then retrofit it to your own product.

Macaron also ran a second distribution lane.

Alongside the copied app-promo videos, the team posted faceless AI-generated story clips using satisfying retention visuals, like cutting boards and other sensory scenes.

These videos pushed constant app branding on screen, usually with the app icon, the name, and text telling people to download the app to read the whole story.

It is a very different format, but the logic is similar.

Low production. High repeatability. Strong curiosity.

The videos are not polished, but they are easy to make and easy to scale.

And according to the App Store reviews, people are explicitly mentioning that they discovered the app through these TikTok stories and ended up liking it.

Macaron is winning because they found two cheap, repeatable content systems: recycled app-promo videos and faceless cliffhanger stories with constant app CTAs.

Even if some of the reach was helped by paid distribution, the strategy itself is still clear: copy what already works, adapt it to a product broad enough to fit many niches, and repeat it until the volume compounds.

article.title: Bible Stories Turned Into Tea: 49M Views
article.content:
Bible BFF just hit another 9.2M views in the last month by pushing a format that feels closer to reaction content than app content.

Creators film themselves listening while Bible stories are retold like millennial gossip with Gen Z phrasing. The format is something in between a story time, reaction content, and a clip from a podcast.

Their main hook driving this wave right now has been as version of:

“God bless the girl who read through the entire Bible but made it sound like tea.”

Several accounts are posting versions of it, and it keeps landing.

One post from their top creator, @tessa.bible, hit 5.4M views on Instagram Reels in three weeks with that exact hook:

“God bless the girl who read through the entire Bible but made it sound like tea.”

She’s sitting at 46.9M views basically repeating the hook while testing different formats.

Another video already crossed 1M views with a slightly different setup: three girls sit in the car, press play, and react while a Bible story is told like gossip.

The app is being packaged as something you listen to for fun first.

If your app has content inside it, you can package that content like entertainment and let the reaction sell the product.

article.title: The Dating Format They Can Repost Forever
article.content:
Cerca has one ambassador rerunning the same 8-second boyfriend checklist every week, while the founder tests a second narrative around escaping dating-app humiliation.

We covered Cerca’s “My application to be your boyfriend” format three months ago. Now it is one of the app’s main growth drivers.

This one creator @ben.ekedahl basically turned one idea into a weekly series’ bringing him up to 14.6M lifetime views and Cerca’s second-best-performing account.

All of his last 50 videos are some variation of the same structure: “My application to be your boyfriend — Ben, 27, 6’3″ — [green flags] — Only on Cerca.”

He pulled 1M views one week ago:

Each new video only needs a slightly different combination of traits “Takes your pictures. Pays for dates. Won’t make you work out ect…“.

So the format stays the same, and you can repeat the same videos endlessly just making enough list changes to create a new comment section.

The CTA “only on Cerca” can always be included.

At the same time, the founder is pushing a different angle.

@cerca.myles first started building his account around an anti-dating-app narrative. The content framed Hinge, Raya, and Tinder as embarrassing and  frustrating to position Cerca as the alternative.

He is at 15.3M views on TikTok and 14.3M views on Instagram.

Now he is trying a newer format: faceless videos with voiceover where he spins a wheel, chooses a follower, then contacts friends to figure out who that person’s crush is and set them up on a date.

One of those already hit 334K views.

article.title: Join the Hottest App Store Category, Steal the Best Formats
article.content:
It’s no secret that language learning is one of the biggest view drivers on TikTok, and the 23 apps on our site make that clear.

So far, the most viral formats in this category are extremely consistent:

1. The “Why is [language] so hard?” emotional close‑up

Template: “Why is [language] so hard 😭🤔” ->Creators film themselves crying into their pillow with the same hook every time.

2. Serialized learning‑journey content

Template: “Day [num] of learning [language]”

here you can see:

We found an app in this category trying to reach the same numbers by copying these proven formats: DuoCards.

DuoCards runs 12 creator accounts, and their first hits only started appearing at the end of 2025.

Despite testing different formats, the only one that actually performed was the already‑proven “Why is [language] so hard?” format.

“Whyy is French soo hard? 😭🤔🇫🇷” → 966.1K views

However, when the same creator tried to repeat the format while replying to a comment, the results dropped significantly.

“Whyy is French soo hard? 😂😭🇫🇷” → 391K views

The app currently has 40K downloads, but if they continue landing hits like the one from two months ago, that number could grow quickly.

article.title: FinanceTok: Finvest’s 3 Promising Formats
article.content:
After two years on the market, Finvest is finally getting some traction on TikTok.

One of the main angles creators focus on is the IRA, an individual retirement account in the US.

Example:

“Finally maxed out my Roth IRA for the first time.” → 216.9K views, 1,062 comments

Since 2025, another format they use is the corporate profit explainer, where creators explain how big companies make money and connect it to larger financial trends.

“Microsoft just made $25.8B in profit — then laid off 7,000 employees. Why? AI.” → 408.8K views

Their only truly viral video comes from a creator who takes random clips and connects them to a financial regret, in this case, not investing in NVIDIA.

“Why didn’t you buy NVIDIA in 2012? Here’s what I was doing in 2012.” → 2.7M views

But this may have been a one‑off. The same account had already posted similar videos with weak results.

Example:

“Me after the $0.47 of NVIDIA dividends hits my Finvest account.” → 954 views

We leave you with a good selection of reads if you’re interested in learning more about the Finance niche.

article.title: Giant AI Platform Scales to 50M+ Views on TikTok
article.content:
If you’re either studying or working, chances are you’ve heard of Gamma, an AI tool for making presentations, docs, and simple webpages fast.

It has become one of the go-to AI platforms for Powerpoint creation without needing design skills.

Founded in 2020, the website started growing much faster in 2024. By March 2026, it is already averaging around 5 million daily organic visits.

And guess what: they didn’t stay out of the TikTok wave.

We found a total of 32 Gamma accounts across TikTok and Instagram, including two main brand pages and a 30-account ambassador army.

Together, those accounts have generated more than 50M views.

Interestingly, their best-performing accounts are still Gamma’s official pages.

Across the two main brand accounts, they have generated 30M views on Instagram and 9M on TikTok.

Their biggest early TikTok win came in 2024 with a very simple hook:

“AI CAN MAKE PRESENTATIONS NOW?”

Across two videos using the same format, Gamma generated a combined 7.8M views and 236K bookmarks. The structure was simple: shocked face first, then app demo. The hook did most of the work, really.

On Instagram, though, Gamma’s biggest wins came through paid partnerships.

The strongest example was a collaboration with creator pictelate, who made more than 15M views by using his usual rage-bait event format and attaching a Gamma promo at the end.

That is a very different kind of distribution from the main TikTok demo posts.

Instead of leading with product shock, it borrowed an already-proven creator format and let the promo land inside content that was built to go viral regardless.

More recently, Gamma launched a large ambassador wave. The campaign started on February 4, 2026. Two months in, most of the ambassador accounts are still below 1M total views. But one creator quickly broke away from the rest.

@chiomasworkdiary has only 10 videos and hit 8.7M views on her very first post. The hook was not product-first at all.

She opened with a story about how both she and her male friend had decided at the same time that they should stop pretending to be just friends. When she went to his house to tell him, he had already prepared a Gamma slide deck asking her out.

The “Gamma PPT” mention is subtle, but that is exactly why it works.

The storytime hook does the heavy lifting, while the product appears almost as a plot detail. Viewers stop for the relationship tension, then end up discovering Gamma through curiosity.

Gamma kept testing across main pages, influencers, and a big ambassador wave until different winners emerged on each platform.

That is what got it past 50M views.

article.title: The Return of Cute BFF Apps: The Friend Breakup
article.content:
Zumi is bringing back the “cute BFF” trend that started last year, with a virtual best friend you can dress up, grow and share parts of your day with.

The app has been growing steadily since September 2025 but the first noticeable traction only happened this year.

Zumi currently runs 23 creator accounts.

We noticed that all of them are following a very similar format, consisting of a close up shot of the creator, paired with a hook about their “best friend,” who is actually their Zumi.

“I saw a quote that said ‘you know you really love someone when you don’t hate them for breaking your heart.’ And that hit pretty hard (my Zumi told me this btw).” -> 731.9K views

Before that, @alexspocketpet tested a different angle, and it worked even better. Instead of focusing on a virtual best friend, she talked about the struggles that come with having one in real life.

Clever move when addressing a younger audience with frequent friendship fallouts and school gossip.

“The one thing I’ve always craved since I was a little girl was a best friend who also thought I was their best friend.” → 965.1K views

“Forget breakups, have you ever slowly stopped contacting your best friend because it felt one‑sided, and now you just don’t speak?” → 1.5M views

Despite the strong formats, not all videos achieve completely organic reach.

What happens next will show if they can turn these wins into a repeatable content system, or if they will end up relying on paid ads again over time.

article.title: Before‑and‑After Format Still Wins: Ecosia
article.content:
You probably know Ecosia, the search engine that uses the ad revenue generated from your searches to fund global reforestation projects.

They released the mobile app in 2023 and currently rank #23.

Ecosia has two official accounts, one on TikTok and one on Instagram. Both are verified and share the same kind of content.

Their videos use a before-and-after transformation format.

They show what a specific region of the planet looked like before Ecosia intervened, and how it looks years later after reforestation.

Even though Instagram has more followers, TikTok is generating far more engagement.

“A year with Ecosia: Top 5 before vs afters” → 2.6M views, 5,438 comments

“There’s no hope for this forest” → 1.6M views

This format is a proven view‑driver, we’ve seen it succeed across multiple categories:

It’s a universal storytelling device: show the past, show the present, and let the viewer connect the emotional gap on their own.

article.title: 8 Viral Hits You Missed This Week
article.content:
Here’s your weekly roundup of the hottest consumer apps trending on TikTok and Instagram Reels. Let’s get into it.

Sherlock, an AI face search app, is only 70 days old and already crushing it.

Four days ago, they posted a video of a creator recording a call with her best friend’s boyfriend, pretending to be a nurse to expose him for cheating.

It is a classic cheating drama playbook that never disappoints, pulling in 7.3M views and 1,994 comments.

BoldVoice’s best creator, Gina, strikes again with a brand new format.

She plays “the long word road,” and below each word she says, she gets a pronunciation score and an error breakdown. It’s genius because this is an app feature, so everyone in the comments is asking for the app reference.

She pulled 7.4M views and over one thousand comments.

Cupidly, the AI rizz keyboard, pulled in 459K views five days ago.

The video starts with a clip of a guy making a basket, with the hook “texting huzz. take notes,” then cuts to a text conversation that smoothly integrates a clear app CTA.

It is their top-performing video so far, built on a format they have tested more than 30 times.

Palteca, a Spanish learning app launched in 2024, has been quiet for a while but just struck gold with a fresh take on a proven format.

Their video, “How secret agents learn Spanish so quickly,” pulled in 7.3M views, 939K likes, and more than 2.1K comments.

A slightly tweaked version of the same hook brought in another 1.8M views from the same creator.

Alta, the fashion app, is now dominating Instagram Reels using the same format they have already perfected on TikTok.

The video opens with “rich in life because I woke up like this,” followed by a fast-paced morning routine that naturally features the app.

It pulled in 6.4M views and more than 1.3K comments.

Yope, the social app, is back with the same wall-of-text UGC format, this time from one of their Indonesian creators.

“I always open my social media archives whenever I feel empty and keep thinking ‘my life used to be so fun, being with my friends.’”

The video hit 1.2M views and over 800 comments just five days ago.

We wrap up with period tracker Musa, and honestly, this comes as no surprise.

Once again, their “Raise your hand if your March period never came” format keeps delivering, month after month.

This one reached 2.2M views and pulled in over 10,000 comments, all about delayed periods.

article.title: Cantina Scales 30M-View Format With Relationship Drama
article.content:

article.title: How Apps Are Hijacking Relationship Drama Right Now
article.content:
Lately, we’ve been noticing an interesting trend among consumer apps.

Relationship drama is dominating TikTok.

It started with the usual suspects, the cheating and couples apps that have been getting views for years. But now, many other unrelated apps are using the same hooks, prompts, and storylines, and putting their own spin on them. From widget apps to Bible apps, everyone is borrowing the same relationship hook.

It no longer matters what you sell. If your app fits inside a breakup story, it can spread.

These apps were made to expose relationship drama:

For them, the story is already there. Suspicious follows, hidden dating profiles, weird notifications, cheating paranoia, proof that something feels off.

The content sells the feeling of catching something you were not supposed to see: The fabricated evidence.

Lately, they’ve been pushing long talking videos with live reactions.

Like this recent one that did 20.9M views from Sherlock.

They are the pioneers of relationship drama format on TikTok.

And now that same emotional structure is spreading far beyond the apps where it naturally fits. Widget apps, fitness apps, music apps, English learning apps, even Bible apps are starting to borrow the exact same tension.

Widgetable turned lock screens and fake notifications into relationship receipts. Their slideshows use fake payment bait like “You’ve received $___ for listening to Spotify,” then hide shocking texts inside the widget setup.

The lock screen becomes both the proof and the CTA. This one below pulled 2.6M views.

It’s subtle, but once you repeat it at scale, and the notification actually fits the story, it can really perform.

Promise, an app that tracks promises and commitment, pushed 5.3M views with two accounts @girlhacksnaomi and @girlhacksbyjas.

The content leaned into fake-notification scroll bait.

“Does the disgusting feeling u get after finding the girls he watches on his phone ever leave?” → 1.4M views

Pure scaled the format even further. They built a whole creator network around staged dating drama. Multiple “@datingwith[name]” accounts recycle the same handful of selfies, slightly vary the hook, then show message receipts with unhinged responses to men’s texts.

Their best performing account @datingwithmads is sitting at 109 million views, built entirely on recycled selfies and conversations screenshots:

This one pulled 16M views.

These are the most fun because the product has no real relationship angle, it is fully made up.

Symmetry is a great example. The Spanish fitness app turns breakup text notifications into a gym call to action.

The product comes in as the second beat. People get pulled in by the relationship story, then see an unexpected notification that ties the breakup to a makeover.

Airbuds plugged music choices into relationship drama with posts like: “broke up w my bf bc im moving 10 hours away and he just favorited this song on airbuds what do i even do”. It hit 2.6M views.

This is where you see how apps so far from relationship drama are including it into their strategy.

Sounter, a language learning app, copied the same breakup-style emotional text structure as Symmetry.

Here the payoff becomes an English-learning CTA instead: “People abandon you, but English will never.”

It’s another strong example of how the narrative can do the heavy lifting even when the product has nothing to do with dating.

This one below did 10.5M views (notice how the picture is with the same creators as above).

Tomo, an AI chatbot, used the same logic with a more absurd twist. In the video, the boyfriend creates a group chat with Tomo and his girlfriend so the chatbot can break up with her for him.

“there’s NO FUCKING WAY my bf just broke up with me in a GROUP CHAT” did 2.9M views.

Then there’s Creed, the Christian Bible chat & companion app, that pulled 18.2M views with a simple on-screen hook about relationship drama.

“I made my boyfriend of 4 years lose contact with his girl bsf because it was becoming weirder than it already was (church tg, bible study tg, creed streaks tg) and I couldn’t take it anymore, now that same ‘girl bsf’ is reposting lala land videos”

A Bible app built around jealousy drama should feel absurd, and that is exactly why it sticks.

That is the bigger shift. Relationship drama is no longer limited to dating apps. It has become a packaging layer that almost any product can use.

What the app does matters less now. What matters is whether it can stand out and get noticed inside the drama.

article.title: Japanese-learning App Finds First Million Views
article.content:
HayaiLearn is a Japanese‑learning app powered by AI and YouTube videos.

This TikTok sample shows HayaiLearn operating through a small cluster of creator-led accounts rather than a single brand voice. Across 4 creators, the network totals 131 videos and 1,088,547 combined views.

Every account is centered on learning Japanese, and every bio reinforces the same core themes: study, learning, immersion, and HayaiLearn branding.

Most videos follow the same visual pattern: faceless study clips.The highest peak view in the sample comes from @irisdreamsjapan, with 474,3K views.

“I want to learn Japanese but don’t know where to start!”

@nihongo.ghoul follows at 339.6K views

“this part of my life is called”

Together, those two accounts make up 74.8% of all peak views in the dataset, setting the highest level of reach in this creator cluster.

All four creators have posted almost the same amount of content, with 32 or 33 videos each.

Despite the app being less than a year old, that alone doesn’t explain why views are still this low. If the goal is to keep the current faceless study format, then the next step is to adapt stronger hooks to match it.

A good reference is the viral POV‑study style video that used the line “studying because I must leave this country.”->3M views

For a Japanese‑learning app, the equivalent would be something like: “Studying Japanese because I need a way out.”

Same format with a stronger pull.

article.content:

article.content:
You remember you have free will, then show the impulsive thing you decided to do because of it.

We could see this hook work well for utility apps. Start with the free-will line, then show the action your product made possible; book the trip, buy the item,  build the website, send the message.

article.title: New Expense Tracker Just Found Its First Outlier
article.content:
A newly launched expense tracker is starting to show early signs of traction with founder-led content.

Costify, released on January 30, 2026, is a simple app for tracking, splitting, and managing expenses on your phone.

The app was created by Marlon Pitters, who also handles distribution himself across TikTok and Instagram, posting in both English and German.

According to his TikTok bio, he is a “design-obsessed iOS dev, trying to build the best expense tracker ever”.

So far, most of the content has stayed in low-view territory.

But a recent video suggests he may have found his first promising format.

On March 31, 2026, he hit 215K views and 1.5K bookmarks with:

“The system I use to track my money”

The video is fully faceless and works as a clean product demo. It opens with a real payment moment, then immediately shows the app recognizing the expense, categorizing it, and tracking it through an automatic pop-up.

This format has also been used by TapSheet, another budgeting app growing quickly.

For an expense tracker, that is likely the right direction.

article.title: “Secret CIA Method” Pushes Spanish App to #5 in the U.S.
article.content:
A Spanish-learning app just peaked at #5 in Education in the U.S. on April 1, 2026. At the end of March, it was still outside the Top 500.

Palteca, launched in June 2024, hit 40K downloads last month.

Palteca currently has three active TikTok ambassadors, and all of them have gone viral. The biggest standout is @trinityren2, who has generated 15.8M views on her own.

In total, Palteca has pulled in more than 23M views, with most of that volume arriving in 2026.

The clearest catalyst behind the app’s sudden rise came from @trinityren2.

On March 27, 2026, she hit 5.5M views, 680K likes, and more than 250K saves with:

“How secret agents learn Spanish so quickly”

The day before, on March 26, 2026, she posted a near-identical version and hit 1.7M views, 250K likes, and 108K saves with:

“How secret agents learn new languages so quickly”

Same idea. Same creator. Same angle. Repeated twice in two days. And both worked tremendously well.

In the videos, she frames the app around a “secret method” supposedly used by CIA agents and government officials to learn Spanish faster. That makes the pitch feel much stronger than a normal app promo, because it sells access to elite knowledge, not just convenience. The logic becomes simple: if this is how the elites learn faster, I want the app too.

The setting helps the format as well. She is lying in bed while explaining the method, which gives the video a relaxed, personal feel. That makes the hook sound less like a polished ad and more like someone casually sharing something valuable.

frameworks.example: Palteca's TikTok videos frame the app as using a 'secret CIA method' to learn Spanish quickly, making viewers want to access this elite knowledge.

article.title: Lovable Finds New Money Hook
article.content:
One recent Lovable partner account, @stevenislovable, started posting two days ago and is repeating a hook structure that’s been working well so far.

The CTA is not only about coding but how easily Lovable can turn a random Google Maps business into a paid website job.

article.title: Teen Social App Gets Heat Before Launching
article.content:
A new under-18 social app is already building early demand before launch.

Kelebek is a teen-only social platform set to launch near the end of summer 2026. It is designed to give teenagers a safer space to talk about their interests, meet new people, play games, and join competitions.

Kelebek is being built by Isla Johnson, who is also handling distribution herself through the @islajohnson.kelebek accounts on Instagram and TikTok.

So far, she has generated 1.2M total views across both platforms, mostly through simple selfie videos.

The biggest hit came on December 12, 2025, with a short video built around the hook:

“Congratulations on making a safe app for teens to connect and make friends. Now you need to post so teens find out about it” (The biggest hit happened on December 12, 2025, when she posted a video with the long hook:

“Congratulations on making a safe app for teens to connect and make friends. Now you need to post so teens find out about it”  (693K views, 4K saves)

She films herself reacting to the reality of having to promote the app, which makes the post feel honest and low-pressure. At the same time, the hook creates genuine curiosity around the concept.

Her best-performing TikTok came a few weeks later, on January 3, 2026.

Instead of a short reaction-style post, this one was a longer founder-led explanation:

“Imagine if there was an app like Snapchat and a making friends app combined, but it was actually made safe for teens” (210K views, 2.7K saves)

The app has not even launched yet, but the founder is already doing two important things at once: building a waitlist and learning what kind of content gets people interested.

That matters even more for a social app, because these products need a community from day one.

article.title: When TikTok Finds Your Next $1M App
article.content:
Most consumer apps start with a product and then search for distribution.

He is doing the reverse.

The publisher behind two fast-growing party game apps seems to be using the same strategy twice: make a simple format go viral through native short-form content, then turn that idea into an app.

One app launched in December and is already doing 20K downloads and around $10K in revenue over the last 30 days.

The second launched in February and hit 10K downloads in its first 24 days.

Behind both projects, there’s Tomi Arakaki.

Before this, he was already active in the short-form app world as a Cluely ambassador. It feels less like a coincidence and more like someone who truly understands how to turn creator content into products from the inside.

His first launch was a “find the impostor” party game.

Released in December 2025, ImposterAI reached 20K downloads and ~$10K in revenue last month.

The app seems to have emerged from a creator account Tomi ran with friends, @tappedinclub, on both TikTok and Instagram.

The concept was simple: a group of friends in a car, a category on screen, and one hidden impostor in the group. The format is instantly understandable, which is exactly why it works so well.

They started uploading in January 2025, and went on to generate 114M views on TikTok and 44.3M on Instagram. After months of going viral by playing the game together, they turned the mechanic into a product so viewers could do the same with their own friends.

Then, they launched separate app accounts under the @imposterai handle on both platforms. Those accounts kept using the same content style, often re-sharing material tied to the original format, but now with the app logo added at the beginning of the video.

No hard sell. No heavy explanation. Only a slightly more productized version of something viewers already understood.

That account alone pulled 15M views on Instagram.

This is the core mindset behind the strategy: build around a game that people naturally want to recreate with friends, and the content starts converting the product almost by itself.

The mechanic is a bit harder to explain than the impostor game, but it works great in short-form content. You see the two extremes, follow the clue, and naturally want to see if the guess lands in the right spot.

Once again, the format went viral before the app even launched.

Except this time, he didn’t create it.

The mechanic is a bit harder to explain than the impostor game, but it works great in short-form content. You see the two extremes, follow the clue, and naturally want to see if the guess lands in the right spot.

Once again, the format went viral before the app even launched.

Except this time, he didn’t create it.

This format took off through other creator accounts like @risingyakult, which generated 84M TikTok views and 51M Instagram views.

They built their audience around “wavelength” videos: a wheel, two opposite options, a hidden target, and the fun of watching people argue their way toward the right answer.

And many other accounts followed.

Just like with the first launch, a separate app account began posting around the same mechanic, using the same logo-first distribution trick. One standalone launch video introducing the app pulled 580K views.

Even as the faces changed, the playbook stayed the same: make a social format go viral first, then turn it into an app.

It works even better because these mechanics are naturally social, so viewers start thinking about who they would play with.

In the end, it does not matter if you create the format or spot it early. The revenue goes to whoever moves fastest to the App Store and turns the viral idea into a dead-simple, highly usable product.

article.title: What About Apple Watch?
article.content:
From what we’ve been seeing lately, it seems like Apple Watch apps on TikTok  are still on the race to find the first consistently viral format.

Livity is a sleep, health, and fitness tracker with 30K downloads and $30K in revenue, launched in April 2024.

We identified 15 TikTok accounts posting content for Livity. And although they started posting for the app in 2024, the first real breakthrough posts did not appear until the end of 2025.

Their content is centered almost entirely around the Apple Watch experience.

“Y’all, I think you’ve been using your Apple Watch wrong” → 1.6M views

Despite the high number of views, the ER% remains consistently low, which strongly indicates that the views are likely not organic.

Across all Apple Watch apps we’ve analyzed, none have shown a solid performance across time, at least not when compared to the engagement we see in adjacent niches.

StressWatch: AI Stress Monitor->3 videos + 2.15M total views = 4.90% ER

PulseBuddy AI: Stress Monitor->9 videos + 4.41M total views = 4.04% ER

PeakWatch: AI Personal Trainer->16 videos + 2.96M total views = 2.90% ER

article.title: AI Language Tutor Hits 38M Views With New UGC Wave
article.content:
Tenmin is an AI language tutor designed to help users practice real conversations.

About a year after launching, it has grown to 30K downloads and reached $20K in monthly recurring revenue last month.

A big part of this growth comes from its UGC strategy.

The app is running a 20-account creator wave that has already generated more than 38M views. Instead of pushing one broad language-learning page, the team seems to be building around creators dedicated to specific languages: Chinese, Korean, Japanese, German, Spanish, and more.

Rather than trying to sell one generic “learn languages with AI” message, they let each creator live inside a single language niche and build content around the jokes, memes, and conversation habits that already exist there.

One creator stands out the most.

@avaaaaa994, who posts Korean-learning content, has already generated more than 10M views across TikTok and Instagram. His format is simple: he talks directly to the app, asks it how to say something, and lets the response become the joke.

One of his best-performing videos used the “67” meme. He asked the app how to say it in Korean, and the AI told him to go away in an annoyed tone. It was not a direct app promo, but the comment section suggests it still worked well as product discovery.

That video alone reached 3.5M views on TikTok and 3.2M on Instagram on January 28, 2026.

Another creator seeing strong traction is @giastudiesjp.

She has generated 7.3M views on Instagram and 3.8M on TikTok with Japanese-learning content, using a very similar strategy: direct-to-app videos built around funny, language-specific moments.

Her best-performing video reached 2.7M views and also played off a meme, this time a Japanese one, with the AI again telling her to stop.

The app has also picked up traction through faceless slideshows.

One faceless ambassador, @violesdcwev on TikTok, reached 750K views and more than 43K saves with “Best Apps to Start Learning Chinese” on August 9, 2025.

So even when the content moves away from direct app conversations, the distribution still stays tightly tied to a specific language-learning niche.

article.title: Albo’s UGC Network: 7 New Accounts
article.content:
When we last covered Albo, the app had just rebranded from Sortd, launched its first UGC creator, and pulled views by letting people watch the product being built in real time.

Two month laters, Albo is now running a total of 17 accounts, 7 of which were launched in the last month.

So far, the strongest traction is coming from founder-led accounts.                     One of Albo’s founders, @karosaves, has been posting consistently across several profiles(@internet.hoarder,@sortdappsupp,@perfectangel214, @kmciol).

One of her videos pulled 122.8K views by using a smart comparison hook referencing a well-known productivity app to frame what Albo does differently.

Outside of the founder accounts, Albo’s creator network is clearly in an experimentation phase testing multiple formats in parallel.

One UGC account is built entirely around trying a new hobby in each post (pottery, journaling, knitting..).

Each video starts with the identity hook (“cool girl hobbies”, “productive girl era”, “things I want to try in 2026”). Then smoothly transitions into how Albo is used to save tutorials, inspiration, and resources for that hobby.

Other creators are experimenting with:

In most cases, the app name is revealed in the comments or bio.

None of these UGC formats have gone truly viral yet.

The next shift will likely come when a format starts exploding and they can start repeating it across their network.

For now you can track their recent accounts here: https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10HXmdQ8qRAv

article.title: Canva-like App for IG Hits       MRR in Four Months
article.content:
A new carousel template editor for social media creators is going viral.

Crsel launched in August 2025.

In the last 30 days, it hit 200K downloads and $70K MRR.

Here’s the growth playbook behind the spike.

This was an audience-led launch.

Founder Georgy built trust with simple phone video tutorials, then productized those filming instincts into a template engine.

But the scaling engine is TikTok.

Two creator accounts pulled 22.6M+ views with faceless app demos.

The content sells the outcome first, then the comments do the conversion.

@emilycreatescontent hit 2.3M views and 50K saves in November with a single demo.

@val_edits162 hit 2.2M views and 86K saves using the same approach.

Fast collage builds, carousel ideas, and satisfying before/after edits.

You can track Crsel’s account collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10ct3CWePYb2

article.title: New Men’s Private Tracker Hits 7K Downloads
article.content:
Men’s insecurity apps went fully mainstream in 2025.

UMAX gamified face ratings. Taller gamified height.

Now the trend moved to a private metric people don’t post openly.

Dih launched in September 2025 and already hit 7K downloads in the last 30 days.

It went viral through 5 different “dih app” accounts on TikTok and Instagram, adding up to 20M+ views.

All 5 accounts upload a specific format 3 times a day.

A few clearly performed better than the rest:

Format 1 -> App Photo (Start vs Now).

“it aint that big” also bro: hit 2.2M views on November 17.

Format 2 -> AI car selfie, then an App Photo.

“but it’s so small” hit 1.2M views on October 31.

Format 3 -> The best “x” to grow your “dih”

These are rankings of habits or foods that help users improve.

“The Best Fruits To Grow your Dih” hit 750K views on September 30.

It’s an off-limits category, but the demand is real.

You can take a look at their collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b108JAyvofXgi

article.title: 7 viral hits you missed last week
article.content:
Yope is tapping into the whole “new year / new memories” energy by pitching a simple Jan 1 ritual anyone can do with their friends.

On-screen hook: “Me telling my friends that we should download Yope and start a secret album on January 1st…”

The creator pitches that if everyone adds one photo a day all year, and by the end of 2026 you’ve basically made a memory movie together.

1.9M views and 35.9k bookmarks, posted last week.

StudyFetch is still thriving on productive chaos and the funniest part is that people are starting to recognize them straight away.

For this video, they used the hook: “Forcing myself to study by chaining myself to the chair and freezing the key 🥴”

It let to 1.8 M views, and one comment “Is it study fetch ?” that pulled 4,354 likes.

She literally locks herself in her chair, drops the key in ice, then goes full on studying mode with a StudyFetch demo.

Language learning pain remains undefeated.

A single Portuguese word inside Airlearn’s app feature (“Cabeleireiro”) made the creator spiral over the pronunciation and pulled 1.7M views in under a week.

Hook: “why tf is Portuguese so hard?”

If you’re still not sold on AI pranks, Yapper’s got another banger for you.

This time: “convincing my dad he’s in the files (gone terribly wrong 😭)”

The creator uses AI to fabricate proof, films the reaction, and lets the confusion do all the work. It pulled 1.4M views in three days.

Grandir posted a “quick hack” format with Sora-style visuals and a fake-urgent “fact” you need to know if you want to grow.

“If you sleep on your back you’re doomed to be 1m65”. An anxiety bait that pulled 401.6K views (and it’s all in French).

This reflection content is right on schedule.

Opal is back with it’s classroom-style breakdown, this time explaining what an end-of-year check-in actually means.

And of course, sliding Opal into the conversation as the tool to track it.

They did 301.5K views with this one.

Iori flashcards pulled 3M views with a street interview style format.

This one hooks you before you even realise it’s an app reveal: “I think I can speak your language”

The creator approaches strangers, attempts their language, then reveals how they’re learning it.

article.title: Roamy’s Viral Hook : 300k Downloads & 30M Views
article.content:
When we last covered Roamy, it had just crossed 100K downloads in two weeks after launching in October, powered by one breakout UGC hook filmed on a plane. Since then, the team hasn’t reinvented the strategy but they’ve leaned harder into it.

As of December 2025, Roamy is now sitting around 300K downloads, and over the last 30 days its UGC network pulled 29.9M views.

Driven largely by the same creator repeating the same winning format across TikTok and Instagram.

In the last six weeks, @marg.roamy posted three near-identical videos using the same hook:“I could LITERALLY kiss the flight attendant that showed me this”.

17.5 M views, posted two weeks ago

7.7 M views, posted 5 weeks ago

9.2 M views, posted 6 weeks ago

In total, that’s 34M views, 6 weeks apart with one format.

Four days ago, the same creator posted a slight variation on her TikTok account, with the hook:

“I could LITERALLY marry the flight attendant that showed me this”

It pulled, 648.2k views:

Another variation that worked, posted by tt@sammy.roamy pulled 1.6 m views: “I could kiss the Japanese man who showed me this”

The format isn’t just driving organic views but it’s driving engagement in the comments. People keep asking the same thing:

And the creator answers with a simple conversion trick that rounded up to 3 136 likes:“Guysss the app is @roamy.travel 🙌”

You can track their accounts here: https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b1099osSV4DMo

article.title: The Faceless Format That Works For Any App
article.content:
Reclip’s co founder went crazy viral on Instagram Reels.

He did it with a faceless format that works for any app in any niche.

One video hit 16.5M views in September 2025.

“BRO doesn’t realize his entire GPT history is on show for the whole class“.

-> Zoom in on a laptop screen showing ChatGPT history.

-> Lecture hall background.

-> Start with the “BRO” hook.

The ChatGPT history is the retention hack, and it also sells the app.

Each chat triggers a different feeling:

Reclip’s collection is available on Shortimize:

article.title: Class Action Settlement App Doing $700K MRR, 60M+ Views
article.content:
This is the top class action app, pulling in over half a million downloads every month.

On TikTok alone, they reached 54 million views. One standout video hit 40 million views by itself and quickly drove 22k comments and 650k bookmarks.

The video is a 57 second talking clip, which likely generated hundreds of thousands in revenue on its own.

They also run several other active, high performing accounts.

We believe they operate more than the 22 visible accounts, with additional ones likely concealed.

There are now over 15,000 posts using the hashtag #settlemate.

article.title: $100K+/mo App. 600 TikToks. Zero Breakout
article.content:
PrivacyHawk had an underwhelming performance on TikTok despite being a strong revenue app.

The app makes well over $100K and experimented with UGC multi account marketing for a few weeks starting in late August.

They tested a format inspired by settlement style ads, using direct talking videos with a warning hook that explains a data breach right away.

They also experimented with wall of text videos that clearly list out every data leak.

None of these approaches worked. Across more than 600 videos and 12 different accounts, not a single video passed 8K views.

metadata.key_principle: Not all content formats or UGC strategies guarantee viral growth; extensive testing and iteration are necessary to find what resonates with the audience.

Despite posting over 600 videos across 12 accounts, none achieved significant views, indicating that even strong apps can struggle with organic TikTok growth without the right content fit.

article.title: Format Idea to Drive IRL Traffic to New Location
article.content:
Turning TikTok and Reels views into real people showing up is often hard to pull off and even harder to track.

This format can work extremely well. Create a multi slide recommendation post with a strong hook around fancy restaurants.

Place your newly opened restaurant between two well known or more expensive spots. Do this again and again until the post gets saved and shared enough times, then let the foot traffic do the rest.

This specific “date night” format would work well in high dating velocity cities like New York, London, or Paris.

frameworks.example: A 'date night' post recommending a new restaurant situated between two famous dining spots in New York, encouraging users to save and share the post, thereby increasing visibility and visits.

By positioning the new spot between two well-known or pricier venues, the post gains credibility and encourages saves and shares, which translates into increased visits, particularly effective in cities with active dating scenes.

article.title: 2025 Growth Strategy Team’s Favorite
article.content:
We picked our favorite growth strategies of 2025.

They might not be the top performers or the highest converting ones, but each of them stood out to us.

They earned our editorial pick because there was something truly special about them.

FocusFlight launched a mass faceless CPM strategy on TikTok, flooding the platform with hundreds of near identical videos at the same time.

Users were encouraged to create a video and only paid by signing up for a free subscription if they hit a specific view count.

Every video was branded with #focusflightchallenge.

Simple faceless StudyTok style demos helped drive more than 200K downloads, perfectly aligned with the back to school moment.

The app itself is highly polished, and interestingly, it is a Chinese app.

OCSN is run by top tier growth engineers who scaled the Status social app to hundreds of thousands of downloads and truly understand niche algorithm marketing.

They nailed a clear social identity built around Original Characters, fandom, and roleplay.

By tapping into a deep existing subculture, they were able to dominate attention and funnel it straight into their product.

They also appear to have brought on the solo founder of Fitdrop, known for mastering wall of text videos that pulled in millions of views.

What really sets the OCSN team apart is how well they activate power users, grouping them in Discord, building hype, and creating strong referral loops.

Tone’s strategy received less attention than we expected, even though it operates at an insane Machiavellian scale.

The approach is simple. It is a massive top of funnel play built on high volume and low conversion. Everything is optimized for hundreds of millions of views and fast account growth using one repeatable format.

In most cases, huge view numbers come from repeating the same format over and over.

Some accounts posted up to 12 times per day, both faceless and on camera.

Even with weak conversion rates, the sheer volume of views makes installs add up quickly.

This one likely doesn’t work anymore — but it was legendary and deserves its place here.

They pushed 67M views across 11 unbranded accounts using just 3 hooks and a single repeatable system.

That machine generated 3.9M shares (at the time of coverage) and roughly $150K in recurring revenue.

“I’m still shocked about this unconventional wedding idea.”

“I went to a wedding that people still talk about 9 months later.”

“The entire internet is buzzing about this unconventional wedding.”

Every video followed the same structure:

an AI character narrating the exact same story, layered over stock footage, all programmatically generated at scale.

No brand. No variation. Just brute-force distribution and repetition.

Today, this is extremely hard to replicate successfully due to saturation and platform shifts — but as a case study in high-volume, systemized storytelling, it was flawless.

With over 100 creator accounts, Nomadtable is a solo founded, solo operated indie social app. It now gets more than 200K downloads every month. Technical founder Jay is moving fast and winning in the space.

Here are a few more direct promotion hooks.

Huge respect for this founder. We wish him a gazillion more downloads in 2026.

And when it comes to indie founders, another one of our favorites is:

Run by a couple, this web scraping Chrome extension gets most of its users from short form video marketing. It is not an obvious channel for this type of app, yet it works incredibly well when you truly master it, like Floor has, especially while no one else is doing it.

They repeat the same format over and over, adjusting it to new trends, hooks, and styles.

They are a big inspiration, and hopefully many indie and bootstrapped founders can learn from what they are doing.

Finally, and even though we could keep going forever because there were so many smart and creative strategies this year, we will end with just one last example.

What really sets them apart is how they scaled the “Angry Professor” format across multiple accounts and reached nearly a billion views, all without using AI.

They also consistently bake one of their app names directly into the video itself, making it a central part of the content.

Another smart move was grabbing domains like ihatereading.com, savemygpa.com, and ratemyprofessor.com, then using them as simple hooks that also generate revenue.

This shows how one strong content format can unlock multiple app ideas.

–

As mentioned earlier, we could honestly keep going. We covered over 400 apps and their strategies. Next year, we plan to cover at least three times more and share even more insights you can use in your everyday marketing.

Happy new year of viral videos and apps.

article.title: New AI Photo Editor Enters the Prank Game
article.content:
After Halo AI and Yapper AI proved that one fake photo + one emotional reaction can print tens of millions of views, another editor app just entered the game 51 days ago: Cocopix.

We’ve only found two Cocopix “prank creator” accounts so far, with the same disguise “I Love Pranking My Friends” and a CTA “since y’all keep asking about the app i use 👉🏼 cocopix“.

tt@riley.595 started posting a month ago and already pulled 12.9 M lifetime views.

And they’re using the same exact format that has already been working:

AI prank-as-content. Again.

Four days ago, she posted a Cocopix prank that hit 3.4M views: “pranking my asian dad I got fat in college (he’s overacting)”

One video opening with a face close-up + reaction format also went viral with 3.2 M views:

Let’s see how many accounts they’ll launch.

Until then, you can track their accounts here: https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b100g8g8oxz6W

article.title: French Taller Copycat Hits 230M Faceless Views
article.content:
We previously covered Taller’s $100K MRR Growth Playbook.

Now, someone cloned the Taller app in French and hit #6 in Health & Fitness.

Here’s how Grandir took over France with a bold copycat play.

Grandir, which means “Grow” in English, launched in July 2025.

The app gives users a personalized height growth plan plus an AI coach.

In the last 30 days, they pulled 50K downloads and $5K MRR.

Grandir runs 4 accounts that together have passed 230M views.

One main account across YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok under the app name, plus a faceless TikTok “ambassador” called @sigmafits.

@sigmafits just crossed 200M views with a fully faceless setup.

The account posted its first video in July 2023 and is now fully sponsored by Grandir.

They stayed viral by leaning on two repeatable height growth formats.

Strategy 1: AI anime stories

Girl rejects short guy -> Guy trains -> Becomes a giant -> App promo.

That same format pushed Grandir’s YouTube page past 8M views.

Strategy 2: the FOMO app formula

Hook: A dramatic claim (If you drink milk, you will never grow past “x” height).

Common habit -> Height shrink -> “Secret” app method -> Height growth.

They also use this on TikTok and Instagram, with one small twist.

Instead of illustrations, they use a mix of height-related clips, and cut the hook claim, going straight to the method.

Grandir took a proven app idea, adapted it for France, and scaled it with two repeatable formats.

You can access all Grandir’s accounts on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10JLa3E3XRO6

article.title: 15M Views in Two Posts
article.content:
Tomo AI first launched on web and on iMessage and SMS, where it offered emotional support and coaching.

Seven months ago, the iOS app launched to grow the ecosystem, but the TikTok content still leans heavily on the website experience.

The main challenge is turning a text-based service into something that feels real on TikTok.

Across all 4 accounts, one profile created two videos that rose above everything else.

First Hook: “ifafterthegreatlockinofaugustodecember2025thingsdontstartgettingbetterformeimgonnadoitthistime”

10.2M views, 1202 comments

First Hook:

Big: “PLEASE HIRE ME”

Small: “You can hire me to text you every single day asking what you got done today.”

5.2M views, 899 comments

metadata.article_summary: Tomo AI, a text-based emotional support service, successfully used TikTok to drive massive organic growth by creating two viral videos with strong, relatable hooks that generated over 15 million views combined. Despite the challenge of translating a text-based service into engaging TikTok content, focusing on authentic emotional hooks helped the brand gain significant attention and engagement.

article.title: Another disappointing text-to-mobile app ugc content strategy
article.content:
Most vibe coding websites are struggling to make mainstream TikTok acquisition work as their main top of funnel channel.

Natively.dev is another good example of that.

3.8M views across more than 1,300 videos is not a strong result. Half of those views come from a 5 second wall of text video that shows nothing about the product and is in French, while the account mainly targets a US audience.

Most of their content does not convert. It relies heavily on text only videos, even though they have recently started switching to formats that actually show the app in action and simple tutorials.

They are still posting and we will keep an eye on them, but based on what we have seen with many similar projects, it is hard to believe they will break through. The mainstream audience does not seem interested in vibecoding at all.

frameworks.example: Switching from text-only videos to showing the app in action and simple tutorials to better demonstrate value and engage viewers.

article.title: This product is naturally going uber viral on TikTok
article.content:
I came across this product called Stickerbox, and it is blowing up on TikTok without trying. It makes total sense. It is built to be content, and it fits perfectly into a simple three act format.

Act 1 is talking to a box.Act 2 is the thinking moment.Act 3 is the reveal and the printing.

Most of the viral videos come from random accounts, often moms posting everyday content that suddenly takes off:

Once it goes viral, they keep posting it. That is the obvious move. When your content usually gets no views and you finally find something that works, you stick with it. If you are making videos at all, attention is part of the goal.

If you check the #stickerbox tag https://www.tiktok.com/tag/stickerbox, you will see hundreds of videos pulling in a massive number of views.

article.title: Gauth’s disappointing 115M views from 79 accounts
article.content:
After Studley, Turbo, and others, we came across another supposed UGC powerhouse. However, it is very unbalanced, with just two accounts driving 65% of the total views.

The numbers look stronger than they really are. Nearly half the views, and likely more, come from short exam skits that do not show the app or include any call to action.

The same pattern appears across their other accounts as well. Almost all of them rely on the exact same approach.

There is only one format. You can see it by checking all their videos.

For a study app like Gauth, which reportedly generates millions in revenue and downloads every month, we would expect much more. They had the opportunity to build a true powerhouse like Studley or Turbo. This proves that capital alone does not win in this space. Strong bottom up execution is required, and that expertise is clearly missing.

frameworks.name: Diversified UGC Content Strategy
frameworks.description: Avoid relying on a single content format or a few accounts for user-generated content to ensure balanced and sustainable growth.
frameworks.when_to_use: When UGC performance is heavily skewed towards a small number of creators or content types, limiting reach and engagement.
frameworks.example: Gauth's UGC was dominated by two accounts and one content format, leading to unbalanced view distribution and missed growth opportunities.

metadata.key_principle: Balanced and diverse UGC content across multiple creators and formats drives more sustainable growth and better conversion potential than concentrated efforts.
metadata.article_summary: Gauth, a study app generating millions in revenue, had 115M views from 79 accounts on TikTok/Instagram, but 65% of views came from just two accounts using a single content format. Nearly half the views were from short exam skits that did not showcase the app or include calls to action, limiting conversion. This case shows that capital alone does not guarantee success; strong, diversified bottom-up execution in UGC strategy is essential.

article.title: 92M views across 9K videos and 142 creators
article.content:
We discovered Pixory without realizing it was such a large creator network promoting a physical product.

Once we saw the product, it immediately stood out as being perfectly suited for TikTok marketing. Across 9K analyzed videos, they generated 92M views.

What makes their product and strategy work so well is how visual and aesthetic it is. This comes through clearly in the content.

The nostalgia angle works extremely well. “Imagine showing your kids…”

article.title: GTA Gameplay, Gamer Codes, 332 Videos, 10M Views
article.content:
Game Maps IRL, which we covered about three months ago when they launched their first account, has scaled to at least 8 TikTok accounts. They are also active on Instagram.

On TikTok, they have seen fewer breakout hits recently, but they have increased their posting volume.

They are now generating over $20K in monthly revenue. Probably closer to $50K.

October and November were especially strong, with some videos clearly showing the app in action reaching up to 750K views and more than 12K bookmarks.

They started out completely faceless and have since shifted to using real creators, which you can see on this account.

They have reached 10M total views across 332 TikTok videos alone, which is very impressive, and they show no signs of slowing down.

One of their early viral videos from three months ago reused multiple codes from gamer content and paired them with GTA gameplay in the background.

This matched the hook well, added context to the app, and stood out due to its high recording quality.

article.title: They Mixed StudyTok and Screen Blocker to Hit 13M Views

Meet Study Guard: Study & Focus.

It’s a focus blocker that makes you study before you can open social media.

They launched in April 2025 and reached 9K downloads in the last 30 days.

They also pulled 13M views across Instagram and TikTok.

All it took was three faceless accounts.

On Instagram, Study Guard took off with one repeatable strategy.

Format: Put a phone over a notes image, then show the app demo.

Hook: “told my mom my phone actually cares about my grades now”

They posted these in early September, right when school started.

Their top video got 37.5K shares and 31K bookmarks.

What’s even better is that their Instagram success came from a TikTok blueprint.

On June 7th, @studyguard.app  uploaded:

Overall, there are two main hook templates that helped them breakthrough.

It’s wild how many TikTok niches screen blockers can fit into.

A few days ago, we wrote about Reload, another scroll blocker app.

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/the-simplest-reels-format-app-blockers-can-copy.

article.title: The Growth Lab: 3.4M Views on X
article.content:
Welcome to a brand new category here on Social Growth Engineers.

The goal of The Growth Lab is to share new ideas and experiments we’re actively running and/or seeing happening around in a how-to, step-by-step way that you can easily implement yourself.

Today’s article is about Twitter marketing, but actually, it’s truly about doing TikTok marketing on Twitter.

That’s where it becomes interesting.

I call it TokTweeting.

After Nikita took over, my account hit a bit of a valley of death, especially after the so-called “threadbois” were hit hard. I’m unsure whether I identify as one. I took the hit anyway.

On any algorithm-driven platform, change is part of the game.

So I changed my approach and began testing high-frequency, low-friction posts rather than publishing one long thread each day.

There was some light success, but nothing crazy. Still, it led to two important realizations.

Shorter and more aggressive hooks matter more than ever. Videos are also being pushed in a massive and disproportionate way.

Let us start with videos.

This was a simple side-by-side A/B test with a short hook and a short 13-sec video, posted one hour apart.

It is not perfectly scientific, but that does not matter. One post hit half a million views with 58 percent retention at completion, while the other only reached 33 percent.

Retention is what seemed to make it go interstellar. It is not only this one. Another post here got two million views.

What stands out is that engagement barely matters anymore.

That video had only 7 comments for 2 million views.

This shows that retention is clearly one key outsized signal in this new video algorithm.

I see the same pattern even with 16 by 9 videos.

One small note on quote tweets. The platform appears to reward discussion more, which is why many quote tweets are being pushed forward.

Now back to Toktweeting. What is it exactly? It is about applying the same growth engineering tactics used on TikTok.

Instead of posting content like this.

These hooks feel mostly informational or like announcements, which is what most startups and founders do.

Instead, you take the opposite approach and TokTweet with hooks like this.

This is a word-for-word copy of a TikTok hook from Nomadtable. I am not sure where it originally came from.

That tweet generated five thousand bookmarks, which is a significant number here.

You get the idea. I quickly made another one titled, “I am addicted to this website.”

For a tweet that took seconds to make, it drove a strong number of sessions. You can see the same exact patterns as on TikTok.

Fast-paced video edits, lots of graphics that grab attention, and a short, intense hook.

So what does this mean in practice?

The TikTok videos I repost with short hooks tend to reach a very mainstream audience. They do not drive many followers, but they spread widely.

That makes them ideal for consumer apps that know how to engineer virality, just like on TikTok.

The direct promotion of TokTweets is even more interesting to me.

People may simply be tired of generic announcements like “We raised a $300M pre-seed round” or “We are launching tool X that will revolutionize AI video”. Instead, like TikTok users, they are more receptive to aggressive, highly engaging, and addictive indirect shills.

Twitter is shifting away from a friend-to-friend network and quickly becoming an everyone-to-everyone platform.

By pushing content from smaller accounts, Nikita is effectively turning Twitter into TikTok, where anyone can go viral and where the same strategies used on TikTok or Reels now apply.

Rather than spending $30K on a perfectly polished launch video and tweet, you take the opposite route. You ship raw, aggressive, TikTok-style tweets.

Food for thought. Experimentation never stops.

article.title: Spicy Cubes Lately: 10 Accounts, 50M Views
article.content:
SpicyCubes is an e-commerce brand selling bite-sized, chili-coated gummy “cubes” marketed as a natural aphrodisiac. They’ve built a multi-account UGC network that packages the product inside messy, close-friends-style storytimes.

We’ve tracked 64 accounts total and multiple pages of profiles are sitting at several million view total:

The top 10 accounts alone add up to ~50M views, which shows how much volume they can generate without needing a single “main” brand page to carry the story.

You can check out all their accounts here: https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10gQ05lV0iuB

In the last month, they pulled 14.7 million views.

One thing we noticed: a creator posted the same storyline on two different accounts, and both versions went viral. But it wasn’t a repost: different outfit, different take but the vibe is the same: filmed in the car, delivered like a private “group chat update.”

“Calling off my engagement” -> 4.2M views

(second take, same plot) -> 2.3M views

2.7 M views

A key shift in how this looks on-feed: the product isn’t being sold in the caption or the comments. Most videos avoid a hard “buy this” push. The strongest CTA is usually just “link in bio.”

The branding is mostly carried by:

So viewers get hooked on the story, then they check the profile for context, parts, or follow-ups and then they can see the product on the profile.

Their hook performance snapshot matches what the feed feels like:

That aligns with what they’re publishing: long, specific, text-heavy setups that sound like you’re watching you friend’s private story.

article.title: GoWish’s Template Prints 14M Views in December
article.content:
Christmas is peak season for a wishlist app. It turns everyone into a last-minute shopper, a gift strategist, and a full-time job.

This time around, GoWish turned that feeling into content.

In the last month, GoWish pulled 14M views across 50 creator accounts by locking into one seasonal behavior: gift planning feels like a job.

You can recognise their English accounts by the usernames (ex: maddie.wishes_, cecilia.wishes, taylor.wishes, savy.wishes).

We covered the breakout in October, when tt@maddie.wishes_ went crazy viral with one POV format: cozy bed / laptop / low-energy grind  and the “work” is shopping, planning gifts, and building the wishlist.

What’s interesting now is the views are still growing.

48.7M views in October → 59.6M views now“when my boyfriend calls mid day but I’m still in bed making my Christmas wishlist”

29.5M views in October → 32M views now“pls don’t be out cheating on me”

They also reposted cross-platform: the same video hit 3.1M views on Instagram with a different hook:“Me suddenly thinking I’m a billionaire when it comes to buying my boyfriend Christmas presents.”

And the newer versions are still printing: 618.8K views on recent posts.

But on top of their English accounts, they’re also running Scandinavian localized pages (their best-performing accounts):

GoWish also ran a Christmas Advent-style giveaway series on their Scandinavian page.

One post per day, same visual template (Christmas tree background, creator talking to camera, holding a product/prize), and the recurring headline (“Today’s giveaway/contest”) + the date.

You can track their accounts here: https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b107lgIjrLIP5
