< 1 min read

Save for later

Cathoven targets non-native English speakers in the U.S., UK, Canada, and Australia, and seems to reach them through Asia-based creators making non-talking videos. They have had a few small wins, nothing huge, but enough to make it work since they can produce content very cheaply abroad.

The hooks are very simple, and so are the formats. Their main advantage is how little they spend on content production.

They may also be using two-step videos mixed with demo clips provided by the team managing the app.

The company also seems to be based in Asia, which likely gives them easy access to these creators. All the hooks are available here:

frameworks.name: Low-Cost Creator Sourcing
frameworks.description: Leverage creators based in lower-cost regions to produce content cheaply while targeting audiences in higher-value markets.
frameworks.when_to_use: When budget constraints limit content production costs but targeting multiple international markets is required.
frameworks.example: IELTS app uses Asia-based creators to produce TikTok videos targeting non-native English speakers in the U.S. and other English-speaking countries.

frameworks.name: Simple Hook and Format Strategy
frameworks.description: Use straightforward, easily replicable hooks and video formats to maximize content output and maintain consistency.
frameworks.when_to_use: When scaling content production rapidly with limited resources and aiming for viral potential.
frameworks.example: IELTS app employs simple hooks and non-talking video formats to engage viewers effectively.

frameworks.name: Two-Step Video Approach
frameworks.description: Combine initial hook videos with follow-up demo clips or product showcases to guide users through awareness to conversion.
frameworks.when_to_use: When the product requires demonstration or explanation after initial engagement to drive conversions.

An AI fashion discovery and try-on platform just hit 60K downloads last month.

Launched 10 months ago, Shoppin lets users upload a photo, find similar fashion pieces, try them on virtually, and shop cheaper alternatives. It turns outfit inspiration into a shoppable feed and shortens the path from discovery to checkout.

When it comes to distribution, the team is not holding back. Shoppin runs a total of 58 accounts across TikTok and Instagram, including official pages, UGC creators, and paid partnerships with larger influencers.

So far, the strongest engine is the main Instagram page. That account alone has generated 35M views. Its best-performing post hit 11M views through a paid partnership with a Hindi-speaking influencer with 4.3M followers.

TikTok looks different. Shoppin has tested more than 30 ambassadors there, but none have broken out hard enough to create a repeatable format for the rest of the network.

The best-performing example came from @mina.shoppin. On Jan 24, 2026, she posted an app demo, but framed it as a hack her cousin had found.

That framing matters. By presenting it as something worth passing along, rather than a direct promotion, the post feels more like a personal recommendation than an ad.

“My cousin is living in 2099” hit 925K views and 37K bookmarks.

Most of Shoppin’s bigger TikTok moments still come from paid partnerships with large creators. The plain is usually the same: they tell viewers they get their clothes through the app and find similar pieces for much less than the original item.

One example came from influencer @__therealnia who reached 2.3M views on Jan 23, 2026.

So structurally, Shoppin is trying almost every distribution play in the book.

The UGC network still has not produced a viral format strong enough to scale across dozens of creators. But the brand is already generating serious reach through its main page and paid influencer deals. If they eventually find a UGC structure that converts and repeats, the upside could be much bigger.

We’ve recently come across another teenager making serious money online with organic TikTok marketing.

EasySlice.ai

is an AI website that automatically generates viral video clips from famous YouTubers. It works by simply taking a channel’s most recent videos and clipping out the most viral moments, allowing users to easily capitalize on trending content.

In just a few weeks, EasySlice has seen impressive growth, averaging 3K+ daily organic traffic, all fueled by a zero-cost, solo-founder strategy.

The founder is an 18-year-old entrepreneur named

Soren Skarsgard

.

Soren developed the website himself and is now going viral by marketing it on Instagram and TikTok.

According to a recent

LinkedIn post

, his clipping business is now generating $40K/month, just four months after being launched.

Soren only runs one Instagram account and one TikTok account.

He has generated over 20 million views, with most of them coming from Instagram. His content focuses on showing the website as a simple tool that lets creators generate clips without doing any manual editing.

The breakthrough moment came on January 9, when he uploaded a quick tutorial on how to use EasySlice to clip viral moments from YouTuber Speed’s channel.

In this video, he also mentions Whop as a way to monetize the clips, offering viewers the whole picture of how they can earn money from viral content.

“Youtube + This Website = money in 2026”

→ 6.3M views

This video also generated 1,900 comments, which is not bad at all when compared to the usual engagement benchmark for Instagram Reels.

On February 26, 2026, Soren went viral again with a similar strategy. This time, he used text to walk viewers through the process, rather than speaking directly on camera.

“How is this legal”

→ 2.5M views

Soren’s approach works because he taps into a single core desire: making money.

Most of his videos follow the same structure, and always include his own face and any sort of website demo.

He might be only 18, but he has extreme clarity about what his audience actually cares about. They want to make money on YouTube in the easiest way possible. So that is what he delivers.

If you look closer, you will see that almost all of his top performing hooks revolve around the idea of earning money, which connects strongly with his viewers.

This story is an inspiring example of how a solo founder can leverage AI tools and useful content to generate impressive revenue without needing a big team or ad spend.

You can learn a lot from the shady businesses online.

Study the scammers. Strip out the scam, and keep what works.

You can learn a lot from the shady businesses online.

SGE Team

•

March 11, 2026

•

< 1 min read

Save for later

Scammers are always one step ahead when it comes to social engineering, and studying them is always worth it. Take away the scam part, and you are left with fresh micro strategies that can level up your viral content. This account posted just one video, and it is a scam that pushes people to a site asking them to install games to get access, but the most interesting part is not the hack, it’s…

The way they built two layers of comments to make people believe it’s real. The top three comments are all from different users mentioning the same website name. Then, when you expand the replies, you see even more different people confirming that it’s legit.

That is some serious multi layer social engineering. And to push those comments to the top, they either use services that sell comment upvotes or phone farms to boost them.

frameworks.description: Create multiple layers of user-generated comments and replies that reinforce each other to build perceived authenticity and trustworthiness around content or offers.
frameworks.when_to_use: When launching new viral content or campaigns that require rapid trust-building and social proof to encourage user engagement or conversions.
frameworks.example: A TikTok video promoting a new app features top comments from different users all endorsing the app, with replies under those comments further confirming the endorsements, making the content appear highly credible.

metadata.key_principle: Leverage the psychological power of social proof by engineering multi-layered, reinforcing user interactions to build trust and virality, while avoiding unethical or deceptive practices.
metadata.article_summary: The article highlights how scammers use sophisticated social engineering tactics, such as multi-layered comment structures and boosted comment visibility, to create perceived legitimacy and virality. By stripping out the unethical elements, growth teams can adopt similar layered social proof strategies to enhance content trustworthiness and organic reach on platforms like TikTok and Instagram.

A new guessing game is starting to become known across Europe with a very simple concept.

Vestige mixes history with geography. Players are shown an iconic image and have to guess the year it was taken.

Launched around three months ago, the app reached 7K downloads in the last 30 days.

The team behind it is French. In a founder-led TikTok post, they explain that five friends locked themselves in an Airbnb for five days to build their dream app.

So far, that story seems to be working.

Their self-described “GeoGuessr of History” is now sitting in the Top 100 Education category in more than 20 European countries.

The app’s first hit came with a founder-led video.

One of the founders, Mart, posted a slideshow introducing the app with the hook: “We mixed GeoGuessr with History and made it an app…” That video reached 1.4M views, with part of the reach appearing to be paid.

Another founder, Fab, also gained traction with a similar app presentation, but used a short-form video and a longer hook instead.

What makes the strategy especially interesting is how the team is structuring distribution.

The founders are posting in English and French, which helps them reach a much wider audience across Europe.

They run one account for each language.

Fab even recreated one of the same videos in French after posting it in English, and that version also gained traction.

That bilingual founder-led approach seems to be a big reason the app is spreading so fast across European markets.

We stumbled across this video promoting a dictation tool.

The account’s strategy is actually not that strong. It feels too direct and not very appealing to the viewer.

But they accidentally found a clever growth hack. This one video went viral and hit 500K views because of a Polaroid photo stuck on the keyboard. Yes, that’s why the video holds attention and got those views. You get hooked right away trying to figure out what it is.

And it’s nothing. Nothing exciting is on the Polaroid.

Can you believe it? If you put something wild on the Polaroid instead of a boring festival photo and act like it’s nothing, then jackpot.

You hook the viewer, keep retention high, get virality, and then just hope they are the right audience for the video or product you’re promoting.

We call this the Easter egg in the MacBook growth hack.

MoonX targets zodiac content like Nebula but uses the wrong format, while Nebula combines all 12 signs in one hook, boos…

SGE Team

•

March 10, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

MoonX is a lunar‑cycle and astrology app that’s been around since 2019.

Even though it ranks surprisingly high in several countries

#1 Panama

#1 Bolivia

#2 Nigeria

#3 Angola

#8 Latvia

#9 Argentina

It still has just 20K downloads.

While digging into their TikTok presence, we found a linked account.

The posting rhythm is inconsistent. Some months are active, while others go completely quiet.

Even so, a few videos still manage to generate real engagement.

Each post focuses on a single zodiac sign.

“Aries at a party is…” → 615.5K views, 1,545 comments

“Gemini me happy with life” → 463.4K views, 830 comments

But here is the real structural issue, and it becomes obvious when you compare MoonX to

Nebula

.

MoonX and Nebula are basically playing the same game-> zodiac identity content built to drive comments.

But they’re doing it in completely different ways.

MoonX posts one sign per video-> You get comments, but only from 1/12 of the audience.

Nebula does the opposite.

They put all 12 signs in one slideshow->Every viewer scans to find their sign, every viewer comments.

That is why Nebula can get 5.7M views on a single post, 2,700 comments, and 45.8M total views across four accounts.

And the hook that unlocks everything is love and relationships.

MoonX needs a stronger structure, one that speaks to all twelve signs at once, uses relationship-based hooks, and naturally moves viewers toward the app instead of leaving them in the comments.

frameworks.description: Create content that includes all 12 zodiac signs in a single post to maximize audience engagement by allowing every viewer to find their sign and comment, rather than segmenting the audience by individual signs.
frameworks.when_to_use: When targeting a broad audience interested in zodiac or identity-based content and aiming to maximize engagement and virality on platforms like TikTok.
frameworks.example: Nebula's slideshow combining all 12 zodiac signs in one video, resulting in 5.7M views and 2,700 comments.

metadata.key_principle: Maximize audience engagement by creating inclusive content that speaks to the entire target segment simultaneously, rather than fragmenting the audience with narrow, single-segment content.
metadata.article_summary: MoonX, a lunar-cycle and astrology app, ranks highly in several countries but is stuck at 20K downloads due to ineffective TikTok content strategy. MoonX posts one zodiac sign per video, limiting engagement to only a fraction of the audience. In contrast, Nebula combines all 12 zodiac signs in one video, using relationship-based hooks to drive massive engagement and views. This inclusive approach leads to significantly higher virality and user interaction, suggesting MoonX should adopt a similar content structure to improve growth.

We’ve been seeing more and more simple talking-style videos pull huge views on TikTok. Just like this cheating-drama format that is being repeated across cheating/drama apps.

The video usually just show someone doing something ordinary in the kitchen, cutting fruit, making a snack, moving around the house, while the whole story sits in one long POV sentence on screen.

Cheaterbuster

posted one five days ago that pulled 20.1M views with this hook:

“POV: your (soon to be ex) husband is mad because you won’t let his girlfriend… the girl he cheated on you with and got pregnant… move into the house with your two kids”

There’s no direct CTA in the video, only a link in bio. This can help the post feel more natural and keeps the comments moving, but it also makes the product easier to miss.

This is not a new format for Cheaterbuster who has already used it in

multiple waves

: affiliate clips, confrontation skits, emotional talking videos.

But the latest is easier to produce and easier to scale.

The open question is conversion.

Sherlock

posted a very similar video five days ago and pulled 6.8M views. Same setup, same emotional hook, same kind of product underneath.

But this time the app is pushed closer to the viewer with a direct caption CTA “use Sherlock app to check ur man”.

On screen hook: “listen to my husband’s reaction when he got caught cheating”

frameworks.description: Use a relatable, emotionally charged POV story as the video hook, presented in a simple talking-style video format with on-screen text narration. This format leverages viewers' empathy and curiosity to drive high engagement and virality.
frameworks.when_to_use: When aiming to create viral organic content that resonates emotionally and encourages viewers to watch and share, especially on TikTok.

frameworks.description: Test the placement and style of call-to-action (CTA) to balance natural content feel and conversion. A soft CTA (link in bio) keeps the content feeling organic and encourages comment engagement but may reduce direct conversions. A direct on-screen CTA pushes the product closer to the viewer, potentially increasing conversion but risking less natural engagement.
frameworks.when_to_use: When optimizing for conversion from viral content, especially when the product is related to the content's emotional hook.
frameworks.example: Cheaterbuster uses a link in bio CTA for natural feel; Sherlock uses a direct caption CTA to prompt app use.

metadata.key_principle: Leveraging emotionally resonant, simple POV storytelling on TikTok can drive massive organic reach; balancing CTA style is critical to convert views into app installs without losing engagement.

One uses a soft CTA (link in bio) to keep the content natural and encourage comments but risks missing conversions. The other uses a direct on-screen CTA to push app installs but with fewer views. The format is simple, scalable, and effective for viral growth.

A simple slideshow format is moving across categories right now: start by rating familiar subject, rate it with short punchy text, and end with an unexpected verdict.

Most videos open with something like “Rating concealers I’ve used…” and move slide by slide through quick scores and short reviews.

Then the last slide flips the format and reveals the real winner:

a friend, a partner, or any person who always has your back with a hook like:  “10000/10 / Knows everything / Doesn’t judge / Backs me up / NEVER SNITCHES.”

780.3k views

46.7K views

What makes it smart is that it uses a familiar product-rating setup to pull people in, then turns into something else by the end.

It catches attention with a format people already know, but the real message is about a person, a relationship, or a different kind of recommendation.

frameworks.name: Bait-and-Switch Rating Format
frameworks.description: Start with a familiar product rating slideshow format with quick scores and punchy text, then end with an unexpected twist revealing a person or relationship as the real 'winner'.
frameworks.when_to_use: Use when you want to leverage a popular, recognizable content format to attract attention but deliver a surprising, emotionally resonant message that encourages sharing and engagement.
frameworks.example: A video starts by rating concealers with quick scores, then ends by rating a friend as '10000/10, knows everything, never snitches', shifting the focus from products to relationships.

metadata.key_principle: Leveraging familiar content formats to hook viewers before delivering an unexpected, emotionally engaging twist increases attention and shareability.
metadata.article_summary: The article describes a trending slideshow format where creators rate familiar products with quick scores and punchy text, then conclude with an unexpected verdict highlighting a person or relationship instead of a product. This bait-and-switch approach uses a known format to attract viewers but surprises them with a meaningful message, boosting engagement and virality.

UsTwo is a shared drawing lock-screen widget designed for couples and friends.

This single-feature app, launched just two weeks ago, has already reached 9K downloads and is currently sitting in the Top 100 in the U.S. Lifestyle category.

So far, the team is running a single TikTok account that has generated 2.1M views. They are posting aggressively, averaging three videos per day, with about 30 videos uploaded so far.

The most successful one hit 1.3M views on March 1, 2026 with the hook:

“making sure me and my bestie are on the same page”

Every video follows the same structure: two phones interacting on the lock screen, followed by a quick app reveal.

This format has become a strong growth engine for long-distance relationship apps because the feature itself is the demo. Viewers instantly understand what the app does in the first second.

We’ve already seen similar growth from apps like

Lovio

,

Lovora

, and

Lovelee

, all experimenting with different hooks while keeping the exact same visual setup.

At this point, the two-phones lockscreen interaction is starting to look like a built-in virality engine for couple apps.

UsTwo essentially showed that it’s still not too late to “abuse” it.

Clove is an AI recipe app that lets users save, import, and organize recipes from TikTok, Instagram, websites, and screenshots.

In the last month, they’ve been growing to 9.1M views using one hook that already proved it can travel across categories.

One video alone brought in more than half the views:

“I’ve been cooking for 2 YEARS & now I see THIS?” -> 5M views

Same format, different creator:

“I’ve been cooking for 5 YEARS and now I see this” -> 1.4M views

The videos open with a slightly shocked expression then move into the app demo.

It’s an easy format to create, get a batch of reaction clips from your creators, swap in different recipe examples, and keep reusing the same hook.

frameworks.example: The cooking app used the hook 'I’ve been cooking for X YEARS & now I see THIS?' with different creators and recipes, generating millions of views.

This format is easy to replicate and scale, driving organic growth and user acquisition.

New AI Closet App Hits 1.5M Views and Top 100 in 6 Countries

An AI wardrobe organizer app hit 1.5M views and Top 100 in six European countries through a simple TikTok strategy.

SGE Team

•

March 9, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Launched just four months ago, Vesta Wardrobe is an AI app designed to help users organize their closet and get personalized outfit suggestions.

Simply upload photos of your clothes, and the app suggests smart outfit combinations for different occasions.

Though the app is still building its download base, it’s already made significant progress, recently climbing into the Top 100 in six different European countries.

The app is driving growth on TikTok with an UGC strategy focused on style inspiration and daily outfit content. With 11 active accounts, they’ve managed to generate 1.5M total views so far.

The best-performing video came from @stylewithavaaa, who posted a pov style skit where she wakes up and opens her closet, using the app to help pick an outfit. The video, titled “unfortunately i do ‘wake up like this’ every morning,” hit 463K views.

Vesta Wardrobe has tapped into a relatable struggle, deciding what to wear.

Creator @delareilley perfectly expressed this frustration in her February 12, 2026, with: “Me: ‘I have nothing to wear.’ My closet:

opens app

.”

The video went viral with 4.7M views, showing the potential for combining relatable content with app demos.

With this type of strategy, Vesta Wardrobe could be on track to increase conversion. We’ll be keeping an eye on how they continue to build momentum.

We’ve recently covered a similar AI closet app playbook here:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/11m-anthropic-backed-ai-clueless-closet-app-pulls-36m-views-in-one-account

Finanz vs Bloom: A Masterclass in What Scales

Two apps in one of the toughest niches to scale.

SGE Team

•

March 6, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Finanz is an Italian educational app about saving and investing. It launched in 2022, and three years later, the numbers are still flat.

6K downloads total.

4M TikTok views since they started posting in July 2025.

The message is always the same” your generation won’t get a state pension, so start saving now”:

“POV: avete 23 anni… la pensione statale la vedrete solo con il binocolo.” → 292.9K views

“POV: You’re 23 and you’ve just discovered that you’ll only see a state pension through binoculars, so you create the Duolingo of finance to allow everyone to build it for themselves :)”

“Io che mi metto in punizione per non aver iniziato ad investire…” → 212.4K views

“Me putting myself in timeout for not starting to invest even just 50€ a month when I started working (It would have cost me nothing) (I don’t even want to know how much I’d have now) (I’m trying to make up for it with the Duolingo of finance)”

And yet, nothing converts.

Bloom

works in the same space, finance education, but uses a totally different approach.

They streamlined the hook that was already effective.

Here’s what that looks like:

20M+ TikTok views, not from one account but from a coordinated network.

Top video: 7M views

A seeded comment->“Bloom is the only reason why I even have 18k lol” -> with 41K likes, posted by another account inside their own network

Bloom sticks to the same format, again and again.

Relatable pain → creator reaction → product embedded. Bloom runs this loop across accounts, endlessly.

Despite Bloom’s success on TikTok, it hasn’t yet scaled, the app sits at only 20K downloads.

frameworks.example: Bloom uses this loop across multiple TikTok accounts, showing relatable financial struggles, creator reactions, and embedding their app as the solution, driving 20M+ views.

metadata.key_principle: Consistent, authentic, and relatable content loops distributed across a coordinated creator network can drive viral growth and user acquisition even in tough niches.

Bloom's approach generates massive views and engagement but has yet to fully scale downloads.

A discipline tracker hit ~12M views by posting faceless “rules + harsh truths” content that people save like self-help,…

March 6, 2026

2 min read

Save for later

A discipline tracker hit ~12M views by running one faceless Instagram page and one faceless TikTok page, and letting the content feel fully organic.

Pattrn is a discipline tracker built around a 60-day challenge, with an AI coach layered in to keep users accountable. It launched in February 2025 and did 9K downloads last month.

Across simply one Instagram and TikTok faceless page with the app’s handle, they managed to hit 12M+ views.

Two videos (one in each platform) stick out for their virality.

On Instagram, they hit 2.1M views on 9 January, 2026, with:

“5 Simple Rules to Master Yourself” -> A faceless short video with generic rules: When you are “x”, do “y”.

The video doesn’t include an app promo in itself, only in the caption.

On TikTok, they hit 3.2M views and 186K bookmarks with:

“6 harsh truths that finally made me grow up”.

Same idea, but as a slideshow.

These slideshows worked very well on TikTok, averaging an insanely high (~20%) engagement rate.

These posts are already doing the hard part (reach + saves).

Even a light, consistent on-screen mention inside the slides would likely turn more of that intent into installs.

This approach led to high engagement and saves, indicating strong user intent that could be converted into installs with light branding.

The “Bookish Spotify” Hook That Drove 9K Downloads

A book-tracking app reached 9K downloads and $20K MRR after one creator found a repeatable reaction hook built on FOMO,…

SGE Team

•

March 6, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

A book-tracking app recently reached 9K downloads and $20K MRR, mostly driven by a single creator.

Bookshelf helps readers log books, track reading habits, and discover new titles. They also feature an AI book scanner tool, which recommends books based on personal interests.

Instead of running a large creator network, the distribution comes from just two accounts, both run by the same creator, Anna, who posts reaction-style videos on TikTok and Instagram.

On September 29, 2025, she hit virality for the first time.

“FCK why I didn’t know about this bookish app earlier????? It is LITERALLY bookish Spotify!!!” hit 1.6M views.

The classic shocked face -> app demo structure plus the hook itself which contains several engagement triggers at once.

First, the punctuation-heavy shock tone (“FCK…?????”) creates urgency and authenticity.

Second, the phrasing triggers FOMO — “why didn’t I know about this earlier?”

Third, the comparison makes the product instantly legible: “Spotify for books.”

So far, that video remains the biggest hit, but similar hooks have produced a few additional 100K+ posts.

They already found a winning strategy, now they need to scale the format across more creators.

If you want a similar case in the same niche, Margins is also gaining traction on BookTok with creator hooks like

“book girlies what book tracking app are we using in 2026 because Goodreads is not it anymore”

(1.5M views).

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/book-tracker-gains-traction-on-booktok

article.title: Wrap a product reveal inside a “Gen Z built this”

Wrap a product reveal inside a “Gen Z built this”

The fastest way to explain your app is: “[famous app], but for [niche].”

SGE Team

•

March 6, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

This is a plug-and-play hook for almost any consumer app:

“I love Gen Z because wdYm they made [famous app] but for [niche].”

Creators starts with “I love Gen Z because…” and then drop a specific example of something clever that someone built.

The hook gets even stronger when creators anchor it to a famous app name. “Tinder but for books” lands faster than “a book discovery app.”  The big brands does the positioning for you.

Here’s how different apps have used it:

StudyFetch

“I love GenZ because wdym someone made a website that is like SUBWAY SURFERS but for STUDYING” → 1.7M views

Raena AI

Another study app

“I love Gen Z because WDYM someone made an app that is FLAPPY BIRD but for STUYDING?”

12.4k views

So brief

“I love genZ because wdym someone made a Tinder for BOOKS” → 1.3M views

Vesta wardrobe

“I love Gen Z because wdYm someone made BARBIES DREAM closet irl”

Shelf

Shelf’s creators ran the same idea but swapped “Gen Z” for founder credibility, and it still worked because the structure is identical: surprising claim → quick explanation → “is this real?” comments.

“wdym the creators of Spotify and Pinterest just made an app tgth??” → 792.1K views

and again at

770.7K views.

Same template every time, better hop on it.

frameworks.name: Famous App but for Niche Hook
frameworks.description: A content hook that explains a new app by comparing it to a well-known app but tailored to a specific niche, e.g., 'Tinder but for books.' This leverages existing brand recognition to quickly communicate the app's value proposition.
frameworks.when_to_use: Use this framework when launching or promoting a new consumer app to quickly convey its purpose and appeal to Gen Z audiences on social platforms like TikTok and Instagram.
frameworks.example: "I love Gen Z because wdym someone made a Tinder for books" which quickly communicates a book discovery app by referencing Tinder.

metadata.key_principle: Leveraging familiar, popular app names as analogies accelerates understanding and piques curiosity, making content more shareable and engaging among Gen Z audiences.

This approach uses the positioning power of big brands to quickly explain the app's purpose, driving viral growth and brand awareness on platforms like TikTok and Instagram. Examples include 'Tinder but for books' and 'Flappy Bird but for studying.' The format encourages surprise and curiosity, leading to high engagement and views.

article.content:
Travel Website Grows on The Back of Viral Hook From Competitor

Layla.ai went from viral travel edits to copycat creator drama, stick with the trend or return to its root.

SGE Team

Travel Website Grows on The Back of Viral Hook From Competitor

Layla.ai went from viral travel edits to copycat creator drama, stick with the trend or return to its root.

SGE Team

•

March 5, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Layla.ai

is a travel‑planning website that has been active on TikTok since 2021.

For years, the brand relied on a simple, visual format that consistently delivered reach. Then, after a long break in 2024, the account returned with a completely different strategy and the results look nothing like before.

For two years, Layla built its TikTok presence around AI‑generated travel inspiration.

The format was unmistakable:

bucket‑list destinations

hotel compilations

“places you’ve never heard of”

“Bucket list places you probably haven’t heard of” -> 42.8M views

At the end of 2024, the account stopped posting for months.

So when Layla returned in late 2025, it wasn’t picking up where it left off, it was starting from zero.

Instead of AI travel visuals, the account shifted to creator headshots reacting dramatically to the site.

“je peux littéralement épouser la meuf qui m’a montré ce site je vous jure” ->2.4M views

“I could literally marry the girl who showed me this site, I swear.”

The videos aren’t all 100% organic.

But just weeks ago, the travel app

Roamy

exploded on TikTok with 17.5M views in a month using a nearly identical structure.

“I could literally kiss the Indian flight attendant who showed me this” -> 2.5M views

It’s almost impossible not to see the connection.

Layla’s new format looks like a direct attempt to replicate Roamy’s breakout.

Now the question is whether Layla will commit even more to the new direction or go back to the format that helped it grow in the first place.

frameworks.name: Trend Hijacking with Format Adaptation
frameworks.description: Identify a viral content format from a competitor and adapt it to your brand's context to quickly gain traction and reach on social platforms.
frameworks.when_to_use: When your existing content strategy plateaus or after a hiatus, and a competitor's viral format aligns with your brand's audience and goals.
frameworks.example: Layla.ai shifted from AI-generated travel visuals to creator reaction videos mimicking Roamy's viral TikTok format, resulting in renewed growth.

metadata.key_principle: Leveraging competitor viral content formats by adapting them authentically can jumpstart growth and re-engage audiences after stagnation or inactivity.

SGE Team

Save for later

Latera is a new travel utility that’s basically “save the spot, map it, and turn it into a trip.” It lets you save places from TikTok/IG/Safari and organize them on a map, so your “future trip” isn’t just screenshots.

Released 52 days ago, they went straight for what’s already working:

Roamy’s hook system

, translated into Spanish.

Their biggest hit so far comes from

@travelwithcande

, who started posting at the end of February and immediately went straight for Roamy’s best-performing lines.

She translated the flight-attendant credibility hook to spanish and got 1.3M views.

“Podría LITERALMENTE casarme con la azafata que me mostró esto”

(“I could literally marry the flight attendant who showed me this.”)

Then she tested another Roamy-style “how did I not know this” discovery hook and it popped too:

“Llevo viajando hace 10 años y RECIÉN me entero de esto???” → 974K views

(“I’ve been traveling for 10 years and I’m only just finding out about this???”)

We’ve already seen apps like

Palima

and

Travy

, where copying Roamy’s biggest lines (“wdym I just spent 3 months planning my trip to Paris and I just found this??”) was enough to get a first break through.

Roamy already proved this format worked over and over again: shocked reaction → panic/discovery hook → relief.

And instead of spending months experimenting, these newer apps can just lift the hooks that are already known to work and use them as a shortcut.

When

PushUp Time

The early play was the exact same format: phone/screen shot → “opening Clash but I have to do push ups to unlock it” → quick demo → “app name?” comments.

Which is a format that still works, Push up time just pulled 827.9K views on YouTube shorts:

Now Wayk is moving to the next phase. It’s testing a broader angle: an alarm that won’t turn off until you complete a task.

A recent video from the founder-led accounts pulled 4.1M views a week ago:

They’re testing a broader angle: an alarm that won’t turn off until you complete a task that opens up endless variations. Push-ups is one joke. Tasks are a whole series.

And it pulls comments automatically because everyone starts saying how they’d try to cheat it instead of doing it.

article.title: The Tip of the Iceberg
article.content:
The Tip of the Iceberg

Viral formats are becoming products, and this is how you stay in the TikTok distribution game in 2026.

SGE Team

•

March 4, 2026

•

6 min read

The Tip of the Iceberg

Viral formats are becoming products, and this is how you stay in the TikTok distribution game in 2026.

SGE Team

•

March 4, 2026

•

6 min read

Save for later

You know what I have been noticing lately?

More and more, the format itself is becoming the product.

Look at Halo and Yapper (AI video prank apps) on one side, and Evry and Wayk (alarm apps) on the other. They are the tip of the iceberg of a much bigger trend.

Take those two alarm apps that came from the viral “Apple alarm not going off?” TikTok format. Both teams saw the format blowing up and built an app directly on top of it. In just a few weeks they were already doing more than $50K+ in revenue (each).

This trend matters a lot for casual consumer mobile/web apps because many of them are quickly becoming commodities.

Of course a company like Duolingo is not going to zero.

It has brand recognition, distribution, and network effects. Simply cloning Duolingo with the same strategy is not the right move. The real strength is not just the software. There is real research behind the learning system.

But the product structure itself can often be moved to another vertical very quickly. Sideme is a good example of that.

From a TikTok marketing perspective, this approach has clear advantages. The format is familiar so people instantly recognize it. Viewers are more interested. The UX and UI are already proven.

The downside is that you are basically doing free market research for companies like Duolingo that can copy you the same way you copied the format. AI is becoming the ultimate equalizer.

Now let’s go back to the format idea.

Take Halo, or a text to brainrot tool I recently found on TikTok.

Do you know how many SaaS products like this exist? There are dozens (if not hundreds) of wrappers around the same AI models. I have seen many of them appear and disappear.

They have almost no moat. So unless you dominate SEO, the only real way to distribute them is to attach the product to a viral format.

That is exactly what they did. They created a video format that reached more than 6 million views and they keep repeating it.

One thing they could improve is the domain name. SEO sites often use names like “PDF to something”. The same idea works for viral tools/apps. Something like BoyfriendToBrainrot . com would immediately capture the use case.

Another strategy would be to break the product into very specific niche use cases and optimize each one for the format that drives traffic. Everything becomes tuned to increase conversion from the viral format.

In other words, the product serves the format.

And if software can soon be generated infinitely and almost for free, this may actually be the future.

What we are seeing now is just the beginning. The tip of the iceberg. Once you notice it, you cannot unsee it.

You might be thinking, “G, how do I actually make money from this?”

My answer is simple. Every day I scroll for about 30 minutes and I look for gold. What you want to find are untapped formats.

Untapped formats are accounts that repeatedly go viral with the same idea or way of presenting information, but they have not fully monetized it or built a product around it.

Here are a few examples I recently found.

One was around Valentine’s Day. Girls started posting funny websites their boyfriends built for them in a 2010 style design. The format kept going viral again and again. If you moved fast, you could have built a product around it.

Speed matters more than ever in a world where nothing is very defensible.

Another example is a creator making videos about commenting on Hinge prompts. The execution is excellent and I have not seen many others doing it yet. It is easy to repeat and clone, and several “rizz” style apps could easily be built around that format.

Then there are formats where many accounts are doing the same thing and all of them keep going viral. I am not even sure what product should be built there yet, but statistically it is a strong and scalable format.

This is why research matters so much. If you find the insight before everyone else, you move faster. Being first is becoming more and more important as we move toward a world of infinite software generation.

When software can be generated instantly, many products start behaving like infoproducts. Timing and distribution become the most important factors.

Formats themselves are not defensible either. Do not fool yourself. The only real advantage is your ability to spot the next format faster than everyone else.

For example, someone on our team created this format below that quickly got adopted by almost every language learning app.

It ended up generating billions of views. Yes, billions.

How much did we capture from it? Probably just a few percent. It still brought a lot of downloads.

This whole game is similar to quant trading. Your trades get picked off by algorithms and arbitrage players.

Your formats get picked off by competitors doing the same thing.

But human traders still make millions by spotting the right opportunity before everyone else.

So you cannot complain about it. You just have to keep getting better and faster.

It really is a brave new world.

Best,

G

Silent study rooms, strangers on camera, and a UGC wave turning “don’t study alone” into the main hook.

SGE Team

March 4, 2026

3 min read

Save for later

You open a room and you’re instantly surrounded by other students studying live from all over the world. Cameras on, audio off. It feels like a virtual library, except you’re not alone, and that’s the point.

StudyStream started back in 2020, but the app version only launched in 2024. It’s still mainly a website and averages around 500K organic visits per month. On the App Store it isn’t a big chart player, but it still holds $7K MRR.

For years they just ran the steady engine: one main Instagram page and one main TikTok page, posting twice per day on both. They’ve been doing that since 2021, and those two accounts alone have made over 30M views.

One of their best promos shows that their niche has real interest:

“pov you finally discover that there are 24/7 study rooms for students from all over the world to focus in” hit 2.2M views plus 39K bookmarks.

Then, since last year, they widened the playbook.

They started leaning heavily into a TikTok-led UGC wave, and it’s already producing viral posts because creators can remix the same visual in different storylines.

@emma.studystream stands out for going viral on both platforms.

She hit 1.7M views on TikTok and 2.3M views on Instagram 1 month later, with:

Another creator, @roux.studystream, got 920K views by marketing it as “study with good-looking guys.”

And @paula.studystream hit 2M views by keeping it even simpler: show the room, show the chat, and sell it as the fix for studying alone at night.

StudyStream won because the concept is instantly clear on camera.

Once the study room visual clicks, creators can wrap it in whatever feeling pulls the viewer in: studying alone at night, needing accountability, chasing motivation, even a little “who’s in this room” curiosity, without changing the product at all.

They spent years making the idea familiar through consistent posting on their main pages, and now the UGC layer is simply scaling the same scene through different storylines until one hits, then repeating it.

SGE Team

A budget app called TapSheet has hit 9K downloads in about a month.

What makes it interesting is that it did not start as an app at all. It started as a simple Google Sheet built to track expenses, then slowly turned into an app once the distribution proved there was demand.

The whole thing is built and marketed by a solo founder, Avian Jonas Leung.

He runs both Instagram and TikTok and posts around twice a day on average.

Before TapSheet became a standalone app, the workflow was pretty much an iPhone shortcut connected to Google Sheets.

Back then he posted a video showing the setup and it hit 600K views and 11.6K saves. The high amount of saves showed that people had interest in his system.

Since then, his content has reached about 3.1M total views, and the shift to an actual app gave him recent virality.

On February 21, 2026, he hit 1.7M views with:

“Showing my friend how I cured overspending (4 steps)”

The only open question is monetization. He appears to be running a subscription model, and budgeting audiences are notoriously price sensitive.

1. Not drunk just together

This one has been trending for months, but it’s still pulling very solid numbers.

You or your creators can show a great bonding moment with friends or a partner. Think laughter, stumbling, and doing stupid, fun things. Then just tie it all together with the hook “not drunk, just together.”

It’s super easy to adapt for travel, couple, and friend group apps because it instantly sells the vibe.

17.8M views

2.4M views

here

.

2. Been waiting on that sunshine

This one is low effort, high reward. You need two slides:

Slide 1: winter you (grey, bundled, low energy).

Slide 2: summer you (outside, glowing, back to life).

Use the viral audio by

Rihanna

, and copy these hooks, one for each picture:

“Been waiting on that sunshine” vs “I think I need that back”.

8.6M views

6.7M views

And more at

3M+ views

here.

3. Do you actually want to do this

This trend revolves around sharing those awkward, funny, or frustrating moments when someone calls you out for not doing something “right” in their eyes, all because it’s something you were kind of forced into.

The more specific the memory, the better it lands.

10.5M views

7.7M views

+more sitting at

3.5M views

here.

4. How it feels to __

A relatable, easy trend to capture a small panic moment, turned POV.

You shake the phone to the beat so it feels intense and slightly chaotic, then drop this line:

“how it feels to ___”

Fill the blank with something weirdly specific (avoidance, social hierarchy, childhood fear, looming responsibilities).

8.5M views

5. The sound I hear when

This one is built for anyone who mentally checks out mid-conversation.

The format: you write “the sound I hear when…”, then finish it with a scenario where you’re instantly tuning out advice you didn’t ask for, instructions you can’t process, someone speaking and your brain just goes offline.

Most creators pair it with a static / distorted noise sound effect to show the internal shutdown.

SGE Team

A new face search app has climbed to around #30 in the U.S. after roughly a month live.

Sherlock lets you search for anyone’s online presence from just a picture of their face.

So far it has hit around 10K downloads and hit 2.4M total views.

They are already running a TikTok led UGC wave made up of 24 creator accounts, who post a wide variety of storyline content.

The other thing that stands out is how the accounts get warmed up.

A lot of ambassadors start with videos that have nothing to do with the app. They use a relatability question to farm engagement first, then pivot into promotion once the account has traction.

For example, the first video ever uploaded from ambassador @alyyycole1 hit 613K views with a 14.2% engagement rate.

After a few breakup relatable posts, she transitioned into app demos framed around catching a boyfriend cheating and using the tool to identify who he was with.

But the breakup angle isn’t the only one being tested.

One creator, @jacob.fitzgerald59, hit 460K views by showing the app as a way to find criminals in the Epstein files.

Another creator, @neezy7753, is growing fast with long car story videos that feel like real time confessionals.

She posts the story in parts, makes it detailed enough to look real, then ties the app into the moment she identifies the girl involved. With less than ten videos she is already at 27K followers, and the comments consistently fill with people asking what she used to find the person.

There are smaller pockets starting too. One account is getting traction with teacher profile searches, using short reaction clips filmed in classroom settings.

Sherlock is stacking medium wins across many creators, with each one testing a different storyline and target audience.

Those pieces add up. And in just a month, it has already been enough to push the app into the U.S. top ranks.

Wayk is on a crazy run right now. Yes, they are clearly running some videos as ads, but they also have some very strong organic content. For example, one video from 6 days ago already has 1.8M views.

We appreciate the sped up format trick and the big watermark logos everywhere. Also, the iPad recording is always a good hack because on TikTok an iPad always looks better than an iPhone. A BeReal alternative just went from 30K to 90K downloads in 30 days.

Buddies is an app built for friend groups, launched during quarantine. Friends can send photos and videos, but nobody can see anything right away, only the next day.

They run an English and French playbook that has made close to 40M views.

Their first good find happened in French, with street-style app presentations and the same hook every time: “The reverse BeReal”.

“Le BeReal inversé” hit 2.4M views (March 14, 2025).

However, the real explosion that tripled their downloads in the last 30 days was a small but efficient primarily english-speaking UGC wave.

Around early February 2026, Buddies decided to start a small ambassador campaign made up of 5 creators.

They started going viral after days. And all they had to do was cut fruit.

@maybelleirl hit

3.8M views

&

60K bookmarks

on TikTok by cutting a mango and presenting the app as a better alternative to Snapchat “do not open” group chats.

A few days later, @faaizslife hit 3.1M views on Instagram with pretty much the same script.

Their strategy always comes down to mainstream app comparisons.

At first, they grew their French audience as “the reverse BeReal”.

Now, they are growing an international audience by comparing themselves to the Snapchat “do not open” group chats.

Breakout Accounts & Apps

Built Workout

Built Workout

reached #74 in the U.S. Health & Fitness category after a single founder-posted Instagram video hit 7.5M views.

The video showed his year-long body transformation, with the app subtly displayed as a small on-screen overlay.

The overlay acted like a workout “receipt,” showing muscles trained and stats without feeling promotional. This subtle placement sparked curiosity in the comments, driving organic interest and App Store traffic.

Oasis – What’s Healthy

Oasis

generated 15M views in the past 30 days using a small number of accounts and repeatable product-rating formats.

Their strongest videos use grocery aisle hooks followed by the app’s score screen, positioning the app result as the natural conclusion and CTA.

On Instagram Reels, videos follow this:

Warning Hook → Explanation → App Result Structure

While TikTok slideshows rank products from worst to best using app scores.

These simple, repeatable formats drive high engagement.

Glowyynnn

A single creator account,

@glowyynnn,

generated 82M views by repeatedly posting the same teeth-whitening transformation format across TikTok and Instagram.

Each video opens with teeth stained purple to create visual shock, then reveals clean white teeth using the whitening kit.

The consistent problem → transformation structure keeps viewers watching and makes the product benefit instantly clear.

Emotional, confession-style captions and dramatic hooks further increase curiosity and engagement.

Newcomers to Watch

Juno: Chronic Illness Support

Juno

is gaining early TikTok traction using faceless, repeatable slideshow formats focused on insomnia hacks and chronic condition tips.

These videos use Pinterest visuals, simple explanations, and relatable hooks, with the app subtly positioned as part of the solution.

Accounts like @potstipsandadvice generated 3.8M views from just two videos using this template.

While others like @chronically_pickle use consistent animated formats to explain conditions.

This repeatable, faceless strategy allows Juno to scale content efficiently and build early momentum.

HabitHands: Quit Nail Biting

A

brand-new habit-breaking app

hit the Top 100 in three countries after a single faceless video (mostly Google images + quick demo) reached 600K views.

The hook focused on a relatable but rarely discussed struggle, making the problem instantly recognizable.

So far, growth has been driven by one breakout, but the category has strong UGC potential if they shift toward consistent creator-led content.

Solaia: Équilibre hormonal

A

hormone-focused meal scanner

app hit $10K MRR in just 3 weeks, powered entirely by a founder-led run on FrenchTok.

The creator was already posting anti-inflammatory recipes and body transformation content. The app was introduced subtly, first in captions (362K TikTok views, 244K on Instagram), then briefly shown on-screen. As soon as the product appeared visually, comments shifted to “What’s the app?”

Winning content → Light mention → On-screen proof

A clean example of founder-led distribution converting directly into revenue.

Innie: Self-Discovery & Care

Just 11 days old,

Innie tested the usual advice-driven formats

across nine creator accounts, but nothing crossed 200K views.

The breakout came from a shift in framing. Instead of listing habits, one post asked for real transformation stories:

“What took you from ‘I hate my life’ to ‘I can’t wait for tomorrow?’” → 421K views, 935 comments.

Growth came when they turned tips into identity-level transformation and community participation.

frameworks.when_to_use: When aiming to produce viral short-form content that resonates with health, fitness, and well-being audiences on TikTok and Instagram, especially for apps or brands wanting to leverage UGC and creator content.

frameworks.description: Develop faceless, repeatable content formats such as slideshows, animated mascots, or simple demos that can be scaled across multiple creator accounts to efficiently build momentum and reach.

frameworks.description: Shift content framing from generic tips to identity-level transformation stories that invite community participation and emotional engagement, increasing comments and retention.

Stateshift succeeded by making users feel anxiety and share their scariest symptoms; now in 2026, the test is whether th…

Stateshift is an app meant to teach body‑based tools for managing stress and anxiety.

So far, their biggest driver is

@issy.stateshift

, now at 10.6 million cumulative views.

For months, this creator has been using a format we’ve seen winning across the anxiety space.

Their competitor

Vent Now

was the first to prove it. Back then, their early growth started with a simple slideshow that listed the anxiety symptoms the creator experienced.

@issy.stateshift

went for the same structure and guess what. It worked.

“You’re healthy, chill out it’s just anxiety” → 688.4K views, 1674 comments

Then she pushed the format further.

Instead of listing her symptoms, she asked the audience about theirs. That changed the whole dynamic and sparked her first true viral hit.

“Pls tell me ur scariest anxiety symptoms, I need to know I’m not alone” → 1.5M views, 6989 comments

However, TikTok formats age fast, and what worked in 2025 is already struggling in 2026.

“you’re healthy, it’s just anxiety”->1,247

The question now is whether this new version will hold up, and we’ll be watching.

The “UMAX for Body” App Pulling 40M Views

A new “UMAX for fitness” app pulled 40M+ views, but only started converting on Youtube Shorts.

SGE Team

•

February 26, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

A new body-rating app is starting to gain traction with a familiar playbook: UMAX-style scoring, but for fitness.

Ujack launched about 4 months ago and is basically “UMAX for the body.”

Users scan their physique, get an overall score, and see ratings for specific body parts.

They’ve already pulled more than 40 million views across Instagram and YouTube Shorts, but the path wasn’t clean from the start.

On Instagram, they grew through a repeatable “winter arc” series built on funny and weird gym training compilations.

The content blew up, but the app barely appeared, so it looked more like audience building than acquisition.

The actual conversion angle started later on YouTube Shorts, once they began using the app directly inside transformation content.

That’s where the format clicked: body transformation videos with app rating.

“

3 year transformation

” hit 3M views & 2K comments (23 Dec, 2025).

They also added a pinned-comment app promo on these posts, which made the funnel clearer than the earlier Instagram phase.

They first proved they could get attention in gym content, then layered the product into a format that actually matches the app.

If you want the original looksmaxxing score-overlay format that likely inspired this, this is the closest reference:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/app-score-overlay

article.title: 5 TikTok Formats = 62 Million Views
article.content:
5 TikTok Formats = 62 Million Views

Travel apps have been winning by repeating 1 or 2 content formats until they blow up, then everyone copies it.

SGE Team

•

February 25, 2026

•

5 min read

5 TikTok Formats = 62 Million Views

Travel apps have been winning by repeating 1 or 2 content formats until they blow up, then everyone copies it.

SGE Team

•

February 25, 2026

•

5 min read

Save for later

Travel apps might seem different at first, but behind the scenes they have built some of the strongest playbooks out there.

Now everyone wants to follow their lead.

As soon as one format works, the whole niche rushes to copy it.

Here is a quick breakdown of the top formats travel apps are using today, so you can learn from them and apply the ideas to your own niche

1)  Shocked Discovery Hook

This is one of the biggest travel formats right now.

The structure is built around a strong emotional reaction, then the app reveal.

The creators start by reacting like they just stumbled into something too good not to share before showing the product.

The clearest example is

Roamy

. One of their biggest hits (posted 10 weeks ago) pulled

28.7M views

with the hook you’ve been seeing all over your FYP:

“I could LITERALLY kiss the flight attendant who showed me this”

”

They repeated the same hook until it compounded and had several big hits. And it worked:

300K downloads off pure hook repetition

.

Nomadtable

also jumped on this format, and tweaked it to:

“This random guy from my hostel just showed me THIS

“, pulling

310K views

.

2) In the moment discovery

This format shows up exactly when the app feels most useful.

Travel moment first → urgency/disbelief line → app reveal.

The creator finds the app

precisely

while traveling: on a plane, at the airport, during a trip, mid-chaos. That context does most of the work. It makes the product feel urgent and the moment real.

This is where the classic hook

“how am I only finding this now?”

style works best.

We’ve seen it in multiple versions:

Roamy pulled

1.4M views

with

“we’re literally leaving for Dubai in 7 minutes and I JUST found this”

Palima

also pulled

633k views

with a French creator:

“I spent 6 months planning a trip and I’m only finding this out NOW??”

We’re now seeing newer apps copy the same structure.

Travy

, just 6 months old, is already running the same UGC format through a 20-account ambassador wave. They pulled

893k views

with:

“wydm I just spent 3 months planning my trip to Paris and I just found this??”

3) Aspirational POV

This format barely looks like app marketing. It’s about showing the aesthetic side of traveling and the adventures you get to go on. Think travel diary, POV slideshows, unreal landscapes.

That’s how

Tripbff

first grew when they started posting in February 2023.

The whole account was faceless, alternating between random repurposed clips and pictures from Pinterest.

Once again, the app is usually secondary because the content sells the feeling first.

Worldpackers

is another great example, as they first started scaling with slideshows and FOMO landscape hooks

Some of their standout posts:

“taste testing durian”

→

10.7M views

“you traveled to China instead of Japan”

→

8.8M views

We’re also seeing early versions of this with

Landa

, another travel tracker.

7.2k views

4) Solo Travel Confession

This one is more personal and more text-heavy.

The format usually entails a girl creator on camera, a long text hook covering a personal solo travel story, and often, a subtle CTA.

It feels like a confession.

Going Solo

—

“How did you meet all those friends in Koh Tao”

(

3.5M views

).

They built their entire brand around the idea of solo travel adventures and meeting people.

Nomadtable

—

“3 years solo travelling and now I find this?”

(

803k views

)

What makes this format so strong is that it turns the app into social proof inside a real story. It’s not “download this app.” It’s “this helped me avoid a bad solo travel experience so I’m happily sharing it with you”.

And we can all agree that’s a much stronger emotional sell.

5) Travel Deal Reader

Not every travel app needs a reaction hook. Some of the performing content in this niche is just useful: a creator behind a laptop, reading deals, explaining routes, or showing how to track prices.

It’s a more practical format, less emotional than the reaction hooks, but it works because it can be genuinely useful. The viewer gets value even before the app is introduced.

The clearest example is

AirClub

with its “Travel Tuesday” format. The creator sits at a laptop and walks through live deals in a repeatable multi-part series. Their best video pulled

3.3M views

.

Tryp

actually mixes the deal-reader setup with a reaction hook: the creator starts with a close up reaction than shows the deal on screen.

It’s a blend of travel deal reader + shocked discovery —

3.2M views

.

The viewer gets value even before the app is introduced.

article.title: Four Calorie Trackers, One Playbook
article.content:
Four Calorie Trackers, One Playbook

In a category where every app shows calories the same way, Counter AI disappears unless it finds a format of its own.

SGE Team

•

February 25, 2026

2 min read

Four Calorie Trackers, One Playbook

In a category where every app shows calories the same way, Counter AI disappears unless it finds a format of its own.

SGE Team

•

February 25, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

In the calorie‑tracking category on TikTok, there’s already a “default format” that every app follows.

The execution varies a bit from app to app, but the core stays the same.

Content is all about showing you how many calories are in the food right in front of you.

Proof:

Kalo

uses slideshows of meals with calorie counts.

Microgram

uses slideshows of supermarket products with calorie counts.

CalScan

compares foods that have the same number of calories.

And now there’s one more to add to this playbook.

Just like CalScan, Counter AI also posts comparisons of foods with identical calorie counts.

The problem is that when every app uses the same calorie‑reveal structure, none of them stand out. And smaller apps like Counter AI become even more invisible.

Counter AI tried to stand out by having creators defend that counting calories “isn’t enough” to lose weight. You still need to hit the gym.

“She doesn’t know it yet, but in 5 min she’s going to pass out at the gym because 1,200 cal wasn’t enough”

->1.7M views

Or that they

“don’t have any calories left for the day.”

“When you have no calories left so you pull out this move”

-> 1.5M views (boosted)

frameworks.when_to_use: When entering a crowded content space where many competitors use similar formats and struggle to differentiate.
frameworks.example: Counter AI used the common calorie comparison format but added creator-driven narratives highlighting the limitations of calorie counting, resulting in viral videos.

metadata.key_principle: In saturated content categories, standing out requires breaking the default format with unique storytelling or perspectives to capture attention and drive viral growth.
metadata.article_summary: The article analyzes how calorie-tracking apps on TikTok use a default content format—showing calorie counts of foods via slideshows or comparisons. Counter AI, a smaller app, struggled to stand out using the same format. By introducing creator-driven narratives that challenge calorie counting norms, Counter AI achieved viral videos with millions of views, demonstrating the importance of format differentiation in content strategy.

Launched about 6 months ago, Travy reached 10K downloads and $5K MRR by entering a niche that already had a proven short-form playbook and executing it well.

Travy is an AI trip planner, a category that already had strong distribution patterns on TikTok and Instagram before they showed up.

They’ve now crossed 5M+ total views by following a very clear playbook.

First, they entered a niche that was already trending.

Second, they added a mascot-style companion to make the branding more recognizable.

Third, they ran the same UGC format that was already working for apps like Roamy and Palima.

That’s the core move. Travy runs a 20-account ambassador wave and leans on the same travel-app structure that already proved itself: curiosity hook, shocked reaction, then quick app demo.

The hook writing is especially close to Roamy’s. Travy leans more on “found this” phrasing, but the overall setup is nearly identical, and it’s working.

Travy entered a validated niche, kept the format familiar, and added just enough branding to make it feel like their version.

That was enough to push them past 5M views, 10K downloads, and $5K MRR in six months.

If you want the closest comparisons in this niche,

Roamy

&

Palima

are the best side-by-side references.

2 min read

This “Shazam for places” app is climbing the U.S. Top 100 with high-intent list content that gets people to save and actually use the app.

The app is called Tabi, and it helps people turn TikTok and Instagram posts into saved places. You share a post into the app, and it finds the locations, pins them to a map, and organizes them into custom tabs.

They’re running a 13-account setup and have generated about 2.6 million views so far.

That’s not huge volume, but several videos crossed 100K+ views with strong engagement, which, especially in the beginning stages, matters more here than raw reach.

The playbook is mostly local list content. Instead of leading with app demos, they lead with useful food and city recommendations, then use Tabi as the place where the full list lives.

The clearest example is @ultimateoclists. The videos feel like normal city food content, but the CTA is the product action: save the full list on Tabi using her code. That works because viewers already want the list before the app is even mentioned.

They also run other list formats built on the same behavior.

One version is faceless celebrity restaurant lists, where the app becomes the place to save all the spots tied to that celebrity.

Another is “best restaurants in [city]” rankings, which are naturally built for saves.

Tabi is growing off regional list content that matches exactly what the product does. High-intent saves beat empty views.

An all-in-one couples widget app is growing fast, and the main playbook is almost a direct copy of a format that already worked in the category.

Lovio launched about 10 months ago and was sitting at 10,000 downloads in January 2026. In February, it’s already around 30K downloads.

They’ve generated 42.8M views across just four accounts, two on Instagram and two on TikTok.

Most of that virality came from one faceless format that looks almost identical to the one that previously drove Lovelee’s growth: the two-phones lock-screen setup.

Their top performer hit 6M views on Instagram on Jan 17, 2026.

The format is almost the same each time: two lock screens, a message sent on one phone, the same message appearing on the other, then the app logo at the end. Same structure, same pacing, same payoff, just a different app.

The only real shift recently is the hook writing. They kept the exact same faceless setup, but started using more specific relationship scenarios, which also helped them break out on TikTok, not just Instagram.

One example from Feb 18, 2026:

We argued last night and I woke up to this → 2.2M views and 13K bookmarks.

They scaled fast by reusing a proven format and tightening the hooks over time.

A new AI audio companion for readers is climbing the charts with a single founder-led TikTok account.

BookScape turns reading into a more immersive experience by adding ambient music and subtle effects that match the book you’re reading.

Launched about a month and a half ago, it’s already sitting in the Top 100 in Books across a big part of North America, South America, and Europe.

Most of that momentum comes from one founder account.

Jonathan, the founder, started building attention while the app was still in beta. On Dec 27, 2025, he posted a video around the beta opening, showing 12 popular books that already had custom soundscapes inside the app and calling on readers to try it if they were reading one of them.

That video hit 350K views and 11K bookmarks.

Now he’s seeing a second spike.

On Feb 22, 2026, he posted another founder-led video and hit 150K views and 3.2K bookmarks with:

“I’m building an app that plays soundscapes for the book you’re reading”

The playbook is simple and working: founder intro, app intro, quick demo.

TikTok is packed with mental health and AI therapy apps, and most of them follow the same playbook… anything that tells you

exactly

what you need to “change your life.”

It’s what the audience expects, and it’s usually the only format that performs. We’ve seen it with

Juno

, for example, where a simple carousel of advice pulled 1.6M views.

But this new app Innie, only 11 days old, is already positioning itself as an outlier.

Innie is still in its experimentation phase on TikTok.

Across their nine creator accounts, they’re trying to replicate the classic “tips” format.

“small habits = big changes” → 138K views

They’re also testing close‑ups with creators speaking directly to the camera, giving out specific advice.

“This is the advice I would give you if you actually wanted to change your life” → 68K views

But unlike Juno, none of these attempts break past the 200K mark.

Except for one video.

One post stood out with 935 comments, not because it listed habits, but because it framed an actual transformation.

“baddie to baddie, what’s something that’s made your mental health go from “i hate my life” to “i can’t wait for tomorrow”?? i don’t mean taking a walk outside or journaling but something actually REVOLUTIONARY. mine is downloading innie, its like my personal therapist”-> 421.7K views

People shared their experiences in the comments.

“understanding that everything is under Allah’s control so basically there s no need to stress”->83 likes

“law of attraction, romanticizing my life, antidepressants and a hobby. It’s all you need”->306 likes

“took antidepressants and developed a mindset “everything happens for a reason” and repeated that to myself 5739304 times a day”->153 likes

Sometimes it’s the smallest tweak that changes everything.

This shift from generic advice to authentic transformation storytelling unlocked significant organic growth and community building.

A book. A big big book.

This guy was stuck on a Japanese island during COVID and turned a survival guide concept into a $3M Kickstarter and 400K+ copies sold worldwide, allegedly.

It’s a 400+ page, hand illustrated encyclopedia that covers thousands of years of human hacks, growth hacks but in real life.

Since a few months ago, a new strategy has been running with 30+ accounts posting talking videos and linking in their bios, all pointing to a 119 euro hardcover book.

Creators are sharing tips directly from the book, often holding the book with the cover facing the camera so viewers can see it. It feels very natural and integrated into the long format content.

Turbo AI

We keep spotting new accounts, now totaling 250+ accounts.

Useful content first, then Turbo AI is introduced

1.1M views creator opens with:

the fruit-cutting study format

.

then shifts into the study method: watch a YouTube explanation, then take notes with Turbo AI.

Turbo’s scale and with 250+ accounts testing variations, they can keep remixing the same core mechanic across:

talking-head website recommendations

moving-object explainer formats

catchy memorization clips

Ludus is a recent AI language‑learning app, but its growth story doesn’t look like the usual “language app on TikTok” playbook.

Even though the brand has only existed for four months, its TikTok presence has been active for much longer.

They already had a website, and @ottodo_, one of Ludus’ main creators, has been creating content on TikTok since 2024.

His growth didn’t come from the usual language‑learning formats. No lessons, no vocabulary bits, nothing that looks like a traditional language app.

Here’s an example:

“pov: your cousin could win the beabadoobee lookalike contest” → 2.2M views, 544 comments

Otto launched a running series documenting how he’s building the Ludus app, and that is when engagement finally exploded.

“LUDUS EP 02” → 299.8K views, 3,334 comments

People comment on these videos like they’re attending a class.

But this format attracts people who want to build apps, not learn a language, which might explain why downloads haven’t followed yet.

An AI shopping assistant is starting to dominate Indian Instagram with a small but effective creator wave.

Zave is built to help users save money and time while shopping. It launched in 2024, but the real breakout only started in the past month.

They’re running an Instagram-only playbook, and the India angle is the whole story.

The main page has gone viral, and so have three ambassadors. What makes it more interesting is how early these creators are, most of them only have around 10 posts, but they started pulling views almost immediately.

The format is simple and repeatable: shocked reaction first, then app demo.

The main page, @zave.app, has already gone viral more than once by reposting ambassador clips and framing the app with simple “saving hack” hooks.

One example: Saved 5000/- this month using this hack hit 1.4M views and 18K comments.

The ambassadors use the same structure, but with more local and specific hooks. That’s where the content gets stronger.

The biggest hit so far came from @roshniwithai on Feb 19, 2026 with a Zomato-led hook:

Wait who hurt Zomato? → 2.6M views

That works because it instantly anchors the app to a brand people in India already use. It doesn’t feel like a generic “save money” app anymore. It feels like a hack for the exact apps and purchases people already make.

That’s the playbook here: Instagram-first, local references, simple reaction-to-demo structure, and creator hooks that make the savings feel specific instead of abstract.

India is a huge market, and with English hooks, they can reach scale fast without needing a huge content machine.

It is possible for a single creator to drive massive views and meaningful downloads.

article.title: 10 Unhinged TikTok Hacks
article.content:
10 Unhinged TikTok Hacks

Time for another round of TikTok strategy cheatcodes.
