10 Unhinged TikTok Hacks

Time for another round of TikTok strategy cheatcodes.

SGE Team

•

February 19, 2026

•

6 min read

Save for later

If you’ve been following us for a while, you know we publish hundreds of posts every week. So we always keep up with what’s working in TikTok and Reels marketing.

Lately, we’ve found a few new hacks that are already showing strong results.

We’re talking views, engagement bait, comment conversions…and a lot more.

Let’s break them down.

1. TikTok Display Name as CTA

Straight from the e commerce brands playbook, this hack has been growing silently on TikTok lately.

Basically, they change their display name, not their username, to “link in bio.”

When you are scrolling on mobile, it appears in the bottom left corner, similar to an ad call to action but without spending money on it. You can even add an emoji for extra impact.

2. Exhaust Your Views

Too often, apps hit 10 million views with one random video and then switch to a totally different content strategy.

In 2026, we are done with that. If something spikes, double down. Repeat it, all of it.

Most formats can easily become a series. Just add “day X of…” and keep going until the views dry up.

If it cannot be a series, that is fine. Stick to the same format and the same hook. The odds of going viral again are strong enough to test it.

3. Founders, Buy a Camera

Another trend we are seeing more often is founder led content.

That does not mean you need to stop working with creators or spend your whole day chasing perfect lighting.

Think of it as your personal lab. Before you scale a format and hand it off to creators, test it yourself. Doing it for a while is cheaper, but more importantly, it helps you understand what really works so you can guide your creators with much more clarity.

4. Stage a Fake Notification

This hack works in almost any niche, especially when paired with a faceless screenshot format.

You tell a story through text messages and notifications, then subtly slide your app’s notification onto the screen without calling attention to it.

The more unusual or controversial the topic, the better. Big money transfers, messy gossip, exposed Tinder profiles, extreme weight loss wins. You know the drill.

Read exactly how to do it

here

.

6. Localize Your Accounts

There is nothing stopping you from translating your content into other languages and posting it again. Even if your main target is the US, you could be leaving foreign demand on the table.

If you are based outside the US, launch a second account for your home country. If you want to expand, reuse your content, translate it, and publish it.

For many apps right now, some of the top performing creators create content in Spanish, French, or Portuguese.

You can go deeper into this strategy

here

.

7. Highjack Comment Sections

You might have noticed that most apps no longer mention their name directly in the content. Instead, they spark the comments with staged questions and replies, those being the real call-to-action.

Recently, though, something new has been happening.

Competitors are jumping into the comment sections and hijacking them. What used to be space for the creator’s CTA is now free promotion for other apps.

We have seen this a lot on BookTok, where open ended question hooks give competitors the perfect chance to slide in and promote their own agenda.

8. Hack Your Customer’s Mind

There is a lot to unpack when it comes to comment sections and open ended hooks. Many apps are now using them to learn exactly what customers want and what frustrates them about competing products.

Imagine you are building a new book tracker app, like so many founders are right now.

If you post something like, “Book lover to book lover, what finally made you switch from [big competitor] to a new app? For me, it was…”, you will likely unlock a wave of detailed feedback. That kind of insight can completely change how you build and position your product.

9. Anchor Your App to the Market Leader

When in doubt, use the name everyone knows.

For vibe coding, that is ChatGPT.

For visual inspiration, that is Pinterest.

For language learning, that is Duolingo.

And so on.

Dropping a well known name gives your hook instant context and makes it easier to grab attention. And it does not have to feel aggressive. You can frame it softly, like, “I used to use … all the time, but lately I have been wanting something better for …” and let the real call to action unfold in the comments.

10. Leak a discount code

Finally, do not underestimate the classic discount code trick.

It can work for almost any app or product. The key is to avoid sounding promotional. Instead, frame it like, “I probably should not be sharing this, but…”

When it feels like insider information or a hidden opportunity, people are much more likely to act on it.

article.title: When to compete, when not to compete
article.content:
When to compete, when not to compete

Should you enter a channel that’s already crowded?

SGE Team

•

February 18, 2026

•

6 min read

When to compete, when not to compete

Should you enter a channel that’s already crowded?

SGE Team

•

February 18, 2026

•

6 min read

Save for later

I am often surprised by founders who choose to enter channels already crowded with bigger players offering similar apps in the same markets.

Yes, it can work. You can still break through. But it is a much tougher game.

Here is why.

When UGC turns into a scale driven game inside a vertical, the biggest operators gain a major advantage.

They can track everything you do, replicate your formats quickly, and outscale you fast, especially if they have (talented) creators who can execute many different styles.

We have seen this clearly in study apps and language apps.

Apps like

StudyFetch

and others in the space constantly copy each other’s formats and feature formats.

A feature format is a product feature designed mainly to become a viral TikTok or Instagram concept. A good example is

the coughing podcast

format used by StudyFetch or

Studley

.

The power of scale

Scale matters because hooks and formats are hard to protect. If you have more than 100 creators and you actively track every breakout idea in your niche, you can quickly spot what works and replicate it.

At that point, it becomes an execution game. You scale operations and move fast on cloning winning content.

The real advantage of scale, though, is speed of testing.

If you are publishing 200 videos a day, you can dedicate 30 percent to testing and 70 percent to scaling. That gives you 60 daily experiments and 140 videos pushing proven winners. Over time, that compounds.

But scale also creates pressure. If everyone is copying, you end up in a constant race. If you only innovate, your ideas get copied fast. You need both.

Take the crying format we created for

Pingo

. It was copied thousands of times, and we were not even the ones with the highest views.

One single video reached 60 million views. Altogether, the format drove between 3 and 5 billion views, and we captured less than 5 percent of that.

You could say innovation is pointless in that scenario. It is not. Being first still gives you a strong share of the upside, even if you do not own the majority of it.

Pre content market fit

Competing in an already crowded space has one big upside. Content market fit is already there.

You do not need to validate demand from scratch or run heavy traction experiments. The market has already proven it works.

The real edge comes from execution. If you can enter and perform better, you can still win.

The Ick

is a strong example. It joined the Instagram stalking niche after apps like RecentFollow and CheaterBuster had validated it, and still scaled past 200,000 dollars in revenue.

No content market fit (yet)

The highest upside often comes from opening a new vertical and capturing virality first.

But this path is riskier. You need sharper instincts or the patience to test until something clicks.

Look at vibe coding apps such as Lovable, Rork, Vibecode, Anything, and others.

Most of them used similar formats and generic messaging, and very few broke through.

Instead of repeating the same playbook, they could have studied why earlier attempts failed and positioned themselves differently.

Tactical positioning

Tactical positioning is about choosing a smarter battlefield. Instead of competing directly, you pick a different vertical.

If everyone is chasing Gen Z, maybe the better opportunity is with people over 40.

Look at

Noise

versus

Home From College

and other similar apps.

While others focused on Gen Z, Noise built 500 accounts targeting stay at home moms and dominated that demographic.

They won by going where no one else was paying attention.

And if you are based in Germany and the United States market already has 10 clones of your app, maybe the best move is to win on German TikTok first.

When not to join the party

Just as important as knowing when to compete is knowing when not to.

I recently spoke with a language app that targets an older audience and has a more text focused product. They assumed a certain channel would work for them because competitors were performing well there.

But that logic can be misleading. Their product and audience might be better suited to other channels where they already have traction. Sometimes the smarter move is to double down on your strengths instead of following the crowd.

Conclusion

Market research matters because it helps you position yourself for maximum virality and lower acquisition costs.

Before committing fully, take the time to:

Map out the entire landscape, especially competitors using multi account strategies.

Break them down by the audiences they target, including age groups and locations.

Assess how much scale each player has and where their real advantages lie.

Decide carefully whether entering that space makes sense for you.

If you choose to compete, move fast and build enough scale to become a leader.

The gap between acting blindly and acting with clear insight is bigger than most people think.

A hormone wellness app that uses AI to help women understand and support hormonal balance hit $10K MRR in 3 weeks, off a founder-led run on FrenchTok.

Solaia’s core feature is simple. You scan your meal and it tells you whether it supports hormonal balance, plus what foods to prioritize.

The growth is tied to a French creator who already had traction with body transformation updates and quick nutrition recipes. The app just becomes part of the routine, the thing she uses behind the scenes.

On Jan 26, 2026, one day before launch, she mentions Solaia for the first time in an anti-inflammatory recipe post, pulling 362K views on TikTok and 244K on Instagram, with the app credited in the caption.

“Anti-inflammatory recipe that helped me lose 6 kg in 2 months”

A couple days later, on Jan 29, 2026, she runs the same hook again, but this time adds a quick in-video app moment, and the comments change immediately, people start asking for the app name.

That’s the founder-led pattern here.

Winning content → light mention → app on-screen.

Akob Kim is a photographer who promotes his work on TikTok and has found a format that’s consistently pulling views.

He only photographs airplanes, but he found a distinctive way to show it though slideshows.

The first slide is always a photo of him, taken from far away, photographing a plane in the sky.

In big text, you read “what I see”. On top of that same image, a small frame is drawn around the plane, and On top that frame, in smaller text, it says “what I take”.

The next slide reveals the actual photo he took.

From there, the pattern repeats-> always a–b, a–b, a–b

6M views

6.5M views

A format like this can easily translate into photography apps.

This app was released in December 2024, but it didn’t really move until late 2025, when one creator landed the perfect hook for this category.

Certainly is an AI glow-up app built around guided plans to level up your look and confidence. It’s closer to a personal glow-up companion than a standard tracker.

They are running three TikTok accounts (two ambassadors + a main page), but in practice one account does all the work: @lizzieee222.

On Nov 18, 2025, she posted a simple before/after glow-up reveal with this POV line:

“pov: you stopped chasing fine shyt and became the fine shyt”

There’s no demo in the video. The app only shows up in the caption (“…and i did it all with a glow up ai app lmao”), then the comments take over. Someone asks for the name, she replies with it, and the link is already sitting in her bio for anyone who’s sold.

That one post hit 1.2M views and drove ~6K downloads last month, mostly off that single moment.

Peekz Campus: College Advice is a mobile app positioned as an AI‑powered personal assistant for navigating college life.

At a first glance, account @rosie.collegetips seems to stand out with 3.7 million views.

But most of her videos don’t feel completely organic.

“Junior year

House parties

Going to bars

Internship

Building resume

Going abroad

Focused on grades” → 963.2K views

The only exception was one post, a selfie with a hook asking people to share their wildest freshman-year stories.

“I’m bored comment ur most INSANE freshman year story. Not just ‘we got caught by the RAs’ like actually unhinged.”

→ 545.9K views and 1,718 comments.

And that’s what people did — they shared the stories.

But she never returned to that format, no have they seemed to use any of these insights to craft better hooks.

Engagement dropped again, and the app hasn’t seen a lift in downloads ever since.

1. Drop your most unhinged tip

This one is a comment-section printer.

Creators open with “I’m bored” and ask people to drop their most unhinged / life-changing tip then force specificity with:

One hook turns vague replies into actual stories. You could adapt this hook and make the prompt about a pain your app solves.

2. Thanks, just what I needed

Early trend spotted with less than 4K videos on the audio, and small creators are already pulling real numbers.

The prompt is simple: share the final straw that made a bad day worse. That one extra thing that shouldn’t matter… but somehow sends you over the edge.

Format: front-cam clip + on-screen context (“after having a bad day…”) → drop the one detail.

The specificity is what makes it funny (and painfully relatable).

This sound is built for anyone waiting on something that’s starting to feel imaginary.

You just need one unexpected scene-stealer.

SGE Team

2 min read

Save for later

A simple app that counts sushi pieces just hit 100K downloads, powered by a TikTok trend plus creator partnerships.

Sushi Score launched in Feb 2025 and grew without ever needing a big creator army.

The app is now ranking strongly in Food & Drink in Spain and Italy, which makes sense because that’s where the trend has traveled the furthest. The content loop is basically a game you can play at any sushi place.

The format is Expectation vs Reality, but with a twist. At the start of the meal, friends or couples type a prediction into the app for how many sushi pieces they think they’ll eat.

After the meal, they reveal the real number and compare it to the prediction.

Some of the biggest clips don’t even feel like “ads” because they’re framed like normal hangout content.

For example, @martinaabiagi hit ~3.1M views despite having a tiny following.

At the other end, bigger creators like @iindaralopeezz_ have also posted versions, pushing the trend into mainstream reach.

Either way, it worked because it’s a repeatable little game people actually want to record.

The reveal is satisfying, the friend competition is built in, and every person who tries it ends up posting an unpaid ad without even thinking of it that way.

The Ear-Ripping Audio That Drove 124M Views for a Utility App

SGE Team

February 17, 2026

Save for later

A long-running utility app just reignited growth by turning a tiny, gross-but-satisfying problem into a faceless format.

Clear Wave fixes something most people don’t even think about until it happens. Phone speaker sounds muffled, you run a sound sequence, and it pushes out dust or water. The promise is dead simple: speaker in, cleaner sound out.

Across just two accounts on TikTok and Instagram, they’ve generated 124,000,0000 views, and most of the breakout has happened in the last 3 months. The creative is faceless and repetitive in the best way. Same setup, same payoff, same hook that does the stopping: Speaker, cleaner sound.

The videos work because they stack two retention triggers at once. First, a visible “problem” you can’t unsee, dust shaking loose from the speaker. Second, an intentionally annoying, ear-grabbing sound that makes you wait for the moment it “clears.”

They also extend the playbook through paid creator partnerships. Those clips usually run the water-damage storyline, dropped in the sink or toilet, then a quick step-by-step using the app to clear the speaker, ending on the sound change as proof.

It’s a good reminder that even established utility apps can spike again when they find a format that’s instantly legible and repeatable, then run it hard.

A single creator account, @glowyynnn, has driven nearly 82 million views across TikTok and Instagram by repeatedly promoting the same whitening bundle.

The engine isn’t the offer, it’s the visual shock.

The format is consistent. The video opens with teeth stained a dark purple shade that instantly stops the scroll. It looks wrong enough to trigger curiosity and retention. Then they rinse it off and reveal clean white-teeth that explains the product without any explanation.

They also layer in hooks that feel personal and dramatic on purpose, long captions that read like a confession or a warning.

The openers lean on the same emotional tone: POV captions, thank-you callouts, and the gross-out line “sorry if you’re eating dinner”.

It’s classic e-com short-form: a highly visual “problem” in the first second, then the transformation.

A ChatGPT-style Bible companion pulled 20,000 downloads and $7,000 in MRR last month.

Amen, Bible Chat launched about 7 months ago and is now climbing on TikTok with a networked approach. Across 20 accounts, they’re nearing 25M total views, mixing faceless content with a small international UGC wave.

The most interesting choice is localization. Instead of going all-in on English, they lean heavily into Spanish and German, with just enough English to keep the main narrative universal.

Most of the viral reach comes from their faceless “Catholic story” videos. The structure is consistent: a simple AI animation shows someone struggling or depressed, then Jesus appears and hugs them.

The CTA is always last. After the hug payoff, they flash the app icon and a quick “download” prompt.

One example, POV: Jesus, hit ~1.1M views and ~30K bookmarks.

But it’s not just faceless animations. They’re also running UGC in parallel, mostly through Spanish and German creators using the classic shocked-face setup, followed by a quick app demo.

A top Spanish hit from @espspio reached ~1.2M views with the hook:

“POV: you wake up to the best wallpaper every day.”

A top German hit from @amen.app1 reached ~750K views with:

“It took me 19 years to find out that our birthdays are Bible verses.”

The UGC remains very simple on purpose: reaction first, then a quick demo.

If you want the closest comparable playbook in this niche, Creed is the adjacent case worth reading:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/how-this-bible-ai-app-hit-20-in-15-countries

They launched two weeks ago and already hit ~10K downloads.

Wayk is an alarm utility positioned as a harder alternative to the default alarm. Instead of letting you dismiss it, you set a mission you have to complete before the alarm turns off.

So far, the distribution is coming from one TikTok account that reads founder-led.

@marsbarz00 broke out with a simple hook:

“My alarm won’t turn off until I do 15 pushups” hit 1.8M views.

He repeated the same idea with a more gamer-coded variation, swapping TikTok for Clash Royale, and that one still pulled ~300K views.

The playbook is straightforward: one creator, one repeatable skit, one mission that’s instantly legible.

Save for later

Benable is a recommendation app where creators share curated lists of products, places, or services. Before launching the app, the brand operated exclusively through the website.

The first signs of organic traction on TikTok started showing up near the end of 2024.

A creator posted on the @benable_hq account using shot where she talks about the brands associated with the platform.

4.3M views.

A year later, another video went viral, this time with a creator showing how she repurposed clothing into a new piece.

“everyone was asking how I made this skirt” -> 3.2M views

Consistent with what we found for

Codibook

, transformation‑based outfit content tends to outperform other formats.

Despite these spikes, the app currently sits at around 20K downloads.

Probably because on TikTok, their call to action still consistently sends people to the website, not the app.

frameworks.example: Benable's TikTok videos went viral but directed traffic to the website instead of the app, resulting in low app adoption despite high engagement.

metadata.key_principle: High engagement content must be paired with aligned conversion pathways to effectively drive user acquisition.

However, despite this high engagement, the app's downloads remain low (~20K) because the TikTok call to action directs users to the website instead of the app, causing a disconnect between content success and app growth.

Kndrd is a social app built around friendships and finding people to hang out with.

Their main creator is @bella__ventura, and in 2024 she had three clips that broke out.

Two were closeup, but each one was grounded in a different story.

One was about the cost of living in New York.

“I was today years old” → 3.2M views

Another was a retelling of a date she had.

“I think I just met the man that I’m going to marry” → 1.6M views

And the third one, she offered her date up to the audience.

“NYC dating is broken so I decided to go on 50 first dates… If I’m not a match with my date, I’ll share him here and connect the two of you…” → 1.5M views

Since then, the tone of her content has shifted.

And the views went down.

Her recent videos focus on the NYC girls’ club she runs, sharing event updates.

“nyc people listen up !! i started a club to make friends and this is ur invitation. we do weekly dinners, workouts, gallery openings, happy hours etc. if u live in nyc and wanna join us, lmk and i’ll send u the deets!”->1,761

Europe Language Jobs has run 18 local TikTok accounts since 2021, but its real organic growth only came in 2025 when the…

SGE Team

•

February 14, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Europe Language Jobs

has been building a multilingual TikTok presence since 2021.

It’s a job portal specialising in roles for multilingual candidates who want to work across Europe.

18 accounts, one for each market, each speaking directly in the local language.

Spanish

French

Romanian

Polish

English

Hungarian

Dutch

Portuguese

Swedish

Greek

Czech

Finnish

Norwegian

Slovak

Danish

Across these accounts, they’ve tested multiple formats over the years.

The first was faceless content about what not to include on a CV.

“Keywords to avoid using on your CV2” → 1.8M views

But none of these videos were organic on any of the accounts.

The second format showed creators talking about the jobs people can find on the site.

“Tu parles 🇫🇷 ? 📍 À distance”(Do you speak 🇫🇷? 📍 Remote) → 1.5M views

The third highlighted the different nationalities represented in their office.

“TODAS LAS NACIONALIDADES de nuestra oficina” (ALL THE NATIONALITIES in our office)→ 1.3M views

But the strongest performance came later, in 2025, from the main English‑language account, @europelanguagejobs.

That account sticks to one format, showing side-by-side comparisons of how the same sentence sounds across different languages.

And one of those clips ended up outperforming everything else across the entire network.

“Romanian vs Italian Which is better? 🇷🇴” → 2M views

Emy Bff

Emy’s plushie drop series just hit its “final fall.” Their whole premise was dropping the mascot 1mm per new follower until they reach their stated Burj Khalifa height target.

Four days ago, the account crossed 830K followers, and after more than a month of silence, they posted the payoff moment: dropping Emy from a helicopter in Dubai. The “final drop” still pulled

2.8 million views

.

BoldVoice

This week, BoldVoice hit

1.8 million views

with their classic UGC clip: close-up cyring face, emotional delivery and the one hook:

“Why is English so hard?”

A little over a week ago, the same creator also reached

10M views

this time by starting her video with a movie scene clip before cutting to her face.

Doodle Couple

Relationship apps are pushing drama formats right now, and Doodle did exactly that. They lead with a big headline question, add a very specific situation, crying face, then cut to a screen recording of the couple widget with the drama message as proof.

“how does my boyfriend have the WORST timing in the world???”

It pulled

567.8k views

.

Tea Dating

When your app sparks controversy, you run with it. After staying quiet for a while, Tea Dating pulled

1.5 million views

this week with a long-hook story time designed to trigger comments.

“My sister called me crying hysterically because her husband had been cheating for over 11 months. So I did what most good sisters would do & snatched the home wrecker’s fiance of 3 years. I love you sis!! ”

Parrot

Parrot is pushing the

“Spanish is so weird

” hooks across a whole creator network. Same playbook here: logic-error sentences you reread twice, with the CTA hidden inside the hook.

This one pulled

1.2 million views

, over 103k likes and 10k bookmarks:

“no one warns you that once you start actually learning spanish for real… i’ve been practicing on parrot and now i’m yapping to myself in spanish”

Creed

Creed keeps growing by mixing faith content with modern relationship drama.

They’re relying on the creator close-up plus long hook combo — and it’s working.

This one did

1M views

five days ago.

“Okay guys is it bad if when someone asked my bf who he would save first on a sinking boat me or Jesus…”.

Halo AI

Halo AI pulled

222.7k views

with another AI prank setup: generate a realistic tattoo edit, then film the reaction like it’s real.

“pranking my dad i got his face tattooed on my back (he freaks out

😭💀

)”

The product is shown through the prompt on screen:

“can you add my dad’s face as a tattoo on my back make it realistic”

Pure

Pure has been turning dating drama into a repeatable template: POV headlines, chat “receipts”, and the brand slipped in as one line or hashtag.

We just published an article on their strategy, check it out

here

.

This version pulled

1.1M views

with the trending hook:

“Sometimes you just gotta traumatise these men back”

Roamy

Travel apps have been winning with this exact urgency format: a countdown, a panic face, and one hyper-specific trip detail that makes people stop scrolling.

This week, Roamy hit

705K views

on Instagram Reels using the same playbook.

“I’m literally leaving for Rome in 4 DAYS and i see THIS???

😳😭

”

Pixory

Pixory pulled

6.1M views

with a UGC clip, and one hook that frames the problem (camera roll chaos) before the product shows up.

“because i REFUSE to show my future grandkids 87,528 screenshots”

Text Receipts + Clapback have been turning relationship drama into a simple “watch me respond” payoff. Creators screen-record a chat, show a low-effort / disrespectful / manipulative message, then type a reply that mirrors the exact energy back.

How creators and apps are packaging it:

work: reused Pinterest pics, neutral backgrounds, or iMessage-style mockups.

Often captioned with the hook

“ sometimes you just have to traumatize men back”.

We’ve seen

apps like Pure

join in and pulling 7M views.

And creators still getting traction 135.2k views

The AI Grandpa Glow-Up: 70M Views in 5 Days

A breakup-style hook plus an AI glow-up reveal turned five posts into 70M views.

SGE Team

February 13, 2026

2 min read

Save for later

A brand new TikTok account posted its first video five days ago and instantly broke out. In under a week, with only a handful of uploads, it’s already at 70.3M total views from one account.

The format is an ultra-realistic AI body transformation storyline that plays like a grandpa thirst-trap. Every clip opens on a “before” version of the same man, older, overweight, and defeated, paired with a blunt breakup-style line.

Then it cuts straight to the reveal: silver-fox beard, great hair, an unreal physique, and a confident flex.

It’s a full revenge arc in seconds, and the 1st post alone cleared 40M views.

The hooks are basically breakup captions dressed as insults. They’re short, a little cruel, and they set the stakes fast, you’re 64 just gave up, one year can’t change a man, I’m not attracted to you anymore, the divorce effect. You don’t click because you want fitness tips. You click to see if the guy “beats” the line.

This is easy to productize. An AI video tool can live in the bio as the “made with” credit. A fitness app can run the same before/after arc too, but keep a tiny corner overlay on-screen the whole time, workouts completed, calories, weight trend, so the transformation feels earned instead of imaginary.

Six Plus is a dating app built around one premise: height.

The app has been live for 5 months, but the team had been laying the groundwork since the year before.

Out of the four accounts they run, one creator consistently gets the strongest performance-> @brooke.dates.

Her clips carry unusually high engagement, especially the ones where she measures her male friends on camera.

“Even your male friends lie about their height” → 95.6K views, 1,445 comments

The comment section turns into a height confession booth. People share how tall they are, how tall they wish they were, or argue about what “counts” as tall.

Another format pushed it even further: one framed as a joke about what men supposedly lack, bringing over 10.2K comments on its own.

“No man has all 5:

A job

A dad

Education

Cooking skills

A height above 6ft” → 844.5K views

Across their table of results, the pattern is clear.

The videos built around height measurement and height‑based lists consistently pull higher views and higher ER% than anything else in the ecosystem.

TikTok’s Obsession = Untapped MRR

January was the month for BookTok apps, and we’re breaking it all down.

TikTok’s Obsession = Untapped MRR

January was the month for BookTok apps, and we’re breaking it all down.

SGE Team

•

February 12, 2026

•

5 min read

Save for later

There’s a niche that’s been taking off since the beginning of 2026. It’s not brand new in the world of consumer apps, but it did stay quiet for a while.

Now, thanks to TikTok making it trendy, the App Store is flooding with new apps in this space.

Can you guess what it is?

Let’s break down the latest developments in the BookTok and book apps space.

The BookTok Giants

It started with three.

Goodreads, one of the first big book tracking apps, launched back in 2010 (yep, that’s 16 years ago, probably older than some of you). Today, it holds a solid spot at #5 in the Books category on the US App Store and brings in about 700,000 new downloads each month.

Fable launched in 2021 and is currently sitting at #10 in the Books category on the US App Store. Just last month, it brought in 300,000 new downloads and made $200,000 from in-app purchases.

Storygraph, also released in 2021, now sitting a bit below, at #20 in the same category, pulling 200,000 downloads a month and over $50,000 in monthly revenue (in-app only).

At the core, these apps do the same thing: they help people track what they’ve read, write reviews, and get fun insights into their reading habits, pace, and preferences.

But in the last few years, the whole industry took a turn:

The rise of BookTok changed a few things:

A huge boost in sales,

with an average 600% increase

when a book is featured in a viral video.

Reading became cool again for a wider crowd.

New genres took off, and both well-known and new authors rushed to grow their online presence and connect with readers.

People start sharing their reading habits and tracking progress, turning a hobby into something more structured (and that you can brag about).

Ratings, reviews, and recommendations matter more than ever.

All of this opened the door for new players, while the older ones had to double down on distribution or risk losing the spotlight they’d held for years.

The Newcomers

Booktok

Yeah, there’s an app called

Booktok

. And it’s not just another book tracking app.

It turns out, unsurprisingly, that so many books are popular now that people want to know the stories without actually reading them.

This app, launched in November 2024, lets users “watch books explained” by turning books into AI-generated animations. It’s bringing in $60,000 a month.

On TikTok, they rely fully on one account: @clarawithbooktok. That account pulled in 52 million views with just a few videos, mostly user reaction clips.

One video hit 30 million views, yet not entirely organic. They stopped posting around the end of summer 2025.

You can read the full story

here

.

Margins

Margins

launched at the same time as Booktok — and yes, it is another book tracker app, but with a few added features like “search books by vibe” and a tool to “block social media while reading.”

They’re seeing 200,000 downloads a month and pulling in $6,000 in monthly recurring revenue. Last month, they pushed hard on distribution and are now in the top 100 apps across most countries.

Their network spans across 20 creator accounts, but one has been leading, with 1.6M views recently, @jenna.thomas3.

The flipside is that, despite getting extremely high engagement, these open hooks create the perfect stage for competitors to hijack the comments and promote their own tools. That’s exactly what happened to her biggest hit.

You can read the full story

here

.

Bookology

Bookology was released just seven months ago and has been hovering around #60 on the App Store. It’s another book tracking app, currently generating $7,000 in monthly recurring revenue.

They’ve gone fully faceless, and it’s working well. Their branded account drives the entire strategy using faceless phone app demos.

The standout feature is the ability to create a virtual TBR (To Be Read) shelf, in true BookTok style. It’s highly visual and distinct, so they don’t need much more than a strong hook and a well-made recording.

So far, this account has collected 2.1M views and engagement keeps rising.

You can read the full story

here

.

Meanwhile, big players like Fable have started moving too. They’ve teamed up with BookTok creators and tested out a few content formats themselves.

We broke it all down in a piece

, including which formats helped them score 23 million views since the end of last year.

We’re expecting a lot more new players to jump into this space, and plenty of clever hacks and micro-strategies from the big names already in the game.

Stay tuned.

What happened to the sweet mascot that has been dropped from the Burj Khalifa?

Emy’s Drop Series Reaches 112.5M Views

What happened to the sweet mascot that has been dropped from the Burj Khalifa?

SGE Team

•

February 12, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Two months ago,

EmyBFF started a stunt series

where they drop their plushie mascot from crazy heights.

The premise:

“Dropping Emy 1mm for every new follower until we reach the Burj Khalifa.”

No product pitch. No app demo. Just an objective viewers can track and influence. It became their main distribution channel.

4 days ago, the account crossed 830K followers (their stated Burj Khalifa height target), and they shipped the “final” moment: dropping Emy from an helicopter in Dubai.

That payoff video did 2.5M views after more than month of no posting.

They took this opportunity to launch their new goal

“100k likes on this comment and we’ll take Emy to space.”

That comment is currently at 14,000 likes.

They also ran this series on TikTok under a separate account; same concept but it stalled early with their last post post being Day 5 (Nov 26) with 1M total views across 5 videos.

As of today, @

emyadventure1

is sitting at:

1M followers

112.5M total views

7 posts total

First post went live ~2 months ago

New objective: Space (they’re framing it as “followers left until dropping Emy from space”  now 237,837 left, implying a 1,237,837 follower target)

This is currently their only account actively posting the series. No new parallel accounts pushing the same format right now.

Right now, the app is posting though only one account

.

On TikTok, they haven’t posted since the end of November, and there haven’t been any new TikTok accounts pushing the format either.

No change in their download and revenues for now:

We’ll keep you updated.

Summary AI is an AI meeting note taker that records audio, turns it into a transcript/summary.

In the last month, they pulled 19.4M views, with a few videos carrying most of the volume.

A few posts look boosted, but we also found clips that drove organic engagement. The insight stays the same: they lead with attention (corporate meeting drama) and slip the product in as the “receipts” using Summary’s transcript as proof mid-argument.

Creators film a fake “meeting” and stage corporate work drama (PTO gets revoked, a manager switches up, HR “changes the rules,” etc.)

There’s usually an iPad in the frame recording the “meeting,” and the creator uses it as the proof mid-argument:

“I have Summary up here’s the transcript from our last meeting.”

A few videos that did well with strong engagement:

14.6M views

And more recent ones from

@wfhgirl4

and

@burnout.lazy.girl

2.2M views

It’s a good format to attract comments. People share their own work experiences and even the ones that know it’s staged, a comment is a comment.

They have a second format that’s more “chaotic workplace POV”.

A creator sets up the scene like: “corporate hack!!” then does something ridiculous (smearing food on her camera) sticks the phone up with Summary running, and walks off to the couch like “I’m done”.

Again, the content holds attention first, and the product is just sitting there as the tool in the moment.

These posts look a bit boosted sometimes, but there is real engagement that proves the format can work organically too.

3.1M views

Here you can find their best hooks they’re repeating that you can adapt:

Pure is an anonymous dating app positioned around honest intentions and clear boundaries.

In the last 30 days, they pulled 56.7 million views while running just under 30 accounts.

Their accounts use the same naming pattern (“datingwith___”) and post relationship content using faceless visuals, Pinterest-style images and movie extraits. The story line is carried by the POV hook + text receipts, not the creator.

The video usually opens with a familiar dating situation (“love bombing,” “mixed signals,” “cheating-adjacent”), then the creator drops the receipts as a chat screenshot.

They sneak in a CTA in a line (“I should’ve been on Pure”) or via the hashtag, so the brand is present without taking over the narrative.

Another version from

A newcomer screen-time app is climbing in the U.S. after a split-screen skit made Apple’s built-in limits look easy to bypass.

Useless is a screen-time control app built around a different idea: to keep scrolling, you have to ask a friend for permission.

Five days ago, they hit 1.9 million views with a split-screen skit: two guys, different screen time. One side shows the “Apple Screen Time” user still clocking 10 hours. The other shows the app user at ~1 hour.

Then, the Apple guy gets blocked and just taps the built-in Ignore button, so nothing changes. The other guy can’t bypass it. If he wants more time, he has to text a friend for permission inside the app.

Same problem, two outcomes. The difference between them is the app.

A small creator may have stumbled into a sticky format.

Cassandra Lovin has around 4,000 followers, but she hit 1.8M views in 18 hours with a simple setup that turns the comments into participation.

On February 10, she posted a car selfie with the hook:

“I’m going to confess to my secret crush tonight.”

The clip climbed to 2 million views and over 10,000 saves.

Then she sets up three outcomes using profile-picture scenarios: my pfp if he says yes, my pfp if he says no, my pfp if I chicken out.

The real trick is the follow-through. People comment, wait, then click her profile to check the profile picture for the “answer.”

Once it changes, the comments flip into congratulations because the story resolves off-video, but the result is still on her profile.

This wasn’t made to sell an app, but it adapts cleanly. The profile picture is the trigger.

The proof should live somewhere readable, like a quick shot of a blurred in-app message thread or a simple “receipt” overlay showing sent, seen, and reply.

article.title: Ditch Your Product, It’s Time For a Viral Collapse
article.content:
Ditch Your Product, It’s Time For a Viral Collapse

Creators aren’t selling products anymore they’re selling drama that makes the product inevitable.

SGE Team

•

February 11, 2026

•

4 min read

Ditch Your Product, It’s Time For a Viral Collapse

Creators aren’t selling products anymore they’re selling drama that makes the product inevitable.

SGE Team

•

February 11, 2026

•

4 min read

Save for later

On TikTok, apps and tools are hardly being pushed head‑on anymore. Lately, we’ve been seeing more and more brands build small, emotional narratives that call for an urgent fix. That opportunity becomes their sales window.

In moments of great tension, FOMO and stress, people don’t think. They are less likely to compare your product to other options, question the price, or go read every single review.

That is why selling on TikTok and Reels today often starts with creating a situation where the consumer feels your product is the only escape.

Below are four types of situations you can recreate to trigger this dramatic effect. What works will differ by use case, so it is up to you to find the sweet spot for your brand. Either way, the underlying mechanisms still apply.

1. The Advantage Glitch

Hook:

“bro why is europe so affordable??”

Views: 3.6M

A €17 flight is enough to stop anyone scrolling. It’s not just because it’s cheap, but it goes beyond that. It feels like a mistake anyone should be taking advantage of.

That “this can’t be right” moment is what drives retention. The app does not need much explanation or any pricing defense.

When the deal can sell out, it works even better. There is a rush attached to it. Users move fast to grab it before others do, and that urgency is what makes this hack work.

2. Community Callout

Hook: “book girlies what book tracking app are we using in 2026 because goodreads is not it for me anymore”

Views: 1.5M

Instead of presenting it as a personal problem, the creator talks as if everyone is looking for a new app together.

This turns a basic complaint into a shared decision. It creates the illusion that the whole community is already moving on, and anyone still using the old app is being left behind.

That feeling alone can be more powerful than any free plan or standout feature, especially for apps that depend on scale to stay relevant, like this one.

3. Systemic Injustice

Hook: “Day was going fine until I got the email saying I didn’t get the KFC job… with a 3.8 GPA and a masters degree… This market is unreal”

Views: 9.7M

The story centers on a mismatch: strong qualifications and a basic job rejection. That contrast hooks viewers because it feels unfair in a way everyone recognizes and relates to.

That shared frustration pulls people together to look for a fix.

In the comments, someone suggests a site that applies to hundreds of jobs automatically, and the creator pins it. The comment racks up thousands of likes and becomes the call to action. The video captures attention, and the pinned comment converts it.

4. Corporate Drama

Hook: “HR said ‘use your sick days when you need them.’ I called out sick with the flu on Friday. my manager replied ‘convenient day to be sick’ and cc’d leadership. I felt embarrassed. I read the employee handbook in the Playbacks app. It says ‘no proof required for one day.’ They treat us like we’re lying children”

Views: 1.6M

Longer stories like this tend to boost watch time because people want to stay until the gossip plays out. Short horror stories about abusive bosses, in particular, have become so relatable that they work perfectly as entry points for apps to introduce their product.

The app shows up close to the end, with no heavy push. It is mentioned casually as something she used during her struggle, and it quietly becomes the “hero” of the plot.

The story gives just enough context to attract the right audience, while staying vague enough to spark curiosity about the app that was named.

It may look different on the surface, but all of these examples follow the same core principle.

A strong feeling is triggered at the start.

The problem is shown quickly.

The product enters quietly when it fits and blends with the story.

The comments push viewers into users.

You use drama as the engine, and your product as the relief.

frameworks.name: Viral Collapse Framework
frameworks.description: Create a dramatic narrative that triggers a strong emotional response, presenting a problem or tension that makes the product feel like the inevitable solution. The product is introduced subtly as the relief, not the main focus, and community engagement (especially comments) is leveraged to convert viewers into users.
frameworks.when_to_use: When launching or promoting consumer apps on short-form video platforms like TikTok or Instagram Reels, especially when direct product pitches are less effective and emotional engagement drives virality.
frameworks.example: A TikTok video telling a relatable story about workplace injustice, ending with a casual mention of an app that helped the creator, with a pinned comment linking to the app, driving millions of views and conversions.

metadata.key_principle: Use emotional, relatable drama to create urgency and FOMO, making the product feel like the only escape, and leverage community engagement to convert viewers into users.
metadata.article_summary: The article explains a shift in TikTok and Reels marketing where creators no longer push products directly but instead build emotional, dramatic narratives that create urgency and FOMO. Four types of viral situations are outlined: Advantage Glitch, Community Callout, Systemic Injustice, and Corporate Drama. Each triggers strong feelings and presents the product as a subtle solution, with community comments driving conversions. This approach leverages emotional storytelling and social proof to drive organic growth and user acquisition.

article.content:

How does a newcomer hit $20K MRR with only 3.2M views?

Slideshow Goes Viral Three Times and Builds a $20K MRR Newcomer

How does a newcomer hit $20K MRR with only 3.2M views?

SGE Team

•

February 11, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

An app that records driving trips and speed is climbing fast.

Released about one month ago, Speed Tracker is already at 60K downloads and $20K MRR.

They’re running this with a faceless network of 13 accounts, and the whole story fits inside a surprisingly small view count: ~3.2M total views so far. What matters is how concentrated that reach was.

Around 90% of the views came in a single day, when the exact same slideshow popped off three different times across three accounts. The title is the hook: How me and bro feel when we drive together.

The actual slideshow is quite simple. The cover shows two airships that look like they’re moving ridiculously fast, which instantly sells the feeling.

Then the final slide lands the prompt: two high-end cars labeled bro and me, with a Speed Tracker app screenshot above them comparing speeds.

It’s basically a friend competition packaged as a shareable joke.

That’s why it converts. It’s not really selling trip tracking. It’s selling a moment you want to recreate with a friend. The comments reflect that too, with people asking for the app name, and the slideshow pulling an unusually high ~15% engagement rate.

frameworks.example: Speed Tracker used a slideshow titled 'How me and bro feel when we drive together' with visuals of fast-moving airships and cars, culminating in a friendly competition prompt featuring their app, driving 3 viral spikes and 15% engagement.

metadata.key_principle: Focus on selling the emotional or social moment users want to experience, not just the product features, to drive shareability and conversion.

The slideshow used a relatable friend competition theme, high-engagement visuals, and a compelling hook title, resulting in ~15% engagement and strong conversion from views to installs.

Many artists grow through TikTok, and @kurttheviolinist, a violinist that plays contemporary music, is one of them.

He’s already at 1.4M followers.

Meanwhile, Tonic Music, a practice‑training app for musicians, saw the opportunity to connect their distribution to his social media success.

But he’s not the only face of the program.

Tonic is now working with two artist accounts-> @kurttheviolinist, and @raychenviolin, a Taiwanese‑Australian violinist with international recognition.

The contrast is clear.

Kurt posts are pure performance.

Ray shows the app in action how he practices, directly linking it to his daily routines.

Despite the star power, the views aren’t translating into downloads, at least not lately. It remains unclear whether the recent push in content toward the end of last year has yielded any significant return.

Alternatively, they could have taken a more “language learning” approach by onboarding creators who are also music beginners and who share their journey and practice streaks through the app (at a fraction of the cost).

We’ll keep an eye on them.

Despite millions of followers and views, the strategy has not clearly translated into app downloads, suggesting a gap between content virality and conversion. An alternative approach could involve onboarding beginner musicians sharing their learning journeys to foster relatable UGC and potentially better conversion at lower cost.

When it launched on TikTok, it skipped the usual productivity tips and tapped straight into the new Gen Z most aspirational trend: financial freedom and burnout relief.

Most of their videos start off with the same hook.

They reference a “faceless Pinterest page” to sell the idea of easy, anonymous income and frame regular jobs as a waste of potential.

PurpleWrite

is just another online tool that “humanizes” AI‑generated text. In one of the most crowded markets right now, they have managed to quietly start building a French content empire on TikTok.

The team has been active on TikTok since June 2025. With just three accounts, it has already pulled 57.2M views.

One account alone is responsible for 42.4M views.

The breakout came from a single format: the same old “Mad Sora Professor”, but this time in French.

““My teacher caught some students using ChatGPT again 😫😫” → 25.9M views

The formula works in any language, and like we predicted

earlier

, it’s official: this format works on any account (for now).

The top six videos follow this exact structure, all variations of the same classroom‑panic setup.

But the team is testing new angles.

“Mon copain est en train d’écrira son partiel. Pas de notes. Pas d’écouteurs. Pas de ChatGPT. Pas de musique. Pas de PurpleWrite.com. Juste lui et ses propres pensées. Il affronte la fac en mode brut, comme un vrai psychopathe.”

Translates to:

“My boyfriend is writing his midterms. No notes. No headphones. No ChatGPT. No music. No PurpleWrite.com. Just him and his own thoughts. He’s raw‑dogging college like a total psychopath.”

The video pulled 980.6k views.

They’ve also tested copying their competitor Real‑Write’s signature format, which you can read about

here

.

The format goes like this:

Creator at the computer

Countdown‑style hook

Upbeat track

Essay typed at 2× speed

Paste into PurpleWrite

Final reveal

“POV: tu as une dissertation à rendre à 23h59 et il est 23h54”

Translating to:

“POV: you have an essay due at 11:59 PM and it’s 11:54 PM” → 969.5K views

The app lets users simulate different wraps, paint, and style changes on cars. It was launched 9 months ago and it’s now sitting at #91 in Graphics and Design category.

The distribution is intentionally faceless and multi-account. They’ve run 7 accounts total, and 3 of them have broken past 1M+ views. In total they’ve driven ~20M views, with a meaningful chunk still coming from paid distribution.

It all comes down to two repeatable story formats: wrap reveals and dream-car pranks.

On May 15, 2025, they pushed their biggest hit with a wrapping hook:

“Wrapping the Stradman’s Nissan GTR.”

Stradman

is a major car creator, so the name does a lot of the initial pull.

The second format is the dream car prank.

“Pranking my buddy by finding his dream car”

hit ~1.6M on Instagram and ~800K on TikTok.

It’s framed as a friend prank, but it’s a demo in disguise. They name the buddy’s dream car, simulate the build in-app, then hold the reveal for the reaction.

1. Plan A vs Plan B

This one keeps is a classic two picture slideshow that basically sums up the two paths you can choose in life.

In this trend, people have two doors:

Plan A = the socially approved path.

Plan B = the one you actually daydream about when you’re procrastinating.

And because it’s text + two clips, it scales across every niche: travel, relationships, career, wellness, soft-life delusion… you name it.

Biggest hit this week: 7.5M views.

7.3M views

4M views

Read the full article

here

.

2. Don’t screw me over

Another Euphoria audio has been trending this week and it’s not a subtle message.

Creators use it as a punchline for the exact moment someone starts soft-launching an excuse in the group chat “I’m tired,” the friend “might be late,” the situationship switching up, the plan about to collapse.

The best versions are face close-ups to show the moment you start to notice the betrayal.

3.1M views

See more examples

here

.

3. You can learn character from a childhood photo

This trend is a personality test disguised as a wholesome post.

Step 1: show your face now with the hook: “You can learn a girl’s character from a childhood photo”

Step 2: drop one childhood photo that explains everything.

It works because everyone loves a throwback, and the comments write themselves:

“oh you were DEFINITELY the problem” / “wait this is so me” / “that photo explains your whole aura.”

2.1M views

See more examples

here

.

4. The Red Flag Test

This is basically a prank disguised as a dating question.

One person reads out a list of “is this a red flag or green flag?” traits like it’s about some random crush… while the person next to them thinks they’re judging hypotheticals.

But halfway through, they realize the list is describing them. So the video becomes a live reaction test.

The setup looks something like this:

“I’m gonna ask my dad / boyfriend / friend if these are red flags or green flags.”

Then you hit them with oddly specific traits:

“He’s always 10 minutes early.”

“He disappears to ‘work’ at 9pm.”

9.2M views

And when legends of cinema join in you know it’s worth watching

Read the full article

here

.

5. Show your iPhone Notes

This format is popping because it turns private thoughts into content without filming anything new.

It’s a screen recording of your Notes app, but the energy is: this should’ve stayed between me and my phone.

Unhinged drafts, delulu lists, situationship math, “things I should not text,” and the occasional calm reminder like:

“drink water” sandwiched between emotional warfare.

Biggest hits right now:

7.8M views

Bonus: the sound itself is doing 10.5M views, so even low-effort formats get carried:

Read the full article

here.

Most EdTech startups start working with large-scale UGC networks straight away, but this one chose a different path and put the founders on camera instead.

King of the Curve is an MCAT prep app for iPhone and iPad built by three med‑school students with real exam experience.

The official account is managed by two of the founders, and their strategy splits into two roles.

William Kelly had the biggest hits.

His videos usually open with a close‑up and a hook about building an app to make studying easier, followed by a quick product reveal.

“just bc you think studying sucks doesn’t mean you can build an app to make it fun” → 19.1M views

However, his videos aren’t fully organic.

yeah so I actually built an app that’s helped over 10,000 students get into medical school” → 9.6M views

Heath Rutledge‑Jukes took the opposite route.

He posted two videos using the same hook, one in 2024 and another in 2025.

Both were fully organic and both strong performers.

“Brown University came out with a study showing that the Flynn effect is no longer a thing | Gen Alpha dropped the ball (and their IQ) | This means Gen Z is the smartest gen of all time.”

2024-> 7.4M views & 9.4k comments

2025-> 2.8M views & 4.1k comments

Despite the visibility, the app launched in 2020 and downloads remain low.

Oasis is running fewer accounts than most health apps.  But the formats that they use are working.

In the last 30 days, they pulled 15M views mostly coming from two accounts.

One format is doing a lot of the work: “grocery aisle hook → Oasis score screenshot.”

A creator films water/food shelves with a scary one-liner (“this is why we’re sick”), then cuts to the app result screen. It hit 4M views with comments that add another chance for a CTA (“ok so what’s the best water?”).

But other than that, they’re not relying on a huge UGC army. Their two strongest accounts are basically their “main” pages, and they use them differently depending on the platform.

Instagram Reels: statement hook → explanation → app result

On Reels, the videos usually start with one warning statement about the food/product that makes you pause. Then the creator explains the point while showing the product in use, and the video ends on the Oasis score / result screen.

The app screen is the CTA.

One example pulled 621K views.

On TikTok, slideshows are doing the heavy lifting (it’s also their second best-performing account format). It’s basically rating products from worst to best, while using the app score. This format is good to print saves and shares when the topic hits.

Each slide is its own retention beat: (claim → product → why it matters → score → next).

And they’ve started expanding to more than just

food and water bottles.

Example: “9 out of 10 toothpastes tested positive for lead in US”

841k views

A faceless AI interior design newcomer hit ~9M views by repeating the same small-space question and letting the comments pick the best makeover.

House AI is a newcomer AI home decor and room planner that launched in December 2025. It generates interior design concepts and layouts from a room photo, aimed at quick inspiration.

They’re running one TikTok and one Instagram page, both faceless, and they’re not experimenting much. They found one repeatable strategy and stuck to it.

Every post is the same slideshow formula.

First slide is the empty room, usually a small, awkward space.

Then each slide is a different AI makeover theme for that exact room, like cozy TV nook, modern office, reading corner, minimal Japandi, and so on.

Same hook every time:

What should I do with this little space?”

This isn’t a new playbook. It’s basically a small-space remix of the same faceless room-makeover strategy that scaled to ~97M views with Room Genius.

If you want the “extended version” of this pattern, that earlier breakdown is worth a read. Same idea, just turned up to 100M:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/ai-interior-designer-verges-on-100m-views-with-faceless-strategy

article.content:

The Fake Tinder Chat Format Behind a $10K MRR AI Keyboard

Why did staged Tinder convos outperform “real” creator UGC for this AI keyboard?

SGE Team

•

February 10, 2026

2 min read

Save for later

An AI “rizz keyboard” launched in January 2025 just did ~$10K MRR last month, and the growth isn’t coming from polished UGC.

It’s coming from faceless Tinder/Hinge conversation loops on their main page.

SmoothSpeak is an AI rizz keyboard built for dating apps. The core promise is simple: you’re mid-conversation on Tinder or Hinge, you hit a wall, and the keyboard feeds you a line that keeps the thread alive.

They tried the “normal UGC” route first, but it didn’t land. From August to October 2025, they had a few ambassadors posting daily videos, and views barely moved.

There was an awkward mismatch in their format, that typically hooks like “In a room full of people I would never dry text you” and then pitching an AI rizz keyboard.

The real use case is helping guys message girls, and polished creator UGC doesn’t read authentic in that context. That flop is what pushed them toward what actually works here: faceless dating content where the punchline is the line.

It’s staged, but the format still sells the outcome.

Match → Conversation → App line → Number.

This faceless loop became the primary acquisition channel behind the ~$10K MRR month, not the UGC wave.

It’s basically a Plug AI-type product in the AI dating assistant niche we’ve covered before.

If you want more tactics from this category, that playbook is worth revisiting:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/100k-mrr-from-minecraft-b-roll-and-text-messages

They pivoted to faceless staged Tinder/Hinge chat loops that authentically demonstrated the product's value in context, resulting in ~$10K MRR. This format sells the outcome by showing a conversation flow, which resonated better with the audience and became the primary acquisition channel.

Professor Curious, formerly known as ZuAI, helps students learn and solve schoolwork with AI.

The app didn’t begin posting consistently until August 2025.

Since then, three videos have clearly outperformed the rest, each with a different format.

#1 – Close‑up shock reaction

A classic TikTok reaction format.

“1000 years of struggling with math and I found out about this today” → 1.2M views

#2 – Headshot + real‑life action

The creator cuts an apple while explaining the benefits of the app, then shows the interface.

1.3M views

However, none of these videos appear to be organic.

#3 – The first truly organic moment

“POV: APUSH DBQ documents in 50 years” → 1.8M views

This is the first video that feels native to student culture. It jokes about the idea that today’s memes and influencers will become “serious historical documents” for future exams.

The post generated 1,076 comments, none of which relate to the app.

Quick context:

APUSH = AP U.S. History (a college‑level high school course)

DBQ = Document‑Based Question (students write an essay analyzing historical documents)

This “red flag / green flag” format is basically a sneaky personality test.

One person reads a list of traits on camera like it’s about a random crush or “the guy I’m talking to.” But the twist is the person sitting next to them is the one being described… and they don’t realize it at first.

So the video becomes a live reaction test.

They set it up with a simple line: “I’m gonna ask my dad/boyfriend/friend if these are red flags or green flags.”

Then they start listing a bunch of very specific things:

“He’s always 10 minutes early.”

“He disappears to ‘work’ at 9pm.”

“He’s obsessed with the gym.”

The other person answers “green” or “red” for each one, thinking it’s hypothetical.

Halfway through, they clock it’s literally them. That’s the payoff moment.

8.9M views

2.2M views

You know the trend is working when legends like Mr. Scorsese join in

1.7M views

An AI study tool is starting to lift on SpanishTok through two channels: a face-to-camera UGC wave, and a parallel faceless wave.

The surprise is that the faceless study tips pages are outperforming the face creators.

StudyOS is an AI study tool released ~7 months ago. Its standout feature is turning uploaded files into flashcards.

It’s now starting to pick up momentum on SpanishTok via a multi-account UGC wave, with 14 TikTok accounts totaling ~25M views.

The two biggest accounts aren’t “study creators” promoting a tool directly.

They’re faceless studytips pages that already have stacked ~9M and ~7M views.

@olivia.studytips hit 2.5M views with a study-methods slideshow: Study methods that will make you the best in the class.

Each slideshow has a specific study method recommendation for a given issue. After trust is built and the slideshow is perceived as authentic, the app promo slide comes:

“Need to study fast and effectively? Use StudyOS.”

@ines.tipsestudio hit 1.8M views with a ranking-style slideshow: Ranking the AIs I used to study

The promo is hidden inside the ranking. She rates ChatGPT 5/10 and StudyOS 100/10, making the install feel like the obvious upgrade.

Face creators are going viral mostly through relatable study-struggle clips, with the product only mentioned in captions.

The installs come from the faceless slideshow pages, which are built to convert.

SGE Team

We last wrote about

Parrot

when it positioned itself as a go-to alternative for anyone checking out language-learning apps, alongside

Pingo AI

and

Airlearn

.

They were running 37 accounts mixing “Spanish” skits, Duolingo shade, and Bad Bunny buzz.

In the last 30 days, Parrot pulled 6.4M views, with most of it coming in the last week.

You can literally see it in the chart: it stays relatively flat, then spikes hard at the end of the window. Which is usually what happens when one format starts working and the whole network copies it.

The biggest post in this wave hit 833.6k views using the classic UGC style: close-up creator plus a long on-screen hook.

“learning spanish is so weird because wdym that to me ‘gracias’ means ‘thank you’ but to a spanish speaker ‘thank you’ means ‘gracias’”

A similar version pulled in 498.8k views two days ago:

“Spanish learners when they realize the word ‘bother’ in Spanish is one of the most offensive acts to exist in English”

For both videos, the CTA is in the caption: “like just a random thought i had while doing my lessons on parrot”.

And the hooks are clearly designed to confuse people on purpose. They’re written like logic errors the kind of sentence you have to reread twice

Some versions push it even harder by putting the CTA directly in the hook, like this one that pulled 317.5k views:

“i’m so jealous of people whose parents spoke to them in two languages… meanwhile i’m fighting for my life on parrot”

They’re finding repeatables format that any creator can run, then scaling it across faces until the algorithm can’t ignore it.

Note: most of their videos are using bad bunny tracks is a smart move considering he just own a grammy.

Studley AI: Notes & Flashcards is one of the big players in StudyTok.

They keep shipping new formats, and they’re especially good at making marketing content that doesn’t read like marketing.

They never lead with the app.

They start with a situation that feels more natural: a grade, a deadline, a roommate “secret,” a small panic moment. Then once you’re hooked, they switch to showing the product.

In the last 30 days they pulled 17.8M views.

One of their best-performing angles right now is surprisingly fully faceless.

The video starts by showing a good grade as visual hook. You don’t see the creator’s face. It’s just the paper and the score, with on-screen text that frames it like a personal win:

“MOM my phone is literally SAVING my grades!!”

Right after that, it jumps into a screen recording of Studley AI: Notes & Flashcards.

Same flow every time: quiz / answer choices / right vs wrong / “Correct answer explained.”

2.3M views posted 5 days ago

And it’s not just one post. That same creator account is the 5th best performer in the network with 7.5M views while staying completely faceless.

They’re also pulling views with talking videos that look like a standard “study tips ad” in the first seconds.

They start with a story time usually with a situation hook tied to a roommate or school stress.  Then, the frame switches into the same payoff: the “secret” reveal, plus the app screen recording. That pivot is doing the work. It keeps the video from feeling like a straight sponsor read, but still lands on the demo.

476.6k views

Catlangu started as a language exchange website that learned how to go semi-viral on Instagram. About a month ago, it finally turned into an app.

The interesting part isn’t that the app launch exploded (it didn’t), but the distribution engine that was built earlier on Instagram, when Catlangu was still pushing the website.

They ran a single-account strategy with 100 videos totaling ~2.4M views, and  all of the meaningful activity happened months before the app launch.

The videos are intentionally simple: a clip of someone doing a shocked/relieved reaction face, followed by a quick product demo.

Example: “2 years of learning a new language and now you found this” hit 840K views (July 5, 2025).

The hooks barely change. It’s always the “years of studying, then the same found this” punchline.

What’s valuable here is the scrappiness.

Not the highest-quality content, but the strategy is proven, and that’s why it still worked.

Deepsearch Converts 84M Views Into 900k Downloads

A background‑check app turned TikTok cheating stories into 84M views and 900K downloads all in a matter of months.

SGE Team

•

February 7, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

It took only a few months for Deepsearch AI to blow up on TikTok.

The app lets you pull public information about people using only a name or username.

In 10 months, it is now at:

#49 overall in the app rankings

Top 10 in multiple countries:

#6 Italy

#2 Switzerland

#20 Thailand

#10 Austria

#11 Philippines

#15 Pakistan

#11 Costa Rica

#13 Panama

#20 Paraguay

#14 El Salvador

All while pulling $700K/month in revenue and over 900,000 monthly downloads.

Across 5 creator accounts, the format has already generated 84.6M views.

Every viral video follows the same structure:

A creator in a tight close‑up, implying they’re about to expose a cheating partner using “something.”

“There’s no way this man doesn’t have a gf…” → 15.1M views

“Everything I signed my gf up for when I found out she cheated” → 4M views

The app is never directly mentioned.

Only the official account

@deepsearchapp

names the product and those videos feel much less organic.

“I searched my bf’s name in DeepSearch, and since his results were SO clean, I said yes to him.” → 6.6M views

The growth curve rises sharply, with he second most‑viewed video being posted just one week ago and hitting 7.7M views:

“Told my husband I was having a sleepover at my friend’s but stayed home to see who he comes home with.” → 7.7M views

Check out here the hooks with the most views and highest ER%.

In the last week alone, @aliradfordd pulled 8.3M views with basically one setup that he repeats with slight tweaks.

The biggest clip hit 6M views, one where he stands on camera holding a stack of books, but you never see what the books are.

Instead, the on-screen text labels the stack like a checklist of the kind of Enemies to Lovers he likes :“she falls first” / “he falls harder” / “YEARNING” / “angry love confession” etc.

There’s no real CTA in the video but there is the opportunity to convert in the comments. People are begging for the book titles.

SGE Team

A newcomer AI photo editor launched in December 2025 is now sitting at #11 in Photo & Video in Spain.

Ploxto AI is getting there with the trending “Prank Your Parents” playbook.

They’re running a TikTok-led setup through three Spanish faceless accounts. Across 72 videos, they’ve already racked up 14.2M views in barely a month.

The format is a repeatable message → proof → reaction cycle.

Each video opens on a text conversation with a familiar target (usually a parent or an ex). The creator tells a lie, the app generates a hyper-realistic image as “evidence,” and the recipient reacts.

Example:

“Le digo a mi padre que he cocinado a su pez de 1000€” (I tell my dad I cooked his €1,000 koi fish) → 4.1M views

Their best performers reuse the same hook language, always starting with:

“Le digo a mi…” (I tell my…)

It’s crazy virality for a faceless strategy. By positioning the app as a prank generator rather than an editor, they’ve turned the download button into a way for users to join the joke and try it themselves.

This cycle creates a compelling narrative that hooks viewers and encourages sharing.

Built Workout

This eight-month-old app hit jackpot this week with a sped-up transformation video.

The guy’s body changes over time, and in the top right corner, an app animation tracks the time passing, over 300 days.

It printed

11.6 million views

just three days ago.

Iori Flashcards

A language learning app pulled in

1.9 million views

five days ago.

They used a staged street interview, where someone walks up to a Japanese woman and she says she doesn’t speak English.

Then the creator switches to Japanese and says he’s only been learning for a month, and she looks surprised at how good he already is.

Creed

Bible app Creed had another hit this week with the same format they’ve been using since the start: a creator headshot recording paired with a long hook.

“knew I was cooked when the sweetest boy at church wanted something serious

with me and I felt nothing but the guy who did me so dirty, didn’t read the Bible / keep a creed streak and only wanted to hangout at night made my heart skip a beat”

It pulled racked up

921k views

and nearly 300 comments.

Airlearn

Another language learning app got

479k views

using the same format that’s already earned them millions.

In the video, the creator tries to finish English words in a funny way, with all of them leading to “b*tch.” They’ve done the same thing before with other similar words.

Studley

Studley’s been trying out a faceless format, and it went viral twice, once five days ago, and again four days ago. Together, those two videos pulled in

7.1 million views

.

The video starts by showing a high grade on a paper, then cuts to a tutorial for an app with the title “how I study.”

The main hook is still the same: “MOM my phone is literally saving my grades!!”

Zest

Cooking app Zest hit

1.1 million views

four days ago.

Same old UGC headshot reaction and the hook:

“am I late or is this actually new?”

A cool spin on a very familiar format.

Simmy

A c(.)ai competitor pulled

1.1 million views

and over 1.4k comments with a UGC-style video.

Like most of these apps, they used the same trick: name-drop the big player, then pitch theirs as the better option.

The video kicks off with: “When someone mentions that phase where I was unfathomably addicted to using c(.)ai every day of my life.”

In the caption, she leaves a soft CTA: “Now I’m addicted to Simmy, check bio.”

Jenni AI

Another StudyTok video where a creator starts off doing something with her hands, and this time it’s a wobbly purple slime.

The post hit

1.1 million views

just four days ago with the hook:

“Day 2 of seeing if my teacher ACTUALLY reads my 3,000-word essay.”

Stella

Last but not least, a new manifestation app recently blew up on TikTok with (also)

1.1M views

on a talking-style UGC video.

It kicks off with,

“if you just had the shittiest past few days of your life”

a line that instantly connects with thousands of people scrolling while feeling off.

The video also sparked huge engagement, pulling in over 3.7K comments, and proving that when astrology and manifestation content is done right, it almost never fails.

→ 57.3K likes

→ 73.8K likes

Following the 18M‑view spike, the format didn’t manage to reach such high numbers again.

@libbiedebtfree → 10.4M views

What makes this case interesting is that the formats are completely different, yet both work.

@financiallyresponsiblemr is doing close‑up confessions. Her videos use tight close-ups, showing her looking straight into the camera and making expressive faces.

The hook is always a financial confession.

“I wish it was socially acceptable to ask about money like are you in debt??? is that normal??? ill go first – im in $78k in debt (student loans and credit cards)” -> 4.7M views

“I’m 60k in debt and i need everybody’s most unhinged hacks on how they saved money. I’m not talking “I ate ramen everyday” I’m talking absolutely diabolical” -> 2M views

@libbiedebtfree leans more into the relationship angle.

Libbie is actually married to the app’s co‑founder, Luis Andino, and most of her videos include him.

The hooks focus on financial vulnerability in relationships.

Her biggest hits revolve around her fiancé/husband reacting to her debt.

“Finally showing my fiancé my student debt total before we get married.” → 2M views

“My fiancé’s reaction after we decided to share finances and he saw how much I owe.” → 2.6M views

TikTok has a soft spot for pre‑exam panic, and Voicenotes accidentally tapped straight into it.

Voicenotes: AI Notes & Meetings is an app that records, transcribes, and summarizes audio from meetings or ideas using AI.

Three months ago, one video stood out from the rest with 4.7M views.

A headshot of the creator before an exam.

“I’ll recognize it when I see it on the exam.”

A competitor, Knowunity, which is a direct rival in the study aid space, saw the chance and took it, by commenting:

“Study with Knowunity guys 🥱”

After that moment, no other video reached similar traction.

In simple terms, the product converts well, but not many people are finding it.

metadata.key_principle: Viral success must be followed by strategic content format development to maintain momentum and prevent competitors from hijacking audience attention.

One week post-launch, it’s already #58 in U.S. Health & Fitness.

The app comes from @hothighpriestess (Sarah Perl), a manifestation creator with 2M+ followers on TikTok and ~1M on Instagram.

She launched both accounts in early January and posts multiple times per day.

On the dedicated Instagram, her “love letter” method hit ~1.1M views on launch day, paired with a “comment ‘app’” CTA (Jan 28, 2026).

We’ll keep tracking and share updates as the growth story unfolds.
