Jenni AI keeps reinventing formats, and that’s why they never leave our FYP.

Their recent viral format is a serial “experiment” creators are running on their teachers: they’ll hide random but provoking lines inside their thesis draft just to see if the professor actually reads it.

“Day 1 seeing if my PROF reads my 3000 word essay”

Then Day 2 / Day 3 versions with the same premise, same stress, and the same comments bait (“WAIT did they notice???”).

It turns the video into a storyline people follow and the comments start doing the work: “remind me when part 2 is out,” “update us,” “did they catch it??”

And it’s working. In the last 30 days, this format helped them stack 5M views:

1M views

61.7k views

The CTA is subtile but there as they’re filming the tool they are using to write their thesis and check sources.

It overlaps with another winning template we’re seeing across StudyTok: the “doing stuff while talking” hook. When the creator is actively doing something on camera here playing with slime.

It keeps people watching long enough for the punchline to land and for the app to appear as the solution.

What’s the secret behind this app’s rapid rise to #1 in Spain and a surge of 200K downloads in just 30 days?

SGE Team

February 5, 2026

•

3 min read

Save for later

With Valentine’s Day around the corner, we’re taking a look at an app that’s blown up recently, growing from 30K downloads in December to 200K in just a month.

Couple360 focuses on a lock screen widget that helps couples share special moments, count down to big dates, and keep track of relationship milestones, all from their phones.

It also has a days counter that shows how long you’ve been together, a feature that’s quickly becoming a hit on TikTok.

An International Campaign

Couple360’s growth is fueled by a diverse ambassador network.

With around 37 accounts, the app has reached roughly 14 million views across English, Spanish, Portuguese, Turkish, and Filipino-speaking communities.

At its core, it’s a large-scale UGC strategy built on hyper-localization: using relatable creators from different regions and languages to make personal connections with local audiences.

The SpanishTok Dominance

Spanish-speaking influencers are the cornerstone of Couple360’s strategy, with videos reaching millions in Spain, Argentina, and Mexico.

In fact, the two most viral creators are Spanish-speaking.

@shanycami

and

@user2019378190

together account for roughly half of the app’s total viewership.

@shanycami

hit 2.6M views on December 27 with a simple shocked face clip, followed by a lock screen recording featuring “days apart” countdown widget:

“HOW CAN I PUT THE NUMBER OF DAYS I’VE BEEN WITH MY GIRLFRIEND ON MY PHONE?!”

@user2019378190

hit virality twice with the same format:

I don’t know how long we’ve been dating, I forgot. 1.7M views (Jan 21, 2026).

FINALLY I LEARNED HOW TO TRACK THE DAYS YOU’VE BEEN WITH YOUR PARTNER!!! 1.6M views (Jan 22, 2026).

Expanding the Viral Reach

You guess what happens next. International ambassadors are replicating the SpanishTok success with content tailored to their own audiences.

@takoyakat

, for instance, hit 715K views on January 25 with a English mixed with Filipino relationship long hook with an app mention:

Looking Ahead: A Global Leader for Couples

With Couple360 now dominating TikTok in multiple Spanish-speaking countries, and with continued growth in English and Filipino-speaking regions, the app is on track to lead the relationship app market worldwide.

Their #1 ranking in Spain is just the beginning.

Expect more viral moments and international expansions.

article.title: StudyTok Formats That  Keep Winning
article.content:
StudyTok Formats That  Keep Winning

StudyTok formats that keep winning.

SGE Team

•

February 5, 2026

•

5 min read

StudyTok Formats That  Keep Winning

StudyTok formats that keep winning.

SGE Team

•

February 5, 2026

•

5 min read

Save for later

StudyTok is by far one of the most innovative niches right now, constantly leading the way with new formats and creative takes.

Sooner or later, the rest of us follow, tweaking those ideas for our own niches.

Here’s a quick look at the top formats study apps are running right now, so you can take notes and get inspired.

1) Busy Hands Study Advice

You’ve probably seen multiple videos where a creator is doing something with their hands while talking to the camera.

Cutting fruit, making tea, peeling an orange, playing with slime… this is not random.

Study apps have been using this visual hook as a stop-scroll hack, while the creator talks about how they study and recommend methods that help.

When done right, you don’t even realize it’s a promo until the very end, when the tool is revealed.

Recent examples include

Studley AI

, pulling 1.7M views just a couple of weeks ago:

And

Turbo AI

, at 1.4M views:

We’ve seen this format spreading fast and you can probably adapt it to any app out there.

2) Mad Professor / Teacher Meltdown Skit

This one is a classic and

has been trending for months

: a classroom clip or skit where the professor has a full-on breakdown because the class used Chat GPT instead of [insert study tool].

It’s chaotic and absurd, which is what gets people to comment and watch.

We’ve seen it evolve from using actors to real humans, to AI-generated professor sketches.

Every single variation has exploded, including Mindgrasp AI with 3.2M views in January:

Turbo AI pulled 9.5M views with an AI version.

3) AI Voice Tutoring

StudyTok creators have been recording themselves studying while an AI voice reads their material out loud (definitions, lecture notes, textbook pages).

Then they interrupt it like its a real tutor:

“wait explain that again,”

“give me an example”

“break it down like I’m 12.”

The best versions cut to the app feature after the back-and-forth starts (notes → flashcards → quiz), so the product appears as the reason why the study session is working.

StudyFetch

has been printing with this: one of their creators @studyfetchbrunette pulled her best views (6.3M) using this exact format and she’s been repeating it over and over again.

4) Toxic Study Motivation

Sometimes all it takes is a bit of tough love to snap you out of it and give you the push you need. A while ago, creators started to tap into these feelings of fear and shame to trigger people to lock in and study.

Hook are almost always short and aggressive

“Lock in.”

“No one is coming to save you.”

“You’re not tired, you’re distracted.”

The rest is just built around the narrative and smoothly linking back to the app.

We’ve seen apps like

Studley AI

doing really well with this format:

This creator pulled 4.9M views with the hook “toxic study motivation for finals”.

And another pulled 2.2M views with a faceless version of the same format.

5) “What’s ur GPA?” / “What do you use to study?”

What started as a trademark from Turbo AI earlier last year is now being recycled all over StudyTok in different shapes and variations.

Someone asks several students in a circle what’s their grade and the tools they use to study, usually keeping it to two types of answers in for contrast:

low GPA → students who claim they don’t study or use Chat GPT

high GPA → students who use the right tool

Here’s an example of Turbo AI that still pulled 235.1k views just one week ago:

You can also do it with a fully AI-generated spin with pictures lined up in a slideshow, similar to this one that hit 448.6k views:

6) The “AI Forgot He’s Not Human” glitch

More recently, creators started filming themselves studying while an AI voice reads in the background until it glitches like it’s human, usually a cough or sneeze.

They act confused and quickly cut to the app feature.

One of the best examples is from @joce.erly for Studley AI at 13.5M views:

Turbo AI also pulled 4.7M views with this one:

WhoLiked is a social party app where friends guess who liked or reposted certain videos.

In just 9 months, it’s already generating $200K/month and has passed 700K downloads.

The growth is clearly visible:

#21 overall on the App Store

Top 10 in multiple countries (#2 France, #6 Switzerland, #2 Poland, #3 Portugal)

The creator network is already international, spanning 5 nationalities.

French and English accounts are driving the biggest hits.

Creators follow the same structure:

filming a group of friends playing the game at a casual hangout.

or four friends face the camera while playing the game.

“Who gave like?” → 1.4M views

Three accounts posted the exact same video, but at different times and in different languages.

The results shift dramatically:

5 months ago (French hook) → 649.5K views

4 months ago (same French hook) → 1.1M views

2 months ago (English hook) → 7.2M views

“Your sign to play Guess Who Reposted at your next Friendsgiving”

After the 7.2M spike, they kept reposting the same video again… and the views collapsed.

frameworks.example: WhoLiked's format where friends play a guessing game about who liked or reposted videos, filmed casually and replicated by creators in multiple languages, leading to millions of views and top App Store rankings.

However, overusing the same content led to view collapse, highlighting the need for content freshness.

Gloss Nail Art is a nail-design app where users generate nail sets, save ideas, and share looks, with creation behind a subscription.

Released in August 2025, it hit ~50,000 downloads last month.

Instead of relying on one brand page, like many apps in the same niche do, Gloss is pushing distribution through a 10 account network (1 Instagram, 9 TikTok), already totaling ~10.8M views.

The first hook that broke them out hit on Dec 15, 2025:

“i could KISS the nail tech that showed me this”

Sounds familiar? It’s a spin-off on Roamy’s viral flight attendant hook, which you can read more about

here

.

It reached 2.7M views on TikTok and 2.6M on Instagram, with roughly 100K saves combined.

The format stays the same: the classic shocked face followed by a fast app demo that reveals the nail idea.

Then they repeated the exact play with a second hook:

“6 years using pinterest for nails just to find this”

It hit 2.0M views on Instagram and 588K on TikTok.

That’s the whole engine: make the app feel like a “finally found it” nail hack, then scale it across a small UGC network until it turns into downloads.

1.7M Views Hit, Then Flat

A 14‑account network couldn’t make the format take off.

SGE Team

3 min read

Save for later

Some formats look scalable on paper, until the numbers say otherwise.

Natively.dev

is a seven‑month‑old platform that uses AI to generate mobile apps from an idea or design.

Across TikTok, we found a network of 14 accounts.

Posting began in June, paused in August, and resumed in October, which turned out to be their strongest month so far.

Format:

a headshot of a creator

acting as a computer‑science student

delivering a scripted hook about job rejection or opportunity

Some creators post in French, others in English. But the structure never changes.

They have two types of hooks.

The rejection hook

Creators act as if they were just rejected from an entry-level role for lacking a CS degree or side projects, then claim the platform could have helped them build apps.

“”J’ai passé une excellente journée jusqu’à ce que je reçoive un nouveau refus pour un poste de débutant (j’ai un diplôme en informatique). C’est tellement difficile de se démarquer sur ce marché du travail ! J’aurais aimé développer des projets parallèles plus tôt à l’université. Il existe aujourd’hui tellement d’outils d’IA qui permettent même de créer des applications : il suffit de saisir une idée et le logiciel génère tout le code standard pour le déployer sur iOS ou Android !””->390.6K views

2. The “born in the right generation” hook

Creators express excitement about living in a time where you can build an app without coding.

“I was clearly born in the right generation — wait, what do you mean there’s a site where you can throw in any app idea (or even just a design) and it builds the whole app for you without coding, then sends it straight to iOS and Android???”

(translated from French) -> 91.5k views

Even with 14 accounts using the same format, most videos still underperform.

But one video went viral, reaching 1.7M views.

“je suis né dans la bonne génération car au lieu de lutter pour me concentrer…”

English version:

“I was born in the right generation because instead of struggling to focus during my studies, I can create an application that contains everything I need to focus: a calendar, a deadline tracker, and a timer.”

It’s the only video that breaks through and none of the replicas manage to repeat the spike.

frameworks.name: Consistent Format with Variable Hooks
frameworks.description: Use a consistent video format with different scripted hooks to test which resonates best with the audience.
frameworks.when_to_use: When launching content campaigns to identify the most engaging messaging for a product or feature.
frameworks.example: A network of 14 TikTok accounts used the same video structure but tested two hooks: job rejection and generational advantage, to promote an AI app builder.

metadata.key_principle: Even with a consistent format and multiple accounts, viral success often depends on unique, authentic hooks that resonate emotionally with viewers, which cannot be easily replicated.
metadata.article_summary: A network of 14 TikTok accounts promoted an AI app-building platform using a consistent video format featuring creators acting as CS students delivering scripted hooks about job rejection or generational advantage. Despite multiple videos and accounts, only one video went viral with 1.7M views, while replicas failed to replicate the success, showing the challenge of scaling viral content through formulaic approaches.

SGE Team

2 min read

Save for later

Tavus is building AI humans.

They are real time video agents that can see, talk, remember, and interact like real people.

They enable face to face AI through APIs and replace static avatars with emotional and context aware conversations.

They are backed by Sequoia, YC, and CRV, betting that the next big interface is not chat but human level video AI.

Their content strategy heavily leans on anti c.ai narratives,

similar to what many competitors are doing.

They push these narratives without branding and then highlight Tavus mainly in the captions. They also try to push in the comments, but it does not always land.

Some of their more extreme engagement farming hooks perform very well, but they likely do not drive much traffic since there is no clear call to action.

You can find their full hook list here.

Even if the results are unclear, it feels like they are steadily increasing posting velocity. Either something is working, or they have strong funding and are focused purely on awareness, or on shifting the narrative away from c.ai and modern app misinformation.

Overall, they are performing fairly well on a global level with only six active accounts.

frameworks.example: Tavus uses anti-c.ai hooks in their TikTok and Instagram posts to engage audiences skeptical of AI-generated content, then highlights their brand in captions.

If you’ve spent any time in TikTok marketing, you’ve likely noticed this: most apps start with a bunch of accounts, but in the end, it’s usually just one or two standout creators carrying the entire view-count.

Gleam is no exception to this.

Even though it’s just 8 months old, it’s already ranked #96 worldwide and sits in the top 50 in Canada, Australia, and Singapore.

In April, a group of six accounts started posting content on TikTok. But shortly after, it became clear that nearly all traction comes from a single creator.

Out of 40.1 million total views, 37.3 million come from @povmaxxed.

His format never changes:

faceless videos

filming strangers walking by

attempting to compliment them (“I like your outfit”)

showing the discomfort

Some videos show him visibly nervous, reinforcing the idea that learning social skills is a process that takes time and effort (and an app).

“Day 2: Overcoming My Social Anxiety”-> 8.3M views

Engagement has been pretty high for most posts, with this video hitting 7,444 comments, most of which are people identifying with the struggle:

“Stuttering/pausing ≠ social anxiety” → 137.8K likes

“the way he stutters it breaks my heart” → 98.5K likes

“I hate having social anxiety” → 48.6K likes

By Day 4, he appears more relaxed.

“Day 4: Overcoming My Social Anxiety” → 1.3M views

The hook never changes:

“Day X: Overcoming My Social Anxiety”

article.title: YAP Notes Hits a Wall in the Career Game
article.content:
YAP Notes Hits a Wall in the Career Game

YAP Notes leans into workplace‑crisis content, but after a year, results remain far behind their competitors.

•

YAP Notes Hits a Wall in the Career Game

YAP Notes leans into workplace‑crisis content, but after a year, results remain far behind their competitors.

SGE Team

•

February 4, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Most apps in this category sell career progress. YAP Notes sells crisis, and the results show the difference.

The app has existed for a year, but consistent posting only started three months later. Two isolated videos show up in October, but the real push for growth begins in November.

Creators follow the exact same script:

They film a tense call with their boss.

The boss demands they return to the office or they’ll be fired.

The creator records the call using the app.

And ends with:

“

Take this to HR.”

“POV: your crazy boss wants to change your remote job to an in‑person position, asked to return to the office” → 72.8K views

While YAP Notes focuses on “record your boss so you don’t get fired,” the top apps in this category take the opposite approach.

Competitors like Proactor AI

position the product as a tool to help with interviews and landing a job. And that opposite strategy is the one pulling in over 100M views.

YAP Notes, meanwhile, doesn’t have any videos that break past 72.8k views.

If the winning strategy is about getting hired rather than getting fired, YAP Notes may need to rethink its angle.

frameworks.name: Problem vs Solution Positioning
frameworks.description: Position your product either as a solution to a positive outcome (e.g., getting hired) or as a tool to manage a negative situation (e.g., workplace crisis). The framing significantly impacts audience engagement and growth potential.
frameworks.when_to_use: Use when defining your product's core messaging and content strategy to maximize appeal and virality.
frameworks.example: YAP Notes positioned as a tool to record workplace crises, resulting in limited views, whereas competitors like Proactor AI positioned as a tool to help with job interviews, achieving over 100M views.

metadata.key_principle: Product positioning and content framing directly influence user engagement and viral growth potential on social platforms.
metadata.article_summary: YAP Notes, an app focused on recording workplace crises, struggled to gain traction compared to competitors who positioned their products around positive career outcomes like job interviews. Despite consistent content posting, YAP Notes' videos capped at around 72.8K views, while competitors reached over 100M views by focusing on aspirational content. This case highlights the importance of framing product messaging to align with user aspirations rather than fears.

Early traction doesn’t always appear in view counts.

Kindred lets users create and experience interactive, AI-guided stories and characters.

The app is barely 2 months old, but creators began posting back in September 2025, though not consistently.

October marked the first real spike. From November to December, there was complete inactivity. In January, posting became consistent, with no gaps.

So far, most of the views come from two creators using opposite formats:

@faye.kindredai->Faceless

Films only the app.

But his best‑performing video had only 344.9K view.

“what are you doing?”

@faye.lovekindred-> Headshot reaction

Opens with a facial expression, then shows the app.

Her top video doesn’t show the app at all. Instead, she used the classic “diss your competitor” trick, naming c.ai and implying that a new app is coming that will be better.

“c.ai girlies, tell me one thing that immediately makes you turn off a character so I don’t include it in my new app”

-> 916.9k views, 8,935 comments

The most viral comments focus on tropes, clichés, and common icks in AI characters.

Another video from @faye.lovekindred hit 8.6% engagement rate.

“When your c.ai app alternative was just an idea last week, and now…”

-> 274.5k views, 1,026 comments

They are still clearly in the experimental phase by testing many different hooks and see what sticks.

While most apps gout there are growing by scaling a network of creators, Goodie AI is trying to bet it all on a single format.

The app is nearly a year old and only began posting on TikTok in March 2025.

There are no creators.

Everything is faceless.

Every piece of content follows the same template.

Following slides: a supermarket product photo->a screenshot of the app analyzing the ingredients

1. We’re so sorry (no we’re not)

This format is exploding because it’s a group skit that reads instantly and forces everyone to self-identify in the comments.

Three people. Same situation. Different reaction type.

And within two seconds you already know which one you are.

The version taking off right now: conflict response types

Type 1: “f

ck you b

tch”

Type 2: “we’re so sorry”

Type 3: “no we’re not”

It’s basically a personality test disguised as a joke so people show up in the comments to assign roles:

“I’M #2” / “my friend is #1” / “we need a #3.”

34.9M views

26.7M views

17.2M views

See the full trend

here

.

2. When Your Mom Says Something You Don’t Wanna Hear

This audio brings you right back to high school.

Creators use it to recreate those ultra-specific “mom moments” where you’re annoyed… because you know she’s right… and that’s what makes it sting.

The best part: small accounts (under 10K) are pulling millions of views.

If it’s specific enough, everyone’s like: “wait why is this MY life?”

6.4M views

See more examples

here

.

3.Sorry I don’t know

Creators with under 4K followers are pulling 2–4M views with one move: acting out the moment someone expects you to have context… and you absolutely do not.

The hook is always a hyper-specific scenario where you should know the answer and the punchline is the deadpan “I don’t know.”

You don’t even have time to scroll before you’ve already thought of your own version.

4.3M views

Read the full trend

here

.

4. Editing like it’s a TV reality show

This one’s fun and you can easily recreate it with footage you probably have sitting on your phone.

Creators are taking regular clips; office day, friend drama, family trip and cutting them like it’s an episode of a reality show.

Quick cuts. Dramatic pauses. Zoom-ins on faces. It’s all in the editing.

Add a few “meanwhile…” / “previously on…” captions and suddenly your friend isn’t just late… she’s the villain of the episode.

61M views

10.5M views

4.7M views

See the full trend

here.

5. Look the other way

Oh what people would do to avoid the ick.

POV: you’re with your partner / crush / friend… and suddenly you remember you have a tiny little thing about you that could be an ick.

So you start acting way too loud, way too helpful, way too “OMG LOOK OVER THERE!!” which, of course, makes it ten times more suspicious.

Creators are using the audio to act out that exact moment you go into distraction mode, and the hook tells you what they’re trying to hide.

4.8M views

Read more examples

here.

Little hacks that solve hard problems keep winning on TikTok.

And Juno fits right in.

It’s a sort of “AI BFF” style of app that supports people living with chronic conditions.

Their first big moment came last August, but the team didn’t commit to regular posting until later on, around October.

There is a clear pattern across all accounts, since all of them post faceless videos with not a single creator in sight.

@potstipsandadvice stands out by pulling in 3.8M views with just two videos.

They both follow the same template: slideshows + pinterest photos + sleep‑fix tips

“Some weird hacks from my psychiatrist to fall asleep” → 1.6M views

This video includes the app in a single slide as part of the solution, while the other does not.

However, the second one does not seem to be fully organic.

“Bizarre insomnia hacks my therapist taught me” → 1M views

Another account that’s also growing is @chronically_pickle.

All of the videos feature the same animated doctor character.

Each time, the video opens with a narrator asking, “What the fuck is ___?”, followed by a simpleexplanation of the disease.

“Finally POTS properly explained”->592.1K views

We’ll keep tracking their growth and keep you updated.

Osta is a recipe-saving app built for TikTok & Reels recipes.

Instead of lost screenshots and chaotic notes, it allows you to save a recipe straight from TikTok, Instagram, or the web into a clean recipe box.

Launched ~9 months ago, it hit 100K downloads and $20K MRR in the last 30 days.

The app was founded by

Ben Chelin

, a recipe creator with 1.3M Instagram followers and 300K on TikTok.

He has been the main acquisition channel: he posts his usual recipe content, adds a “comment Recipe” CTA, and routes commenters to a link that sends them into Osta to save it.

But the recent lift isn’t exclusively founder-led.

Around November 2025, Osta started an ambassador wave, and a few accounts are now repeating the same template at scale.

@cookedbysammy

made 14.2M total views with a simple repeated strategy:

Shocked face + “found out this” hooks + app demo.

And

@eatwithsid

is starting to go viral too with the same strategy:

“wait so I’ve been cooking for 3 years and I never knew about this??”

1.3M views & 25K saves (23 Jan, 2026).

The shift is visible in output, with performance moving from occasional founder spikes to a steadier stream of UGC that carries the app in someone else’s voice.

This monthly growth guide keeps you updated on trending formats, viral hooks, and new apps, and gives you the tools you need to plan your strategy for the month ahead.

An overview of what happened in the last 30 days

Top hooks and formats to test in February

The hottest breakout accounts and apps

Access to a full list of hundreds of videos you can explore with our advanced analytics

A full dataset on current UGC formats and hooks so you can look beyond what apps are doing and get inspired by the best organic content out there

Use it to spot trends early, borrow what’s already working, and avoid wasting time on formats that are already outdated.

Let’s get started.

Niche Snapshot

Over the past 30 days, Health, Fitness & Well-Being content has pulled

286.1M

views, with an average

5.35%

engagement rate across the niche. On average, that’s roughly

9.3M

views per day, making this one of the most consistently active content categories on short-form platforms.

We analyzed the best

450+

accounts and

88k+

videos to understand what’s driving performance in this space.

These numbers comes for performance across founder, UGC, ambassador, and network accounts, broken out by views, engagement, likes, comments, shares, and saves.

The data shows just how quickly this content gets consumed. Short-length videos and even slideshows carry most of the performance. The content was diverse and offered flexibility to creators and apps with formats and hooks.

Every month comes with its own spikes and dips. So we reverse-engineered the tactics behind what worked (and why), which accounts outperformed the rest, the hooks and formats that went viral, and the repeatable patterns behind them, broken down below.

Top Hooks & Formats to Test

1.

“empezar bien el año….”

or

“Start the year off right…”

in english.

From:

Musa

Hook type:

Fresh start / self-improvement cue

3.5M views

220.3k engagement

Format:

Lifestyle glow-up slideshow

Type:

Face

What it looks like:

A woman posing confidently, followed by aesthetic shots of healthy food or habits, ending with an app screenshot as the “start right” solution moment.

2.

“

2 dumbbells, 1 mat, and results you’ll feel in 2 weeks and see in 4 weeks. We start Dec 29th. You in?!”

From:

Fit With Coco

Hook type:

Results-driven challenge invite

3.5M views

220.3k engagement

Format:

At-home workout demo

Type:

Face

What it looks like:

A woman doing simple exercises with dumbbells and a mat, showing how minimal equipment leads to visible results, paired with a clear start-date CTA.

3.

“Worst waters of 2025”

From:

Oasis

Hook type:

Ranking / negative callout

3.1M views

53k engagement

Format:

In-store product breakdown

Type:

Face

What it looks like:

Someone standing in a grocery aisle with water brands behind them, ranking or calling out the worst options while explaining why on camera.

4.

“60kg”

From:

Tone AI

Hook type:

Curiosity bait / transformation signal

2.4M views

318.5k engagement

Format:

Body reveal POV

Type:

Faceless

What it looks like:

A woman confidently showing her fit physique, letting the short “60kg” hook spark curiosity about her journey or results.

5.

“2-Ingredient Japanese Cheesecake. This cheesecake hack that’s going viral in Japan”

From:

ReciMe

Hook type:

Viral trend / simplicity appeal

1.6M views

22.9k engagement

Format:

Recipe demo + taste test

Type:

Face

What it looks like:

A creator quickly making the cheesecake step-by-step, then cutting and trying it on camera for the satisfying payoff.

6.

“You BECOME who and what you surround yourself with”

From:

Innertune

Hook type:

Life lesson / mindset truth

1.1M views

34.8k engagement

Format:

Visual metaphor demo

Type:

Faceless

What it looks like:

Someone showing one rotten fruit causing another to spoil, using the visual as a metaphor for how environments and people shape behavior.

Apart from these top-performing hooks, you’ll find a detailed collection of over 400 hooks that are performing well in this niche.

UGC Hooks

We’ve pulled together the best hooks from viral UGC creators in the space. This is usually the hardest stuff to track down since it’s scattered across TikTok, so we’ve done the work for you.

These are the top-performing hooks you need to keep up with rising trends. Take a handful of them, give them your own spin, and test them out over the month.

Breakout Accounts & Apps

Wellspoken

Wellspoken

is going founder-led: the founder’s TikTok is basically the whole growth engine, pulling 10M views.

Yes, this app doesn’t quite fit the typical “health” category, but that’s how it’s listed in the App Store.

It’s the founder-as-teacher format with blunt problem → transformation hooks: “improving word retrieval” (2.3M), “Monotone voice? No more!” (1.2M), “Become Articulate in 21 Days” (836.8K), “Stop Mumbling” (478.1K).

Symmetry

Symmetry

is still printing, hitting #1 in Spain. 26.9M views in 30 days, led by one breakup-style TikTok that did most of the lifting (13.3M).

A 2-photo slideshow: “we were fine… then this happened”

Breakup hook → lock-screen breakup text → hard cut to a Symmetry training notification as the punchline.

Two other winners: @symmetry.gaizka (1.5M).

And @elpana.musculo (1.2M).

Musa

Musa

just landed 40.8M views in 30 days, with multiple creators hitting different lanes (curiosity bait, relatable self-care, and launch content).

The biggest video this month was a slideshow that hit 3.5M views.

The classic face-cam panic hook still works too: “WAIT… nipple hairs can be a sign of something serious???” → 546.7K.

They usually don’t name the app in the video; it shows up in the comments when people ask/share symptoms.

They also announced the Android launch and pulled 693.1K views with 26K+ likes.

Mesmerize

And finally, on this month’s podium, we have a meditation app,

Mesmerize

.

It hit $60,000 in MRR in the last 30 days, by consistently posting faceless immersive hypnotic visuals.

It’s worth a quick look.

Breakout Accounts/Apps

The outlier is @seharstudies: 7.5M views off mostly faceless laptop-screen vids (PowerPoint slides + blunt hooks). Biggest hit: “ap classes that are useless” → 2.5M views.

Other accounts like @giaonthephone are running the familiar Face-to-Face Pep Talk format. Top hooks: “EVIL study methods that will get you a 4.0” → 764.5K, and “The EVIL way to pull an all nighter” → 537.5K.

Airlearn

In the last 30 days,

Airlearn’s creator network

pulled 26.4M views, and they’ve scaled to 200+ accounts (up 40 since November).

But most of the reach is still coming from one stupid-simple loop: tight frame + wet eyes + one line of pain. The repeatable hook is always some version of: “Why is

__

so hard??”

It’s popping across accounts like @learnwithantony1 (“why tf is Portuguese so hard?” → 1.8M)

And @learnwithshrimpik (“Why tf is Russian so hardd?!??” → 519.1K).

The biggest engine is @bayleeonajourney at 16.7M views, basically running the “Why is Spanish so hard??” series on repeat (2.2M and 1.4M hits).

went viral with one static AI image + job-market despair copy. A single post hit 9.7M views on Dec 24: “didn’t get the KFC job… with a 3.8 GPA and a masters…”

The CTA is in a pinned comment, and it got 21K likes, turning the pitch into social proof.

BookTok

This app is literally called “

BookTok

” and it’s piggybacking the #BookTok wave with one main account that’s already hit 52.7M views.

They keep the format dead simple (close-up reaction → quick app demo), but the hooks are the real engine. First posted Mar 19, 2025 and flopped, then a month later a tweaked version landed 332.7K views: “I just found out you can make your own fantasy movie in like 2 mins?!?!?!”

Now it’s reportedly at $70K+/month off 50K new downloads.

Iori Flashcards

Iori’s street-interview

“language surprise” skits are still printing: 13.6M views in 30 days

.

Same loop every time (ask where they’re from → switch languages → “I learned it with Iori”), now posted in English to push beyond FrenchTok.

Two @ioriflashcards hits reached 3.5M views each, and a Reels repost pulled 1.4M.

This is not unheard of. It comes straight from Studley’s playbook, which you can also check out

While it’s still too early to tell, it seems like they’re on to something with this “you have a strict mom” format:

Lately, we’ve seen a clear shift in this niche, with more apps putting their money into creators who can talk in engaging ways. There’s almost always some kind of visual hook too, like spinning a globe or cutting fruit.

article.title: This B2B Company Is Doing UGC Marketing Now?

This B2B Company Is Doing UGC Marketing Now?

That was my first reaction. If you are in tech, you almost certainly know the company.

SGE Team

•

January 29, 2026

2 min read

Save for later

Yes, they are.

And the company is… *drumrolls* … Deel.

Yes, Deel, the HR and payroll app.

It is new, it is fresh. Just 19 accounts and 173 videos so far, but already 3.7M views.

At first glance, you might think, wow, this is already a big win.

But if you look closer, you realize the videos are completely indirect.

They focus on HR comedy, not on selling the product.

Which actually makes a lot of sense, because making a B2B app go viral directly is… almost impossible.

So it is straight comedy.

What is the point? (Heard you thinking out loud).

If you are a small company, probably not much. But if you are a large one, awareness becomes the real game.

At that scale, the lifetime value of a customer/company choosing Deel over Remote is massive.

Their cost to acquire a customer is likely in the hundreds, maybe even thousands, of dollars.

Think about Ramp. Ramp sponsors almost every podcast, so the logo is everywhere. When you start a company and hesitate between Ramp and Brex or another provider, you naturally lean toward Ramp.

That is what awareness (at scale) does.

With Deel, though, there is no logo, no product mention, nothing at all. So maybe they plan to connect the dots later.

A B2B company that has been doing this for some time is tl;dv.

The difference is that they use branded accounts with their name and logo, which feels closer to an awareness first, Ramp style approach.

So what is Deel actually attempting here? Most likely, they do not know yet. They are experimenting, learning what gets views and how views are created. Once they understand that, they will start fine tuning the strategy.

Something unusual happened on TikTok on September 9th.

One account posted 9 videos in a single day, and that sudden burst led to their biggest spike of the year.

The account belonged to

Fastic-Weight Loss & Fasting

, a health app launched in 2019.

The videos all follow a similar format: creators film their plates to show how they track their calories.

“pov: you think you’re hungry but you’re actually just thirsty” ->713.9k views

This video may not have been fully organic.

Was it a test? A paid push? Whatever it was, it doesn’t seem like it was a strategy. Since late September, Fastic has returned to posting sporadically, without any regular cadence.

Finance App Manufactures Conversations With 20M Views

They don’t invent hooks. They steal proven ones and deploy them systematically.

SGE Team

•

January 28, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

It’s Blooming.

This personal finance education app branded as “learn to invest” has been absolutely crushing UGC marketing, and it’s worth studying.

Let’s break down what they’re doing.

At the core of their strategy is engagement hook farming, and they execute it really well.

They seed comments early and push them to the top to drive conversation.

Take their most viral video with over 7M views.

The top comment has 41K likes and says, “Bloom is the only reason why I even have 18k lol.”

That comment comes from another account inside their creator network.

They repeat the same play on this video and many others.

When you study their content closely, you start to notice the same hook patterns showing up over and over.

The real lesson here is how deeply they research the personal finance space and the exact language people use.

One of their viral videos from three days ago is almost a direct copy of a hook from a random influencer.

The same thing applies to their main hook from early December. “I’m 22 with $1,000 in checking, $23k in savings, and no debt. I think I’m fine.”

This format is a somewhat proven personal finance trendy hook. You list your checking, savings, and debt, and let the comments do the rest. Naturally, people jump in and start sharing their own numbers.

This kind of consistent vertical research matters most when running comment farming strategies.

Conversation starting hooks from a year ago can still be reused and go viral today if they tap into the same core emotions and questions.

frameworks.example: A personal finance app copies a trending hook format listing financial stats, seeds top comments from creator accounts to spark discussion, resulting in millions of views and thousands of comment likes.

This week’s trends are giving: fake rich energy, dating reality checks, main-character friend groups, and 2026 as a full-time personality project.

Welcome to The Trend Radar – Week 4

1) “I got like hella money”

A random guy singing “I got like hella money” in his car turned into the internet’s new catchphrase.

The original clip got deleted after it reached 5.2 M likes, but the sound lived on and now it’s getting used as a meme, an audio and even sticker.

19.5M view

12.8M views

11.4M views

We even saw an app jump on it (PushUp Time) and pull

71.8K views

with the sound.

Get the sound

here.

2) My emergency contact is in the same emergency as me

This one is back and it’s a classic plot twist you can recreate with videos you probably already have on your phone. (And yes, you could probably fake the whole thing with AI if you want.)

The joke: you’re in a crisis → you go to call your emergency contact → and then you realize… they’re in the situation with you (or they caused it).

It’s quick, visual, and easy to adapt for apps in photo/AI editing/couples.

7M views

4.2M views

See the full format

here

.

3) The thought of having a BF/GF…

This trend is one hook + pure honesty:

“The thought of having a boyfriend/girlfriend…”

…and then people finish the sentence with what they usually keep to themselves.

It’s cute in theory until you remember the real parts: texting, being reachable 24/7, location sharing, “wyd,” social media, and the obligation that comes with it.

Works just as well with faceless text-on-screen.

5.8M views

Check all examples

here.

4. The Year of Side Quests

TikTok has officially decided 2026 isn’t a glow-up year. It’s a side quest year.

Think:

“I’m adding random missions so life feels fun again.”

Expect lists, series, and people treating their planner like one big side mission. A face close-up works just as well:

13.9M views

Read more about it

here

.

5. The Friend Hype Tunnel

And lastly: this one is pure fun. It’s giving “movie scene” comeback moment. Recreate it with any group; friends, family, colleagues… or even your bosses if they’re as cool as mine.

Get them to clap/scream → form two lines → and choose that one person to walk down the middle like he/she just won an award.

The caption that keeps printing:

“She’s free.”

(Usually breakup-coded, but it works for anything that feels like a comeback.)

32.8M views

21M views

15.4M views

See the full trend

here

.

When Ozempic Is Not Enough

MeAgain keeps posting, but nothing passes 279K. In a niche this active, that’s on the content.

SGE Team

•

January 27, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

For a GLP‑1 app in a niche with massive cultural attention, failing to break 279K views says everything.

MeAgain: GLP‑1 has been posting on TikTok since August, using multiple creators and multiple formats, but nothing has managed to break past 279K views.

Not once.

Not even with trends.

Not even when creators share their own weight loss journeys.

Across the account, two main formats appear.

Creators show their progress over time, habits, weight changes, routines.

“GLP-1 changed my body & my brain… and not always how I expected”->14K views

The other format is a slideshow list-> things you can/can’t do with the medicine

“Dos and Don’ts on a GLP-1”-> 141K views

None of these formats are creating lasting momentum.

In November, one creator tried to ride a trending audio used by people documenting their diet progress.

But instead of using the trend’s visual style of healthy meals, she swapped the food for the items she was tracking in the app.

The trend didn’t translate.

The video stalled at 279K views, while others using the same audio were pulling far higher numbers.

frameworks.example: MeAgain tried progress updates and slideshow lists but neither broke 279K views, indicating a need to rethink content approach.

Attempts to leverage trending audio failed because the visual style did not match the trend's expectations, resulting in stalled growth despite the niche's high cultural attention.

Widgettable’s latest breakout isn’t just about long distance couple widgets, it’s about a single notification that makes people stop scrolling.

In the last week, their “long distance lockscreen slideshow” format has pulled

3.3M views

A lot of these slideshows look like the normal “

long distance tips

The kind you

shouldn’t

be reading on someone’s lockscreen which turns the slideshow into a mini-drama and pushes comments.

But they didn’t stop there, they’ve also been adding some payment baits like:

“You’ve received $___ for listening to Spotify.”

Different accounts are testing the exact same structure.We’ve already seen multiple versions perform:

They seem to have been pushing the shock formats lately with their previous hits being showing big age gaps that made people react and it’s working.

Everyone Wants The Noise Playbook

But can they run it like them?

SGE Team

•

January 26, 2026

•

< 1 min read

Save for later

PostForBrand(dot)Com is essentially like Noise but web only, and they attempted to run the exact same playbook and…

…kinda failed (for now).

Some of their accounts did get decent views, but they have been running since

December 20 and are still active, so it might just need more time.

Same playbook overall, at home mums posting about earning extra cash to help with bills and mortgage payments.

The issue with this approach is that hooks are not tightly controlled and the content quality sits on the lower end. To make that work, you need a massive network of posters to balance it out.

Once a few hooks show promise, you double down on them and try to scale and spread them across the network.

Right now, their main challenge is ramping up posting volume quickly. That is hard to do and requires strong operational execution.

frameworks.name: Controlled Hook and Content Quality Playbook
frameworks.description: A content strategy framework where hooks (the initial attention-grabbing element) are tightly controlled and content quality is maintained at a high standard to maximize viral potential and engagement. This requires a network of content creators who can produce consistent, high-quality posts with proven hooks. Once effective hooks are identified, the strategy involves doubling down on them and scaling their use across the network to drive growth.
frameworks.when_to_use: Use this framework when trying to scale organic content growth on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, especially when relying on user-generated content and viral hooks to drive engagement and acquisition.
frameworks.example: Noise's approach where at-home moms post about earning extra cash with tightly controlled hooks and high-quality content, enabling viral growth and network scaling.

Their main challenge is scaling posting volume, which requires strong operational execution. Noise's success comes from tightly controlled hooks, high content quality, and scaling proven hooks across a large network.

How One TikTok Video Pushed a Social App Into the U.S. Top 20 Overnight

A single TikTok shoutout triggered a rapid “exit wave” to a new social app built around anti-censorship positioning.

SGE Team

•

January 26, 2026

•

< 1 min read

Save for later

UpScrolled is a social media platform built by Palestinians.

It launched in June 2025 and stayed quiet at first.

Then one video pushed it all the way to number 19 in the U.S.

Guy Christensen

, a pro-Palestinian TikToker with 3.4M followers, posted a video calling UpScrolled an alternative to TikTok that is not owned by “billionaires with biased interests.”

The video was uploaded in January 22, 2026 and hit 313K views.

A few hours later, he uploaded a second video with a clearer tactic:

spread the app through TikTok comment sections

across the U.S. feed.

In the same videos, he claims that U.S TikTok is now controlled by Larry Ellison and that this will lead to increased censorship of pro-Palestinian speech.

He also says UpScrolled was built by Palestinians connected to the Palestinian liberation movement.

There’s an interesting mechanic here:

Creator-led distribution + urgency framing + a simple, repeatable action (comments) that scales.

The creator used urgency framing about censorship and a simple call to action—spreading the app through TikTok comments—to create a scalable viral growth loop.

From TikTok Beginner to 45M Views in 60 Days

5 lessons learned from going from 0 to 45M views on TikTok.

SGE Team

•

January 26, 2026

•

4 min read

Save for later

45M views, 49 videos, 3 audios, 2 hooks, 1 format, 1 account.

This is how I got here as someone who had never created content before November.

I’m currently Chief of Staff at Alta, an AI personal stylist app backed by the LVMH family office and Anthropic. Alta has been featured in Vogue, Elle, TIME Best Inventions 2025, TechCrunch, Forbes, Fast Company, and more.

We all know consumer apps often leverage UGC to fuel growth.

Aware of this, I started posting and experimenting after researching on Twitter and reading resources like Social Growth Engineers. What actually worked came from treating content like a science, not an art. And once one format clicked, it became repeatable across videos, amassing 45M views over 49 videos on my account.

Here are my biggest takeaways if I had to start over:

1. Find a format that’s unique to your product

In a saturated UGC space, the content that wins is the content that shows the product’s value without feeling like an ad. It has to feel native to how someone would actually discover something.

Strong formats usually come from having someone in-house who can lead content ideation and clearly translate the product into visuals (reposting Daniel, ex-CMO of Cluely below on this). Your UGC creators can’t be guessing how to show your product, you need to give them clear examples.

Here’s what worked for us:

2. Audio

actually

matters

Find audio that sonically fits the content. If you watch my posts, you’ll notice the beats match when I swipe through the Alta app UI.

This is not accidental; you need to find ways to make your content riveting and satisfying to watch. Short-form content is a viewer retention game. Bonus points if the artist comments on your video (thank you Laufey)!!

3. Don’t be precious

Create with the assumption that most people will not care. They’re scrolling fast and trying to understand everything at 2x speed.

We cut way more than felt comfortable and just kept doubling down on what worked. Kill your darlings, distill fluffy copy, iterate quickly!

4. Use the comment section

People feel special when a creator responds. They’re more incentivized to engage (and maybe even download an app) when someone has taken the time to tell them about the app.

5. Interact like a real account

For your UGC account to get healthy views, you need the account itself to be in good shape.

That means consistently leaving relevant comments on videos in your niche, following new people you come across on your FYP, making sure you scroll periodically. A lot of creators will post on the app and disengage immediately.

Think like an influencer trying to grow, and act like one!

How an AI Assistant Hit $70K MRR by Remaking Viral AI Videos

An AI assistant app hit $70K MRR by taking viral videos, then adding the prompt and their app.

SGE Team

•

January 25, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Flibbo AI

is an all-in-one AI assistant built for content creation.

Users generate videos and copy ideas that are already working.

In the last 30 days, it hit $70K MRR and crossed 50K downloads.

On TikTok, Flibbo’s

main account

has generated ~198M views (some of that reach seems paid).

Format 1: The AI Ambassador

Early on, Flibbo used an AI character as the “creator.”

The character writes the prompt, reacts to the output, and sells it as something anyone can recreate if they follow the guide.

“

Flibbo Ai video generator

” 21.2M views (Aug 21, 2025).

Format 2: Viral clip + app tutorial

Their core strategy is simple.

They find a viral video concept that already has millions of views, remake it, then add a quick tutorial so viewers can re-do it.

The app is shown as the tool that makes the viral result easy to do.

One example: an AI creator posted a POV scene with movie characters in a wooden shack. It hit 44.4M views on Dec 19, 2025.

Flibbo posted a very similar version soon after, then added a “how to” segment. It highlighted the prompt and ended with a direct call to download the app. That one reached 1.1M views on Dec 30, 2025.

They essentially start with a proven viral scene, reveal the prompt, then show how to generate it in the app.

We recently stumbled upon a TikTok format that feels very similar to the “World in Statistics” style Twitter account, but adapted perfectly for short form video.

One airport‑shot clip broke months of flat performance, pulling 3.3M views

Until November 26, JetBack’s TikTok presence had been steady but flat.

Since September, JetBack has posted regularly using the same formula.

creators filming themselves at the airport->a quick flash of the app.

“I could KISS the flight attendant who showed me this has!”->509.2K views

For months, no video crossed 700K view.

In November, one video finally escaped the pattern.

“I could literally kiss the flight attendant that showed me this hack.”-> 3.3M views.

Even with that hit, there hasn’t been another success since, and this video doesn’t feel fully organic. Still, the app brings in about $80K in monthly revenue.

Follow Jesus is only 20 days old and it’s already sitting in the top 50 of the ranking.

The app launched with a face who is, by himself, a powerful reach machine. Timothy Bruce is one of the most influential Christian creators on TikTok and has 1.8M followers on his main account.

And long before the app existed, the audience was already there.

The app has been posting steadily since March, and it keeps getting regular hits.

All of them follow the same core structure.

He speaks directly to the camera.

He delivers an inspiring message about faith and spiritual growth.

“MESSAGE FROM GOD FOR A YOUNG WOMAN” – 6.3M views”

11.3K comments

The comment “HOW DID YOU KNOW” alone reached 92.3K likes.

You can notice the pattern: most hooks are almost always aimed at young women.

But he doesn’t work alone. His wife, Marthaa, has two more accounts where she uses the same structure but in Spanish.

“DIOS QUIERE HABLAR CON UNA JOVEN” (the Spanish version of “MESSAGE FROM GOD FOR A YOUNG WOMAN”)

6.2M views

All of this shows why the app climbed into the top 50 in under three weeks. It wasn’t starting from scratch.

The Faith App Remixing Genesis’s Ritual for 161M Views

Sanctify remixed Genesis’s ritual into 161.2M views, with one creator leading and a tone that moves between calm and urg…

SGE Team

•

January 23, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Three and a half months, that’s all it took for Sanctify, a direct competitor to Genesis, to rack up 161.2M views.

But Sanctify didn’t create a new format. It actually took the Genesis ritual format and reworked it into its own style.

Format 1: The Genesis Adaptation

A Bible verse illustration opens the video.

The creator delivers the recurring line: “Can you help me spread the word of God by sharing this with everyone, can you?”

The verse is read aloud.

The app appears at the end as the call‑to‑action.

4.2M views

They also replicate Genesis’s original structure.

But while Genesis pushes this format to peaks of nearly 14.7M views in 2025, Sanctify’s version usually reaches only about 415.1K views.

Format 2: The “Don’t Scroll” Spiritual Confrontation

Sanctify’s second format doesn’t try to copy what Genesis does, and it still performs well on its own.

It starts with a random clip and then suddenly cuts to the creator delivering a sharp and confrontational hook.

“The devil hopes you scroll past this because he doesn’t want to give back what he stole from you. I encourage you to save this and share it with the first person God puts in your mind…”

As he starts to pray, a montage of dramatic and symbolic clips appears on the screen.

3.9M Views

This whole week is a mix of nostalgia, faceless mood boards, and low-effort formats that reveal your true self.

Also: TikTok has decided we’re back in 2016, so prepare your throwback.

Welcome to The Trend Radar — Week 3.

1) 2016 is back

Apparently 2026 is the new 2016. Vogue said it, celebrities posted throwbacks, and now socials are treating 2016 like a mythical era we all lived together.

The format: quick 2016 throwback → old pics / old outfits / old music -> “this was my era” reveal.

It works because everyone wants to comment their own era (“this was my peak” / “why did we dress like that” / “take me back”).

5.6M views

“I heard were bringing back 2016 so I bring you freshman year”

Check all examples

here.

2) This & No Stress

The perfect hook for anyone trying to romanticize their life.

Creators slap “this & no stress” on a cinematic shot or anything that makes you forget about your problems (ocean, sunsets, mountain views, city nights, girls trips) — and it just prints.

You can make it a faceless template because the visual does the storytelling.

12.3M views

10M views

Read more about the format

here.

3) One Text Away From Leaving

This one is all about showing your side quest energy which 2026 is all about.

This micro-trend is popping where creators admit they’re basically one message away from abandoning their whole day.

“I’m one text away from leaving my house”

and show how easily you’ll say yes to a random plan or chaotic detour.

7.9M views

“How easy it is to convince me to go on a side quest because i’ll literally do anything”

4M views

“How easy it is to convince me to go anywhere to do anything cus I love a side quest”

More examples

here

.

4) I’m bored, Show me a picture

Creators post a nice photo (travel, camera roll, scenery) with one on-screen hook: “I’m bored. Show me your last

_

pic. Here’s mine.”

This one is low-effort and works in basically any niche: from couples content to travel to study setups.

Anything that can prompt a “show me yours.”

8.7 M views

1.1M views

Check all examples

here.

5) Private Story vs Public Story

This one is a few weeks old, but it’s the kind of format that can print any time because it’s built on a universal truth: everyone has two personalities online.

Expose the gap between what you post to your private Instagram story vs what you let the public see.

It pulled

massive views

because people just love to see the behind the scenes chaos.

134.7M views

and 25M likes.

43.7M views

37.8M views

Read about it

here.

Go hop on these while they’re still hot.

Musa just put up 40.8M views in the last 30 days.

And what’s interesting is that several different creators are behind this surge of views, with multiple formats hitting different parts of the algorithm: curiosity bait, relatable self-care, and a launch product moment.

Musa usually wins with face-cam, story time, and “period POV” content but their most viral video this month is a slideshow that hit 3.5M views.

The classic bait still works: close-up face + panic hook. But this time it was one of their English creators.

“WAIT… nipple hairs can be a sign of something serious???”

->  546.7k views

Once again the app name isn’t mentioned in the video. Instead, she makes sure it shows up in the comments replying directly when someone asks / when someone shares a symptom. That’s deliberate:

They also announced the Android launch and pulled  693.1k views and 26K+ likes

EN: “Girls, the wait is finally over! Musa is out on Android!”

Their team is running 47 TikTok accounts.

All of the formats they use come down to the same theme: date ideas.

Each slide shows 4 photos, and each group of photos represents a different date idea.

“2026 date ideas” → 547K views

The same structure used by their competitor

Loverzz

.

One LDR hook, two phones and a matching widget.

Same template, far lower impact.

Even though views and engagement remain quite low across all accounts, the app still reached 30K monthly downloads.

Noise’s “Mom Network” Gets 4.1M Views

Noise is blowing up with “mom side hustle” creators promising extra cash for quick posts, and it still pulled 4.1M views…

SGE Team

•

January 19, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Noise is a pay-per-view creator platform where anyone can earn cash by posting short content on TikTok and Reels.

Creators post, and get paid based on performance, which is why it’s blowing up with “side money” creators right now.

They’re recruiting small, everyday creators (mostly moms) and pushing one simple promise: “make extra money by posting.”

Scroll the network and the profiles bios are basically copy-paste:

“mom of 2,” “single mom,” “side hustle,” “use my code,”

and a quick bonus line.

The interesting part: their network is huge, but the activity is unequal. Noise now sits at 345 tracked accounts in the ecosystem.

Some post a few times a week, others go quiet. So it’s not every account firing daily, it’s more like a bunch of creators, some active, many inactive, and a few doing the heavy lifting.

Yet… the views still add up fast.

In the last 30 days, the ecosystem pulled 4.1M views

This isn’t one massive breakout carrying the month. It’s lots of small wins stacking, plus a few mid-sized spikes, the kind you’d expect from a network where content is constantly being re-posted and recycled across variations.

The top of the funnel is still a handful of accounts:

katie.side.hustle0

(~7.2M total views)

keke.estoff

(~4.5M)

tashmanifests

(~2.4M)

mammaofcuties

(~1.3M)

Lately, they’ve moved on to pushing this hook:

“She doesn’t know it yet, but a post she made yesterday is going viral and her Noise app earnings will pay for her vacation.”

-> 27.1k views

“She doesn’t know it yet, but a post she made yesterday will hit 3M views and her Noise earnings will pay for her rent this month.”

-> 2.3k views

•

Fly Vaunt, a “fly private” membership app, just hit 20,000 downloads in 30 days, with a $2,995/year subscription plan.

The business model leverages “empty leg” flights, last-minute, one-way repositioning routes that would otherwise fly at $0 revenue.

For a single annual fee, members get unlimited access to these routes via app waitlists.

Fly Vaunt’s pages have pulled about 7.2M total views across Instagram (4.4M) and TikTok (2.8M), driven mainly by repeatable street-interview formats.

“

How much does it cost to fly private?

” hit 1.2M views (Jan 2, 2026).

These videos work by highlighting the massive gap between the perceived value (a $50,000 private jet flight) and the actual cost ($2,995 for the year).

“

How much do you think it costs to charter a private jet?

” 735K (Jan 10, 2026)

By “ambushing” a stranger, the creator turns a cold sales pitch into an accessible lifestyle “glitch” for the viewers.

AI Apply is a website that automates the job search.

AI crying image →  relatable job-market hook → pinned comment CTA.

BoldVoice

is going all in with one repeatable series that’s going viral on a  weekly basis.

And being honest, that’s the only one that matters.

4.7M views

10 Viral Hits You Missed This Week

SGE Team

4 min read

Save for later

Sounter

We’ve seen this “angry professor sketch” format at least a million times with study apps. But Sounter just showed it can work just as well for language learning apps.

One AI-generated mad professor clip, uploaded just 3 days ago, hit

11.1 million views

and 8,428 comments.

Same energy, same punchline and easily replicable with AI —

“

My English teacher got really mad

🥺”

RealYou AI

This one’s not your typical “AI prank” video. It’s more of a cover story about “fake hobbies that might help you get a boyfriend,” and she’s asking the public for their take on it.

“HELP i told him I’m really into pottery… which studio pic looks real

😭

”.

It did

690.1K views

and the comment section quickly turned into a group chat vote.

Cray Cray

Another UGC-style slideshow is blowing up from the couple’s game app Cray cray.

This time, it was posted by one of their French creators, who went for the usual aesthetic couples pictures and simple hook.

“Wallpaper ideas to do as a couple

🫶

”

pulled

616.3K views

and 19.5K bookmarks.

It’s cute, simple, and feels like a mini Pinterest board while being insanely easy to produce at scale.

Lori Flashcards

Lori flashcards hits again.

1.8 million of views

with a quick street interview and language flex. He walks up to a stranger, asks one question, figures out their language and flex his fluency.

“You can speak?”

That response sets up the app reveal instantly.

Rebrain

This is one of those relatable videos where the hook does all the targeting.

A few days ago, Rebrain pulled

1.3 million views

with:

“Having both ADHD & Autism be like”

Nothing much to report here, it’s a safe bet that actually worked.

Musa

Musa is still winning with their female led creator accounts.

One of their Spanish creators posted an announcement of their Android launch with:

“

Girls, the wait is finally over!

💜

MUSA IS OUT FOR ANDROID

💜

”

It did

683.3K views

and just over 1,600 comments.

Widgetable

Couples slideshows are still printing, but Widgetable took it a step further with a shock twist: age gap shock value. The hook is simple but uncomfortable enough that people stop scrolling:

“You know he’s younger right?”

It racked up

4.9 millions of views

and over 15,000 bookmarks in a simple slideshow format.

Playbacks

Playbacks just pulled in

1.2 million views

with one long on-screen text that feels like a personal confession. The hook is basically a corporate horror story and sneaks in a CTA:

Word-for-word:

“HR said “use your sick days when you need them.” I called out sick with the flu on Friday. my manager replied “convenient day to be sick” and cc’d leadership. I felt embarrassed. I read the employee handbook in the Playbacks app. It says “no proof required for one day.” They treat us like we’re lying children”

Coursicle

Coursicle hit with a classic face close-up and a desperation bait (in a good way).

“Disorganized college students LET ME HELP U I BEG”

hit

474.6K views

and over 80,000 likes.

It’s chaotic, direct, and the hook seems effective at targeting the right audience.

Airlearn

Airlearn, the language-learning app pulled

15.6 million views

and nearly a million likes. It’s basically a game show for English learners disguise under a trap format.

The hook:

“What is this called?”

It tricks you into typing an answer and that’s how they got to 11,100 comments.

A subtle CTA is included in the post’s caption.

Or at least that’s what Cosmos creators want you to believe.

A wave of creators is framing Cosmos as the escape app for creatives who are tired of Pinterest being “all ads + AI,” then dropping a comment-gated CTA to pull people into DMs.

And it’s working. They’ve pulled 4.2M views in the last 30 days, mostly on Reels.

Now that we’ve got the headline numbers, let’s look at the content.

One format is clearly winning right now and it’s easily repeatable:

name-drop a massive platform → panic line → “switch to Cosmos”

.

You can see the pattern across the top clips:

“

Open ai buying pinterest is the modern day burning of the library of alexandria. PLEASE start using cosmos. boycott the billionaires

” -> 1.3M views

“

can we boycott anything and everything ai? bc wdym open ai is buying pinterest?? it’s already filled with ads and ai… time to use cosmos ig

” -> 75.6k views

And TikTok is running the same angle:

“

I miss the rage (

“I miss when Pinterest wasn’t full of AI + ads… so we switched to apps like Cosmos.”

)

” -> 89.6k views

Different wording, same core move: fear + nostalgia + exit.

(if you want to copy it for another app)

Pick a “declining giant” in your niche

Write the doom line (“it’s cooked or it’s all ads now”)

Position your product as the exit door

You can track their accounts here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10UAGPtW1IUP

Huzz AI is a 7 month old tool that helps people write messages for chats and dating app.

Even though the brand runs 17 TikTok accounts, it still hasn’t gained real traction.

All accounts have been pushing the same format: a message exchange with the app

“how to make her blush (take notes)”->623.3K views

“how to make her want u (3am razz)”-> 312.6K views

Yet, among the 17 accounts repeating the same idea, one of them finally decided to try something different.

Instead of endlessly chatting with the app, now this creator is using the app to ask a “real” girl out on a date. It instantly become their top hit:

“shooting in ig dms part 1”-> 1.1M views

The next day he posted part 2, which only got to 49.9k views.

“shooting in ig dms part 2”

Still, taking the risk of testing a new format seems to have paid off, as Huzz AI now shows signs of a potential new direction.

What remains unanswered is whether this format can work at scale.

We’ll keep you in the loop.

article.title: One Female Founder, Two Viral Apps
article.content:
One Female Founder, Two Viral Apps

171 million views on Instagram Reels and 37 million on TikTok.

SGE Team

•

January 15, 2026

•

4 min read

One Female Founder, Two Viral Apps

171 million views on Instagram Reels and 37 million on TikTok.

SGE Team

•

January 15, 2026

•

4 min read

Save for later

Most of you probably know her as the founder of Going Solo, one of the top Gen Z social travel apps using UGC marketing at scale.

Now, she’s working on a brand new app with the same mission: tackling modern loneliness.

Today, we’re diving into her strategies and how she’s scaling them as a solo founder.

—

Ashley Pokorski, a young U.S.-based entrepreneur who launched Going Solo in January 2023 to help solo travelers meet and connect.

Then, just 87 days ago, she rolled out Soir, a new app created to bring city people together for chill, personalized hangouts.

Going Solo

Going Solo+ 1 year: $79.99

Going Solo+ 1 week: $4.99

Travel Buddy Matching: $3.99

Going Solo+ 1 month: $9.99

Buddy Matching: $2.99

Soir

Soir Plus Weekly: $9.99

Soir Plus Monthly: $19.99

Soir Plus Yearly: $89.99

The Strategies

Going Solo

Going Solo now runs 12 accounts and has hit a total of 171.8 million views.

You can track all videos

here

.

They started posting on Instagram in 2023, and since then, their strategy has focused on three main formats.

Format #1 – Quick clips

These are 6–10 second videos featuring a minimalist hook and an app CTA, using screenshots or video demo.

“How did you meet all those friends in Koh tao?” pulled 3.5M views.

Format #2 – Image sequence

This format consists of 10–15 Pinterest travel-related images, each lasting 1–2 seconds, with a static hook overlay and no CTA.

Hooks are usually more generic and aspirational:

“life’s too short to be mysterious. be wildly obsessed with the things and people you love.” did 590.1k views two months ago.

Format #3 – Movie/TV clips

This format is all about short videos from popular series or movie scenes, often featuring aspirational characters.

In December 2024, the team introduced new TikTok accounts featuring different creators.

The TikTok videos with the highest views all came from the @goingsolo.app account, even though some of them were not fully organic.

“wonders if I’ll meet any new friends in Australia” pulled 3.4M views nine months ago, with the app CTA loud and clear on the post’s caption.

“I want to travel the world but no one to go with” hit 3.9M views at the same time.

Soir

Soir is already running eight accounts and has racked up 37.6 million views so far.

You can track them all

here

.

Unlike what she did for Going Solo, Ashley’s strategy for this new app is primarily focused on TikTok.

Most of her videos for Soir feature close-up shots with a hook focusing on city loneliness and bringing women together through a supportive community.

What’s interesting is that this time, she’s leaning heavily into headshot-style, founder-led content — and she’s boosting her own reach by showing up as different creators across several accounts.

Out of the eight accounts:

five feature Ashley in most videos (despite different names in handle)

two are faceless, posting Pinterest-style slideshows

only one is run by another creator, Lexie (@lexiequinnn)

Still, it’s clear that for now, her main TikTok account, where she’s been posting since 2021 and promoting both apps, is the one performing the best.

With this app, she’s also leaning more into wall-of-text hooks, a clear shift from the strategy she used with Going Solo.

Will she be able to replicate her 171M Instagram views on TikTok?

Time to place your bets.

A new AI gym format has been going viral this week.

POV: your muscle is the one talking.

Creator

@gym.shorts0

posts simple AI mascots (muscle, creatine, pills) with eyes and legs, giving first-person fitness takes.

On January 7, 2026, a muscle mascot called out the cold shower myth:

“

I’m Muscle, Cold showers don’t burn fat

” hit 2.1M views and 42K saves.

Three days later, same AI voice, same setup:

“

I’m your Muscle, Where’s my protein?

” hit 2.1M views and 32K saves.

The AI Body Part or Supplement POV is what keeps people watching.

The strategy

Hook

: “I’m your [muscle/creatine/etc].”

Take

: Fitness mainstream advice or myth-busting topics.

Cadence

: 7 to 8 short AI clips together (1 minute videos).

To adapt it for a fitness app, let the mascot call out a mistake, then make the app the resolution:

“I’m your muscle. Where’s my protein? → open the app → build a meal that hits it.”

Swap the narrator (muscle → creatine → pills) to refresh the same format without changing the structure.

New Year’s “pixel” habits are going viral.

Pixa is a journaling app where each day becomes a color-coded square.

The promise is simple: “Log your year in pixels.”

In December, Pixa was at ~30K iOS downloads and ~$7K MRR.

In January, it jumped to 80K iOS downloads and $30K MRR, while Android moved from 20K to 50K downloads.

The growth is not accidental.

Pixa is turning “daily pixels” into a New Year ritual, then scaling it through a TikTok-led official account (

@pixa_app

) built on repeatable, faceless templates:

Format 1: Sketch → App (before/after slideshow)

An effective way to position the app as a digital alternative to paper tracking.

1.6M views & 20K saves (Dec 30, 2025).

460K views & 10K saves (Dec 14, 2025).

Format 2: “That girl” positioning (slideshow)

Packaging the tracker as a lifestyle essential rather than a utility.

“that girl” must-have app

1.1M views (Jan 13, 2025).

“that girl” must-have app you need to try

1.7M views (Jan 29, 2025).

Format 3: One-category grid (single-theme pixel year)

The same mechanic, but applied to a single category (“crying,” “health,” etc.) to make the pixel grid instantly relatable and commentable.

“

Is this a lot of crying for one year?

” 565K views (Dec 12, 2025).

“

I’ve been tracking my health all year

” 575K views (Dec 28, 2025).

The pixel grid is the distribution engine.

One of the most viral forgotten formats.

Me and the app I found years ago where I can watch EVERYTHING against the world

”

9.8M views, 1.1M likes, 368K saves, 37K shares.

The video never shows an app name, only the screen.

23M Views, 2.7K Videos, 18 Accounts: The Largest Goodreads Alternative

BookTok is booming, and mainstream apps are betting everything on TikTok organic marketing to claim the largest piece.

SGE Team

•

January 14, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Fable, the largest app on BookTok, has been running UGC marketing for some time, with a strong acceleration starting in September this year, as shown in the graph.

Results have been ok/good, reaching 23.7 million views from 2.7k videos across 18 different accounts, all on TikTok.

While some videos appear clearly boosted, the majority seem to be fully organic.

Their approach breaks down into two main video types. One focuses on classic BookTok skits with no direct app mention, mainly farming views and occasionally adding a reference in the caption.

The other type uses a quick hook paired with on screen visuals, often highlighting stats or similar callouts.

They also put a strong emphasis on BookTok romance reading, which is one of the most active and competitive verticals on the platform.

On top of that, they often position Fable as a replacement for Goodreads, the long standing and established player in the space.

frameworks.example: Fable uses BookTok skits without direct app mention to gain views and occasional captions referencing the app, alongside videos with hooks and stats to position themselves as a Goodreads alternative.

Their strategy involved two main video types: organic BookTok skits without direct app mention to farm views and build community, and videos with hooks and on-screen stats to highlight the app's value. They focused on the competitive romance reading vertical and positioned themselves as a replacement for Goodreads, achieving strong organic growth on TikTok.

article.content:
