How Copying Cluely Got Me Millions of Views

As a UGC’er I have one ground rule: if it goes viral once, repeat it a thousand times.

SGE Team

•

January 12, 2026

•

5 min read

Save for later

As a UGC’er I have one ground rule: “if it goes viral once, repeat it a thousand times”.

Something I like to do to find viral videos is look at other UGC creators, and during the summer Cluely was hard to miss. They just hired a huge team of creators and were pushing new UGC formats out

en masse

. A big opportunity that I, of course, couldn’t let pass.

So let me explain how I used their content as inspiration, successfully created my own videos based on their format and how you can use this strategy for infinite viral video ideas.

A quick rundown about Cluely

The AI startup Cluely was basically founded on virality. When one of the founders, Roy Lee, used his newly created AI tool to ‘cheat’ his way through job interviews he got expelled from University, tweeted about it and blew up on X. From then on he went all in on Cluely, an AI assistant for meetings.

Past summer Katie Xu (

@katiexsocials on X

), the head of marketing at Cluely, started a huge UGC campaign, hiring around 100 creators. Each creator had a 30 day trial, needing to hit certain milestones to stay for a longer term.

Katie describes how with only one format they managed to hit their first 50 millions views on socials, which is exactly the format I decided to copy.

Finding viral videos

Cluely’s UGC campaign was REALLY hard to miss. They were literally all over social media. I remember tweeting:

Since the campaign started I had followed as many of their creators as I could on Instagram and kept up with their progress. Looking at what type of videos they were posting, what hooks they were using, which videos were going viral but most importantly: which videos were going viral on

multiple different accounts

. Those videos were my gold. Not only did they go viral once, I had proof that they could go viral for other creators too.

Creating your own version

During the campaign I noticed Cluely’s target audience consisted primarily of students so their audience was quite different from mine (professionals). And besides that, I had slight doubts about the

conversion rate

of their videos which was later confirmed by Roy in a blog post*. He explained that some of their most viral videos did not end up converting people to download and use their tool. It was clear that some tweaks were needed to apply their viral format for our own tool

Ultimate Web Scraper

.

The first thing I did was identify some of the main elements in their video format, which consisted of:

Brief face reaction, then demo of the tool

Catchy gen z vibe hook with emojis

Environmental sound & talking by the UGC’ers (no music or TikTok sounds)

Now that I had the building blocks, I got to work. What I kept most and foremost was the ‘vibe’ of their videos which was curiosity driven and casual without much editing. I liked the environmental sound, and chose to talk in the videos as the Cluely creators were doing. Plus I used the emojis they put in their hooks.

What I had to change were the hooks themselves. They did not suit our tool so copying them one-to-one would have made no sense. I came up with some of my own hooks that applied to what I was doing in my videos.

Finally, I used the ‘face reaction and then demo’ video flow. But instead of only showing a small feature very shortly, as the Cluely creators were doing, I did a more in depth demo of our tool, lingering longer on our main features to help with conversion.

All in all I kept the format very similar and primarily altered the elements needed to successfully showcase our product. It worked! With the inspiration from the Cluely format, and the tweaks to suit our tool I managed to create multiple viral videos both on TikTok and Instagram.

Infinite video ideas

The best thing about this strategy is that you can apply it over and over again! Old formats go out of style, and new ideas pop up. The important thing is that you keep your eyes open for when they do and don’t hesitate to try them out when you think a format has potential.

I apply this strategy constantly. It helped me get over 30 million views and is very scalable. You can even copy yourself plenty of times before your audience gets format fatigue 😉

So, now it’s your turn to do some doom scrolling and get inspired by a good format!!

Good luck 🙂

Floor

The 50M Views Faceless PC Build App Strategy

Are faceless 3D PC build clips the simplest way to hit 150K downloads in a month?

SGE Team

•

January 10, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

BuildCores is a 3D PC part picker that lets people visualize a desktop build and performance before they buy anything.

Last month, the app passed an estimated 150K downloads.

It’s now a top 100 utility app across much of Central and Eastern Europe.

BuildCores also runs a 42-account network with 21 Instagram accounts and 21 TikTok accounts.

So far, they’ve driven 29.5M views on Instagram and 19.5M on TikTok, for 49M total views.

One Instagram account,

@mo_buildcores

, generated 21M views by itself.

It posts faceless 3D PC builds paired with short, relatable PC gamer hooks.

“

If i lag again I’m ending it all

” hit 6.5M views, 48K shares and 55K saves.

It even went viral twice using the exact same hook.

“

Ofc I found this website after building my PC

” pulled:

4.9M views and 105K saves + 1.9M views and 35K saves.

BuildCores scales reach through “satellite” accounts that look like creators, but mostly post faceless content.

About 88% of those accounts include “buildcores” in the handle, and they generate roughly 94% of the total tracked views.

This is a distribution system:

One hero creator for breakout reach → a cloned identity setup for attribution → reposting across Instagram and TikTok to stack views.

Track their entire collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10npQ8SJOzNj

Genmoji Wave Lifts AI Emoji App to $100K MRR

What happens when a “new iPhone” feature goes viral, and you sell that feature to everyone who can’t use it?

SGE Team

•

January 10, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Gmoji is an AI emoji-maker app that helps people create custom emojis and reaction stickers.

Users can type a prompt, remix existing emojis, or blend emojis into photos.

Last month, the app hit $100K MRR and passed 200K downloads.

Apple’s Genmoji feature made AI emojis mainstream, then the iOS 26 cycle triggered a viral wave of “custom emoji” demos.

One example: “

When iOS 26 gets too real

” hit 9.5M views on September 20, 2025.

The comments were packed with people on older iPhones asking how to do it.

That was Gmoji’s opening.

They started posting similar videos and pointed viewers to their app.

On September 28, they reached 13M views with this hook:

“

how to create genmojis if you have old iPhone 11, 12, 13…

“

Then, on October 1, 2025, they hit 56M views with another hook:

“

emojiholic

“

Note: some of these view totals include paid amplification, so treat them as blended (organic + paid).

Even after the Genmoji trend cooled off, they kept getting views by turning trending shows and events into emoji content.

On December 3, 2025, they pulled 2.4M views with a Stranger Things spin:

“

PICK YOUR STRANGER THINGS EMOJI

“

Their best performing hook styles were “How to,” “Pick your,” and “emojiholic.”

Gmoji launched in 2024, before Apple’s Genmoji push, and used the platform shift as distribution fuel instead of getting wiped out by it.

Track their collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10ixDb5Un3lf

frameworks.when_to_use: When a major platform or competitor launches a popular feature that excludes a large user base, and you can replicate or approximate that feature.
frameworks.example: Gmoji capitalized on Apple's Genmoji feature by creating AI emojis for users with older iPhones who couldn't access the native feature, driving viral content and app downloads.

frameworks.example: Gmoji's best performing videos used hooks like 'How to create genmojis if you have old iPhone' and 'Pick your Stranger Things emoji' to drive millions of views.

frameworks.description: Sustain content momentum after a trend cools by creating themed content around popular shows or events to maintain engagement and reach.
frameworks.when_to_use: After the initial viral trend fades, to keep audience interest and continue growth.
frameworks.example: Gmoji created Stranger Things-themed emoji content to pull 2.4M views after the Genmoji trend cooled off.

Photogeniq

Looks like AI pranks aren’t going anywhere. The AI image app Photogeniq went viral six days ago with a video that racked up 6.8 million views and over 1,000 comments.

The video came from one of their Spanish creators, with the hook translating to:

“I pranked my boyfriend by pretending I got his name tattooed, and it went really badly.”

This prank format has been popping up a lot lately, but for Photogeniq, it’s a shift in direction. Until now, the app had mostly focused on aspirational, Pinterest-style slideshows.

Musa

The period tracker app Musa keeps pulling in views with UGC-style slideshows.

In this one, they tapped into the New Year energy, using a cover photo with the hook “starting the year right…”, originally written in Spanish.

The second slide shows a screenshot of the app, with a ❤️ emoji showing up in the first few days of the calendar. They tried to boost engagement by timing it with her period, but judging by the comments, it didn’t really land.

Still, the video pulled 3.4 million views and nearly 3,000 comments, and it quickly became the creator’s most-watched post so far.

Symmetry

Another UGC-style slideshow is blowing up, this time from the fitness app Symmetry.

They took a bit of a gamble here, and it worked. Instead of the usual fitness angle, they tapped into relationship drama to make their app name stick. It paid off.

The first slide shows a couple hugging, with the hook (in Spanish again, not on purpose):

“4 years in a relationship and out of the blue she just sent me this…”

The second slide shows two notifications: one from his girlfriend, softly breaking up with him, and right below it, a reminder from Symmetry to train.

12.7 million views, nearly a million likes, and close to 14,000 comments.

Pixory Travel Books

These photo albums have been blowing up on TikTok lately, proving again that UGC doesn’t only work for apps.

“Imagine your future daughter seeing how rich your 20s were

🥺😭

✈️”

She flips the camera around to reveal a huge stack of photo albums, then opens a few to show what’s inside.

The video went up last week and hit 6 million views, 701k likes, and 1.6k comments.

Loverzz

Loverzz is an eight-month old couples app featuring little games and widgets.

A few days ago, one of their talking, couple videos went viral and pulled 1.3 million views.

It sticks to their usual format: a “would you rather” style game where the couple plays together while the app shows each question on screen.

Widgetable

Last but not least, another couples-focused widget app.

One of their creators pulled in 768k views six days ago with a four-slide carousel post.

The hook

“texts from my ex vs my bf”

was paired with screenshots of the widgets, which had people in the comments asking what app it was.

21.8M Views, 70,000 Downloads in 2 Months

They drove 21.8M views and 70K downloads in just 2 months by repeating one faceless, zero-cost video format.

SGE Team

•

January 9, 2026

•

2 min read

Save for later

Lovelee is a widget couples app that puts your partner on your home screen.

In just two months, it reached 70K downloads and 21.8M total views.

They only run two official accounts, TikTok and Instagram, both called lovelee_app, and they post the same videos on both.

On TikTok, they hit 5.1M views and 47K saves on November 28, 2025 with this hook:

“

may this type of love find and heal you

“

One day earlier on November 27, 2025, they also hit 5.1M views on Instagram and got 100K shares with a very similar hook:

“

may this type of love & care find you

“

Beyond the “may this type of love” hooks, they also blew up with POV hooks.

“

pov: you found the best way to ask your bf to make u tacos

” hit 2.8M on IG and 880K on TikTok.

“

pov: reminding your bf to feed you

” got 1.9M on IG and 980K on TikTok.

The top 10 most viewed videos all followed the same pattern.

They used either a “may this type of love” hook or a “pov” hook.

They also used the same faceless, zero cost format every time:

Scene: two phones on a lock screen + a candle.

Action: type a message on one phone, show it pop up on the other.

CTA: end on the app name + logo.

One format, two accounts, and two hook styles led to 21.8M views and 70K downloads.

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10zSGHEwS09Q

SGE Team

2 min read

Math AI was already featured

here

, a couple of weeks ago.

But since then, things have changed for them

For a while, they kept repeating the same hooks across multiple accounts.

“What plays in my head while taking the math exam worth 40% of my grade”

They never showed or mentioned the app.

None of those videos was getting real traction.

Until four days ago, when @learningwithrishab released a video that quickly went viral.

“POV: when you’re having fun and suddenly you realize where you are gonna be tomorrow at 8AM”

-> 2.9M views

This video pulled over 4,300 comments (and still counting).

One of the top comments came from Alarmy, another app.

Will they keep milking this format until one billion views?

We’ll keep you on the loop.

Creators are now using taboo openers, such as drinking before exams, to capture initial attention and land a study-app promo.

How 2 Billion Views Built a $20M Jet Broker

A desk, a phone call, and zero polish turned into 2B views, top-of-mind dominance, and a fast-growing jet brokerage wher…

SGE Team

•

January 7, 2026

•

5 min read

Save for later

This 24 year old is building a private jet chartering company almost entirely through TikTok and Instagram Reels.

You have likely seen his videos already. His main TikTok account alone has done over 1.5 billion views, with another 95 million on secondary accounts and 89 million on a personally named but branded account. That is just on TikTok.

On Instagram, the numbers add up to hundreds of millions more.

All in, the brand has crossed 2 billion views, most of them generated in just the last one or two years.

It is a massive awareness engine, very different from anything most jet companies are doing, and clearly inspired by shows like Below Deck and similar reality TV formats.

The content comes in several formats. First, it is worth looking at what made it work, then at the business behind it, based on publicly available information.

The most viral videos all follow the same structure. They show the CEO on a booking call, dealing with wild and often outrageous scenarios.

It feels less like marketing and more like a reality show. That is exactly why it works.

In a high ticket business where a single booking can mean thousands of dollars in fees, being the first brand people think of when they consider chartering a jet is an extremely strong strategy.

Before expanding into other formats, the early content is worth revisiting.

At first, they posted random videos before landing on the desk question format. The setup was basic, the audio was raw, and nothing looked polished. It did not matter. Within a short time, they hit their first one million view video.

It is unclear whether Colin expected this to become the main acquisition channel, or if it started as a fun experiment by a social media intern back in 2022.

Either way, they doubled down. By 2024, the desk was upgraded, the background looked intentionally expensive, and a proper microphone was added. That timing suggests the business was starting to gain traction.

One video in particular marked the breakthrough. It ran for four minutes and clearly defined the winning format.

From there, TikTok became the main growth driver. Production quality steadily improved, with faster cuts, on screen screenshots, and a style that feels familiar to anyone used to high performing TikTok content.

The secondary account now focuses on skits and humorous company related videos.

The account under his own name is centered on personal branding, company building, and longer storytelling that does not fit the other pages.

At this point, the obvious question is how much real business comes from all these views. A quick Google search for “is Amalfi Jets real?” surfaces a lot of negative discussion.

Some of it may be staged or driven by competitors. This kind of Reddit driven criticism is a common tactic in competitive markets.

The calls themselves are likely staged, but that is not a problem. They function as skits, and they do that job extremely well.

From an traffic perspective, the company has a 34 DR and around 5.6K in monthly organic traffic according to Ahrefs, mostly from branded searches.

That is relatively low, although many bookings may happen directly through phone calls listed on profiles and Google.

The app also shows limited downloads, which is not surprising given the niche and price point of private jet chartering.

Based on deep(er) research, the company operates as a Part 395 private jet charter broker with estimated revenue as follows:

2021:

~$1.7M

2022:

~$3.5M

2023:

~$6.5–7.0M

2024:

~$14–18M (marketing claims higher, audited reality lower)

2025 (forecast):

~$25–30M

This makes it a relatively small but fast growing brokerage with thin margins of about 10 to 12 percent, likely close to break even. The brand reach is far larger than the financial scale of the company.

That gap is what makes this such an interesting case study. It shows how dominating content in a single vertical can create a real business from scratch.

The strength of the brand alone could justify a higher acquisition price for a larger competitor looking to enter this channel quickly.

It is also a strong example of B2B content driving real growth by leaning into something people already love watching, how wealthy people live. Real estate has used this playbook for years.

The content potential here is almost unlimited. They effectively own the niche as a reality style TikTok brand and are now scaling through multiple in house channels across platforms.

Long term, this could also open the door to major monetization opportunities, from aircraft model placement to partnerships with other high value luxury brands.

SGE Team

New year, new me. Or at least, that’s what’s showing up all over our FYP.

It’s January, which means TikTok and Reels are packed with resolutions, drastic glow-up plans, and even some surprisingly dark confessions.

That’s where we come in—to help you break down the trends, go viral, and boost your app straight to the top of the charts.

Welcome to the first edition of The Trend Radar: Week 1 of 2026.

The 2026 Rebrand

Before the glow-up comes the planning spiral.

Creators are turning their reset mission into a full-time job. And, of course, letting us all in on the behind-the-scenes.

Think Pinterest boards, ChatGPT prompts, planners, and chaotic “2am I’m fixing my life” energy.

One example pulled 5.4M views “How serious i’m taking this 2026 rebrand”.

It’s a perfect format for a sneaky app name drop.

Check all examples here.

2) Start 2025 vs End 2025

No glow-up season would be complete without some hardcore proof.

Naturally, people are rushing to show off their biggest accomplishments all over TikTok, with special highlight to physical transformations.

One hook, two pictures is all you need. Then just let the contrast do the work.

One of these videos hit 6.3M views, coming from a creator that had less than 5,000 followers at the time she posted:

“Start 2025 / End 2025 / two different people.”

More examples here.

3) Things I Regret in 2025

Every ‘new me’ era comes with a confession scene, and this one is all about laying down your deepest regrets.

Or, of course, you can just put a funny spin on it. Up to you.

Loop one clip and drop a regret list that’s somewhere between serious and ridiculous.

Just like this creator did in a video that passed 1M views → “My 2025 regrets: nothing. I’m an icon and I literally did my best”

Or this one, who pulled 781.2k views with a slightly more detailed breakdown:

“Things I regret: bleaching my hair, buying a van that broke down the day I got it, trusting boys to borrow my car, not learning Spanish as a kid, literally nothing else because it’s all for the plot”.

Last one did 458.8k views with “Things I regret this year: halloweekend actions, double texting, being icked out by all men, my winter fits, caring too much”.

People just love to read confessions and comment… Read them all here.

4) 2025 Achievement Cake

Once the reflections period hits, people want a way to celebrate the wins.

This time, people went as far as making a cake for their 2025 achievements. Yes, an actual cake.

Each flag represents a win.

It’s super easy to recreate, even if you’ve never baked before. And it’s still pulling in millions of views…

4.5M views → “2025 achievements 🤍”

Have fun looking into all the viral videos.

5) Entering 2026 with a Song

And finally, every new era needs a soundtrack and this one is the easiest wrapper.

From “my exit song for 2025” to “my 2026 entry song”, creators are picking a theme song to leave 2025 behind and one to enter the “new” season.

You’ve still got a few days, but you better hurry for this one.

Two faceless formats pulled 3.9M views and 2.7M views respectively.

Exit song: 3.9M views.

Entry song: 2.7M views.

Read more here.

Your turn to hop on these while they’re still hot.

A sun tracking app hit 10K downloads and reached $8K MRR using a simple faceless video format.

The app is called Sunlitt.

It uses AR to preview sun direction and shadow coverage in a specific location at a certain time. It was built for creators and explorers, but went viral by aiming straight at photographers on TikTok.

On December 4, Sunlitt was ranked #215 in the U.S. Weather category.

By December 5, it jumped to #7.

Now it sits in the top 100 for Weather in most countries.

That rise aligned with a single faceless TikTok video.

@goldenhourgirlll

uploaded a video with the hook:

“

POV: you’re a photographer & trying to figure out the best time to shoot photos without the sun being harsh

“.

It pulled 650K views and 11.6K saves on Dec. 4.

The video is a visual app demo.

It shows Sunlitt’s shadow map over Central Park, letting users preview where shadows will fall at a specific time, directly in AR.

@goldenhourgirlll

is still posting similar videos, trying to reproduce the same virality.

In format terms, the loop is simple.

Problem POV → visual proof → save utility → distribution.

They took the product to a market where timing matters (photographers), named the pain point (“harsh sun”), and the value became obvious.

A simple app for checking a room for hidden cameras just hit $40K MRR.

Peek lets you do a fast “something feels off” scan for secret cameras and other recording devices.

It’s made for hotels, rentals, and any place you don’t know well.

The app also hit 40K downloads in the past 30 days.

This niche does not feel like it was built for easy social content, but Peek found a UGC play that worked, and drove over 9M views across 25 accounts in summer 2025.

@travelwithandreea5

A short, crying selfie video with a “

You think you can hurt me?

” long hook.

Another ambassador,

@detectionmodewith

Her hook started with “nothing can embarrass me anymore.”

The pattern is clear.

Dramatic hooks about discovering hidden cameras, often tied to someone close to them such as parents or a boyfriend, to trigger emotion and keep people watching.

They show a faceless clip of a recording device found in a hotel shower handle, then show the scan inside the app.

“

How do you know if your AirBNB or hotel room has hidden camera?

These videos make viewers feel uneasy and unsure, which leads some to download the app and scan their own rooms.

This 143 day old finance app is getting views from a single hook and one widget.

SGE Team

•

January 5, 2026

< 1 min read

Save for later

Originally branded as Duolingo for Money, the 143-day-old app Milo has been running about nine UGC accounts.

Only one is really working.

She has three viral videos out of around 30, adding up to almost 1M views. They all rely on the same hook.

“Only people in their 20s will understand this one… keeping your budget on your home screen”

The videos use their cute personal finance BFF icon and the home screen widget. The demo is simple and only shows the remaining budget on the home screen.

On the branded page, they first paired it next to the Duolingo streak widget. This was a smart move because it uses something familiar without competing with their own widget.

On this UGC page, they could push this winning hook way more. They only tested it a few times. When a hook and format work, they should be repeated as aggressively as possible.

If you remember Brainly, they hit

25 million views in 90 days

back in May.

Since then, they have built a network of over 30 accounts.

After pausing in June, they have restarted around October 20, fully ready for exam season.

This time, they’re mostly working with new creators, but results have been limited.

Only one video has crossed 300K views, and it doesn’t even mention the app.

The next best performer is sitting at around 40K views.

They’re leaning into an engagement farming, pre-exam manifestation tactic where students comment variations of “claim”.

So far, it hasn’t worked very well, but they could still see a breakout closer to exams.

That said, the content quality feels lower than their previous creator batch.

It could also be that Studytok is getting more competitive for apps this year, and the bar for standout content is simply higher.

•

2 min read

Launched in 2024, Quest: Sleep Better Tonight looks like a simple sleep app at first glance.

On TikTok, though, it exploded, pulling in millions of views by pushing content that goes beyond the app’s core features, building prolific channels with long term views.

The app runs just one TikTok account, created in April 2025.

That single account has already generated an impressive 245.2 million views.

Everything revolves around one repeatable format.

Each video opens with an AI clip about the human body, completely unrelated to sleep.

Moments later, it cuts to the app’s content with a short, catchy good night message.

That opening hook does all the heavy lifting.

One video posted seven months ago reached 65.1 million views and made 170,600 comments.

Despite the unrelated opening, most comments come from people admitting they are still awake, even though it is late at night.

The posts timing is key here.

This app did not blow up just because it helps people sleep. It blew up because of how it is packaged. Unexpected AI clips hook viewers, and the calm good night message closes the loop.

frameworks.description: Start content with an unexpected, attention-grabbing element unrelated to the core product to hook viewers, then quickly transition to a relevant message that ties back to the product, creating a memorable and engaging experience.
frameworks.when_to_use: Use when launching content on platforms like TikTok where initial seconds determine viewer retention and when the product category is competitive or not inherently viral.
frameworks.example: Quest: Sleep Better Tonight uses random AI clips about the human body unrelated to sleep as the opening hook, then closes with a calm good night message promoting the app.

metadata.key_principle: Leveraging unexpected, unrelated hooks in content captures attention and drives viral engagement, while a relevant closing message ties back to the product, enhancing brand recall and user connection.
metadata.article_summary: Quest: Sleep Better Tonight, a sleep app launched in 2024, achieved viral success on TikTok by using a single account that posts videos starting with random AI clips about the human body unrelated to sleep, followed by a calm good night message promoting the app. This unexpected hook strategy generated over 245 million views and a video with 65 million views and 170k comments, mostly from users engaging late at night. The timing and packaging of content, rather than just the app's features, drove its viral growth.

article.title: Can’t believe they got this domain name
article.content:
Can’t believe they got this domain name

Uncovering the truth behind a new, mysterious network of TikTok accounts.

Can’t believe they got this domain name

Uncovering the truth behind a new, mysterious network of TikTok accounts.

SGE Team

•

December 11, 2025

•

5 min read

Save for later

We found an incredible upcoming app scheme strategy.

It is an unreleased app with this domain name: atc.com.

They have a three-letter domain name that is the acronym for Air Traffic Control. The domain was first listed in 1990, mind you. It was then updated in 2025.

The first thought was that the initial holder simply abandoned the domain and some kids snapped it up.

That was our initial impression because the content looks like this, with a video that has 1.4 million views.

It clearly feels like something youngsters would make, a TikTok-style mobile app concept. And that is not all.

There are three accounts like this.

All started a few days ago, and each has at least one video with over fifty thousand views.

That is an incredible sign of content-market fit.

Out of twelve videos, one went viral with 1.4 million views and each of the three accounts already has at least one outlier.

This kind of content makes it easy to spark virality, as the comments show.

They can also invent any story they want and pair it with smooth, realistic air traffic control audio, which makes the videos highly potent in virality.

Hooks they use such as “me boarding the plane ready to monitor my pilot the whole flight” you can imagine from all the people feared of flying that relate to wanting to sneak into the pilot comms.

They also appear to use very similar clips.

In this niche, we have noticed that airplane footage keeps people watching longer because viewers are more curious about it and do not see these kinds of shots as often.

Digging deeper, we found that there is a way to get a live feed, or at least to tune in to the Air Traffic Control company.

If they target the consumer market, it is a smart move since the only competing app costs $4, looks outdated, has a poor UI, and has not been updated in ten months.

Looking more closely, we discovered that it is not just “kids” making an app. It is an actual Y Combinator company.

It is made by two former professional pilots who also previously sold a company and are now building a new one together from this winter batch.

This is probably how they paid ($$$$$$) for atc.com from its original owner.

They are building datasets and recruiting AI engineers to build AI air traffic control applications.

Why they are promoting it as a consumer app with such hooks and scenarios is still a mystery, but as they get closer to releasing the app, we will know more about their intention and strategy.

We like it A LOT here at Social Growth Engineers.

It is well executed and sits in a part of the travel vertical we have not yet explored, so we are ecstatic about where it is going.

Recently, the travel UGC category unraveling for travel app marketing. We saw many large-scale strategies, such as:

Roamy, doing one 100,000 downloads in two weeks.

Or Tryp, gaining millions of views while promoting its cheap flights platform.

And of course, Nomadtable, which we are big fans of.

And others like TripBff, Triips, and more.

It is a growing vertical and a huge niche across TikTok and Instagram. We expect many more apps to start using this channel to acquire users.

And as ATC shows, there are plenty of app ideas in this space that have not yet been explored.

A 3M-download, $2.6M MRR language app just turned TikTok envy of native speakers into its main growth engine. Now 25 cre…

SGE Team

•

December 11, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

Language-learning TikTok may have just found its new main character.

Launched in 2024, the app has already reached 3M downloads and roughly $2.6M in monthly recurring revenue across iOS and Android.

Learna AI

is an AI language tutor built for English and Spanish learners.

Today, the app is in the top 100 charts in almost every country in the world.

Right now it also holds the number #1 spot in Education in 10 different countries.

Before we zoom in on UGC, it helps to see the full machine.

Across TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube, Learna AI now runs 28 active accounts that together have generated 35.5 million views.

Three of these are the main brand hubs: @learna.ai on TikTok and Instagram, plus @AILearna on YouTube. Combined, they account for 19.3 million views.

On Instagram alone, the account has nearly 15 million views and 600K followers, though most of that volume comes from paid amplification and Spark-style boosting instead of pure organic reach.

The other 25 accounts are ambassadors.

Their posts drive 16.2 million views that are much more organic.

The interesting part is that the UGC push did not start as a big planned campaign.

The first clear signal came from a Turkish creator who started posting Learna content in July, before any of the others.

She pulled in 13.6M views with a couple of partially boosted viral videos over the summer, then went quiet, and came back on November 3 when the rest of the ambassadors started posting.

Looking back, her summer posts were the prototype.

Localized language, sharp hooks, and just enough boosted spend to see if the idea could work.

The November wave simply took that pattern and spread it across 25 creators.

@alterxo hit 700K views on December 1 with this long hook:

“

I envy people who learned English first. You’re telling me you somehow naturally knew the difference between “complement” and “compliment”? Come on now.

“

She only mentions the app in the caption.

The same structure helped @

learna.aaron

to reach 285K views in November,

And

@learndailywithsol

reached 160K views around the same time.

Crying or sad face -> envy native English speakers hook -> Learna AI caption.

That format is really a remix of an older viral idea.

Back in December 2023, videos with this kind of joke started going extremely viral

Two years later, the concept came back and went viral again in many versions, like:

“

POV: When you have a boyfriend that you only speak english with, He’ll never know how funny and smart you are in your own language

” 2.3M views

More recently, the same structure has been used across several language-learning apps.

Their UGC layer is still a small part of total views, but having 25 creators testing and tweaking these formats at the same time is a strong signal of where growth is heading.

You can explore Learna’s full collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10De94DZDS5j

Copia just went through a major rebrand.

They now go under the name Era as a stress and sleep tracker.

Unlike most rebrands where companies keep the same accounts and swap a logo…

(eg:

Albo)

, Era rebuilt their entire identity and their network:

New logo + brand colours

New storyline around astrology, mindset, routines, and personal growth

New promise:

“no more crashing out”

What’s more interesting though, Copia’s network went quiet.

When we last covered their strategy, they went from 4 to 40 ambassadors all female, scaling

17M+ views in 60 days.

Now, only one person is still posting consistently, the founder, with two separate accounts:

@chloeegaynor

&

@chloe.manifests

.

Every other ambassador account is inactive. Copia’s main account hasn’t posted since the 5th of May.

Their main account Copia used to run almost entirely on faceless aesthetic slideshows: Pinterest-style photo dumps, aspirational vibes and “manifesting this life” edits.

After the rebrand, Era’s content moved almost fully to talking videos: face close-ups, all delivered by one person: the founder, Chloe.

Although their last post was in August.

Chloe’s videos now focus on:

personal routines

gym lifestyle

startup founder lessons

astrology hooks

motivational POVs

burnout & mental health

“building your dream life” narratives

You can track their accounts here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10g958QWwP5c

For now, no major growth in terms of downloads or revenue. We’ll keep you posted as this rebranding unfolds.

article.content:
Alpha Bro Apps

Faceless self-help apps are blowing up on TikTok and Instagram. Two launched this year and one already hit 84.7M views.…

4 min read

Alpha Bro Apps

Faceless self-help apps are blowing up on TikTok and Instagram. Two launched this year and one already hit 84.7M views.…

SGE Team

•

December 11, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

Many people still believe self-discipline apps only take off when there’s a coach, influencer, or well-known face behind them.

But now, some of the fastest-growing apps are suggesting the opposite.

Streaks, challenges, dashboards, and gamified progress are going viral on TikTok and Instagram, generating millions of views without relying on anyone’s face or name.

For these apps, the story is the user’s journey.

Two of these apps are standing out in the alpha-male-self-improvement niche.

Both apps were launched this year.

DAWG

was released six months ago and captured 84.7 million views, with a strategy heavily focused on Instagram Reels.

Access all data here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b100NYjYNTE08

Endeavorise

was released around the same time, back in May.

They’ve racked up 18.5 million views so far, mostly from TikTok.

Access all videos here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10bZe5rTJeIZ

Last month,

we published an article

about the format that Endeavorise used to generate over 10,000 downloads.

It was always the same, repeated every single day — a faceless 20-second clip fading in to highlight an app feature (usually a colorful chart), paired with a relatable hook about self-improvement, breakups, or motivation.

Every video shows the Wojak meme guy, and since he’s part of a real app screenshot, it gets way more conversions than a regular funny meme post. Or at least, it should…

The

top-performing video

has hit 3.1 million views and 1,361 comments, mostly from male users showing their progress in the app or talking about what keeps them motivated.

The app mainly targets groups of friends and people into self-improvement, but its focus is clearly on men, especially those in “Bro culture” and aspiring entrepreneurs.

DAWG is following a similar path. The team is sticking to one format on both platforms, and it’s gotten quite some traction already, especially on Instagram.

Each video is about 8 seconds long and uses a hook similar to their competitor:

“bro 2 months ago vs bro now 💀💀 💀” →

6.2M views

“every MALE group has that one guy…🥶🤕 💀☠️ “ →

10M views

“tag bro w this build 💀🥀” →

1.1M views

Their

most popular video

has 13.9 million views and 1200 comments. It doesn’t use the Wojak character, but the hook is a meme in itself, playing with the idea that men do change when their girlfriends make them.

Again, most of the comments are from guys sharing how their relationships have messed with their performance.

It’s pretty clear they’re both going after a mostly male audience using love and relationship content. Turns out, talking about relationships works, regardless of you’re pushing a long-distance love app, a cheater detector, or some alpha-bro tool.

DAWG’s interface looks a bit different from Endeavorise’s, but it works the same way. The hexagon chart tracks how the user’s lifestyle scores change over six areas:

Physical

Ambition

Relationship

Discipline

Mental

Intelect

Same audience, same targeting, similar format.

In both cases, even though the apps got a bunch of comments, monthly downloads are still low.

Can this kind of faceless, meme-heavy format really hold up as a long-term marketing plan?

We’ll find out in a few months.

article.title: One Video, Two Different Outcomes
article.content:
One Video, Two Different Outcomes

Magibook posted the same TikTok twice and sparked two totally different debates in the comments. The video didn’t change…

2 min read

One Video, Two Different Outcomes

Magibook posted the same TikTok twice and sparked two totally different debates in the comments. The video didn’t change…

SGE Team

December 10, 2025

•

2 min read

Save for later

Since launching in 2024,

Magibook

has gotten some attention for a surprising twist: using the same video on TikTok and getting two totally different outcomes.

The app is running a single TikTok account, and so far, totaling 2.8M views since they started posting, in August.

Lately, the app has been using the same formula over and over: a phone-shot video of a kid using the app, with a hook written in a banner at the top.

Recently, two of these videos stood out, one with 1.2 million views, the other with 1.5 million.

They always use the same trick. Both videos feature this kid reading books that are way above his age level (sometimes even above an average adult’s IQ to be fair).

“Caught my 8y old reading Nietzsche” (when this kid is 4 maximum)

“I caught my 7y old reading “Crime and Punishment”

“Is this normal?? What is bro preparing for??”

Meanwhile, the visual hook of the iPad implies that it’s the app making those books easier to read and become age appropriate.

These videos triggered a flood of comments, with most of the discussion centered around a heated debate on whether it’s even ethical or possible for Magibook to heavily simplify classic literature.

More videos in the same style were posted on the account, with different reaction levels.

We’ll keep an eye on any new viral formats they experiment with.

frameworks.description: Posting the same content multiple times to the same platform can yield different audience reactions and engagement levels depending on timing, context, and framing (such as captions or banners). This approach leverages the unpredictability of social media virality and audience sentiment to maximize reach and engagement.
frameworks.when_to_use: When you have a content format that resonates but want to test different audience reactions or spark varied discussions without creating new content from scratch.
frameworks.example: Magibook posted the same TikTok video twice with different captions/banners, resulting in two distinct debates in the comments and high view counts.

metadata.key_principle: The same piece of content can generate different engagement and community reactions depending on subtle contextual changes and timing, enabling efficient content reuse to maximize organic growth.

The videos featured a child reading complex literature, with captions implying the app simplifies these books for kids. article.title: Bad Dates Turned $1.6M In Seed Fund
article.content:
Bad Dates Turned $1.6M In Seed Fund

How Cerca Dating app went from 0 to 45M views in 10 months using the power of founder-led content.

SGE Team

•

December 9, 2025

•

4 min read

Bad Dates Turned $1.6M In Seed Fund

How Cerca Dating app went from 0 to 45M views in 10 months using the power of founder-led content.

SGE Team

•

December 9, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

After completing a banking internship in New York City, Myles Slaytonfound himself and his friends stuck in the same loop: endless swiping, awkward first dates, and a deep mistrust of everyone behind the screen.

So instead of trying to build a “better algorithm,” he and his co-founders Willy Conzelman and Carter Munk flipped the entire logic of dating apps and rebuilt dating for Gen Z.

And that’s how

Cerca

was founded. The app that matches you through your existing social graph your contacts, mutuals, and extended circles.

Just months after launch, Cerca raised $1.6M in seed funding and attracted 60,000 users, mostly across New York City and U.S. university campuses.

The Shift: From UGC Network to Founder-Led Storytelling

Most consumer apps scale TikTok through mass UGC.

Cerca didn’t.

Instead of spinning up hundreds of faceless creator accounts, Cerca put its founders directly on camera. Each founder runs multiple accounts across TikTok and Instagram, turning personal storytelling into the brand’s main growth channel.

With fewer accounts than most social-first apps, Cerca has pulled:

44.3M+ lifetime views

Across just 60+ creator accounts in under 10 months since launch.

Over the last month alone, Cerca pulled 24.2M views from one format: founder-led, face-to-camera storytelling.

One of their engine is “Bad Dates → Better App.” And that format still runs.

The most viral videos this month came directly from Myles’ own account,

with 3.4M views on a single post

telling how

“emails are in”.

In this video, he talks about how he walked up to a girl outside and asked for her email. The video got over 2,000 comments, but since he didn’t mention the app or tie the story back to Cerca, all the comments missed the point and didn’t lead to any conversions.

Another hit from his Instagram account was a

“bad Hinge date story”

that pulled

1.9 million views:

In this one, he talks about a weird date he went on, and two smart details stand out:

Mentioning a well-known app like Hinge makes the story instantly click with people who use it too, and it feels more natural.

He purposely misspells “Labubu” to spark comments, and it worked. One of them got over 10K likes.

Still, even with all the engagement, the story didn’t drive significant conversions. It was fun and relatable, but not built to get downloads. The only app CTA is on the post’s caption, but it seems to go unnoticed by most viewers.

The same thing happened with another post, this time about a “Raya breakdown.” Raya is a members-only dating app that some people online are calling “Tinder for the Illuminati.”

The video got

1.5 million views,

but again, no one paid attention to the mention of the Cerca app in the caption. All the comments were either roasting Raya or just reacting to the story.

So far, it seems that all of their content is relying in this one single strategy:

Storytime hook → Personal failure → Emotional shift

They’ve got the hook down. The talking format works, and even their founders are doing a solid job on camera, which isn’t always easy, especially with this kind of headshot, talking content.

But something’s still off. The team hasn’t figured out how to tie the viral content back to the product. They need a smoother way to weave the app into the story—either as how it all starts, or as the better option compared to the big dating apps they keep roasting.

Some other accounts are pulling solid views, but most fall into the same trap.

You can track them all here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10eSEqynevRW

This Study app format strategy is making a hard comeback on StudyTok (it actually never left) and exploding again, with different apps using it and getting multi-million views.

We noticed it first a few weeks ago, but the earliest big example was in a Turbolearn video.

The format works like this: you film yourself studying, while an AI voice talks in the background.

The AI suddenly coughs.

You cut to a one-second slow-motion shocked reaction, then grab your phone, turn it toward the screen, pause the AI podcast and ask why it coughed.

The AI replies that it cannot cough and gives some explanation.

Turbo AI did not just post it once. They repeated the format again here:

Then we found another app, Studley AI.

They work with

more than 100 creators

and they are using the same format, including a video that reached 7.4M views.

The creator’s account is interesting too. If you look closely, they began with a totally different style, tested a bunch of StudyTok formats and eventually landed on this one, copying the original almost frame by frame.

What started as a tiny underground joke on TikTok, is now a full app where besides watching memes, you get to bet on which ones will go viral.

Giggles is a meme social app that mixes TikTok energy, prediction markets, and crypto vibes.

Instead of only scrolling and liking, you put money on posts, creators, and trends you think will blow up, and you earn “aura” when you are right.

Giggles launched in April and has now hit 10,000 monthly downloads.

They are now in the top 100 in multiple countries, including the U.S.

And it is not a surprise how they got there.

Their main TikTok

account

pulled in over 75M views before the app even existed.

Back in 2021, they found a weird but winning content formula that turned into a meme.

The creator posted “can’t rn” hooks while replying to viewers’ dares.

In their most popular video, he shows a viewer comment:

“be a human then”, and replies with:

“

can’t rn im flying

” -> 27.2M views and 130K saves.

Pure OG brainrot.

The account has been inactive since 2022, but it still promotes the app in the bio, which makes it clear the app devs are the same people behind that old viral TikTok account.

The funny twist is that Instagram Reels now feel even more “memeable” and brainrot than TikTok.

Giggles started posting Reels in August, and now has 117K followers and around 6M views since then.

They leaned into edgy memes and app promo hooks to reach virality.

That is their main content format.

Their best performing Reel used the trendy “

Chicken Stars

” meme at the time.

“

Average meal while scrolling Giggles 24/7

” hit 1.9M views in October.

They also pushed “brainrot” skits that included the app name in the hook, like:

“

Giggles CEO think I’m paying attention but the whole time I’m just watching da bob

” which hit 360K views in September.

Their very first Instagram Reel was an app intro.

They showed a black & white montage of the edgiest and most popular memes of 2025, then plugged the app at the end.

“

steve jobs did NOT die for ts

” 650K views in August.

In the end, Giggles is a rare case of a meme outliving its original platform.

They took a 2021 TikTok “can’t rn” brainrot format, turned it into a viral account, and then into a meme betting app that is now quietly growing on Instagram Reels and closing in on its first 10K downloads.

You can track and analyze both their new and old viral accounts on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10ow1V5bJRQK

In a world already overflowing with photo-editing apps, very few have done what Halo AI has done in such a short time. After just two months on the market, it’s already crossed 100,000 downloads and grabbed >20% market share.

This week, it made another big move, jumping to rank #53 in the Photo & Video charts and quickly catching up the top players.

Even with just 8 official social media accounts, the app has already gained over 73,3 million views since it was launched.

The app originally took off on the

@halo.ai0

account with simple food prank videos. They reused the same frying pan photo, turned it into a fake AI image, and showed people’s reactions on WhatsApp after getting it. None of the videos showed any faces.

The video hooks always highlight the prank scenario, usually something related to the kitchen or a strange AI-generated “creature.” That initial shock is what grabs attention.

But slowly, the newer creators have started gaining more and more traction.

They initially started with a headshot format: the video starts with the creator on camera, either talking or reacting with a bold expression, and there’s always music playing. Right away, the hook explains what they’re about to do with the app, then they walk through the steps, one by one.

But interestingly, this format didn’t do as well.

The videos that actually went viral stick to the same formula as the first one: no faces, a clear step-by-step of editing a photo with the app, and a prank at the end using the final image.

This video got 2,158 comments, mostly from people laughing in reaction to the prank.

Humor has become their most powerful trigger to views and engagement.

If the app’s done this much in just two months, it might hit the number-one spot soon if it keeps growing like this. We’ll keep you posted on this one.

A creator films themselves standing in front of a mirror or in their bedroom.  The framing is focused around their waistband, shows their silhouette.

This format comes from the @dumbhotshow account and features short, on-the-street interviews.

The interviewer mainly talks to people who are seen as really attractive or good-looking. The person they stop agrees to play a quick trivia game, usually based on general knowledge.

The player has 30 seconds to answer as many trivia questions as possible, with both the questions and timer clearly shown on screen so the audience can follow along.

Based on how many questions they get right, the person is put into one of two fun categories that match the show’s title:

Dumb Hot (good-looking but not very smart)

Beautiful Genius (smart and attractive)

You can take this concept and apply it in many different ways, including a faceless slideshow with controversial ratings and some good old engagement farming.

Another week, another viral StudyFetch trend. This time, it’s a twist on the usual “studying until my ice melts” with a small change:

She records herself studying at her desk with time stamps, then shifts to recording her laptop screen while using the website.

Yapper

😂

”

The video blew up with

, 2 million likes, and almost 10,000 comments.

here

.

These two videos have each pulled in 2.6 million views (with a possible slight paid boost).

Same format, same hook, different faces.

😭😭

”

Video 1 –

here

here

Screen blocker app Opal hit

426K views just three days ago

with a talking head format where the creator goes through a list of

“how to make your life interesting again — no money needed

”).

Symmetry

Wrapping things up with a viral slideshow (because what’s a Maria’s roundup without one?)

Symmetry, the Spanish fitness app, has been on a roll with its

“Ranking every training split after 6 years in the gym”

format.

The latest post, from four days ago,

brought in 271K views

.

We’ve recently published an in-depth piece on how they managed to reach #1 in Fitness in under five months — read it

here

.

This is a creative format that turns cultural knowledge into a street-style guessing game.

An interviewer stops someone on the street and says, “Tell me where you’re from, without actually saying it.”

It can be a good format for travel, trivia and social apps.

A gamified self-improvement app turned Gen Z “level up in real life” into 80M+ views. They just show one clean stat scre…

Yes, another “level up in real life” app for Gen Z gamers.

The app is called

DAWG

, and it cracked a winning faceless format.

On Instagram, they run @

dawg.app

, an account that has pulled in over 83M views.

All powered by one main faceless format.

DAWG posts videos that highlight the app’s main feature.

They start with a strong hook at the top, then use a fade-in to reveal the app’s key feature and tie it back to that hook.

The key feature is a hexagon with six self-improvement areas, each scored from 0 to 100: Physical, Relationship, Discipline, Mental, Intellect, and Ambition.

Each number goes up or down based on the story in the hook.

For example:

“

every MALE group has that one guy…

” -> 10M views on April 3

Five months later, they went viral again using the same hook:

“

every MALE group has that one guy…

” -> 3.7M views on September 22

DAWG leans into engagement farming hooks that fit this format.

That is why their best performers use words like “bro” or “boys” in the opening line.

DAWG proves how far one tight format can go when it is built on a clear visual and repeatable hooks.

They turn basic app demo footage into share bait.

By doing this they pushed a single account past 80M views without having to show their faces or pay any creator.

Potential niches: motivation, self-improvement, social, productivity

You can track DAWG’s collection and analyze their strategy on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b100NYjYNTE08

After just three months on the market,

Eat Well

has started to gain some traction. Recently, one of their videos went viral on TikTok and turned quite some attention towards the app.

The app’s social media account has already reached 18.2 million views.

At the end of August, a vido by creator @jess.healthyeating racked up 11 million views, 1.5 million likes and over 3,000 comments.

The post opens with a hook that might look familiar if you’ve been following recent trends ->

“You look happier”

The format is a simple slideshow made exclusively with Pinterest photos featuring meals, short captions over each dish pointing out its benefits.

Unlike most of their other videos, this one doesn’t start with a “POV”. Instead, it uses a testimonial-style hook, while the others stick to a callout format.

This video alone makes up 66.7% of their lifetime views.

All the videos use the same format. The only real difference is the hook, proving once again that riding a viral trend can easily become your entry point into a whole new market.

Made popular by the account

@streethearts

The interviewer creates a quirky date setup right in the middle of the street, table and all.

Two strangers are asked to sit down across from each other.

Both people wear blindfolds for most of the date, so they have no idea what the person sitting across from them looks like.

The interviewer sits in the middle and asks both people questions, helping guide the conversation and build a connection.

After spending some time talking and connecting with the blindfolds on, they’re asked to take them off.

Once they see each other, they have to decide right away if they want a second date, based on the connection they felt and their first look.

article.title: 20y old founders land #1 in Spain
article.content:
20y old founders land #1 in Spain

In just five months, they’ve built the most promising Spanish fitness app.

SGE Team

•

December 3, 2025

•

6 min read

20y old founders land #1 in Spain

In just five months, they’ve built the most promising Spanish fitness app.

SGE Team

•

December 3, 2025

•

6 min read

Save for later

Spain’s GymTok has officially found its own personal trainer.

A small Spanish team spent a few months turning a diverse playbook into the fastest growing fitness app in the country.

Symmetry started out as a dare, but ended up peaking at #1 in Health & Fitness on the Spanish App Store, with 100K+ installs on Android.

Symmetry’s story started with a challenge.

In the beginning of 2025, co-founders

Mauro Botanes

,

Miguel Ortiz

, and

Diego Moreno

set themselves a challenge: ship a new gym app in 40 days and make €10,000.

They started building in public, posting daily and documenting the entire progress.

Just three 20 year old guys with no external investment, mentors or previous experience.

On June 6, Symmetry launched on both the App Store and Google Play.

The app made over 200K downloads in the first three months, while climbing to the top spots in multiple Spanish speaking countries.

The concept is pretty simple: you take a full-body picture, AI scans it and you get a score and a personalized workout plan to reach your weight goal.

The app has a free version with all basic features and no ads. Users who want more advanced options, they can sign up to the pro subscription for €12.99/month or €49.99/ year.

Social Growth Empire

Miguel, one of the Co-Founders, already had his own personal brand, including a self-improvement YouTube channel with 350K subscribers.

Symmetry is managing a total of 55 accounts and made over 83 million views.

Breaking them down by platform, they did:

55 million views on Instagram across 14 accounts;

27.6 million views on TikTok across 39 accounts;

320K views on YouTube across 2 accounts.

Instagram Faceless Powerhouse

Symmetry runs three faceless Instagram accounts that are going insanely viral. @symmetry.club is the biggest one, at 25.9 million views.

It blew up by using simple, relatable and shareable self improvement hooks at the top, then adding a fade in effect that reveals images matching the hook with quick tips and guides.

The top performing videos use that same format:

“Bro, ¿por qué estás tan feliz todo el tiempo?” yo mostrándole esto a mi bro

“Bro, why are you so happy all the time?” me showing this to my bro

The video below pulled 3M views on July 20:

@symmetry_.app followed as second with 15.2 million views, using the same faceless strategy, but with black and white anime pictures.

Cómo se siente cuando todos los de nuestra edad salen de fiesta y se dr*gan, pero tú y tu bro estáis intentando ser mejor cada dia:

How it feels when everyone our age goes out partying and dr*gs themselves, but you and your bro are trying to get better every day:

This video from July 24 hit 4.5 million views.

Then there’s @symmetryybro with 11.5M views.

This account posts 3D body images that show their app ranking system.

They managed to turn a core format and “bro” hooks into 3 faceless accounts that made over 50+ million views.

A multifaceted TikTok plan

Symmetry blew up on TikTok through two main strategies. One of them is a UGC wave built around Spanish Gen Z fitness creators.

There are 19 accounts branded “name.symmetry” that have already generated 8.8M views since launching in October.

These accounts mostly post slideshow videos that share fitness tips and then show the app on the final slide.

“Clasificando cada rutina que he hecho (como coach online con más de 10 años de experiencia y natural)”

“Ranking every routine I’ve done (as an online coach with over 10 years of experience and natural)”

500,000 views on November 11:

Their second strategy, and also their most successful one, is using faceless non branded accounts. The only 10M+ TikTok account is one of those and is called @elpana.musculo.

This account went viral using the same format — fitness advice slideshows plus app promo. The only difference is that all the pictures are taken straight from the internet.

#1:

5 tips to increase your muscle mass

→ 3.2M views and 112K saves

#2:

10 rules for your Winter Arc

→ 900K views and 50K saves

#3:

Ranking the best training apps

→ 1.1M views and 40K saves

Numbered and a “list” hooks worked best for these slideshows.

You can check the full analysis here:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/analysis/38e7f893-7b7d-4123-a801-4374c48c6351

In only five months, three 20-year-old founders turned a 40-day dare into Spain’s go to GymTok trainer.

Symmetry is still a small startup on paper, but it already owns the Spanish fitness feed. It is a clear example of how far you can scale without ever using English content.

Their full collection is available on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10XiZkADi7tE

Duolingo style apps are becoming a cheat code for niche MRR, and Paladin is a clear example. Choose a niche, give it the Duolingo treatment, and craft one viral line that makes people stop and think:

Undercover App Account Hits 650K followers and 50M views in 5 days

In 5 days, a brand new Instagram account went from 1 follower to 650K by dropping a cute mascot 1mm for every new follow…

SGE Team

3 min read

Undercover App Account Hits 650K followers and 50M views in 5 days

In 5 days, a brand new Instagram account went from 1 follower to 650K by dropping a cute mascot 1mm for every new follow…

SGE Team

•

December 3, 2025

•

3 min read

Save for later

A new Instagram account just took over Instagram Reels with a mascot series.

Remember

EmyBFF

? We

wrote about them

when they were first starting out back in April.

A few days ago, they decided to launch the account @

emyadventure1

.

At a first glance, nothing connects it to the app.

With just four videos, it hit around 650K followers and more than 50 million views.

The account exists for one simple format:

Day “x” of dropping Emy 1mm for every follower until we reach the Burj Khalifa

Emy is their app mascot, but they are not saying that publicly yet.

The account is blowing up, and they chose not to promote the app in an obvious way. People who use the app can see it right away, because the name and the mascot are the same.

Most viewers, though, have never heard of it.

They are just hooked on the series while quietly building a bond with the mascot behind the product.

The first video in the series did 28.5 million views and over 10K comments.

It was uploaded on a brand new account with only 1 follower at the time.

The comments were full of people calling the series “peak” and claiming to be “OG”.

In one move, they built a global crowd of people who want to see Emy fall.

Then, they get the creator to comment as Emy, feeding into the buzz (23K likes on a single comment).

Right now, the account is at 656K followers, meaning that Emy is supposed to fall 656 meters in total.

The Burj Khalifa is 830 meters tall, so the series is already close to the physical limit of what they can film.

In a few days, they will likely pass the Burj Khalifa.

Will they wrap up the series in just 5 videos?

Or will they find a creative way to keep it going and push for even more virality?

They currently have a website link in their account with a countdown timer.

Supposedly there a few hours left until we see what will happen, but it may be an app promo:

“OG Tickets Only”

https://emyadventure.com

We will keep you updated as this series evolves.

You can check out EmyBFF’s collection on Shortimize here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10t5wQ4Vi2Xv

article.title: 100K downloads in 2 weeks
article.content:
100K downloads in 2 weeks

Another Gen Z consumer app hit shaking up the App Store.

SGE Team

•

•

6 min read

100K downloads in 2 weeks

Another Gen Z consumer app hit shaking up the App Store.

SGE Team

•

December 2, 2025

•

6 min read

Save for later

This new app went from unknown to one of the most downloaded in the travel niche, in several countries, in about two weeks.

Roamy is an AI trip planner that turns social media “travel inspo” into real itineraries you can actually follow.

In just two weeks after launching, in late October 2025, Roamy passed 100,000 downloads and climbed into the top travel charts across Europe.

The Core Feature

Roamy leans into a very common habit.

We save endless TikTok and Instagram travel videos, then never turn them into a real trip.

Roamy takes every location mentioned in a saved video, pins them on a map and builds a day by day route based on how long you are traveling.

The Beginning

Roamy was created by

Logos Studio Inc.

, a small app studio founded in 2024, as its first move into travel tech.

Founder

Frank Chen

is a Toronto-based developer who had already shipped several AI apps in other niches, all the way from e-readers to chatbots.

He was tired of how hard it was to turn saved travel posts into a real plan, so he built the tool he wanted for himself and discovered that many others had the same problem.

Early Success

Launched on October 28, 2025, Roamy took off within days, climbing app store charts on the back of viral TikTok and Instagram content.

Built as a small, bootstrapped project, it landed at the perfect moment, fixing the “saved posts overload” problem for a new wave of social media driven travelers.

The Business Model

Roamy is free to download and runs on a freemium model.

Its paid plan, Roamy Pro, is priced at $12.99 per month or $39.99 per year in the US.

Core features such as importing locations and generating auto itineraries are free, so new users can see value right away.

Right now their focus is on growth, with the team clearly prioritizing viral adoption first and potentially leaning into deeper monetization at a later stage, once enough travelers are using the app often.

The UGC Push

Roamy’s breakout has been driven by a solid TikTok and Instagram move based on UGC content.

The team is working with 12 ambassadors who run “name.roamy” accounts and post a Roamy demo every single day on both platforms.

You can take a look at all their ambassador accounts on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b1099osSV4DMo

The playbook is simple and familiar from other viral app stories we’ve covered before.

Launch many themed accounts, test lots of hook variations on UGC selfies and let the algorithm pick the winners.

It only took one creator hitting millions of views for downloads to jump and for Roamy to blow up in the app store charts.

This creator was

@

marg.roamy

, who hit virality on both Instagram and TikTok with the same clip, spotting the winning hook.

“i could LITERALLY KISS the flight attendant that showed me this”

This first video, uploaded on November 13, pulled 4.8M views on

TikTok

and 2.8M views on

Instagram

.

Because she filmed it on a plane, the whole thing felt like a genuine recommendation, not an ad.

And the numbers that followed are wild.

More than 337K bookmarks and 92K shares on her TikTok so far, from an account that only started posting in early November.

The next day she posted another video.

That one pulled in 890,000 views and 40,000 saves.

“

Been saving travel videos for 4 years and NOW i find this?

“

The UGC push only started about two weeks ago, but each account already has around 20 videos, and winning patterns are starting to get crystal clear for them.

Another creator,

@denise.roamy

was the first to land consistent hits on Instagram with hooks like:

“

so apparently I’ve been planning my trips wrong

“

Again, shocked face thumbnails and airplane shots helped sell the story.

The videos are proven converters.

The comments are full of people asking for the app name and getting tagged with “Roamy” by the creator, an interesting small trick to make sure viewers get notified and come back to the post to read the reply.

The organic reach is amplified by people tagging friends and partners and sharing clips to Instagram Stories and group chats.

The Hooks

We’ve analyzed all Roamy’s TikTok UGC videos, and found that their best performing hooks tap into curiosity and shame emotions, mixing both with an effectively crafted “FOMO” feeling.

For instance:

i could LITERALLY KISS the flight attendant that showed me this

→ Curiosity

Sooo apparently I’ve been planning my trips WRONG???

→ Shame

You can consult the full hook analysis here:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/analysis/37d852a9-ce00-48cd-a39d-4691f4c42225

What’s Next

Roamy’s growth team started with a solid grasp of UGC culture and kept the strategy very simple. In a matter of days, they turned into a must try app for Gen Z and millennial travelers.

It’s a sharp example of a small team using AI and social virality to compete against much larger companies in the consumer app space.

AI Face Coach Crosses $20,000 MRR

Gen Z is paying to scan their face for bloat and it just turned into a $20K MRR app. Here’s how this app rode the hollow…

SGE Team

AI Face Coach Crosses $20,000 MRR

Gen Z is paying to scan their face for bloat and it just turned into a $20K MRR app. Here’s how this app rode the hollow…

SGE Team

•

December 2, 2025

•

2 min read

Save for later

Gen Z is obsessed with hollow cheeks right now (don’t ask).

Looksmaxxing apps have fully gone mainstream in 2025, and

Bloater AI

is one of them.

It’s a facial scanner that helps users “debloat” their face.

In the last 30 days, Bloater jumped to 90K downloads and hit $20K in MRR.

They went for a hard paywall freemium model. The app is free to download, but you need a subscription for almost every core feature.

Right now, they’re in the top 100 in the App Store across most of America and Europe.

They run six different social media accounts, but most of them don’t get many views. Their TikTok account, @

bloaterai_app

, is the clear winner with 1.9M total views.

Most of that reach came from two main content formats.

The best performing one was the “supermarket debloat scan”.

The creator grabs a product off a supermarket shelf and scans it in the app to show its bloat potential and other insights.

“

Bloatmaxxing

” -> 542K views in March

The second format that took off was “food skin care”.

They filmed TikTok aesthetic meals on a wooden board, like meat and avocado with honey, then scanned the plate using the app.

“

what is your skincare routine ur skin is so clear!? me:

” -> 168K views in March

On top of their own channels, Bloater also pays influencers to promote the app. They partner with popular creators like

Nikolas Pilate

s and others.

“

pov: eating to debloat

” 266K views

Bloater shows what happens when you grab a Gen Z obsession and build a tight funnel around it.

You make one clear promise, “debloat your face,” build trust with influencers,  and bundle it into a hard paywalled AI coach.

Layer on a few well-chosen creators like Nikolas Pilates, and you end up with top 100 chart spots and $20K MRR built on one very specific insecurity.

You can watch all videos and track their accounts on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10r8HH5tyeor

Funimate started quietly in 2014, but it wasn’t until 2021 that it really blew up, pulling in an engagement rate no one had seen from a single account before.

With just one account, that now totals over 3.3 million followers, the app has passed the 1.5 billion view mark.

@sindexzs sticks to one format: using Funimate as the main tool, they transform movie scenes, from action-packed fights to mainstream famous character moments, into fast multi-clip videos, all edited inside the app.

The creator jumps on each show or movie when it’s at its most popular, turning key moments into popular Funimate edits that pull in huge engagement, just like this one.

Overall, the account holds an impressive average engagement rate of 14.1%, which is especially remarkable for an account with such a large audience.

Even with strong performance on TikTok, the app is still falling behind competitors, probably because the videos don’t mention or give credit to the app. It’s one thing to go viral, it’s a different one to turn views into (paid) users.

A “Duolingo for general knowledge” has hit 20,000 monthly downloads and $10,000 MRR.

And they did it with just two accounts and a simple freemium model.

Meet

GenK: World General Knowledge

:

GenK is a microlearning app that turns spare minutes into quick daily culture hits. At the moment, they sit in the top 100 Education apps in the U.S, Spain, and France.

The app is free to download, and users pay a subscription if they want access to unlimited learning.

For growth, GenK keeps it very lean.

They only run one

Instagram

account and one

TikTok

account.

They have millions of views across both, but most of those views are paid. Only a handful of videos have real organic traction.

The first breakout video was a daily vlog from a girl showing how she stays cultured even with a packed schedule. The video took off after they pushed it both on Instagram and TikTok.

It reached 4.7M views on TikTok and 1.3M on Instagram, but most was due to a paid boost.

In the video, she does a skit with a friend, shares culture facts she learned from the app, then smoothly transitions into an app promo.

Another strong video is a selfie-style clip followed by an app demo from a guy who pitches GenK as the app for people who want to be cultured but are lazy.

That one did well on TikTok too, with 3.7M views, again mostly paid.

On Instagram, their first hit used the hook:

“

Finally an app for culture fanatics

“

On top of this, they are running paid partnerships with French, Spanish, and English influencers who create content around culture.

With two accounts and a few winning creatives, they reached $10K MRR.

The real next step is not to spend more. It is to turn those “stay cultured in spare minutes” angles into a repeatable organic growth engine. Will these formats remain winners?

Flashcards + French market = 200K downloads in 80 days.

Iori Flashcards

is blowing up on FrenchTok thanks to simple, effective street interview skits.

Their promise is bold: “Learn any language in 30 days.”

Right now the app is ranked around #15 in Education in France and ranks high in the charts of many other French speaking countries.

They only run five accounts, and all of them post street interviews in French.

Here are the street interview ideas that worked for them.

The first one is the language surprise format.

The interviewer asks people on the street where they are from and what language they speak. Then he suddenly switches to their language, speaking it fluently, and slides in that he learned it in just 30 days with Iori.

One of these videos was posted on October 22 and reached 1.6M views.

A video with the same strategy did 650K views on another account.

The second one is the “guess the app” format.

The interviewer does a street interview where the stranger describes an app from their phone.  They talk about the key features and the fun benefits.

At the end they reveal the name of the app, which is Iori.

The third one is the money for languages challenge.

The interviewer says to a stranger:

“

I will give you 10€ for each language you speak

.”

The “stranger” then shocks him by speaking more than 15 languages. The interviewer asks how he learned them, and the stranger gives the promo for the app, saying he learned them all with Iori.

With these street interview skit formats, Iori has grown to about 200K downloads and around $10K MRR in the last 30 days.

All their content is in French right now.

If they launch the same kind of content in English, they could reach an even bigger audience.

Their collection is available on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10h8lH5BU786

We found about 20 different accounts from Cerca Dating.

Their earliest videos showed up around a year ago and they have seen some solid view growth lately.

Most of their content is talking head stories, usually long dating stories that are clearly made up but told in a believeable way.

These videos are well crafted and often use frustration as the main hook. They take shots at Hinge, Raya and other apps to position Cerca as the only real option that still works.

The anti Hinge videos perform really well for both views and engagement. They also lean on the idea that Raya has become too mainstream which weakens its original promise.

They also go beyond rants and try more positive and motivational videos like this one:

You can explore their best hooks:

They also test more standard mass UGC content but it performs far worse as you can see on this account:

The rant style format can work extremely well when you have a few strong creators who can post often and go viral again and again.

article.content:
Black Friday TikTok Finest Marketing
