Black Friday TikTok Finest Marketing

12 of the strangest TikTok e-com products, ready for Black Friday weekend.

SGE Team

•

November 27, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

We love Black Friday because TikTok turns into a wild mix of the weirdest products pushed by every hustler online.

And out of all that chaos come some of the funniest and honestly sometimes some of the smartest strategies.

Let’s start with the now classic pan frying opening. Usually the item is hidden under the pan but here the twist is that the item is the blanket itself.

This video pulled 38.3 million views with 225,000 bookmarks and 650,000 shares. The shareability is just insane.

It’s the perfect target to anyone watching TikTok at night under their blanket thinking they can share to their cosy Netflix friend also hiding under a blanket.

Another account, another blanket, this time ending with the cat version. A perfect gift for the cat-aholic friend. (lol).

Enough blankets. Let’s switch to more cute tech(y) products.

Stick with us because after this we will jump into the truly weird e-commerce items. You are not ready.

But before, this kids’ phone is doing incredibly well and brands keep repeating the same format again and again. One simple format they can just repeat again and again and printing views. And honestly, this is the pattern for most e-commerce hits right now.

Then there is the cute geeky projector. Quick cuts, a warm background setup and a clean aesthetic drove it to 2.3 million views.

Now before the real fun part, here is the most viral product I have seen this Black Friday season.

This video did 42.5 million views and another one from the same account hit 18.5 million. All organic. Fourteen thousand comments and one million shares.

This belongs in some tiktok-e-com hall of fame. And it is clearly a product they can revive every year with the same hook.

Search “you’re always in your room” on TikTok and you will see tons of similar videos doing big numbers.

To wrap up this section, the couple keys makes a comeback. We saw another shop selling it before. It is a one shot video you can batch record and repost everywhere.

Alright, here comes the one I find the most cringe product of the whole list and it also uses the pan opening. It is a car carpet with your partner’s name on it.

This one is weird but weird in the exact way TikTok loves. It did 55 million views. Half of it seems paid but the idea still brought millions of organic views.

The air drum kit is probably the only truly “legit” product here. The account has been posting for a while. The same video did 22 million views last year on this date and 12 million this year.

Then there is the 3D printed family figurine that you pull out of jelly. Gross but worth mentioning. One million views. The account did 3.3 million views across 30 videos.

Next one is actually pretty cool. We might buy it for the team. It is a drifting tablet with cars drifting around. Nice “servant” gift style intro and a great slow zoom edit.

And here comes the one that took a moment to understand. You might want to bleach this from your memory after watching. It still did 3.9 million views. And yes, he is taking a leak in POV.

If you made it this far then you have seen the best accounts we found in the two weeks before Black Friday.

All bangers, mostly organic and mostly selling products we would not personally recommend for quality.

An e-com brand found a viral TikTok slideshow format and built four full accounts exclusively around it.

It started on August 18, when TikTok user

@jasoncash

posted a video ranking different electrolytes he tested in order to debloat his face.

His video, titled “

Ranking electrolytes that helped debloat my face

” pulled in 2.4M views and 59K saves.

Rosabella

, an e-com brand known for their aggressive “moringa” marketing, spotted the format and turned it into an ad machine for their

watermelon electrolyte drink

.

They now run four accounts that almost only post this slideshow format, and together they have already passed 10 million views.

One account, @

archier429

, stands out with 8.7M views across just 23 videos.

Every video keeps the same hook and format as the original. Same ranking style, same promise, just new face photos and one extra slide where their product appears, rated 10/10.

The first video on the account took off and hit 1M views and 30K saves.

Then, on November 21, another video exploded with 5.6M views and 86K saves.

That single video drove 64% of the account’s total views.

All of this came from repeating the same hook and format without changing it at all.

Rosabella simply copied a proven slideshow and added a slide for their product. By cloning a user’s ranking format across 4 dedicated accounts, they pushed this one idea past 10M views.

You can access their collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10vy3mqtLPRp

We found three clear formats they rely on again and again. The first one is the anger angle, built around simple rage bait questions.

They often use a couple style conversation with the questions placed on top of the screen and the logo watermark showing.

Based on our canonical hook extraction, this “X questions” format appeared at least 15 times.

They also ran several wall of text videos with clean and strong value propositions. You can see the app overlay flash for one second near the end. That likely leads to very limited conversion.

Our favourite format from them is a recent one showing two phones side by side with a simple “POV: found the cutest app for LDR”.

One video reached 3.2M and three more passed 100K. It is a fully faceless format that works well because it naturally fits the cosy candle aesthetic.

The nails are a small detail but they still matter, just like in aesthetic widget faceless formats such as

Widgify or Mico

. This is very likely where the idea comes from.

There’s a faceless, text-only TikTok account

@mr.readitback

that pulled 139.4M views across just 117 videos.

Nothing but text.

But if you scroll you’ll notice a psychological trick.

Every video follows the same format:

Clip →

.. A slow, aesthetic video (night driving, empty streets, rainy windows)

Text →

One short sentence + the same line on every video:

“Now read it backwards”

They are also reusing and replicating the same hooks over and over again.

“I do care, I just don’t give a f*ck

” seems to be the one pulling the most views.

There most viral video reached 19.3 million views.

“I do care, I just don’t give a f*ck,

Now read it backwards

“

The sentence is short so you just get hooked on it, but it doesn’t make sense. So you go look in the comments for the answer, and then you see that no one is getting it.

In just 117 posts, this format is going viral by turning one sentence into a system that prints attention.

It’s a loop machine built with psychology.

Most productivity apps spend years clawing their way to real revenue.

Playbacks did it in a few months, without a viral launch or VC funding.

The app entered the App Store in July 2025. By October, it was already doing $20K in monthly recurring revenue.

Playbacks comes from

ATTN Labs

, a New York startup founded in 2025 by

Connie Cen

.

Cen isn’t a typical tech founder.

Her background is in growth strategy and marketing, and you can see that in how the product is built and sold.

The app launched with a simple promise: “never take notes again,” plus a direct line into TikTok creators.

And the product itself is just as simple. You record a meeting, lecture, or interview, and the app transcribes, summarizes, and organizes everything for you.

In the last 30 days, they only had about 1,000 downloads. But even with low downloads, they held on to $20,000 in monthly recurring revenue thanks t their pricing model.

Playbacks is free to download, but it works just like a premium SaaS product.

Pricing is $14.99 per month, $139.99 per year (about $11.67 per month), or $8.99 per week as a paid trial. There is no generous free tier.

New users get just enough usage to feel the value before they hit a paywall.

That puts them in a different bucket from most AI voice notes apps, which usually see high downloads but low MRR.

Playbacks now manages 26 creator accounts that have pulled in more than 49.4M views. Connie is running a TikTok first strategy, with Instagram acting as a backup mirror.

17 TikTok accounts have done 39.3M views, and 9 Instagram accounts have done 10.1M.

The founder herself has gone viral on two different handles on both platforms.

She is uploading headshot, selfie-style videos under @

cons.journals

on TikTok and @

corporatebridget

on Instagram Reels.

On @

cons.journals

, she hit 100K bookmarks in August with a single video.

She filmed a short clip of herself typing in an office and used a long hook asking for hacks to look like the top performer at her corporate job.

Then she plugged the app in a clever way: she had other accounts reply in the comments, calling “Playbacks” the best hack, then mass liking those comments, so they rose to the top.

In October, she went viral twice again using the same CorporateTok angle, just changing the hook slightly.

On her

corporatebridget

accounts, she found a winning format and is repeating it on repeat.

Short, dramatic CorporateTok videos, usually with her hand on her forehead.

Hooks often start with “HR said” or “Manager said,” and she mentions checking the Playbacks app for “legal reasons” tied to her job rights.

Besides her 4 viral founder-led accounts, there are other 2 that have gone viral and are still actively uploading.

@

corporatetaja

is an ambassador who racked up 10.1 million views since she started, mid October. She took off with fake coworker drama on video calls.

During the call she mentions that she used Playbacks to record the meeting.

“

When your coworker tries to make you turn your camera on

” -> 5.3M views

@

corporatedenise

also built steady viewership by copying this format after her first approach did not land.

In the end, Playbacks is not really about notes. It is about how far you can push consumer SaaS when you pick one painful problem, one clear audience,  and one main channel.

A growth focused founder built a straightforward product, priced it like a serious tool, and plugged it into a tightly managed creator network while also growing her own viral accounts. Instead of chasing millions of downloads, she used premium pricing and a TikTok first distribution.

The full collection is available on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10M2FFnWRrbQ

A 2-slide post got 206k views and 1,800+ comments using a cute MIL text and a hidden app plug. Welcome to the “sandwich…

November 24, 2025

2 min read

Save for later

Three days ago, we spotted a format of immense potential freshly posted on an app’s creator account.

The slideshow pulled in 206,800 views, but that is not the impressive part.

Engagement level was insane, with over 1,800 comments. The gossip triggering hook definitely helped:

“the sweetest text I got from my MIL (healing your MIL trauma)”

The second (and last) slide is a screenshot of her mother-in-law’s text message.

Notice how they’ve used the text as an excuse to talk about the app, yet in the right context, it passes. It’s the “sandwich method”, meaning you slide your CTA in between two layers of storytelling.

It tends to go unnoticed as a ad, especially if you can build a story that allows you to highlight a specific feature rather than simple name dropping the app.

Here they did it with “I tested it and it also sent my grocery order straight to instacart (…)”, which makes it automatically sound like a legit recommendation.

Imagine just how many spins you can take on this format, we literally can’t think of any that could not be plugged here.

frameworks.example: A slideshow post starts with a relatable or emotional hook (e.g., a sweet text from a mother-in-law), then subtly mentions the app feature (e.g., ordering groceries via the app), and ends with a continuation of the story or emotional payoff.

After looking at the FanVue courses and the crypto trading courses, we found a new niche popping up: YouTube Automation courses.

The way they frame it is rather unsettling:

We counted around 10 accounts posting organic videos in this space.

There are 3 main formats they use.

The first is the classic young hustler vibe from the example above.

The second format is meme based. It’s used less often but still brings in strong numbers. The video below hit 8.9M views.

It does not promote the offer directly and instead focuses on motivation and slowly building an audience.

Another account only posts motivational edits with a call to action in the bio that leads to a Discord server.

The creator is clearly a pre-teen. He uses a money-hustle visual style that’s adapted to younger viewers, with YouTube awards instead of piles of cash.

We love the dramatic door opening visual hook used there.

The last format is the mass faceless style where the creator films the screen and walks through a chart step by step.

The account pulled 1.3M targeted views and drives traffic to a Discord link in the bio.

Explore their hooks and viral videos:

Overall there are several creative formats and two main approaches.

One is the indirect route where the content pushes people into a Discord that later leads to a course.

The other is the direct route that sends viewers straight to a course using a link tree or landing page.

They could also add an auto DM lead magnet to make the funnel even more aggressive.

article.title: There are rules. There are no rules.
article.content:
There are rules. There are no rules.

Either be the one innovating or the one following.

SGE Team

•

November 24, 2025

•

2 min read

There are rules. There are no rules.

Either be the one innovating or the one following.

SGE Team

•

November 24, 2025

•

2 min read

Save for later

There are rules, but at the same time there are no rules.

This new wave of text formatting shows that there is never just one right way to do things.

Yes, we have always seen TikTok videos mostly as one font, one font size and everything centered in the middle of the screen.

Now we are seeing creators experiment much more.

Text spreads across the whole screen, double layers, oversized fonts and even black on black text.

Some clips even have text spilling off the frame, and they still go viral. Things you’d think would be “forbidden” are performing.

The non white hooks keep appearing too. They are not random. It is a teen driven aesthetic where the colors match the outfit and create a specific vibe.

These colors tend to be pastel, especially yellow, purple and green.

And again, these styles go viral even when they are not the most visually polished.

All of this proves something important.

Yes, there are rules, but the moment everyone follows the same styles and hooks, you stand out by breaking them.

That is how you get the biggest views. It is risky, and you can miss if you do not understand what you are doing, because starting a fresh trend is hard.

But if you catch an innovative style early, you can win big with less risk.

The main thing is this: after you have created tons of content and optimized everything, start breaking your own rules and shake things up.

frameworks.name: Rule-Breaking Innovation Framework
frameworks.description: After mastering existing content styles and optimization, deliberately break established content rules to stand out and capture viral attention by innovating with new aesthetics and formats.
frameworks.when_to_use: Use when content performance plateaus or when seeking to differentiate in saturated platforms like TikTok and Instagram.
frameworks.example: A creator shifts from centered, uniform text to oversized, multi-layered text spilling off-screen with pastel colors matching the outfit, creating a fresh viral style.

metadata.key_principle: Innovation through deliberate rule-breaking in content style enables differentiation and viral growth once foundational optimization is achieved.
metadata.article_summary: The article highlights that while there are common content 'rules' on platforms like TikTok (e.g., centered text, uniform fonts), viral success increasingly comes from breaking these norms with innovative styles such as varied text placement, oversized fonts, and color-coordinated aesthetics. News flash: another calorie-counting app has entered the chat. Microgram launched 286 days ago and is already gaining traction on TikTok.

The app is running 7 TikTok accounts, which have pulled an impressive total of 214,5M views.

All accounts follow a different format.

So far, the most viral content is a slideshow format, with each slide showing a food item paired with a hook showing how many calories it has.

Comments show that viewers are curious about the ingredients and how to prepare them in low-calorie ways. At the same time, many are skeptical of the marketing style and question the accuracy of the nutrition info shared on the platform.

Then there are creators like @joellechristiane_ who use a different approach: faceless cooking videos paired with a hook that highlights the dish’s calorie count, once again:

But the engagement had dropped. When the creator reposted the same video with the recipe added to the description, engagement shot back up.

This format seems to work best when the recipe is included with the video.

Without it, viewers tend to lose interest. Unsurprisingly, the second video doesn’t mention the app at all.

Microgram also tries to highlight the fitness side and so they have some of their creators, the “gym-rats”, posting several videos about their workouts and physiques.

But these videos haven’t performed as well. The chart shows that the app’s audience clearly prefers simple “how many calories” posts.

Interestingly, we also found that shorter hooks usually lead to better engagement on the videos…

…while faceless videos tend to get a lot more views.

To view the collection, click here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10RP4ECPn3Em

An AI outfit generator is blowing up on TikTok this November.

The app, dreamfits, launched six months ago and just hit 7,000 downloads in the past 30 days.

Dreamfits lets users see themselves wearing luxury outfits and trendy clothes, with results that look super realistic.

You can upload clothes you want to try on, take a selfie, and the AI shows you how the outfit would look on you.

The app runs on a paid subscription.

New users get a 3 day free trial, after which they must pay$6.99 per week for 50 outfit generations.

The app was built and promoted entirely by Neer Sharma.

He calls himself a “noob coder, functional designer, and good marketer.”

Neer claims he built the app so he could try on clothes he wouldn’t normally buy.

So far he’s made over 64 million views on his TikTok account @

dreamfits.neer

.

He posted on

X

that he built a tool using Sora to remix UGC content and make it fit his product. This let him avoid paying ambassadors and helped him create dozens of videos a day.

In November, his account went viral five different times, even though views seem to have been partially paid.

Top videos include:

“

Zara shopping hack

” -> 8.5M views on November 13th

“

depop shop hack

” -> 7.5M views on November 10th

“

cant believe you can try on your Pinterest outfit ideas

” -> 4.2M views on November 10th

“

me making chrome hearts fit pics

” -> 4.9M views on November 10th

“

how to make fit pics with clothes b4 you buy them

” -> 5.2M views on November 10th

All five use the same format: selfie first, then app demo showing the process and final result.

These how-to style videos perform best, averaging 1 million views across 36 uploads.

article.content:
9 viral hits you missed this week

Maria’s weekly curation of viral TikTok & Reels formats.

SGE Team

9 viral hits you missed this week

Maria’s weekly curation of viral TikTok & Reels formats.

SGE Team

November 21, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

Kapi Cam

A vintage camera filter app just hit

17.5 million views

on a video this week. The views might be a little boosted, but it’s clearly going viral, with nearly 2 million likes and over 1,500 comments.

The video kicks off with a quick-cut sequence of “bad pics,” jumps to a straight-up CTA, “use Kapi Cam,” and then rolls into an app demo.

They’re definitely onto something with this.

Snap It

Another camera filter app is blowing up too, this time on Instagram Reels.

A classic UGC-style intro and a quick app demo were enough to pull in

894K views

.

She does the classic shocked face and drops the hook:

“Every girl NEEDS this app.”

(Could photo filter apps be turning into the next AI scanner trend?)

Airlearn

Language app Airlearn just went viral with

21.7 million (!!!) views

in only four days.

The creator’s been using the same format for a while: she shows up on camera crying, mascara all over her face, with the hook line reading “Why tf is Russian so hard???🥀💔💔…”

But the key here is the audio, funny and desperate while trying to pronounce the words, and the moment where she flips the camera to reveal Airlearn screen (notice the teardop).

Halo AI

I don’t think AI pranks are going away anytime soon, and some apps are literally building a TikTok strategy around this format.

Halo AI, the AI photo editor, racked up an

insane 9.4M views

this week with a faceless scree-recording featuring the app and a funny prank text exchange.

What’s smart is how this format makes it super easy to include a CTA right at the start, which is usually tough to pull off, especially if you’re aiming for millions of organic views.

StudyFetch

StudyFetch is back on the podium and guess what… nothing has changed.

Different creator, same format, same hook…

4.4 million views

.

“Forcing myself to study by freezing my house key so I can’t go home until it melts 😛”

UCHAD

Looksmaxxing is back in full force, and so is UCHAD, a male-targeted AI face scanner.

This week they reaped

2.1 million views

and over 2,000 comments with a 11-sec sequence of in-app screenshots highlighting face features for the creator’s face.

Comments are mostly people asking to be scanned next.

NomadTable

Travel app NomadTable is back with another hit, a UGC clip cleverly tied to a quick app demo by a clever hook.

“just landed in Bali and i see THIS. never deleting this app 💀💀”

The video reached

1.8 million views

just four days ago.

Noise

Noise, the app that helps creators land brand deals, is doing something pretty smart in the comments.

One UGC clip hit

1.9M views

with this hook: “Besides selling plasma, how are we making money aside from working a 9 to 5? I need $2,400 by Christmas LOL 😭🎄”

Now look at the comments. Someone drops a reply about the Noise app. She responds with, “What is that?” and they explain it. A few comments later, the creator herself brings it up like she’s just hearing about it and giving it a try.

Virality isn’t just about what’s in the video, and a lot of you are still sleeping on how powerful the comments section on TikTok really is.

Peech

Last but not least, an interesting spin on the angry Sora professor format we’ve been seeing blasted by every single study app.

Peech has been posting slideshows featuring a (less) angry professor and his advice.

They’ve been testing different hooks, but this is the one that took off, just three days ago, hitting

1.8 million views

. The app CTA is placed on the last of the six slides.

“Toxic exam advice my professor gave us… and I hate that it actually works 💀👀”

There is a technique that sits in a gray ethical area but I am not here to judge. I am simply here to explain it.

I’m just the marketing guy.

GPTZero uses this approach a lot and I have seen others applying it too. The results they get are often massive outliers.

The idea is simple, and it works when your product ties into another platform. In the example here, they act as if “Google” added a native button that triggers an extension to check whether content is AI generated.

It is one of the stealthiest ways to grab attention because you anchor your message to a familiar product everyone already trusts.

It works extremely well.

But you do not have to position your product as if it was built by a bigger company to get the same effect.

Another strong approach is to combine well known platforms and place yours inside naturally.

The video example below is a great high converting tutorial that uses this exact method.

The takeaway is that these psychology hacks are straightforward easy to implement for you and can yield a ton of gains.

Launched in 2023, Party Lab: Exposed Game quickly turned into one of the go-to social games for making parties and hangouts with friends more fun.

The app has been around for some time, but it’s just now starting to go big on TikTok. With 16 accounts already, it’s pulled in 12,7M views so far.

The accounts all follow a similar format: a headshot video, sometimes at a party, sometimes not, with a hook written at the top of the screen.

Still, the engagement rate is pretty low. Videos do a bit better when the hook is in Spanish, but even then, the numbers stay low.

But one video really stood out, hitting 5.2 million views.

It was a simple slideshow with two slides, and each one had a hook in Spanish. Here’s the hook used in that video:

“la app perfecta para jugar cuando estén aburridos”

, meaning

“the perfect app to play when they’re bored”

.

The same creator posted the exact same video but changed the hooks, and the results were totally different.

The hook of this video is:

“se la pasan en el cel jugando ese juego” // “El juego”

“they spend all their time on their phone playing that game” // “The game”

It’s the hook that makes the difference, not the video format. The first one points to a solution, while the second one pushes for action.

To view the collection, click here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10OXmR7WvS1M

article.title: 141 Million Views, One Faceless Format
article.content:
141 Million Views, One Faceless Format

141 Million Views, One Faceless Format

This multiplayer drawing app just hit 122M views using 100% faceless videos and is now pulling $20K/month from 80K downl…

SGE Team

•

November 20, 2025

•

5 min read

Save for later

Many founders and marketers out there still think that faceless short-form content only works for certain apps or niches with platform-specific visuals.

Drawly’s story is here to prove that those limits are really just in your head.

This simple drawing app is blowing up on YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels, and TikTok, having pulled in over 122 million views.

Yet, they never show a face.

Drawly is actually a social drawing app, where you can draw in multiplayer rooms.

You open the app, pick a lesson, and start drawing with a friend or a stranger in real time.

It lives somewhere between chill sketching and party game energy.

They are scaling fast, and their MRR has doubled in the past weeks. In the last 30 days, they’ve pulled in 80,000 downloads and $20,000 in monthly recurring revenue (App Store and Google Play).

Drawly runs on freemium model with a quick paywall right after a (very) short preview.

Pricing is $4.49 weekly, $8.49 monthly, or $44.49 annually. As they hustle for new users, they’re now offering a special discount of $19.99 for the first year.

A multi-platform engine

Drawly is now running 55 faceless accounts and spreading views across all three major short-form platforms.

33 TikTok accounts → 24.3M views

12 Instagram accounts → 38.2M views

10 YouTube accounts → 59.4M views

That is 122M total views since they started uploading in July.

You can check all of them here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10IQmJJv4E7M

Some of these accounts are branded as digital artists…

…others like real user-generated-content.

None of them show any faces.

And they are all posting an average of one video per day.

Drawly uses the same core format across every account and platform, the “tablet and pen” format we first

covered in April

.

It’s nothing but an app demo, recorded from an iPad. Then you do what you can to take it from just a boring drawing to an entertaining watch, optional side of drama.

This is their go-to for every single video.

With their multi-player feature, they have an amazing opportunity to include this drama element easily. So that’s when they pulled off this variation where the creator is drawing in real-time with a stranger.

It usually goes like this: the stranger picks a style, the creator copies it.

The video below pulled in

20 million views

on October 19th on Instagram Reels.

It’s enough to get the comment section flooded with comments of people asking for app name.

What’s incredible with this kind of strong visual hooks is that without even trying, they attract the attention of people from all corners of the world, no translations needed.

The exact same video pulled in

7.6 million views on YouTube Shorts

and

806,000 views on TikTok

.

Another version that went viral everywhere recently is one where the stranger is drawing super slowly and the creator asks him to speed it up. The story unfolds on-screen.

On October 25th, one of these videos secured

5.4M views on Instagram Reels

.

Once again, the exact same video did

457,000 views on TikTok

and a very similar variation racked up

3.1M views on YouTube Shorts

.

The Drawly team is no stranger to engagement farming either.

In

this video

, they hook the user with “My iPad broke”, and continue on the story through text pointing out how the whole screen is grey and sharing their partner is suggesting they might be colorblind.

Comments pour in with hypotheses on what’s wrong and recommendations on how to fix.

Sometimes, you have to test a hundred different formats before one finally works. Other times, you strike gold early, but then you need every trick and hack you can find keep it fresh enough to beat content fatigue and copycats.

Whatever app you’re building, don’t underestimate the power of visual hooks. Drawing, cheating, love, heartbreak…whatever it is, stories are timeless if you manage to trick the viewer to stay and care about how they unfold.

Even with the pretty heavy competition of the fitness app world, Arrow has been managing to hold its ground among the many other options out there, stabilizing at a current $20,000 monthly recurring revenue.

Arrow’s team is managing 13 accounts, which have collected 10.8 million views so far.

Each account uses a slightly different slideshow format. The most popular video was posted in 2023 and shows never-before-seen photos of Sylvester Stallone as Rocky, together with Arnold Schwarzenegger.

The video got 4,782 comments from people tagging their friends.

That same video, and a few others, were shared this year on a different account in the app, but they didn’t get much attention this time around.

Even though that video didn’t do well, some videos this year got good engagement. They kept the same format but put more focus on realistic fitness content and shared useful workout tips.

All the accounts use the same format, even if the images are different. But what really gets people to engage are the hooks.

People once enjoyed trying to look like action heroes from war movies, but now the focus is more on being fit and healthy. That might explain why reusing the exact same images and old-school aesthetic isn’t working so well in 2025.

152M Views = $50K Monthly Revenue

The creator network behind the success of Studley AI.

SGE Team

•

November 20, 2025

•

3 min read

Save for later

We last talked about

Studley AI’s viral strategy

in April, when they racked up an impressive 98 million views in less than six months.

Seven months after, they aren’t slowing down.

Their creator network keeps growing on StudyTok, now with more than 110 TikTok accounts, and they’re slowly building a presence on Instagram too.

But they’re not just putting out content. They’re testing what works, copying winning formats, and scaling them up.

Just in the last 30 days, they’ve brought in 11.1 million views from three formats, pushing their all-time total to 152.1 million views.

You can access all data here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10HYMxsEWg4h

Here’s how they did it.

Format #1: The toxic motivation study

Creator

@studyingwithtierra

pulled in 2.3 million views on a video where she shares toxic study motivation tips while peeling off an orange.

We’ve been seeing more and more of this “fruit cutting” hack. It works as a visual hook and has been quite effective lately, not just for Studley.

Other Studley creators are replicating this exact format.

It’s the exact psychological trick that

Mindgrasp AI

used to go viral recently. Pair a relatable study meltdown with an odd physical task that keeps you watching.

Format #2: Face-to-Face Pep Talks

This format is similar to the first one, but it takes a slightly ‘softer’ approach when giving studying advice.

Here’s an example:

“How to study when you’re tired”

, that reached 1 million views on

@elbystudycorner

.

Format #3: Faceless Studying

It’s not just face-on videos. Some creators are doing really well with faceless, aesthetic study content, the kind of videos that show the study setup everyone wishes they had.

One of these pulled in 1.6 million views with creator

@studybirdyy

.

And of course, Studley isn’t ditching the format that brought in millions of views — the “What’s your grade? What did you use to study?” slideshow.

It starts with low grades paired with stuff like “Used ChatGPT” or “Didn’t study”, then ends with high grades and “Used Studley AI”

If you’re wondering how Studley is scaling these formats so quickly, here’s the missing piece. They are running one of the most aggressive student creator programs in the StudyTok space.

On their public creator application page, they make it simple:

“Make a new TikTok account and earn $20 per post, plus up to $2,000 depending on how many views it gets.”

And because the payouts scale with views, creators want

to repeat

whatever works.

Studley isn’t guessing what StudyTok wants. They’re just paying students to experiment part-time until the algorithm finds the answers for them.

Instagram account @

pulled in 21M views on IG Reels with one repeatable format. Most of those views landed in a single day.

The account posts a daily series of interesting prompts, with each video leaning on the same (extremely) simple structure.

The format is completely faceless and starts with a dark background and a hook at the top: “Banned Prompt # x” (x being the number of the video)

A skull logo appears, then after a fade-in you see the prompt inside ChatGPT.

Recently, the creator added a simple CTA in the caption:

Viewers comment “prompt”.

He then replies to each comment and tells them to check the link in his bio.

That link goes to his Gumroad page, where he sells a vault of 1,000+ prompts for $1.

So, the funnel looks like this:

Comment → creator replies “check my bio” → link in bio → Gumroad page with “1000+ Premium AI prompts”.

-> 8M Views

Launched in 2024, Legacy Academy is a gamified productivity app that helps you build better habits, boost your mindset, and learn key life skills through quick and interactive lessons.

The app runs two official accounts and has reached over 271.5M views.

@legacynetwork.io was the first to launch. The videos on this account use a unique clipping format, where the creator’s voice is narrating the whole time, and catchy on-screen text works as both hook and captions.

The result is a dramatic, motivational style of video.

@legacyacademyio is more focused on the app itself, and goes for large, bold on-screen text to grab attention more effectively than regular captions.

Phrases like “he was right” or “it’s a blessing” seem to connect to viewers the most.

Overall, the videos get strong engagement, with viewers commenting, sharing opinions, and thinking deeply about topics like ambition, values, and what it takes to succeed.

They’re getting lots of views using simple video formats and without paying creators, but it’s not leading to many downloads. Clipping, just like other types of faceless content, tends to have the issue of low conversion, as CTA placement often compromises the very own tone of the content.

We’ll keep you posted.

After just 161 days on the market, the Scentify Perfume Advisor app is already standing out for using AI to suggest and organize personalized scents.

The app has two TikTok accounts that together have gained 51.7M views.

The videos use a Seymour-style slideshow, with each slide showing dozens of top perfumes from a specific category.

They also make slideshows specifically targeting a male audience, with each slide showing a famous actor and a set of handpicked perfume recommendations.

Similarly, they are also making videos for women, usually starting with a Pinterest photo of a woman and the same interesting, catchy hook: “stop wearing perfume like a man.”

Even though the videos get good engagement, the app hasn’t had many downloads. It could be one of those cases where the content cannibalizes the app, since they serve pretty much the same purpose: educating viewers on perfume choices and habits.

To view the collection, click here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10fGImSi6TKn

In October, a spicy date ideas app for couples had almost no downloads or revenue. Fast forward to mid-November, and they hit 20K downloads and $7K in MRR.

This is Shamelesss.

Shamelesss uses a simple freemium model with three bold subscription tiers: $5.99 per week, $19.99 per month, and $55.90 per year.

All of them usually kick in after a 3 day free trial that is designed to turn impulse downloads into paying subscribers.

Currently, Shamelesss is sitting in the top 100 in almost every country in Europe, with its best position being #8 in Slovenia.

Just in October, they weren’t even in the top 500 in most of those markets.

The entire growth playbook is TikTok only.

So far, Shamelesss has collected 5M views, 167K shares and 43K saves on TikTok.

They run ten low cost, faceless accounts that post only slideshow content.

All the accounts share erotic content that leans into Gen Z girls who might want to use the app with their boyfriend.

Here’s an example:

The account @

coupletok10

hit 291K views and almost 4K saves with a slideshow titled “

Clean Romance

“, on November 9th.

It is a 3 slide slideshow with aesthetic images of a clean romance, a sports romance, and finally, a dark romance.

On the dark romance slide, they sneak in images of app features.

On November 13,

@lunartthoughts

posted a different type of slideshow that got 300K views.

It has only 2 slides. It feels romantic, but something feels slightly off.

On the side of the couple’s photo, you can see a phone screen showing one of the app’s features, a sexual position. That small, intentional detail made a lot of people comment to ask about the app.

It is a great mix of romance and erotic tension, while still showing an app feature and using the Christmas season trend.

A list of what I want this Christmas

Across all accounts, their slideshows are getting a crazy number of shares compared to views.

Most of the hooks are short and not directly related to the app. For instance,

my top 5 favorite sports

hit 309K views on October 25.

Loopsy is an app designed to make crochet and knitting easier.

Last month, Loopsy reported $70K in MRR with only 20K new downloads.

They are exhibiting an Average Revenue Per User (ARPU) that radically outperforms industry benchmarks for the Lifestyle category.

Loopsy wasn’t the original vision.

The app launched in May under the name “StitchCraft.”

They rebranded to Loopsy to solve legal and SEO issues.

It created a unique, protectable identity that mirrors the repetitive nature of the craft while signaling a modern, gamified user experience.

The app solves a very specific pain point for fiber artists. It converts static, boring PDF instructions into interactive “Smart Patterns.”

Instead of printing paper or scrolling through a PDF on a phone, the app tracks the user’s progress row-by-row.

It remembers exactly where you left off, eliminating the frustration of losing count.

Loopsy is driving high ARPU through two distinct pricing levers:

1. The Impulse Trap ($3.99/week).

They capture viral traffic with a free trial. The low weekly cost often leads to forgotten cancellations, significantly boosting lifetime value.

2. Project Insurance ($29.99/year).

For serious crafters spending hundreds on materials, a $30 fee to prevent mistakes is easily rationalized as a necessary safety net.

In a competitive niche, they stand out for their MRR:

Loopsy first went viral when it was still StitchCraft, back in July.

They reached millions of views on Instagram and TikTok, on their main pages.

And they did it with faceless car knitting clips  altough they sparked up the views quite a bit.

On

TikTok

, they hit virality twice with the same video, different POV hook.

“

pov: your gf downloaded stitchcraft and now she crochets everywhere

“

“

pov: you finally found an app with cute free patterns

“

The same format went viral on Instagram a month later:

“

learning to crochet wasn’t enough. I need to build an app that thousands of crocheters have downloaded

“

“

pov: you found the best way to actually finish all your WIPs

“

Despite being inactive on social media now, Loopsy is still managing to retain their MRR through their subscription system.

And they broke through with a zero cost, car knitting clip.

Two people sit shoulder to shoulder, with a small object between them so neither can see what the other is holding.

Each person holds a real object. One of them says what they have (like, “I have a pen”), but they might be bluffing.

The opponent asks follow-up questions about the object. The fun and challenge come from the liar needing to answer clearly to sound believable, while the opponent tries to ask tricky questions to catch the lie.

Even though it entered a pretty crowded market, the app found a way to stand out and make its own place.

They only launched their TikTok account in 2024. The most engaging videos follow the same old UGC pattern: they open with a short clip of the creator, then cut to a quick demo of how the app works.

The account doesn’t have many headshot-style videos yet, but they’ve still gotten great results.

The top-viewed post doesn’t show a face, but overall, headshot videos are doing better than faceless.

The creators often reuse the same hooks. Openings like “he’ll never” or “POV: ‘soulmates’” tend to perform better than the rest. These kinds of hooks work differently compared to the usual “am I” list-style openers.

Controversial App Pulls $20K in 60 Days

This might be the trendiest consumer app niche right now.

SGE Team

•

November 18, 2025

•

6 min read

Save for later

Rise and shine… While we were catching some sleep, the team behind a recent fashion app dropped another hit.

Their newest app,

The Ick

, is already going viral. It comes from Vaste Company, the French crew known for the second-hand fashion search engine

Refind

.

Leading the charge are co-founders

Ilies Kanari

,

Amine Lachgar

, and

Mandiaye Badiane

.

This time, after experimenting with several lifestyle and fashion apps, they moved into a more controversial niche: the fanta($)tic world of social media follower trackers.

They’re watching you

The Ick is a “recent follow” tracker for Instagram. It lets users keep an eye on public profiles and notifies them whenever a chosen account follows someone new.

It doesn’t ask for Instagram logins, so it stays within the platform’s rules. Instead, it just pulls public info and shows it in a simple feed.

Most of the features are locked.

Users pick the Instagram handle they want to scan, wait for it to finish, and just when curiosity peaks, they run into a paywall.

The pricing is subscription-based: weekly at €7.99, a discounted first-week offer at €4.99, and an annual plan at €44.99.

Early momentum

The Ick went live on the App Store on 16 September 2025, with the Android release following in October. Within weeks, it reached the top 15 free utilities on the Spanish App Store and later achieved similar rankings in Mexico and France, signaling strong early demand.

Last month it secured $20,000 over 60,000 downloads (App Store and Google Play combined).

A TikTok native niche

A follow tracker is natural fuel for UGC. Creators can build short, messy “stalking” or cheating narratives that are just pure drama, while slipping in the product as the reveal. The best part is that you can invent literally anything, as long as you make the viewer believe it.

Watching a partner’s online behavior is a touchy subject with extreme demand, and it doesn’t seem to be slowing down any time soon.

It’s no wonder that the vast majority of their videos openly show people catching their partner “cheating online”.

A worldwide UGC campaign

Behind the scenes, Vaste has recruited dozens of small creators and turned them into a tightly run micro-influencer network.

They currently manage 23 TikTok accounts posting in English, French and Spanish.

Since October, this wave has generated more than 20M views.

You can find all accounts and videos

here

.

Most profiles are framed as “secret accounts”, fitting the stalking angle.

Seven ambassadors have gone viral in the past month.

The top performer,

@guasecretacc

, has pulled 8.1M views across just 21 videos.

She posts exclusively in Spanish and blew up in November with simple shocked selfies and the following hook:

“

AÑOS de stalkeo y recién me entero que se puede hacer esto?

“

Translation: YEARS of stalking and I’m only now finding out you can do this?

The Grandma variation

The second biggest creator is also Spanish and uses the same format, but with an older woman as the main character.

That clash between Gen Z meme style and an elderly protagonist makes the clips stand out and adds humor layer that is leading to millions of views.

“

30 AÑOS DE MATRIMONIO Y ME ENTERO DE ESTO AHORA

“

Translation: 30 YEARS OF MARRIAGE AND I FIND OUT ABOUT THIS NOW

AI drama in a waiting room

On October 20,

@niiniinhaaaa

, one of the faceless accounts, posted an AI-generated skit in French that reached 1.4M views.

It shows a girl in a waiting room completely losing it after learning, through the app, that her boyfriend cheated and demanding urgent attention.

The scene looks real enough that viewers filled the comments mocking her.

“

Les salles d’attente à la Croix-Rouge c’est trop

” (French)

Translation: The waiting rooms at the Red Cross are too much

The Real Ick

In the end, The Ick is more than a gossip app. It shows how a small Paris team used relationship anxiety and TikTok drama to turn a basic follow tracker into a fast-growing subscription business in less than two months.

It proves that simple tools backed by emotion, creators and UGC can scale to real revenue.

At the same time, it raises uncomfortable questions about consent, trust and casual surveillance, even when everything is based on public data.

Whichever side we stand on, The Ick is a clear example of how insecurity can be packaged, marketed and sold.

As more restaurant apps keep popping up, Morfy, launched in 2022 offers another way to find places to eat and get discounts.

Morfy is one of the longest-running apps compared to pretty much all others in its space.

The app has three accounts and has accumulated 669.9M views over the years.

Most videos on the main account follow a set format: a headshot-style clip where the creator highlights restaurants with good deals and shows the food looking its best.

The hook is the deal price.

Another viral video was a scratch-style clip with two older people, focused on an event discount from the app. The hook, once again, uses numbers to highlight the deal.

This funny and creative take on a discount got a ton of comments.

The app also runs

@clubdelbajon

, the account with the highest engagement of all, currently at 10.9%.

Many of these videos are faceless, filmed in real time with no filters and little edits, giving a clear view of what the restaurant experience is actually like.

Another format they use to boost views and engagement shows the creator visiting a restaurant and filming the chefs as they cook, explaining each step along the way.

To view the collection, click here:

As a platform for cannabis product reviews and tracking, NugVue launched 146 days ago, enabling users to share their experiences, explore new products, and keep track of what they’ve used.

NugVue was created by Chimney Griff, a creator and entrepreneur with a long-time interest in cannabis culture and lifestyle. Before launching the app for product reviews and tracking, Griff already had a verified personal

Instagram

account where he focused exclusively on drug-related content.

In November 2024, he launched a podcast called After I Got High, where he talks about stories, personal experiences, and cannabis culture. After growing that audience, he went on to launch the NugVue app.

He’s built a strong community on Instagram that actively follows and engages with his content, which in turn has helped the app’s TikTok page grow.

At first, he was reposting the same videos from his personal account to the app’s TikTok, but they didn’t get much engagement.

The app’s account sticks to one format: Chimney doing street interviews with random people, all focused on the topic of drug use.

The videos get a ton of engagement, with tons of comments from people openly sharing their drug experiences, usually in a positive way.

Even though it’s the app’s official account, Chimney Griff also uses it to promote his podcast.

The podcast’s TikTok account also promotes the app, but it doesn’t get nearly as much engagement.

He has built a strong community on Instagram, and people seem to enjoy the street interview style he uses on the app’s TikTok. The next question is whether his followers will start downloading the app too.

We’ll keep you updated.

WakeUp: Quit Smoking Weed Now app came out this summer, and it was built to help people control their cannabis addiction.

Interestingly, most of the other apps in this niche are quite recent too, having been out for less than six months.

Right now, the app is running a single TikTok account, with 1.4 million views collected so far.

One of their typical formats are faceless style, low-quality clips that usually just show someone’s feet. The main point isn’t the video itself, but the hook: a short, motivational line pushing viewers to quit a bad habit (called ‘ZA’ or ‘za’) so they can level up and improve their lives.

These videos tend to generate quite some comments from people who use or used to use cannabis, opening up about their own experiences.

Another type of video that’s starting to get more attention is a headshot format where the creator looks surprised. Like before, the main focus is the message showing that the app helped him beat his addiction.

In the comments, people talk about cutting back or fully quitting their drug use.

Sometimes, elaborate videos aren’t necessary. Simply positioning oneself similarly to the target audience and showing vulnerability can increase engagement. But will these formats be enough to drive real conversions beyond the initial buzz?

We’ll keep you posted.

AI Instagram Hits $80K MRR Last Month

An AI, single-player “Instagram dupe” just hit $80K MRR on a $39.99 a year Pro plan, powered by two branded accounts and…

SGE Team

•

November 17, 2025

•

3 min read

Save for later

Aspect is an AI social media app where you are the only human.

Think Instagram, single player mode.

The app launched in June 2024 and hit $80K MRR and 30K downloads last month.

It is now ranked in the top 100 Social Networking charts in more than 30 countries.

Aspect uses a hard gated freemium model with an “Aspect Pro” subscription.

Without the subscription, you can only post once a day, you cannot comment on posts, and your messages are very limited.

The only option is a yearly plan at $39.99.

Their growth engine is set on a branded Instagram page, another on TikTok, and 15 TikTok ambassadors.

So far, those two main pages have generated 45.7M views on TikTok and 18.6M views on Instagram, mostly from two viral videos.

They first blew up in December 2024 with a short faceless video using a fade in effect and a meme GTA6 hook, calling Aspect a single player instagram:

“

We got single-player instagram before GTA6

” -> 27.5M views / Tiktok

“

We got single-player instagram before GTA6

” -> 6.7M views / Instagram

They went viral again in June with another short video, this time a shocked face selfie-style. The hook was tuned for Gen Z:

“

Wdym there’s an ai only instagram that you’re the only human there

” -> 13.6M views / Tiktok

“

Wdym there’s an ai only instagram that you’re the only human there

” ->  9.7M views / Instagram

Besides the main accounts, they also kicked off a TikTok UGC wave this year.

So far, only

@joajoaaa5

has gone viral, hitting 1.2M views in August with a car selfie and a POV style hook:

“

pov: you’re in a y/n fanfic acting like your bias know you

“

Overall, the hired creators post short videos with long hooks and position the app as “insta sims” or “AI instagram”.

Aspect shows how far a single player social media can go, as an “AI Instagram” where you’re the only human, being pushed almost entirely through TikTok and Instagram.

For builders, this is  a clear example that if the concept is strong and resembles a mainstream app (like Instagram), you can combine strict monetization with aggressive social growth and still scale.

Full collection available on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10MBz8RHiMKv

We found three new gym tracking apps, all released in less than three months, with the newest one released only 41 days ago.

These are

LFTR

,

Gymeo

and

Odyssey

.

We found four accounts, with three of them linked to Gymeo and Odyssey. They publish Pinterest and AI generated slideshow listicles. Here is the type of slideshows they post.

These slideshows use AI generated images and are pushed out in large volumes. The numbers on these three accounts are strong.

They repeat the same hooks often. A few openings perform much better than others, like “muscles i” or “train harder.” These work differently compared to the usual “3 tip…” type of listicle openers.

You can find all their best hooks here.

This listicle style usually needs a lot more views. If you share six tips and only one mentions your app then you get about one sixth of the conversion rate. But the upside is that this broad content can pull in six times more views.

Many apps like this are showing up now. They are often clones of Lyfta or other gym trackers.

It feels similar to when new Gen Z developers start building apps and pick a gym planner as their first project, the same way many pick a simple to do list as their starter idea.

article.title: When The Format Copycat Wins
article.content:
When The Format Copycat Wins

A perfect hook is powerful but temporary. You can repeat it for a while and win big, but anyone can copy it and out-exec…

SGE Team

November 15, 2025

•

2 min read

When The Format Copycat Wins

A perfect hook is powerful but temporary. You can repeat it for a while and win big, but anyone can copy it and out-exec…

SGE Team

•

November 15, 2025

•

2 min read

Save for later

We have learned this many times.

Once you find the right hook, the one that fits perfectly, you can repeat it almost endlessly until you hit full fatigue.

It works the same way paid ads work.

You can keep showing the same creative to people until they convert. At some point the audience gets tired, the performance dies, and you have to move to the next hook.

You should try to protect your viral hook at all cost.

The reality is that it is almost impossible. Someone always copies it, optimizes it, and ends up doing even better.

This is exactly what is happening across the UGC marketplace space. One brand finds a viral hook. Another runs the same structure with a cleaner version and more creators. And they outperform it.

The hook we are referring to is this one:

It is a strong hook/format.

It stacks numbers in a wall of text, uses dollar amounts, plays on a “bad maths” trick, and ends with strong time pressure. It is a classic problem and solution breakdown that performs extremely well.

It did 1.3M views and more than 20K bookmarks. Highly relatable. The only issue is that they did not start the campaign in the strongest way.

Another creator reused the same structure five days ago and hit 3.6M views with 35.4K bookmarks:

This account reached 5.7M views in only five weeks.

Onghost is an AI agent to help creators get brand deals faster. But we then noticed Pitch’Em, a mobile app that started posting four weeks earlier.

And they used the exact same hook. It is the one that drove their first virality in October:

The numbers are different but the structure is identical. They had only twelve creators and already started repeating the hook.

So the competitor simply reused the exact same idea with three times more creators and completely overtook them.

Same hook.

Bigger scale.

Better result.

frameworks.name: Hook Format Replication and Scaling
frameworks.description: Identify a viral content hook or format that resonates strongly with the target audience, then replicate it consistently across multiple creators or channels to scale reach and engagement.
frameworks.when_to_use: When a content hook or format has proven viral success but faces competition or fatigue, and you want to maximize organic growth by leveraging scale and creator diversity.
frameworks.example: A mobile app brand finds a viral TikTok video format stacking numbers and dollar amounts with time pressure, then deploys the same format across a larger creator network to surpass competitors' reach.

metadata.key_principle: A viral content hook is powerful but temporary; scaling its impact requires replication across multiple creators and continuous optimization to outpace competitors who will inevitably copy the format.
metadata.article_summary: The article explains that while a perfect viral hook can drive significant engagement temporarily, it is easily copied by competitors who can out-execute by scaling the format across more creators. The example given shows a mobile app using a strong hook format repeatedly with more creators to achieve higher views and bookmarks, overtaking the original creator. The key insight is that protecting a viral hook is nearly impossible, so growth teams should focus on scaling and optimizing the format rather than relying on a single creator or iteration.

StudyFetch

StudyFetch is back with another viral Reels after riding a StudyTok trend — “studying until my ice melts”.

The video hit

4.4M views

just six days ago.

Ghost

Ghost, a recent AI platform that helps content creators find brand deals, went viral with a TikTok video that pulled in

3.7M views

.

It features a desk recording of the UGC creator drinking a juice at a cafe, her laptop open, paired with a long hook.

They use multiple numbers throughout the wall of text to trigger a stop-scrolling effect. The hook ends with “that’s $15K just from sending emails”, making people comment asking how she did it. She then replies with the link to the website.

Cosmos

Creative app Cosmos went viral with a quick UGC clip and app recording combo that pulled in 3.7M views and almost 3,000 comments.

She leads with the hook

“ai generated images are KILLING the planet so here is an eco friendly alternative”

, then moves on to showing said alternative.

Fluently

The language app Fluently has fully embraced AI avatars and just had its first viral moment because of it.

They stuck to the same format they’ve been using for a while, a split-screen showing what to say and what not to say.

The video hit

2.9 million views

, but with most of the 1.2K comments being totally random, it seems like the conversion message didn’t quite land.

Inflow

ADHD app Inflow went viral four days ago with a meme video format they’ve been using for years.

The hook “People with ADHD when something doesn’t fall into place like they wanted it to, and overreact just a little bit…” got the video to

2.4M views

(slightly boosted), but the complete lack of CTA suggests low effectiveness.

Viggle AI

Video editor Viggle AI jumped on the news of GTA 6 getting delayed to next year and turned it into a funny meme that racked up

2.1 million views

and over 2,000 comments.

With tools like this, the edit itself becomes the CTA.

Visualize AI

Last but not least, another AI editor scored a solid win, this time in the home decor space.

The classic “what should I do with this space?” slideshow kicks off with a shot of a plain corner, followed by a series of decor ideas, all generated with the app.

It pulled in

1 million views

and more than 1,200 comments.

An app went from unknown to 1.3M downloads in a month using TikTok baddies and beauty girl collabs.

SGE Team

•

November 14, 2025

•

3 min read

Save for later

Kapi Cam is a vintage digital camera app that turns your phone into a retro digicam. It comes with a bunch of retro-style filters and simple effects so people can capture their favorite throwback photos.

Built by a small Chinese team, the app launched on Google Play in January 2024 and on the App Store in March 2025.

Last month, Kapi Cam hit 1.3 million downloads across both platforms.

Right now, it sits inside the top 100 charts in dozens of countries.

A big reason for this is that they pulled in over 118 million views in the last 30 days with one Tiktok account and a worlwide influencer campaign.

Their TikTok account

@kapi.cam

, went fully viral in October and is still trending in November.

It posts fast edits of multiple attractive girls using the “retro” filter, paired with aesthetic songs that match the vibe.

Straight after that, they follow up with a short app demo that shows how to copy the exact camera effect.

One of the videos exploded:

“

in another life i’m a baddie taking a low quality pic

” -> 30.6M views on Oct 1

Since then, the account has kept using this same format and has landed several more viral videos in the last weeks.

The other strategy relies on paid partnerships with big beauty and fashion influencers. These collabs are doing insanely well, and they are working with creators in multiple languages.

For example,

@rose_zzzzz

posted a “retro chic vibe” photo tutorial that went crazy.

“

How to turn normal light street photos into retro chic vibes

” 39.2M views

This video shows how strong the demand is for a good “retro filter”, and how many Gen Z girls want to copy their favourite creators’ filters.

Paid collab videos have become their main user acquisition engine, and they are working pretty well.

Becoming a TikTok trendsetter is the quickest way to push your app into the mainstream.

Take a look at their collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10NBRDZfnV73

With 7M views this month alone, Mindgrasp is leading a wave of raw, viral study content, mocking ChatGPT, calling out sl…

SGE Team

•

5 min read

Save for later

Study apps are having their moment, and with exam season coming up, it’s the perfect time for them to get noticed.

From “toxic study motivation” to “Chat GPT takedowns,” academic productivity has gone fully viral.

And

Mindgrasp

, the “AI study assistant,” is right in the middle of it.

Launched in 2022 by Apricot AI, the app helps students quickly summarize lectures, take notes, and generate proper citations. It’s positioning itself as the trustworthy, citation-safe alternative to Chat GPT (but aren’t they all…).

At the moment, the app is pulling in 9,000 downloads a month and bringing in $10,000 in revenue.

Mindgrasp has been quietly building a small but growing media engine.

They’ve hit 39 million lifetime views, with some clear peaks, and 7 million views in the last 30 days alone.

Right now, they’re running 15 TikTok accounts, including 4 new UGC-style pages that popped up in the past two months.

You can access all data here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10I4TDRPKibB

Across these accounts, two content formats are clearly leading the charge.

Format #1: Toxic Study Motivation

We’ve covered this growing trend more than once. It’s raw, a bit guilt-trippy, and speaks straight to your face, part tough love, part therapy. Most importantly, if done well, it has an insane viral potential.

This video got

2.7 million views

, and it’s just one of several posted by different creators. In the clip, she starts with the hook,

“Aw, you’re too tired to study?”

then rolls into a list of tough-love consequences for slacking off, like:

“All good, all good. Just imagine your boss calling you replaceable and they’re right.”

Then the they introduce the solution

“That’s why I use Mindgrasp

“

Once you start watching, you can’t stop. These videos feel like your friend staring straight at you through the screen except instead of comforting you, they’re calling you out.

Format #2: ChatGPT Takedowns

There’s another mini-trend making the rounds in the study app space: mocking the unreliable rival while hyping your own app as the “only one you can trust.”

Creators film themselves talking straight to the camera, with a meme-style caption on top like:

“pov everyone’s finding out ChatGPT gives fake citations but I’m safe because I only use Mindgrasp it’s actually RELIABLE and I can’t risk that degree”

This video pulled in

1M views

:

And this one

766K views

→

“If you use ChatGPT you’re COOKED

“

The tone is half rant, half PSA. You feel like you’re hearing a hot take from a classmate.

This account launched less than a month ago, and it’s already their top performer.

It pulled in

12.5M views

with one single format.

It’s the same setup every time: one creator, one pose, a thousand hook possibilities. Here are some of them:

“When you’re so deep into your research you start recognizing authors like they’re celebrities.”

“POV: everyone’s finding out ChatGPT gives fake citations but I’m safe because I use Mindgrasp.”

“POV: you finish 5 papers in 2 hours because the PhD student next to you was using Mindgrasp.”

But this isn’t Mindgrasp first viral streak.

Back in 2024, they jumped on

the “angry professor” trend

, a skit where students poked fun at strict teachers (played by actors). They brought it back in February, and one of the new videos took off with

15.2 million views

.

Mindgrasp has proven it can read the room and insert itself into study-culture trends.

Now, they’re doubling down on their ecosystem. Under the same developer Apricot AI, two new apps just dropped:

LecturePro AI

→ transcribes live lectures and turns them into notes.

NotesPro AI

→ organizes and rewrites notes in cleaner, structured formats.

NotesPro is already being soft-promoted through Mindgrasp’s creator network.

One

recent post to promote NotesPro AI

did just a few hundred views with this hook:

“I got asked to try out this brand new note taking app that just release..”

No major UGC rollouts yet but this slow promoting hints at a cross-promotion strategy similar to how

StudyFetch

scaled in 2024: use one app’s virality to funnel traffic to the next.

HeightFuel has been changing the way people feel every day, helping them stand taller and improve their posture since launching, just 86 days ago.

The app is running 5 accounts and has gathered 57M views on TikTok so far.

All the accounts use the same format, but

@heightfuel

stands out because it gets by far the most engagement.

This account shares three types of content that are getting tons of views, mostly slideshows with AI-created illustrations.

The most popular videos kick off with the hook, “Habits that make you grow taller.” Each slide shows a habit, a matching illustration, and a quick line that explains it.

This video got over six thousand comments, and many people were skeptical about the tips it shared.

This version also got a lot of views. It used the same style of illustrations but flipped the hook to the opposite: “Habits that make you shorter.”

Unlike the first video, this one got comments from people thanking them for the tips and saying they want to try them out.

This version still uses a slideshow with AI-made illustrations, but it’s a little simpler to show that the topic is different. It’s about guessing a person’s height based on how tall their parents are.

This video got the most comments, with people posting their own height guesses in reply.

The other accounts use the same format with different illustrations, but their hooks convey the same idea as the others, just phrased differently.

Like

‘Unusual Habits Killing HEIGHT GROWTH’

or

‘Signs You Will Grow WAY Taller.’

This subtle difference makes a big impact: the videos aren’t as clear or catchy, so they didn’t get as many views.

$100K Revenue in 22 Days

How this AI copycat has nailed TikTok marketing in under a month.

SGE Team

•

November 13, 2025

4 min read

Save for later

A new app hit $100K in monthly revenue and around 100K downloads just 22 days after launching.

TruthSeek

, which came out exactly a month ago, helps people find social profiles and public info.

You type in a name, email, or username, and it searches major platforms to show possible matches.

The idea isn’t new.

Apps like

Deepsearch AI

already pull in over a million downloads each month and around $1M in monthly recurring revenue.

Several other AI people-search apps are doing well too.

What sets TruthSeek apart is the speed.

Right now, it’s growing faster than any other app in the space.

Turning “stalking” into money

They are monetizing the app by locking the core search feature behind a paywall and using auto-renewing subscriptions.

Plans start at $9.99 weekly, $14.99 monthly, or $54.99 for lifetime access.

You type a name, email, or username, it scans, then results are kept behind a subscription.

There’s no real free preview. Everything is kept behind a paywall.

The growth playbook

Their distribution model runs on a faceless TikTok strategy.

They manage 18 accounts that have pulled in about 350 million views — some of which include paid traffic.

You can access all data here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10UPMufrBM7w

Their posting speed is way higher than any competitor, which each account putting out an insane average of 30+ videos a day.

One of them posted 725 videos last week alone, showing just how far they’re willing to push it.

TruthSeek’s team is operating a network of 18 accounts with seemingly random usernames, each one linking back to the app in the bio.

They repeat the same content formula across all their accounts: short, emotional B-roll of someone breaking down, paired with a dramatic story about a relationship or cheating, all tied to “searching a name and finding out X.”

In most videos, the creators are in a car, crying their eyes out over the heartbreak of finding out they’re being cheated on.

Here are some examples:

“

When you search your boyfriend’s name and find out he’s still texting his ex every night

.”

“

When you search your boyfriend’s name and discover he’s on FaceTime with his ex at 2 a.m… while you’re sleeping next to him

.”

(in Spanish)

“

POV: When you type your boyfriend’s name into TruthSeek and discover his secret with your bestfriend

“

Clips are constantly recycled, only the hook lines are iterated.

Why it works

No other app posts at this volume. Not in this niche or anywhere else, really.

Most of their videos are average, but putting out hundreds daily creates a solid baseline and leaves room for hits to pop off. It really is a numbers game, and they’re nailing it.

Then, once the viewer is pulled in, the paywall hits right at peak curiosity, pushing them into a trial or subscription right after the hook lands.

That’s how you turn quiet scrolling into money.

article.title: 6 Viral Pro Hacks

6 Viral Pro Hacks

The secret organic engine behind breakout consumer apps.

5 min read

6 Viral Pro Hacks

The secret organic engine behind breakout consumer apps.

SGE Team

•

November 13, 2025

•

5 min read

Save for later

Organic acquisition is the only real foundation of a growth engine.

Unlike paid, it builds momentum over time.

Every piece of content becomes discoverable. Every account becomes a distribution channel. Every iteration improves performance.

And when done right, it compounds.

Here are the six best ways to ensure you’re investing your time and money in building a sustainable growth machine, not just posting to go viral once or twice.

Three posts a day, hook rotation

This is the fastest way to find content-market fit, hands down.

Posting different hooks on a daily basis will give you the data you need to know what the winning formats are,

especially

if you’re just getting started.

Take a look at

Cray Cray

, launched in January 2024: they’ve been slowly shifting gears, moving from faceless slideshows to UGC and are currently testing different formats and hooks around LDR heartbreak.

Reborn Nutrition

also did some testing of their own, having narrowed it down to just 4 winning formats.

Expand branded accounts

Most apps set up a brand account and stick to dull formats that don’t perform well organically. Then they bring in a bunch of creators and lean on them completely. By the time they’re ready to post, the brand account already feels like a ghost town.

Here’s the thing. If your strategy depends on faceless content or stuff anyone can create, you might as well use that to your advantage. Instead of sticking to one generic brand account, why not build several and let each focus on a specific format?

You can divide them like:

@appname.hacks — shortcuts & tutorials

@appname.results — user transformations & stories

@appname.behindthebuild — BTS + team

This way, you can cover all kinds of content that help grow and support your brand. Educational posts, short high-converting hooks, and “build-in-public” updates can all have a fair shot at the same time. Splitting them across different accounts lowers the risk of putting everything in one place and makes it easier to hand things off to different team members.

Activate your team

On that note, get every marketer, intern, and founder on your team posting like a creator. Let them run personal accounts and share daily POV or vlog-style updates about the journey of building.

That’s exactly how we do it at Social Growth Engineers. Every team member makes content, and it turns us into brand advocates who share what we’re learning and doing along the way.

Product decisions;

Roadmap thinking;

Growth experiments;

Engineering or product breakdowns;

Lessons learned while scaling;

…

This helps build trust and makes your app feel more human, while also boosting your reach and making people believe in what you’re offering. You won’t fully understand the power of organic until that one random video from your 18-year old intern blows up overnight.

The smaller, the better

If you want to try UGC without going all in, start by finding as many nano-influencers in your niche as you can. Look for at least a couple of outliers who perform 10x better than the average.

This isn’t just about saving you some money. Paying big for one collab with a huge influencer won’t teach you anything about product–market fit or even content–market fit. The only way to get actual insights is to order a batch of videos from smaller creators who’ll work with you on nailing the right formats and hooks.

Snap It

, currently at 200k downloads/month, started with working with small influencers posting from their own accounts. Since mid-July, they’ve made a strong comeback by bringing in waves of creators and using the content formats they figured out during that first round of testing, pulling in over 22.4 million views.

Become a “format repeater”

It’s just like repeating outfits. You think everyone is noticing your lack of creativity when in reality no one cares.

Create single-format accounts and post daily. It’s super simple to manage and helps you quickly see what works so you can scale it across other channels.

Pick one content template and run it 100+ times with different variations.

If you need ideas, check out our Resource section, especially the

Faceless Guide to 50 Viral Formats

.

Endeavorise, a recent self-improvement app, has just reached 10,000 downloads with a single format repeated on TikTok and Instagram — read the

full article here

.

Multiply by language

If your app solves a universal problem or targets a global audience, language scaling is one of the fastest ways to grow. Just repurpose your top-performing content:

One account per market = one language

Use the same scripts, hooks, and formats… just translated.

Sitly

did this with one video in four different languages and hit 100 million views, bringing in $250K in monthly recurring revenue.

The best part is that since all their videos were silent UGC clips with text overlays, they didn’t need new creators for each language. They just had someone check the translations and hit post. Genius or genius?

SGE Team
