New AI Skincare App Hits 26.4M Views in 60 Days

63 days in, this app has 26.4M views from six AI faces that feel real.

SGE Team

•

November 13, 2025

•

3 min read

Save for later

Just 63 days in, Dewly is already aiming to change how we do skincare with smart, AI-driven personal recommendations.

The app is still new, with just six active accounts so far, but it’s already racked up 26.4M views. A few of their posts look like they were boosted, but most have picked up organic traction on their own.

All the accounts on the app follow a similar pattern, using AI-generated headshots. The videos are short and only show a small movement to highlight the condition of their skin.

The videos show two kinds of AI-generated girls. One type has skin covered in pimples and marks, and the captions focus on how acne affects self-esteem and mental health, the ongoing struggle, the emotional toll, and the feeling of vulnerability.

Some of their best hooks:

“do u ever feel pretty then see ur acne in a mirror and say nvm”

“a little kid just asked me why my face looked like that”

“no matter how much I spend or what I do I wake up like this anyways what’s the point”

“maybe if I fell in love with my acne it would leave me too”

“tysm for pointing out my acne and ruining the rest of my day as I pretend it didn’t affect me”

Then there are the videos where the creator shows her now-clear skin. These focus on the healing journey and the emotional change after treatment, the sense of relief, the joy of moving past a tough time, and the renewed confidence that comes with recovery.

Here are examples of the hooks from these videos:

“it took nuking my mental health and skin before the acne went away 🫠”

“I wouldn’t wish the acne I had on my literal worst enemy”

“how I got rid of my acne”

“friendly reminder u haven’t lost ur spark u just need clear skin ✨”

This small detail changes everything. The second type of video gets almost no engagement  and what little it does get feels paid, while the first type draws strong, natural interaction.

This video got a lot of comments because people relate to the situation, many have gone through it themselves.

A lot of the videos don’t mention the app directly or show any links. Instead, the creators drop the app’s name in comments on each other’s posts.

To view the collection, click here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10XVcI1ylylt

Icare is a new mindful browser for social media that helps you focus.

It removes addictive features like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts.

On November 11, it reached #7 in Social Networking in France.

Icare was created by

His team is now running 7 accounts, 4 on Instagram and 3 on TikTok.

“

I am

” is a lock screen widget that shows daily affirmations.

Last month they reached 400K downloads and $600K MRR.

Back in  March, we broke down their

Instagram Reels

play, which remains their main acquisition channel.

From May to October, they went for a TikTok format that pulled in over 20 million views, although some might have been sparked.

The move was quite simple: open with a strong “how-to” hook, then deliver a fast demo.

Everything centers on the hook:

“How to put affirmations on your lock screen (it changes every day).”

It starts with a 1 to 3 second visual of an AI model smiling and looking calm or confident. It’s the “feeling” the user is chasing.

Then, they end it with an app tutorial, cutting to a screen recording and showing the exact steps.

The hook works because it teaches something, targets a high-visibility spot on the phone, and promises fresh value every day with almost no effort.

It works because it links the emotional “why” to the easy “how,” all in under 10 seconds.

This format, made popular by creator @a_vmack, mixes two kinds of content to reach different audiences and hold the viewer’s attention.

It follows the “Get Ready With Me” (GRWM) format, where the creator does their makeup or gets ready while chatting.

At the same time, the creator shares niche facts, surprising details, or controversial takes on a specific topic.

Example

:

“things about Harvard that would send people from others schools into a coma”

The creator keeps the viewer engaged by doing a familiar and satisfying task, like putting on makeup or following a skincare routine. It breaks up the info-heavy content and draws in beauty and routine-loving audiences.

This format is designed to pull in two types of viewers at once:

Niche: Those curious about the topic being discussed (like students or academics).

Mass: Viewers who enjoy beauty routines, calming visuals, or background noise while they scroll.

The best part is that this can work in any niche. You can tweak the “rant” style to fit whatever you’re focusing on, like “Truths About Health I Learned Too Late” or “How I Actually Learned Japanese Without a Tutor.”

The app often picks a comment and posts a video reply, keeping the comment visible on the screen and adding a hook, as if the dog is the one talking.

Even though the videos don’t get a lot of views, they get a good number of comments compared to how many people watch them.

Around 48 hours ago, they tried a new format that focused more on the staff, using an interview with a hook to give some background.

Even though both apps are connected to Destination Pet, the TikTok account belongs to just one of them. It could be a good idea to post videos that promote both apps on the same channel.

A new fitness app is gaining traction with viral slideshows, creator transformations, and nearly 520K views, mirroring t…

Save for later

Just six days ago, a new nutrition and calorie-tracking app called Kalo launched on the App Store. It’s stepping into the spotlight to compete with Cal AI, which has been leading the space in recent weeks, as the health-tech market gets more crowded.

So far, the app has 16 creator accounts and has already gained 519,6K views. Some of these videos have gained traction organically, some other were also boosted by paid ads.

Even though the view count is still modest, the data shows strong and steady growth in all engagement metrics.

The app’s main account has been testing different types of content. The most viewed post so far is a video showing a creator’s body transformation, before and after, ending with the reveal: the app made it possible.

The official account mainly shares slideshows with meal ideas. Each slide uses a few short hooks to highlight the ingredients in the dish.

Most creators post around living a healthy, gym-focused lifestyle, posting slideshows that mix workout photos, healthy meals, and with a small screenshot of the app in the corner displaying the calorie count.

Even though Kalo still has a low number of views, it’s following a pattern similar to what Cal AI showed in its early days. Back then, Cal AI also had a lower engagement rate compared to its view count, as pointed out in this

article

.

At first, Cal AI’s creators used a format a lot like the one Kalo’s team is using now, a slideshow that starts with a photo of the fit creator, followed by healthy meal photos.

The main difference is that Cal AI only showed the app in the last slide, instead of throughout the slideshow.

As noted in an older

article

, one of the best-performing formats was a slideshow that compared healthy and processed foods, using a clear hook to show which one is seen as the “enemy” and which one isn’t.

The key to boosting Kalo’s views might be keeping the slideshow format but shifting the concept, focusing less on the creator and their meals and more on showing what shouldn’t be eaten versus what actually can be, contrary to common belief.

To view the collection, click here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10PE7eF3mGCT

Fitness Screen Time Hits $36K MRR

This app trades pushups for screen time and hit $36K MRR. One founder, a few viral skits, 37M views.

SGE Team

•

November 11, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

Pushscroll is an app that trades pushups for scrolling time.

It unlocks minutes of scrolling through quick sets like push-ups and squats.

It is a 3-in-1 -> exercise-based app timer, smart app blocker, and gamified fitness in one place.

Launched in June, it has suddenly spiked in the last 30 days:

30K downloads and $30K MRR on the App Store.

100K downloads and $6K MRR on Google Play.

The app works with a subscription that includes a 7-day free trial which renews automatically.

You’ll need a subscription to access the main features, for the price of €9.99 per month or €30.99 per year.

The founder is

Alejandro Sanchez

, known as @skyirezumi on every platform.

He has started multiple startups and went viral with founder-led videos.

He also shares his journey on

X

.

The growth playbook is TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube.

They run 12 accounts that have pulled in over 37M views, with about 95% of views coming from his founder-led accounts.

There are two pillars.

First, the founder account, @skyirezumi, posting punchy videos across platforms.

Second, the official

Pushscroll

Instagram, which reposts influencer videos originally made on TikTok.

That page has not gone truly viral yet, but posts with bigger creators sometimes hit solid viewership.

But the real engine is still the founder’s content.

On YouTube, he went viral twice with push-up skits that demo the app.

“

My phone makes me do 5 Push-Ups before the snap

“

-> 4.5M views

“

My phone won’t let me scroll on reels until I did pushups

” -> 2.1M views

He doomscrolls, gets locked, then does push-ups to add minutes, showing the core feature in just a few seconds.

On Instagram, one format exploded in September. Two near identical videos with sharp hooks and a direct CTA. Comment “APP,” get a DM, convert.

“

Bro is doing pushups to unlock insta

” -> 6.8M views + 6.5M views

On TikTok, he has not hit massive virality yet, but he is building a founder storyline, documenting the struggles and the build. It strengthens the app’s identity.

With Pushscroll, Alejandro shows how a founder can drive about 95% of 37M views by shipping one native demo per social media platform.

Founder feed plus brand reposts, with strict repurposing.

That focus turned a June launch into $36K MRR with minimal spend.

Ship the demo that sells itself, keep it founder-led until the brand page starts to hit, then scale creators around the proven format.

Pushscroll’s full collection is available to track on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10nMDxTOG8r4

This is one of those dropshipped products that pops up around Christmas.

There are plenty others like it, but this one stands out — over 60M organic views on a single account using the same hook and video format.

That’s not all. It’s also being resold by other accounts and featured in dozens of videos across TikTok. Let’s start by looking at this main account.

One of their videos went viral organically, reaching 40M views just two weeks ago.

The hook ““you’re always in your room” also my room” is quite genius. It’s simple, relatable, and hits those at-home scrollers that are in that exact setup. They didn’t invent it though; a quick search shows plenty of older videos using the same line months before.

What we love about e-commerce edits is how fast-paced and visually catchy they are from the very first second. The execution is often spotless, and their mega viral rate sits at around 4%, which is impressive.

We also found individual videos on other accounts promoting the same product, like this one that got 12.9M views.

Plus, there are many competitors selling the same item through different stores, all getting great results with nearly identical hooks and formats.

Scroll through this TikTok search and you’ll find even more examples:

https://www.tiktok.com/search?q=your%20always%20in%20your%20room&t=1762774634352

We’ll likely see even more accounts like this appear as Black Friday and the Christmas season approach.

you’ve changed

Showing the progress on the app in the second slide.

Japanese culture is trending among Gen Z, and language learning apps are catching up.

Apps like

Pingo AI

Realizing the opportunity in this demand,

Hanashi

chose a clear angle, launching as an app that only teaches Japanese.

Launched in June, Hanashi is now at $8K MRR, with 15,000 monthly downloads on Android and iOS.

Monetization is simple: a premium auto-renewing subscription.

Users try a few lessons, then hit a paywall. It charges $14.99 per month or $99.99 per year.

Hanashi was founded by Eion, an Irish builder who moved to Tokyo in early 2025.

He made Hanashi after ChatGPT kept interrupting him and losing the thread.

Distribution is 100% reliant on TikTok.

They are running eight accounts and have collected a total of 3 million views since May.

The top account is

tokyo.hanashi

.

It took the viral “

Why is Japanese so hard

” format, and added a twist. They kept the video faceless, and recorded the app roasting the user’s Japanese.

They also renamed Japanese to “Japanknees”, to farm engagement.

“

Why is Japanknees so hard!?

” 700K views / October 7

“

Why is Japaknees so hard !?

” 300K views / October 10

Eoin also posted a longer headshot video with app picks for beginners, claiming that Hanashi was the one that finally got him speaking.

That video drove almost 9K bookmarks.

Back in June,

studyjp.me

did a faceless slideshow rating three apps.

It hit almost 300K views and 30K bookmarks, which helped build trust.

“

Rating Japanese learning apps for beginners>>

“

They also tapped on the “

Mad Sora Professor

” trend we covered two weeks ago, and that keeps going viral for countless study apps these days.

“

yo why is my japanese teacher crashing out on us

” 212K / Oct. 18

“

yo why did our japanese teacher go so hard

” 171K / Oct. 18

Hanashi got to $8K by studying what works in its niche, riding trends, and adding its own touch.

We’ll keep you posted on their progress. Meanwhile, you can access all accounts and videos here:

The app was actually created by a group of four friends, who are now posting from their own TikTok accounts to promote the app and the events they host. They share short videos from these events to give followers a peek at what’s happening.

They have also been testing a slideshow format, showcasing the event with each photo paired with a fun comment or hook, so followers can really get a feel for what it was like.

People usually leave more comments on the videos format because they give a clearer idea of what the event was like.

At the same time, they continue producing headshot, green-screen videos where they talk on camera while showing the app in the background.

Along with promoting their app, the four creators also share videos about their lives in London, where all the app’s events are held.

But even though people are saving the videos, they’re not getting much interaction.

The main account sticks to the same style but also shares videos discussing the behind-the-scenes process of building the app.

Their events draw big crowds, but the content isn’t getting the same kind of engagement, at least not yet.

article.content:

Two 19-year old college students have conquered the fantasy sports niche and grown their app to $2.4M yearly recurring r…

Two 19-year old college students have conquered the fantasy sports niche and grown their app to $2.4M yearly recurring r…

SGE Team

•

November 6, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

In 2019, two Ithaca College students, Sam Factor and Dylan Shane, turned a simple school project into one of the most promising startups in fantasy football.

It started in a machine learning class, where they built an algorithm that could accurately predict player performance. They named it Walter.

At first, Walter was just their final project. They tested it using past NFL data, a method called back testing. But the real challenge came in the fall of 2019, after graduation, when they decided to test the algorithm on live games.

The results were impressive. The predictions were so accurate that Sam started seeing real business potential in Walter.

Today,

WalterPicks

processes more than 20 million data points collected over 10 years of American football.

They’re now making around $2,400,000 in yearly recurring revenue.

The fantasy sports market was already massive back then, worth about $8.88 billion in 2021, and led by giants like

ESPN

and

DraftKings

.

WalterPicks stood out with an algorithm that’s said to be 17% more accurate than predictions from ESPN and Yahoo.

As of 2025, though, some competitors remain extremely difficult to beat.

WalterPicks soon realized that having a great algorithm wasn’t enough, it also needed strong distribution.

So the team launched an ambitious TikTok strategy, creating accounts dedicated to each of the 32 NFL teams, as well as pages for basketball and hockey (NHL).

In total, it now manages 35 accounts, with over 700,000 followers combined.

As of today, they’ve racked up 118.7 million views.

Access all data here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10rbUlfLUvDA

Every account is managed by a different creator. The first videos they posted were simple app introductions, and many of those are still the most viewed.

Each video uses the same green-screen style, with the creator’s face in front of the app. They go through how it works, using examples from their favorite team to catch the attention of that team’s fans.

Matt Kane, one of creators on the team, runs

@bengals.walterpicks

, which has gained over 33,000 followers on its own. It’s a clear example of how this type of focused, niche content can help grow the brand.

Interestingly enough, Matt found out about them through TikTok, when he came across a video they posted while hiring for social media creators.

It’s not just TikTok anymore.

Earlier this year, the WalterPicks team brought

their blog

back to life.

They’re also active on

YouTube

, sharing both long and short videos, much like what they already do on TikTok. Sure, views aren’t as high just yet, but it allows them to start tapping into a whole new audience of fantasy sports fans who don’t get their news from TikTok.

Still, they’re about to cross the 16K subscriber mark.

When the app launched, Sam mentioned that the algorithm was just one part of the puzzle. The real impact came from their smart social strategy and the tools they built right into the app.

Throne is a wishlist app made for creators.

It lets fans send gifts without ever revealing real names or addresses.

The app launched on iOS on July 1, 2023, and hit 200K downloads just last month.

Throne typically sits around the top 200 in the U.S. Social Networking charts, but one viral video recently sparked a huge spike in reach and a major jump in rankings.

In late September, Throne ran a paid collaboration with @

kilo6814

, a TikTok creator known for his slow motion videos and catchy hooks about random topics.

That video took off, earning 19.2M views, 168K shares, 313K saves and over 5,000 comments.

“So you’re telling me there’s a new site where you can post what you want to buy, and billionaires who don’t know what to do with their money can buy it for you?”

That one clip took Throne from #242 to #18 in two days.

The hook spoke to a core desire: money.

“Billionaires buying your wishlist” reframed gifting as a personal win.

The value was clear in a single line, persuading people to believe they could get free items by using Throne.

Debuting in September 2024, RealYou AI made its entrance into the market with the goal of redefining the landscape of AI-powered photo and image creation apps.

With just two accounts, the app has already racked up over 71 million views.

The app’s official account tried out a few different formats, but the only one that got real engagement was a video of YouTuber

Kai Cenat

, who has a following of over 14M in his YT channel alone, showing a before-and-after of his photo using the app.

Since Kai Cenat is one of the biggest names online, known for his funny streams and videos, turning him into a “character” in the video made it even funnier and almost certain to get engagement.

The first video was such a hit that someone in the comments even asked them to always use Kai Cenat in their videos.

RealYou AI recently brought back the same format with Kai Cenat, and once again, it got a ton of engagement.

They also tested a different video with Kai Cenat, this time using a slideshow of AI-made photos showing him as a Marvel character, with a hook pointing that out, but it didn’t get nearly as much engagement.

The app recently launched a new account with a female creator who uses a totally different style, mostly the typical headshot videos where she looks surprised.

In each one, she says she told a guy she was something specific, then used the app to create photos of her doing that, and shows the results.

All these videos lean into the same format, and they usually get more views when the AI images look more realistic.

Because she always uses the same format and hook, some people are starting to question the story and leave comments about it.

The two formats are different and meant for different groups: the older one on the official account targets a YouTube-focused, mostly male audience, while the newer one is aimed at younger, mostly female viewers.

Check out all videos here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b100Xbp2SsFap

11 months ago, HOPECORE entered the photo and video scene and hasn’t stopped attracting attention on social media since.

With two TikTok accounts and one Instagram account, the app has already earned 440M views across social media.

All three accounts follow the same format, and some of the videos are doing really well on social media, especially on

Instagram

.

The video uses the app’s signature style, making it feel like it was made entirely in the app. It begins with a popular video from social media to catch attention, then shifts into a montage of other clips.

It’s the perfect blend between traditional clipping strategies and app demos.

Each video starts with a strong hook, uses a one-of-a-kind font, and is created completely inside the app.

The videos cover all kinds of themes, from drama to comedy. The main goal is to show off the app’s format using clips that get people to engage.

The Top 3 most popular videos were all posted on Instagram.

Featuring clips from TikTok creators who already get good engagement helps bring even more attention to the app’s account.

Even big TikTok names like

@grandma_droniak

engage with these videos, proving that the app’s format can catch the attention of top creators on the platform.

Even with all the viral success, conversions just aren’t landing. Their videos are pulling in tens of millions of views, thousands of comments, and tons of hype from viewers everywhere.

But the app still isn’t turning that buzz into real downloads or revenue. That’s the risk of leaning too hard on funny content and meme-style clips. People love them, even share them, without realizing there’s an app behind it.

A bit more focus on the edit could help. Even something as small as a line like

“I made this with [app name]”

might be enough to shift attention toward the product.

We’ll be watching to see what they try next.

Access all videos here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10CWhMyiz5ed

3 min read

After going nearly silent across their main pages,

Aavia

, the period and cycle tracking app, just pulled a subtle comeback through a handful of UGC creators who launched accounts this summer.

In the last 30 days, one account has driven

688.5K views

giving a nearly dormant app a second wind.

One account, one format, one potential comeback?

The top videos come from

@pmsjas

, and they all share one thing: face-to-camera storytelling with sharp text hook overlays.

351.9K views

“Women’s health fact they don’t teach you in school: your pain tolerance is highest in the follicular phase […] and apps like Aavia make it so much easier to track this”

58.6K views

“Your period isn’t just blood it’s […] tracking this is way easier with apps like Aavia.”

It’s a format that easy to replicate: face close ups + educational text overlay+ subtle product integration.

There’s infinite variations you can use:

Educational Hooks:

“Women’s health fact they

don’t teach you in school

👇”

“Your pain tolerance is actually highest

right after your period.

”

“Your period isn’t just blood  it’s your uterus shedding

actual tissue.

”

“No one talks about this part of your cycle, but it changes everything.”

“If you’ve been planning a tattoo or workout, do it

in this phase

of your cycle.”

Personal / Relatable Hooks:

“This is why my cramps were so bad and I didn’t even know it 😭”

“Tracking my cycle literally changed how I schedule my week.”

“POV: realizing women’s health should’ve been taught in school.”

Product Tie-In Hooks:

“I only figured this out after tracking it on Aavia.”

“Apps like Aavia make it

so much easier

to understand your body.”

“I use Aavia to know when I’ll actually feel like myself again.”

When your app goes silent, the best move isn’t always to restart your main account,  but rather to slowly seed small creator voices and start noticinh what sticks.

If Aavia scaled this model with, let’s say, 20 UGC creators posting weekly with this same “health myth + product tie-in” flow, it could easily boost their visibility.

Here’s a playbook can should use:

Launch a few UGC accounts.

Let creators experiment with formats and tones.

Track what hits.

Use view data, spikes and identify the winning content type.

Replicate and scale.

Build an ambassador program or replicate the top-performing creators’ styles.

You can track their accounts here:

has earned 26M+ views with this single format and has gone viral more than five times.

Viewers watch a small investment grow across years, then end on a clean, satisfying reveal.

The assets are familiar and easy to care about, including Bitcoin, CS2 skins and popular stocks.

The payoff is purely visual, and the build only needs data and motion.

This format boosts retention through the simple pleasure of watching a line rise over time.

Two variations perform best.

Single asset POV

Pick one asset strong enough to carry the full minute, such as Bitcoin, NVDA, Monster, or an iconic CS2 case.

Use one clear line and make the final number impossible to miss.

Head-to-head comparison

When rivalry drives interest, chart two assets on the same scale and the same start date, for example BTC vs ETH, NVDA vs AMD, or Prisma vs Spectrum.

Consistency makes the system work.

Keep covers, typography, and hook language aligned across playlists so every upload is instantly recognizable and easy to repeat.

The outcome is a sustainable content engine with clear rules, familiar assets, a satisfying reveal, and endless combinations that viewers will request in the comments.

Potential niches: finance, investing, widget

Last summer,

The same layout repeats for wavy, curly, and coily hair.

That recommendation slide can also double as a soft promo for apps, products, or tools.

And when one part starts trending, the key is speed.

Post 3 or more parts within 24–48 hours using the same hook and cover to build momentum.

Over the past few months, more apps have been popping up to help students manage their notes and study better.

About seven months ago, a new one came out, DocScribe, this time made specifically for medical students.

The app is linked to the

Memrizz

website, an AI platform that focuses on medical learning and practice. It’s often called “Memrizz Docscribe,” showing that both are part of the same digital system.

Even though the app is part of the same platform, it takes a different approach on TikTok.

DocScribe runs 9 accounts and has reached a total of 203,1K views so far.

All creators are medical students, and their videos focus mostly on studying. Most of them start with a shocked expression close-up, then move on to showing how the app works.

Each video begins with a hook that relates to the daily challenges of medical students or people in clinical training.

Another type of video shows the creator’s daily routine as a medical student. They talk throughout the video, with subtitles on the screen, and end by showing how the app fits into their day.

Even though the videos are made for the app’s audience, they haven’t been getting much engagement.

Because the app is part of the same platform, some DocScribe creators also promote Memrizz, using the same video style.

Memrizz launched before the app and was already using a different approach. It teamed up with medical students who already had TikTok accounts and were creating content.

It’s been seven months, and DocScribe is still struggling to scale its formats into significant views, and those views into users. Can they carve out a space in one of TikTok’s most crowded markets right now?

We’ll keep you posted, but in the meantime, you can check all their accounts here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10eqxVingBjt

He Vibe Coded a $20K MRR App in 14 Days

He Vibe Coded a $20K MRR App in 14 Days

He vibe coded an app to $20K MRR in 14 days. From $7 in the bank to a simple app that finds class-action cash, scaled by…

SGE Team

•

November 4, 2025

•

5 min read

Save for later

At the start of 2024, Connor Burd had $7 in his bank account and no job.

One year later, he has run multiple iOS apps bringing in over $700K ARR, without any investors or outside funding.

Fresh out of UC Santa Cruz, the 23-year-old had already built and launched several consumer apps before joining Origami as a founding engineer.

That hands-on shipping muscle, paired with his speed-first mindset, set the tone for what came next.

Last summer, Connor joined Shipaton 2025, RevenueCat’s global mobile hackathon, and turned it into a personal two-week sprint to build something big.

That

something

was Payout, an app now making around $20K a month. It also won Shipathon’s Grand Prize, landing him a $60K cash reward.

What is Payout?

Payout helps people find class-action settlements they’re already eligible for. Basically, free money most consumers never realize they can claim.

The app simplifies a messy legal process into a few taps. It scans open settlements, estimates potential payouts, and sends alerts when new cases appear.

Millions of dollars go unclaimed every year, and Payout turns that overlooked reality into an opportunity.

Built entirely with AI

Connor built the whole thing using Claude Code and Cursor.

Not a single line written by hand.

He launched it on August 2, and within weeks it crossed 10,000 downloads and $20,000 in monthly recurring revenue.

Picking a niche that sells itself

Everyone wants to make money, it’s one of human’s core desires.

Connor studied competitors like

Settlemate

and

Claim

, borrowed what worked, and added his own spin.

The $20,000 paywall

Payout runs on a subscription model that gives users unlimited settlements. It’s $9.99 for weekly access or $39.99 for the full year.

Connor’s goal is obviously to nudge users toward the yearly plan, since it brings in the highest lifetime value per customer.

The growth playbook

Connor’s main growth lever was influencer partnerships.

Instead of traditional UGC, he worked with large Instagram creators who already had audience trust.

One of them was @

casper.capital

, a personal finance influencer with 2.7M followers. Casper’s paid collabs drove thousands of users directly to the app.

The formula relied on relatable, viral videos that feel spontaneous but lead straight to downloads.

A typical post starts with a hook:

“

Class Action Side Hustle!

“

Next comes a short skit featuring a brand most viewers recognize, like Temu:

“Hey Temu, Is it true that I can make $1000 from your lawsuit?”

That curiosity pulls viewers in, followed by a quick step-by-step walkthrough of how to claim money through the app.

The CTA is always the same:

“Comment ‘Claim,’ and I’ll send you the app.”

That simple DM funnel drives conversions while keeping engagement high.

Connor now tracks which organic videos perform best so he can turn them into paid ads later.

Based on how they’ve already done, he has a good idea of which ones will work.

Connor now tracks which organic videos perform best so he can turn them into paid ads later. Based on how they’ve already done, he has a good idea of which ones will work.

From Hackathon Sprint to Payout

What began as a 14-day hackathon project became a $20K MRR success story.

Connor scaled fast by understanding app niches, leveraging influencer campaigns, and running smart paid ads, without writing a single line of code.

You can check out an interview he did recently for

Starter Story

here

.

Using only one account and a single content format, the app has hit 107,4 million views.

Every video sticks to the same format: no faces, just split-screen clips comparing calories in healthy meals versus small portions of processed food.

Some viewers ask for the app name in comments, others question if it’s all even real, since a few of the comparisons seem over-the-top and hard to believe.

The comparisons may not be entirely accurate, but they’re eye-catching, like seeing a small bowl of candy with the same calories as two full meals. It grabs attention, drives massive engagement, and makes people question their choices without the help of the app.

Launched in June 2024, the Trimmi Calorie Counter app stepped into the market to go head-to-head with platforms like Cal AI, Nourri AI, and NutrIA, bringing a fresh and personalized way to track calories and manage nutrition.

They are running five official accounts that have collectively reached 14.1 million views.

A top-performing format on the official account is the slideshow series.

Each slide features a food photo from Pinterest, with the dish name as a short hook overlaid on the image.

This video gathered 5.3M views, 30.4K likes, 88 comments, and 10.1K bookmarks, boosted by paid ads.

The official account, @trimmi_app, used a trending format with a popular audio clip that quickly went viral and gave their views a big boost.

However, the official page isn’t the only one getting attention. The creator account

@get.trimmi

is also seeing great results with its own style of content.

One popular format on the page is a short headshot video that starts with a strong hook and goes on about why it’s important to adjust your lifestyle, to match the different phases of the female hormonal cycle, a subject that’s often missing from traditional education.

This video received 1.5 million views, 377,000 thousand likes, 513 comments, and 38,000 thousand bookmarks.

It’s clear that in wide and competitive spaces like nutrition, the best content often sits where two niches overlap—in this case, diet and menstrual cycles.

This is exactly the type of content gets people talking, as it encourages viewers to share their own experiences and thoughts in the comments.

They’ve been leaning towards long hooks that blend these two worlds:

“Your hormones are doing something every single day. This changes your energy levels, focus, sleep, exercise tolerance, food cravings and body temperature. You cannot be the same every single day. You need to adjust your routine to be in sync with your hormones.”

“Estrogen is a powerful neuro-protector. It helps memory, focus, sleep, and mood. Progesterone is your calming hormone. This is why you feel a dip in brain power right before your period. You need to support your brain with the right foods and nutrients in each phase of your cycle.”

“If you try to push hard every day, you’ll burn out and create more stress hormones (cortisol). Learn to work with your body’s natural phases: high energy for the first half of the cycle, and restorative, self-care energy for the second half. This is called ‘Cycle Syncing’.”

Another creator,

@fitwithcal8

doesn’t fall behind, using a simple style where shorter hooks do most of the work. The entire account is running on faceless content, and it’s also slowly gaining traction.

These videos always use the same faceless view and start with a short hook. They focus on promoting a high-protein, high-fiber diet to improve digestion, support gut health, and help prevent illness.

This video received 1 million views, 155.7 thousand likes, 123 comments, and 20.1 thousand bookmarks.

A few of the hooks “she” has been using:

“Not enough talk about scooping food out of the way. If you have a scoop it is literally a pick me up for your gut.”

“Me every day: I’m getting chia from colon cancer not protein deficiency.”

“Remember that the nutrients are the food you eat, but actually because of how you are”

Trimmi keeps it simple with easy formats and catchy hooks to draw people in. Now it’s all about whether they can scale it and grab a piece of this super competitive market.

Keep them under your radar:

Endeavorise is a recent gamified self-improvement app that turns personal growth into a game. It tracks different areas of your life as levels and achievements, making progress feel rewarding and addicting.

Launched in May by a small Swedish team, the app has quickly picked up momentum.

In the past month alone, Endeavorise passed 10K downloads on Google Play, with most of its users coming from European countries.

The team runs three social accounts on different platforms, and together they just passed 25 million views.

They’ve uploaded about 300 short videos on each, reusing the same content across all of them.

All videos stick to the same simple, faceless format: a 20-second clip that fades in to highlight an app feature, paired with a relatable hook about self-improvement, breakups, or motivation.

Each video features a

Wojak character

with a visible rank, while bars representing areas of life rise or fall depending on the story’s message.

It’s a mix of memes, storytelling, and gamified progress.

On YouTube, Endeavorise hit virality once with a “cooked” relatable meme:

“When life is so cooked that you have to pull this combo…”

This video pulled in 1.3M views on September 9th.

On Instagram, they also went viral once, thanks to a “bro” meme:

“

every MALE group has that one bro

”

TikTok has been their biggest source of new users. They’ve gained over 17 million views there and gone viral multiple times.

The top-performing TikTok reused the exact same hook as the previous Instagram hit:

“

Every MALE friend group has that ONE  bro…

“

Their feed shows a consistent pattern. Same video style, slight hook variations, and repeated virality through familiar themes for Gen Z boys.

Endeavorise’s rise highlights how powerful a focused strategy can be.

The team hit 10K downloads using just one faceless video style and reposting it on TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube. Each video mixes product exposure with emotion, turning progress bars into short stories about motivation and self-discipline.

This consistent format keeps costs low while boosting reach across platforms.

You can access all accounts and videos here:

In 306 days since launching, Beli has hit $8K in monthly revenue and 200K downloads a month, making waves in the restaurant discovery space.

In a relatively short time, Beli has already pulled ahead of its competitors in the niche.

With just 7 accounts, they have already racked up an impressive 988 million views.

Even though the app is still new, the official account

@beli_eats

has been around for a while, posting videos that highlight restaurants, just like the app with some reaching as many as 63.5 million views.

Disclaimer: most videos in this account include paid ads.

This video received 63.5M views, 1.5M likes, 2.5K comments, and 66.4K bookmarks.

Using a simple format, a 7-second video, without showing any faces, it sparked huge engagement just by highlighting something tasty.

Now that the account has become the app’s main way of reaching users, it still uses the same format, just with better quality.

Recently they’ve added a new format: street interviews where people choose between restaurants, but it hasn’t gained much traction yet.

This video got 65.5K views, 2.5K likes, 25 comments, and 268 bookmarks.

Interestingly, when the same interview format is posted from a creator’s account, the results tend to be way better.

To perhaps remain loyal to the app’s original concept, Beli works with creators who were already posting food content and sharing restaurant experiences on their own pages.

This video, for instance, hit 42.2M views, 169.2K likes and over one thousand comments.

Their videos always follow the same style: close-up shots of them trying food, with catchy captions that match what they’re saying.

Since they had a solid following already before launching the app, and it’s the same kind of audience, it’s no wonder they were able to get good results from very early-on.

To view the collection, click here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10CrUQREkgJk

Millions of young men are fighting porn addiction.

On TikTok, the topic has blown up.

“Quit porn” videos go viral all the time.

And every November, the buzz peaks with No Nut November, the popular challenge that pushes people to stay away from porn and masturbation for the whole month.

For apps in this space, that trend is pure gold.

Searches increase, motivation goes up, and social feeds overflow with challenge-related content.

This year,

Overcomer

was the first to really ride this wave.

They’re a small player with only about 10K monthly downloads:

Yet right now they’re ranking above mainstream apps like QUITRR and Unchaind.

Currently, Overcomer sits at #64 in Health & Fitness, while QUITRR is at #80 and Unchaind trails at #240.

It was out of the top 500 just a few days ago.

Their jump came from one smart move: a single viral video tied to the trend.

They partnered with a TikTok creator and streamer with 3.7M followers, and an audience of mostly Gen Z guys.

“

No Nut November is in 4 days

” 1.9M views / 6.8K comments / 30K saves

In it, the creator promises to pay $100 to anyone who completes the challenge and proves it through the “Overcomer” app.

That hook instantly got the community interested in installing the app. Most of the viewers already wanted to join the challenge, so it worked as both motivation and reward.

We’ll keep tracking this niche as it hits its golden month.

About eight months ago, a new app called Dawdle AI joined the world of productivity and digital well-being.

Even though the app is still new, it’s already delivering results much like its competitors.

The app runs three accounts and has reached 771.2K views.

One of those accounts belongs to the founder, who posted a video that sparked a huge buzz in the comments.

The video above racked up 376.8K views, 63.9K likes, 891 comments, and 5,317 bookmarks.

The video is a headshot-style clip with her talking straight to the camera, using catchy captions as hooks. Rather than focusing on the app itself, she plays up its message in a dramatic and over-the-top way, though in the video description she makes it clear she’s joking.

People are in on the joke and playing along.

Another post that caught people’s attention was a slideshow the founder shared, highlighting what she worked on that week to build the app.

That video collected 376.8K views, 932 likes, 134 comments, and 299 bookmarks.

The first slide starts with a strong hook that grabs attention. She hints there’s a secret at the end, which makes people want to watch the whole video to see what it is.

Hook :

“My startup’s progress through the week (With a secret at the end)”

The @dawdleapp account has a cool format, but it’s not getting much engagement overall.

Overall, the app hasn’t generated many views, but the secret might be to create more videos like the first format, more motivational, headshot-style clips.

To view the app’s collection, click here:

Meet UCHAD, another AI Looksmax Face Rating App.

Launched in September, it’s already hit over 8,000 downloads.

Even without any unique features, its quick growth shows just how strong the demand for this niche is on TikTok.

The concept is simple.

You download the app, snap a selfie, and get a full analysis of your facial features.

But there’s a catch.

The app is free and clean of ads, but access comes with strings attached.

Users must rate it five stars before scanning, then pay for “gems” to see their full results.

A deceptive model that trades curiosity for ratings and revenue.

UCHAD grew their app on TikTok without using a full account strategy.

They currently run five faceless accounts, but most of their views come from paid collab videos.

They work with looksmax influencers who have small to medium followings, and the approach is clearly paying off.

UCHAD has made almost 10M views in just one month.

In this niche, most “looksmax” influencers grow by showing their “ascension”.

A big transformation that makes them look much better than before.

The creators with the most dramatic changes often go viral, with viewers wondering how they did it.

UCHAD partners with these influencers for “facial transformation” edits, where they use the app’s face scan overlay or show the app at the end of the video.

They also mention the app name in the caption to drive more attention.

UCHAD’s rise shows how fast a copycat can take off when paired with the right creators.

article.title: How to kill your app
article.content:
How to kill your app

5 most common mistakes that could be silently tanking your downloads.

SGE Team

•

October 30, 2025

•

4 min read

How to kill your app

5 most common mistakes that could be silently tanking your downloads.

SGE Team

•

October 30, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

If you’re launching an app, you’re probably guilty of self-sabotaging your marketing efforts without even realizing.

Here are five common mistakes founders often make. See if any sound familiar and fix them before they end up costing you thousands in MRR.

1. No app in sight

This is by far the most common one.

Here’s the thing: most app founders leave out their app name or link in posts to keep things mysterious and avoid looking like a paid ad.

We get it, and for the most part, we stand by it.

But if your content doesn’t give

any

clue about

any

app, people won’t know what to search for.

That’s exactly what happened with

Bible Project

, an app launched by a massive TikTok creator in the biblical space. He had over 200 million views, but most people had no idea he’d launched an app, simply because he didn’t mention it in 9 out of 10 videos.

There’s a clear trade-off here. Sure, it’s way easier to go viral when there’s no mention of a product or app, but at what cost? You could be burning money on creators, editors, and more, and still see zero return.

Going viral feels great, but watch out for the “empty views” trap. If you’re not giving people a clear way to find your app, don’t expect them to magically figure it out.

2. Following trends blindly

Trends can be your best friend. Think of them like having free proven hooks and formats that keep refreshing every day, while you can just plug and play them as you wish.

But here’s the catch: too many creators follow trends blindly. If you’re not tailoring them to your niche and audience, they’ll probably fall flat. And if you’re not linking them to your CTA in some way, you’re just collecting empty views.

Bottom line: don’t waste your reach on content that doesn’t drive downloads.

3. Not iterating on content that works

It might seem obvious, but a lot of founders still fall into the “original content” trap.

If something works, keep using it. Swap “mom” for “sister” in the hook, wear a green shirt instead of a blue one. Small tweaks are all it takes. The key is to spread that same viral format across all your ambassadors.

Only after you’ve fully tapped out a winning idea should you start chasing the next big thing.

Just look at

InsideLux

. Their whole strategy was built on smart iteration, consistently repeating the exact same AI-generated format and script over and over again, simply swapping brands and places that were mentioned. They pulled in 42M views in 42 days.

4. All eggs in one basket

One account can get shadow-banned, pushed down by the algorithm, or just never take off. And when that happens, you’re back to square one.

Spread the risk and accelerate learning by launching multiple accounts and creators. Put together a handful of formats, a few dozen (of researched and proven) hooks, and blast them everywhere.

It’s the only way to actually rule out the poor performers from the hits, while multiplying your chances by ruling out external factors.

Emmy BFF

felt the impact of relying on a single TikTok account. Despite having a decent number of views, this took a toll on their early growth, as their reach was capped from the start, no matter what they did.

5. All or nothing

Believe it or not, you don’t always need to promote your app as a whole.

Focus on your highlight features and, if you don’t have any, go make some from scratch.

Take it from

Copia

, who designed features optimized for virality, or from

Couple Joy

, who drove most downloads through their lock screen widget feature.

A small Bible game with barely 5K downloads is pulling $6K a month. Proof that loyal fans can beat virality every time.

SGE Team

October 30, 2025

2 min read

Save for later

Ascend is a Bible study game that turns traditional Scripture reading into an engaging learning experience.

With the help of an AI Pet Phoenix, users can build a daily Bible study habit through gamified learning.

Think Duolingo for Bible.

After launching, earlier this year, Ascend initially struggled to gain traction.

Even during September they were still below 5K downloads.

But despite having such few downloads, they managed to keep $6K MRR.

This is because they run a paid-subscription only model.

This growth has been fueled by their social media strategy.

They have made 3.2M views and run a total of 38 accounts.

They are trying everything, from faceless slideshow accounts to UGCs.

But virality has been scarce.

The only viral video they have gotten so far was uploaded by Instagram ambassador

bruce.ascend

:

Only 3 people in the Bible were taken to heaven without dying. Guess who?

A bible quiz hook, with a selfie shot.

App promo in the caption –> “Ascend” has the answer.

maddie.ascend

hit a 468K views faceless slideshow with bible stories.

The last slide being an app promo.

This format worked extremely well, with almost 50K saves and an engagement rate of 36%.

Their team is clearly testing every possible growth lever, from quiz-style hooks to faceless Bible story slideshows.

They seem to have slowed down on the content recently, and while virality hasn’t fully hit yet, the foundation for it is already there: a relatively small but loyal paying audience, that leads them to a consistent $6K MRR.

Only 82 days ago, a new app showed up in the period and self‑care space.

Naturally, Aoife is still lagging behind its competitors, but its moving fast on distribution.

With only one account, the app has already managed to get 24,5M views.

So far, the team has been testing out different formats, with two of them standing out with 7.8M and 11.2M views.

The most popular video is a slideshow made with phone photos taken around the house. Each slide shares a hook with a tip about what not to do during your period.

This video has 11.2M views, 315.7K likes, 4,296 comments, and 71.2K bookmarks.

A straightforward format that tackles a common issue and sparks lots of comments.

The other video uses a popular meme to show how over-the-top period feelings can be, making fun of the experience. It also includes a hook that drives the point home.

This video has 11.2M views, 398.2K likes, 5,380 comments, and 24.2K bookmarks.

Hook:

“POV: You’re on your period and your boyfriend is just existing”

Even though this video got less views, it had better engagement. Because it’s funny, people are more likely to leave comments.

While those two formats stood out, the app also has other posts that performed well, like a slideshow that uses some graphic design. It includes a hook at the top and a drawing sticker at the bottom to show the question.

This video got 1M views, 53.9K likes, 596 comments, and 32K bookmarks.

This format is meant to be done with someone else, kind of like a game, with each slide showing a question you can ask your boyfriend.

Along with the interactive style, they also enjoy using existing clips or well-known characters. One format, for example, shows a scene from an animated movie with a funny hook added at the top.

This video got 1M views, 87.8K likes, 287 comments, and 7,103 bookmarks

Aoife isn’t just about sharing useful info, it mixes in humor too. By using memes and movie clips, it connects with more people. Now it’s just a wait to see if all those views lead to downloads.

Two new apps are making waves in the productivity and wellness space: Erly, launched just 56 days ago, and Rise, which came out in August 2024.

Erly may be way more recent, but it already has 5 accounts and 2.4 million views.

Rise, on the other hand, has only one account and has racked up 4.8 million views.

The two apps are getting very different results, likely because they use very different formats.

Erly’s creators stick to a familiar format: “Come spend a day with me” videos that show their daily routines, starting with their alarm going off in the morning.

The video did 1.6K views, 359 likes, 4 comments, and 15 bookmarks.

This format tends to use two kinds of hooks, one that carries through the whole video.

Some of their hooks:

“spend an early morning with me 6AM”

“morning is my life, nothing feels happier 8AM – 9AM”

“spend the morning getting ready 7AM”

“we dont have time to study anymore!!! 11AM”

Or multiple quick hooks, each focusing on a different moment in the day.

This one got 124.4K views, 13K likes, 140 comments, and 1,269 bookmarks.

Like Rise, Erly has an official account that sticks to a consistent format: slideshows of photos, mostly showing beds pulled from Pinterest. The hooks highlight tips, habits, and routines, often centered around productivity and success.

This video got 35.4K views, 2,330 likes, 40 comments, and 597 bookmarks.

Hook examples:

“ways to actually wake up early”

“10 INNOCENT HABITS that are actually destroying your grades”

“The best early morning wake up advice I was ever given”

Even though the formats are straightforward, the videos get relatively low engagement.

Rise, even with just one account, uses a format that drives much higher engagement.

With a simple 2x speed screen recording of the app, it managed to get 1.4M views.

But it was the hook that truly made it stand out.

Hook:

“he doesn’t know it yet but after spending 6 months making an app no one will use it.”

The app leans into dark humor and negativity to grab attention, and it worked. One person reacted to the humor, sparking a wave of buzz.

But it wasn’t just that one video that got attention, another video hit 1 million views, showing the app and the user struggling to complete a basic account setup.

Most of the comments aren’t about the app, they’re about the user struggling to set up their math account.

Rise shares unfiltered, behind-the-scenes videos about the app’s development, while Erly shows how the app fits into everyday life.

Even though Rise’s videos stir some controversy, they’re getting more engagement on social media.

Save for later

This format starts with a short selfie video and a simple list-style hook.

Example: “

7 weight loss rules every girly should know.

”

The video ends almost right away, leaving the full list in the caption.

Each rule or tip is written in short, easy-to-read paragraphs.

The final tip usually connects to the app, but without saying its name directly.

“Follow a system, I use an AI app that builds my plan.”

If you want more engagement, you can add:

Drop a comment to get the app link! I’ll DM you.

“

These videos are super easy for UGC creators to recreate.

All it takes is a short clip that teases a list, explains it in the caption, and subtly points to your app as the “system” behind it.

It’s a simple, flexible, and highly effective format.

It works in any niche.

Swap the topic, keep the structure: “X rules / Y mistakes / Z hacks” → bio paragraphs → “follow a system” → your app.

This approach can also work for AI-generated UGC, since the video only needs a face on camera.

Descriptive tags: headshot, indoors, selfie, UGC, guide, AI

Potential niches: all

An AI weight loss app went from zero to $10K MRR in 30 days by doubling down on one viral UGC format, proving that one g…

•

3 min read

Save for later

Glow Diet, an AI weight loss app, just launched just three months ago.

The app acts as a personal AI coach that builds custom workouts and meal plans to help users lose weight.

Just last month, they had no downloads or monthly recurring revenue.

Now, in only 30 days, they’ve reached 20K downloads and $10K in monthly recurring revenue.

And they did it in a competitive niche, competing with well-known apps like

Simple

and

WeGrow

.

Their rapid rise came from the explosive growth of their social media engine.

They run 10 accounts and have already reached 26.8M views and 459K saves.

Their big break came from a wave of viral UGC videos, with five accounts taking off.

@roslyn.glow went viral on both TikTok (4.2M views) and Instagram (7.1M views).

Her first viral moment came on TikTok, on August 31, with a short selfie video titled:

7 weight loss tips skinny girls don’t share

It pulled in 2.3M views.

She keeps gaining traction by posting quick tips and weight loss “rules.”

Her Instagram blew up again recently with two more hits:

How to lose 30lbs (14kgs) in 30 days

–> 3.2M views / October 21st

Crazy Korean Diet Plan to lose 30lbs (14kg) in one month–>2.4M views / October 17th

@amy_health

, another Korean creator, also went viral using the “text in caption” video format and a simple hook, starting her videos by sipping a drink.

Most of the UGC growth actually came from these “weight loss text in caption” videos.

karlie.healthy

took a different route with longer talking videos instead of quick lists, but the theme stayed the same: weight loss advice.

Glow Diet’s growth from zero to $10K MRR in 30 days shows a powerful lesson for new founders: you don’t need a big budget, just one winning content format that works.

They leaned on a proven, repeatable UGC style: “secret tips in the bio” videos. That single strategy turned a new app into a six-figure business almost overnight.

If your app solves a big global problem like weight loss, it can still go viral and grow fast, even in a crowded space.

Bro lives on your lock screen as a calm and supportive friend.

Ready to listen when you need to talk about work, relationships, or whatever.

Bro helps you stay centered and on track.

(yes, it’s really called Bro)

The app officially launched on October 28th and quickly hit #1 in the U.S. Lifestyle category.

But signs show the app had been live months before the public launch.

The oldest visible review dates back to May 2025.

It looks like Bro quietly launched in May, kept improving through the summer while creators posted about it, and then made a big push with its official launch on October 28th.

This move was clearly planned, and now they’re using the #1 ranking to fuel their marketing.

They shared a post on their website saying they “

woke up to Bro sitting at #1 in Lifestyle and #6 overall

.”

Their subscription model is simple: $2.99 per week or $74.99 per year.

A big reason for their early traction was TikTok.

They pulled in about 10 million total views, although some included paid ads.

Their top video reached 7.8 million views back in July.

It’s a faceless clip showing “Bro” helping the user text her crush.

A smart way to show the app’s value.

Then, just before launch, on October 19th, another UGC video went viral with the same idea.

This time, the creator added a shocked reaction at the start and told a short, personal story.

The comments flooded in asking for the app name.

She replied, telling everyone to wait.

It was launching soon.

That one video, along with a push on TikTok ads, turned out to be the perfect boost for Bro’s official debut.

TLDL is winning: $90K a month, 50K downloads, 105M views. Here’s the full breakdown.

SGE Team

•

October 29, 2025

•

3 min read

Save for later

TLDL is bringing in $90K a month and getting around 50K downloads every month.

The app already has over 50K users and has now hit 105 million views.

Views began to spike last month, with one video hitting 18.6 million views.

A quick 7-second video plays up and pokes fun at study stress, with the hook: “POV: when you’re too tired to study but you can’t sleep ’cause you need to study but you’re too tired to study.”

The video got 3,668 relatable comments, and the creator replied, saying the app saved them.

Other formats stood out too, this time a headshot video, which hit 11 million views.

The video opens with the hook: “POV: you have an exam TOMORROW and JUST found this now 💀”, which grabs attention right away. It’s another example of a hook that taps into panic and pressure. After that, the creator walks viewers through how to use the app.

It’s not just the creators finding what works, the official

@tldlnotesapp

account has its own standout content style too.

The post sparked 7.5 million views, 1,511 comments, 430.3K likes, and 49.6K bookmarks.

The standout format is a quick on-campus interview consisting of just two main questions:

“What’s your GPA?”

“What do you study with?”

The video follows a simple, effective pattern: students with low GPAs use other apps, while high-GPA students use TLDL, and the pattern repeats.

The comments section blew up with people sharing their GPAs and the apps they use.

Even with some standout formats, most videos stick to the same structure, a headshot of someone studying, then a screen showing the app in use. The main thing that changes from video to video is the hook.

The post got 4.4 million views, 843 comments, 155.6K likes, and 76.5K bookmarks.

A few hook examples:

POV: why EVERYONE deleted ChatGPT

POV: you found out why everyone deleted chat gpt

POV: your teacher said to use this for an A in the Syllabu

POV: you find out why EVERYONE is deleting ChatGPT

In addition to the main creators, TLDL has a few study pages, like

@study.lyfe

that use such similar formats, they could easily be run by the same person.

These pages follow a faceless format like the main creators, simple, but it work.

The post got 1 million views, 524 comments, 26.3K likes, and 5,284 bookmarks.

Somme more hooks:

I wish I get these grades without studying

POV: you got all A+ grades without studying

You definitely cheated to get these grades!!

The app’s strong performance proves that sometimes, a good hook is all you need.

In the AI note-taking space, Flownote AI has started to feel some strong competition from Summary AI, a more recent app which has rapidly gained momentum.

Summary AI, released six months after Flownote, currently leads with around 300,000 downloads and $700,000 in revenue.

Flownote stays in the game with 20,000 downloads and roughly $100,000 in revenue.

Even with those numbers, Flownote AI has actually pulled in more views, 21 million, compared to Summary AI’s 14.1 million.

@thestudygirlyy is playing a big part in driving up views for Flownote.

Despite being the newest account, her videos are pulling in the most engagement, and one of them has the most views overall.

It’s a straightforward, headshot-style video where the creator talks through how she uses the app on her iPad. There are no flashy edits or hooks, just a clear explanation.

What really grabs people, though, is the “what I do every lecture to keep my 4.0!!” It instantly catches attention and encourages viewers to comment.

While Summary doesn’t have as many views overall, one video style stands out.

Creator

@wfhgabriela

has hit 10.4 million views with this format. These videos show AI being used in interview-style clips or staged scenes where it looks like someone is secretly recording a meeting.

Her hooks are doing particularly well and sparking a lot of conversation in the comments:

Some of her hooks:

“POV: Your boss forgot they approved your time off…”

“POV: You’re getting accused of saying it. A Slack detective story. 🕵🏼‍♀️ (no hate reasons)”

The Single-Task Method: New App Idea

Productivity apps are in need of some fresh innovation, so here’s an idea for you.

SGE Team

•

October 28, 2025

•

3 min read

Save for later

Picture this:

You open your productivity app tomorrow morning and instead of a long intimidating task list, you only see your next step.

One task only. Until you complete it. Then you see the next one.

And the one after, until all your tasks (or your day) is done.

No clutter. No endless open tabs in your brain. No tasks fighting for attention. Just progress.

Sounds like a dream, but it’s one you can

actually

build.

Maybe you’re thinking this is too crowded of a niche, but think again. With the right distribution strategy, you can separate yourself from the rest and win big, just as apps in neighbor niches, like

Reborn Nutrition

, are doing.

The Angle

“The Problem Isn’t Your To-Do List. It’s Your Brain.”

Most productivity systems are built on the idea that humans perform better when they can see everything they need to do.

In reality, the opposite is true. Especially if you have ADHD or other type of attention disorder.

When your brain sees 17 unfinished tasks staring back at you, it doesn’t process it as “opportunity.” It processes it as threat.

Stress response = dopamine crash = avoidance behavior =  procrastination.

Why It Works

Humans fail when given big goals. They win when given clear next steps.

This app would be a behavior-guide tool, backed by neuroscience, not just annother list display.

The brain gets one clear target, reducing stress

Each completed task means a quick dopamine win

It’s ADHD-friendly (the clear structure prevents paralysis)

It converts chaos into a linear path forward, lowering anxiety

The Strategy

The key is positioning: don’t sell an app, create a movement.

Start by building awareness and waitlist signups, converting viewers into believers and believers into users.

Agitate overwhelm (problem)

Introduce method (solution)

Build trust and belonging (community)

Faceless slideshows and UGC are perfect for this.

And, let’s face it, the hooks basically write themselves…

“Your to-do list is ruining your brain”

“You’re not lazy, just overloaded. Here’s proof.”

“The brain can’t multitask (proof)”

“I simply could NOT focus. Until I found this simple hack. It literally changed my life”

“I can’t believe I’ve been doing life tasks wrong all this time”

“In case no one told you, you’re not supposed to wake up with a huge to-do list already on your mind”

…

The next generation of productivity apps won’t be about AI, more features or bigger systems. They’ll be about simplicity, and how well you are able to frame the same problems under new lenses.

Call it focus engineering, if you will.

Taller’s Copycat Hits 20K Downloads

Launched in June, this height-tracking app jumped from 9K to 20K downloads in a month, driven by 28 creator accounts.

SGE Team

•

October 28, 2025

•

4 min read

Save for later

GoTall is a growth-tracking app that helps people understand and improve their natural height potential. It uses CDC data and blends genetics, habits, and lifestyle insights to create a plan for each user.

They use inputs like tracking family height, nutrition, sleep and activity to get more accurate height predictions.

Users get daily exercises, nutrition tips, and easy tracking tools to maximize their height goals.

Just like

Taller

, GoTall uses a freemium model.

Basic features are free. Core features require a paid plan.

The team is entering a crowded AI niche driven by aggressive Gen Z marketing.

Launched in June, GoTall is gaining momentum, with downloads climbing from 9K in September to 20K over the last 30 days.

It is now ranking in the top 100 in dozens of countries, suggesting real global potential.

GoTall was founded by university students from

NYU’s Stern School of Business

.

The team started uploading in June and currently owns 28 accounts.

They have done a total of 14.6 million views so far.

Most views came from 4 tiktok accounts that hit virality.

immogg3d

found a consistent strategy to reach 4.2M views.

He uploads “viewer height prediction series.”

In each video, he uses viewers’ questions as hooks to showcase the GoTall height calculator.

Viewers comment their age, height, and parents’ height, and he calculates their potential height while demonstrating how the app works.

Comment reading  –> Data input on app –> CTA comment –> App Result

This format leads to consistent high viewership and high engagement.

kevinliutalks

reached 2.7M views using exactly the same strategy.

Meanwhile,

dobbingotall

grew his audience by debunking height growth myths.

He opens with shocking hooks like:

“If you have facial hair at 16 your growth plates are closed”

And follows up with “People actually think this is real information”.

Even the one of the founders,

@daniel.how.to.grow

, has pulled in over 600K views in one video by fun facts and tips about height growth.

In only four months, GoTall has grown from a student’s experiment into a 20K-download app backed by 14 million TikTok views.

What began as a clear Taller copycat soon evolved as the team discovered a format that not only goes viral but actually drives conversions.

By mixing engaging app demos with real viewer interactions, they’ve created a content loop that turns education into downloads.

“

This hook has quietly gone viral for months across unrelated accounts. A clear sign it’s one of those evergreen lines that can be used again and again.

A new pregnancy app quietly launched 113 days ago and already hit 25 million views, all from just 19 accounts using the…

SGE Team

Save for later

A new pregnancy tracking app was launched almost four months ago.

The app has 19 active accounts and has already pulled in 25.4 million views.

The app is seeing strong engagement, perhaps because the formats are so simple.

One video pulled in 2.3 million views, 22.6K likes, 131 comments, and 10K bookmarks.

It’s just a single slide from an informational brochure made in Canva. Simple, clear, effective.

Another solid format is an informative slideshow, with each slide covering one key point. These are also made in Canva and perform well.

This video reached 2 million views, with 55.7K likes, 300 comments, and 19.3K bookmarks.

This format performs well because of its clear illustrations. It begins with an engaging hook and is simple to follow all through the end.

The app has two creators,

@emilyjames963

and

@katewolf2

, each posting two types of AI videos. One shows a doctor yelling at a patient, starting with a hook explaining his anger:

It got 6,404 views, 31 likes, 3 comments, and 2 bookmarks.

The second AI-generated video shows a baby in the womb with a hook mentioning the number of weeks.

It got just 2,087 views, 79 likes, 1 comment, and 3 bookmarks.

Even though this format is more interactive, it isn’t really taking off.

Since both creators only post AI content and reuse the same slideshow videos across accounts, it’s likely the same person is running all of them. They’ll probably keep launching new ones to boost their odds with the algorithm.

To view the collection, click here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b1080Nu4QhWlq

Peek’s empty reach trap

They are going viral without saying their own name. 24 million views, zero conversions. All it takes is one shift.

SGE Team

•

October 24, 2025

•

2 min read

Save for later

Peek is a simple AI money coach that “turns financial stress into financial progress.”

The app was released in March and is still struggling to convert.

They are pushing a wide TikTok engine with 35 accounts and more than 24 million views.

Most of their content is pure UGC.

Some accounts run as “financebestie,” others as “dollarsign,” and others as “peeklife”. They all post once a day.

Only 6 of these accounts have surpassed 1M total views.

financebestiechloe

is the standout, hitting 8.8 million with two breakout videos:

“Tell me the BEST thing you’ve ever spent your money on. Idc if it is $1 or $10K

“

“sorry I can’t go out, I’m broke”

These clips are short with long, catchy hooks and no app mention.

Great for reach, weak for conversion.

The same pattern shows up across other viral creators.

They’re getting views, but only by relying on “no app mention” hooks.

They are on-topic for the niche (saving money) but not turning viewers into users.

Most videos skip the app entirely. There is no demo and no clear feature tie-in. Comments do not bring up the app either.

They’re not clearly framing a problem and then positioning the app as the solution.

With 35 TikTok accounts and over 24 million views, it’s clear that “saving money” culture hooks work. But without the product, those views don’t compound.

The upside is huge: keep the same UGC engine, but reframe every viral trope into a problem → product → proof arc.

If they make that shift, the next 24 million views could drive real users, instead of just reach.

Access all accounts here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10CK9yquzXf2

Just launched two months ago, its creators are already pulling millions of views by betting with friends and doing wild…

SGE Team

•

October 23, 2025

3 min read

Save for later

A new app called Rounder, focused on social and friend betting, launched around 65 days ago.

Despite being so recent, they are already managing 13 TikTok accounts, out of which they’ve managed to hit 3.7M views.

Most creators follow a similar format: a headshot video of themselves doing a challenge after losing a bet on the app.

Each one starts with a hook explaining they lost and what the challenge is.

One example got 15.1K views, 163 likes, 1 comment, and 3 bookmarks.

Some sample hooks:

“Forced to walk the busy streets of japan since i lost my rounder bet yesterday”

“Making my friends refill the penny mayonnaise jar after losing our bet on the rounder app”

“Going through all the laundry i have to wash and fold after losing my bet on rounder”

In general, the videos are getting low engagement.

Only one video stood out, with 1.3 million views, 277K likes,1.3K comments, and 22.1K bookmarks.

It followed the usual format, except this time she hadn’t done the challenge yet — she was just announcing it. And it was the kind of challenge people were actually excited to watch.

An unusual object in the video also got people talking in the comments.

The app’s official page has just a few videos and follows one format, but it hasn’t gotten much attention so far.

The videos on the official page use a simple slideshow format, showing screenshots of the app.

Their most-viewed video only got 135 views.

They’re still early in the process, but they’re starting to build a network of creators. The views aren’t high yet, but the app is already starting to get people talking.

Check out the full collection here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2b10FyIET6zcFm

This TikTok account blew up with simple slideshows and a hook that made 15M people stop scrolling.

3 min read

Save for later

There are plenty of healthy recipe pages out there, but @reborn_nutrition managed to land four hit videos in just four months, with the biggest one hitting 4.2 million views.

In just three months, they posted 128 videos and racked up 15.3 million views in total.

Format 1

The most viral video uses a simple format,  just a slideshow made up of 16 photos.

The video includes three types of photos: a cover image, pictures of the dishes, and a slide showing the dish description.

The video opens with the hook “healthy food is boring…”. It’s paired with a photo of a tasty-looking dish (the kind anyone could take), followed by a slide listing the ingredients plus the macros.

This pattern repeats through the rest of the video.

The video gets flooded with comments — some say the real problem isn’t that healthy food is boring, it’s that it costs too much. Others are just amazed by how good the dishes look.

What makes it work is the mix of natural, good-looking photos and info that’s easy to follow.

Format 2

On this other video, they stick to the same format, a slideshow, starting with a Pinterest photo. The hook introduces an idea that sounds impossible at first.

Hook: “Here’s what clean eating actually looks like”

Each slide shows a dish that looks like it came straight from Pinterest, with a hook at the top pointing out the benefits of its ingredients.

Format 3

The video is a slideshow of close-up dessert shots, each with a short hook at the top saying what it is. What really pulls people in is the photos.

They skip the recipe on purpose, which gets people talking in the comments.

The video pulled in 2 million views, along with 200.8K likes, 378 comments, and 101K saves.

Format 4

The fourth video is a slideshow that could use some tweaks. Each slide shows a dish with ingredients and macro details, but it didn’t do as well.

The photos aren’t zoomed in, there’s too much text, which makes the video harder to follow and less engaging.
