The one “single shot text overlay” format pioneered by Airbuds works particularly well with consumer social and targeted consumer apps where messaging hits Gen Alpha/Z.

That’s how they go:

It’s 6 to 9-second videos with a block of text telling a story, and the creator in the background.

Check a viral one here:

https://www.tiktok.com/@lois.airbuds/video/7433506099686313249

SUSH

has 8+ accounts

Pengu

has 6+ accounts

Airbuds has dozens of accounts

And I’ve gathered a collection of other apps with similar accounts/strategy.

It looks simple, but it’s complex to execute properly.

The economics behind it truly only work with a certain scale.

To make it work at scale, you’ll need a lot of accounts and you’ll need to reach a velocity of at least 50 to 100+ videos posted a day.

If you analyze the accounts of apps mentioned above, you’ll find that you need:

Every account posting 2 to 3 videos a day.

Around 1 out of 25 videos to do 25/50x median and 1 out of 50 or 1 out of 100 to do 200x+ median (going viral).

With 100 videos a day doing only 1,000 views, you’ll get 100K views. The aim is for the videos to average out so that you reach 1M views/day with the odds above.

It’s exactly like a VC fund. 1 out of 100 will become a unicorn. 9 out of 100 will perform okay/good.

The rest will fail.

It’s a power law distribution.

Once accounts are built up, they’ll perform at higher rates.

Every other month, you need to get rid of the lowest-performing ones and scale up the highest-performing ones.

It works insanely well if your app is already known, as you’ll have people understanding your problem/solution hooks and interacting, saying things like:

“Ohhhh, [app name] is also [solving the problem] for me.”

Three things you need to make sure of prior to testing this:

1) It’s all about the messaging and stories you tell through captions, so it should be thought through deeply ahead of time.

2) You need to iterate fast when you find storylines that work.

3) You should follow current trends closely to use and adapt them to your vertical and storylines.

It requires some operations to manage dozens of ambassadors like that (often young & inexperienced), and you’ll have to pay them mainly through CPM bonuses.

The good side is that you can train almost anyone to do those videos; hence, the base fee can be lowered to make economics work on your side.

This specific strategy was unlocked by Airbuds (#9 music) before becoming widespread throughout many consumer social apps.

Shareable Collection Of Viral Accounts

We’ve launched Public Collections on Shortimize, something we’ve been thinking about for a while.

It’s a way to create collections of viral TikTok/Reel accounts and share them publicly.

I made a few collections for the apps I’m mentioning above, so you can explore their viral content for free:

SUSH:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a10o5zJmVIsd4

Locket:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a10eVaER0AvfO

Jammable:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a10vZHFsAdbXd

It’s another piece of infrastructure that gets us closer to our vision to drastically improve short-form video marketing and creator marketing.

We’ve shipped something else this week:

socialgrowthengineers.com

Today it’s impossible to find a consistent and trustworthy source of social organic marketing strategies that work.

So after posting dozens of strategies on Twitter that were read more than 10,000,000 times, we’ve decided to launch:

A dedicated website for those strategies. It’s an extension of this newsletter.

We moved and categorized 50+ strategies we’ve written about on Twitter to socialgrowthengineers.com.

This is only the beginning.

It’s going to be big.

> #8 in Health & Fitness on App Store

How Sweat Coin created an app around their affiliate program:

Sweat Coin (released in 2016), is a step-tracking app that allows users to turn their everyday walks into points. “Sweat coins” can then be used to purchase in-app rewards (ex: Walmart/Amazon voucher, discounts on Apple Watched, etc)

But there’s a catch:

Some users don’t realise they are limited to the app’s offers and get frustrated trying to cash-out. And when they ask how they can withdraw their balance, Sweat Coin’s team:

=> If users get 20+ new customers, they unlock the Influencer Hub and can get real money. It’s sketchy, and it’s genius:

Turns out they’re just trying to get most users to join their affiliate program:

1. Download the app and invite 20 friends

2. Only then, you become a Sweat Coin “Influencer”

3. Get resources from the library, post and make money for each new user w/ unique URL

Speaking of resource library:

They provide video/story/post assets for IG, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat… Including the same faceless intro video in 7 different languages.

And a section on memes, with different ones per language:

They even have a blog to guide influencers through issues. Ex: Oct 10, TikTok was blocking all of their links, and they issued a blog post on how to fix it.

The program became so big, that last year, they got over 80,000 influencer sign-ups. That means 80K x 20 friends each => 1,600,000 new users just from the program.

Meanwhile, on Tiktok & Reels…

IG –

@promotesweatcoin

=> they’re promoting competitions among influencers, to encourage them to create viral content.

Reminds me of Cheater Buster:

https://www.socialgrowthengineers.com/cheater-buster-ais-affiliate-program-350m-views-in-6-months

There’s hundreds of accounts across all platforms, I’ve collected a few in this public Shortimize collection:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a10PgG66r70fE

This family-owned company has achieved over: 1.5 BILLION views on TikTok & Reels in 25 months. Posting an average of 4 videos per day, everyday.

This is how a 19y-old girl scaled a DIY shirt into a million dollar business.

Keida Dervishi was 19 when she had the idea to launch a custom-gift business. For her mother’s 50th birthday, she embroidered a picture of them on a sweatshirt and a few days later, she was starting her business plan.

She’s targeting couple’s gifts, a huge niche on TikTok that keeps growing day by day.

Keida is the face of almost every single video she’s posting on TikTok and Reels… And that’s at least 4 per day, every day:

TikTok : @soulmatecustoms => 634.9K followers & over 500,000,000 views

IG: @

soulmatecustomss

=> 443K followers & over 1,000,000,000 views

Results are crazy, and so are the engagement levels of almost every single video:

TT => 36.6M views // 2.6M likes // 10,500 comments // 83,500 saves

Reels => 69M views // 825,000 likes // 4,365 comments

Keida says the #1 (and hardest) part of owning her business is to create content every single day.

Breakdown of her top 3 content formats:

1. Show the behind-the-scene

Many posts are filmed at the production site. Great, cause users love to access the backstage + it’s relatively easy to film in bulk

@soulmatecustoms

Omg the quote ????????????????????

#dogpassedaway

#doggrief

#customtshirt

♬ sparks – favsoundds

2. Share “peculiar” orders

They can be real or made-up, what matters is that it’s highly scalable and taps into people’s curiosity to know about other people’s romantic lives.

@soulmatecustoms

I. AM. SO. JEALOUS. ????????????

#giftsforhim

#anniversarygift

#swolemates

#gymcrush

#gymcouple

♬ big boy sza – normusreedus

3. “She got THIS for her husband”

Great hook + surprised expression always works.

People click to see what “THIS” is (especially when it hints to spicy content).

Interestingly, last year they launched an affiliate program (

@soulmate_ambassadors

). But it doesn’t seem like much happened there…

Keida’s business made over 1,000,000 dollars in less than a year. Now at 23y old and with 60,000 customers, she says her #1 priority is make sure she posts 3-6 videos per day on social media.

Distribution > Product

5 min read

Save for later

Creative Apps, Faceless Content, Clipping & Platform Arbitrage

Hey!

To all the newcomers, thanks for subscribing.

This edition is a walkthrough of my thought explorations from last week, along with some organic marketing ideas and insights I picked up along the way.

Creative Apps’ Endless Distribution

Daze Chat is a great example of the organic distribution you can achieve with a creative app. They’ve hit 54M views across two accounts (some of those views were paid).

They could have scaled even further by multiplying across more accounts.

They had endless creative assets to fuel their pre-launch strategy.

If you’re interested in scaling creative-driven app distribution, check out how Humans Anonymous scaled faceless creatives across a dozen accounts, or how Jammable is pushing their infinite creatives through hundreds of affiliate accounts.

I wouldn’t build a consumer app again without designing the UI with TikTok distribution in mind.

I made this mistake twice… in a row.

With consumer apps, success is tied to your ability to distribute. And to distribute fast. Especially when a network effect is involved.

Faceless or Not Faceless

When starting organic social growth, everyone’s first instinct is to figure out how to execute and scale faceless creatives.

It seems easier than “faceful” content since one doesn’t have to put himself out there.

It’s often an illusion. Faceless competition is fearless.

Low-quality faceless content is doomed. It doesn’t stand a chance.

And low-quality faceless AI content is even worse.

Don’t you find it “strange” that none of the auto AI short generator apps have managed to get a viral video on their main accounts (I’ve documented 50+):

Still, there are too many success stories for you to ignore.

There are no secrets, to nail it, you have to experiment with hundreds, if not thousands, of videos or posts, until you hit the jackpot.

The scientific approach is to use one format across three accounts. And to test multiple formats at the same time.

This helps reduce the “luck” factor and turn the process into… science.

Rizz, Astro and ColorAnalysis AI are excellent reads on faceless strategies.

Clipping, Clipping, Clipping

Last week, I talked to someone who manages mass content production for the movie industry.

They have a team of 300+ clippers who, for every movie or TV show release, create accounts, make clips, and distribute them—getting paid based on views.

I found it fascinating.

If you listen to major YouTubers, they’re constantly being clipped, with shorts they didn’t create themselves getting millions of views.

It could be seen as a huge loss, but instead, the smartest of them view it as free distribution (not that they have much choice).

The real money is in long-form content, and the real value is in long-term users.

The magic of clipping is that it helps your content spread faster without you having to do anything.

I do believe that every long-form podcaster or YouTuber should have a clipping team or agency spreading perfectly optimized clips… even slightly ahead of release.

Similar to mobile app “waitlist” strategies.

Platform To Platform Clipping Arbitrage

To go deeper into clipping, the real gains for you & me, come from platform-to-platform content arbitrage.

Clipping and sharing YouTube content on TikTok or Twitter within your niche will yield views by tapping into the unique audiences on those platforms.

I do this myself on Twitter, clipping YouTube podcasts and reframing them.

This clip got a quarter million views, and this one hit half a million views.

On TikTok, you can find examples like Hawk Motivation (covered here) and hundreds of similar pages doing millions of impressions through platform arbitrage.

Make sure to find a way to use clipping to boost your distribution:

Any fresh content you can find, remix, and repurpose to promote your narrative is an opportunity you should take advantage of.

If you don’t do it, someone else will.

Engagement Groups & Weaker Algorithms

Note: This newsletter is completely apolitical.

I just saw this political tweet a few days ago, and it reminded me that engagement groups (or sometimes botnets) are incredibly effective at manipulating social platforms with weaker algorithms like Reddit, LinkedIn or Twitter.

Reddit manipulation is so easy & quite interesting now that most posts rank high in SERPs, so just by pushing up comments to the top of a thread, you can rack up hundreds of clicks.

A few years back, I made a botnet on Quora and made a few thousand dollars by pushing affiliate links through NordVPN answers.

Then I realized that I wasn’t alone. A way bigger botnet was pushing my answers down and outranking me with theirs. It became a constant fight, and i lost…

But again… game theory.

If you don’t do it, someone else will.

All these games are rigged anyway, so why wouldn’t you?

Take LinkedIn’s friend-to-friend algorithm. It’s packed with engagement groups. A good friend of mine walked me through how LinkedIn creators use them.

Those are often paid groups.

It’s become a huge business. And as the creator economy grows, it’ll just keep getting bigger.

If Tim Urban and Bryan Johnson had an app together it would be Death Clock AI.

This app tells you exactly when you’re gonna die… and why.

Only 5-mo old & 40K downloads/mo. Simple TikTok distribution strategy:

Most Days Inc, founded by Brent Franson, has two well-being apps on the App Store. One is Most Days, a habit tracker for better daily routines, launched in 2020. It has less than 5K downloads and it’s not generating much revenue..

So they launched a new app in 2024, with a way more aggressive approach to health & self-improvement:

Death Clock AI => combines psychology and AI to provide you a date for your death… and all the habits you can change to improve it.

They got over 40,000/mo downloads since May. They’ve reached 4.3M views on TikTok in 4 months (

@deathclockai

@deathclockai

They’ve been doing ~1 post a day of (usually) Brent (founder) in a podcast format, stating how many years are left at each age.

Ex: “The avg 40y old has 32 years left, are 52% done with their time, 432 full-moons left,…”

How Much Life a 50-year-old Has Left

#wisdom

SGE Team

October 30, 2024

2 min read

Save for later

This legal Delta-8 THC edibles company made: $ millions with a multi-account strategy on TikTok/Reels.

They tested more than 55 accounts on 2 channels over 3 years.

Multi-account video content strategy:

Baking Bags is an edibles company from LA. They have 100,000+ customers and sell 4 different edibles – ice cream cones, cookie dough, candy, lemonade and pre-rolls.

Today they have more than 37 accounts on Tiktok, but those barely reached 2M views through ALL accounts combined.

Three main reasons for this failure:

No consistency => didnt post everyday in none of the accs

No resilience => most accs stayed active for less than 2 months

Product-focus => create content solely abt the product (visual + text)

However on IG Reels, with “only” 19 accs, they reached

– 1,017,498,890 views => 366x more than TikTok

– 939,300 followers => 20x more than TikTok

Posting 2,721 posted videos => twice as much as they posted on all TT accounts

On top of that, on IG, they have been experimenting with new hook and formats:

“POV: Your sister is an actual idiot and ate your edibles without realizing”

“I’ve been snacking on these for the past few hours without realizing…”

Hooks are slight variations of the same and video is usually a recording of the edibles bag + someone with red eyes after eating them

Plus one text hook + viral/clownlike audio song:

https://www.instagram.com/p/DBw5hwLyowp

They post on avg 1 video daily on each IG account.

Lessons learned:

1. Consistency pays off, results can take time

2. Spread risks over multiple platforms

3. Experiment diff types of content + adapt to current trends

Shares are often the biggest algorithmic factor for your video to go viral, with engagement coming in second.

If your content is good and hooks the viewer, it will mechanically trigger him go to check out the comment section.

This applies across platforms, not just TikTok.

In most cases, you want to ensure that an engagement hook is baked into the video to kickstart this comment section.

The typical approach is to use content that’s highly controversial as it naturally triggers engagement.

If you don’t have super controversial content, there are other ways to do so (or to stack on top of controversial content).

Here are 13 engagement farming strategies that i’ve seen crushing on TikTok:

1. Don’t mention the name of the app

Show off the app, but don’t mention its name or any other way to find it. This is a classic strategy and one of the most straight-forward.

The idea behind keeping the app’s name a mystery is that when the video blows up, it triggers massive FOMO. Goal is to get people to comment “what’s the app?”.

+ because you don’t mention the app, the video doesn’t feel like a direct “promotion”.

Let them FOMO.

2. “Forgetting” the link

Say “link below” and “link in bio” but don’t actually post any link to the app.

When the video starts getting traction, everyone will go crazy asking for the link and telling you it’s not there and they can’t find it.

Let them cook, then drop the link.

3. User input for customized app output

Color Analysis (tt@coloranalyses) did this recently, and did it really well.

In this micro-strategy, you post specific combinations of answers within the app to deliver a targeted result.

Viewers can’t see their combo which triggers their desire for personal recognition and will automatically comment to ask the creator to do their own (e.g. here: A – blue eyes, A – blonde hair, C – pale skin = AAC = “Bright Summer Palette”).

Let them be ego-centric.

4. Intentionally saying something wrong

In one of the WhatColors (tt@whatcolors.fashion) video, the guy says that “Billie Eye-Lash” is wearing a green shirt when she is wearing a blue one.

This strategy triggers an instant compulsion to correct, tapping into the viewer’s desire to showcase his knowledge.

Everyone went to correct him.

Let them show-off.

5. Writing with typos

Similar to making a “mistake”, you spell some word wrong on purpose.

It’ll trigger the same behavior as in the previous strategy.

Again, people love to correct and fix others and they will engage in comments.

Let them be grammar purists.

6. Adding an “irrelevant” detail on the video

TogetherKeys’ (tt@togetherkeys1) videos are meant to showcase keychain holders, but they intentionally use Ferrari and Porsche car keys to subtly trigger you.

This approach pushes the watchers to notice and point out the insane “detail.”

Clever tactic, especially when paired with a consistent posting format.

They found this format that continuously performs, and further optimize by adding smart, eye-catching details like this one.

Let them be detectives.

7. Self-categorization

Color Widgets (@color.widgets) uses a slideshow post to showcase different app aesthetics, asking, “Which one are you?”

This triggers self-identification with categories like zodiac signs, aesthetics, color palettes, etc.

You can see similar behavior with astrology slideshows, where viewers comment on what resonates with them personally.

This self-categorization also encourages a sharing effect. If you know someone with the same sign, you’re likely to share it with them.

Let them identify.

8. Share an exclusive, non-available feature of your app

SUSH app (tt@sush_app) is executing this strategy really well.

They post a feature for the app that requires a code, but don’t share the code.

It leads people to get impatient and flood the comment section asking for the code.

Let them cook more.

9. Cognitive challenge

Question AI (@question.ai.mathworld) posts math quizzes for people to solve.

It’s pushes users to showcase their skills, gain social recognition, and engage in debates about the correctness and reasoning behind their answers.

Let them create discussion.

10. Forget a category

Like “forget the link” strategy, you can forget an entire category.

It’s done repeatedly in those astrology slideshows, removing one or two categories on purpose. In their case about 1 out of 12 people will be affected and likely comment:

«What about me?»

Let them feel left out.

11. Replying to:

Replying to user comments in following posts. This is big on TikTok.

People see you replying to others and comment with their own requests, hoping to be answered next.

Let them ask for it.

12. Referral code

Glam Up recently tried this strategy: they launched an app where users can earn free credits with a referral code.

Since they’re targeting teenage girls who might not have much to spend, this effectively drives them back to the video.

There, they post their referral codes.

Some of them are sharing their codes on every video from the account.

Let them ask for free stuff.

13.

Waitlist or gated app

Multiple apps ran this strategy successfully.

Especially ones with a waitlist or running pre-launch viral strategies.

They show a crazy new app on TikTok, people get excited, go to the App store, see the waitlist, come back to the video and comment that it’s not yet live or that they need a code to get in.

It can also work with a non-crazy/exciting app. As long as the video goes viral and the FOMO is triggered.

So let them FOMO even more.

Until next time

Adapt each one to fit your product and context.

Creating a viral video or post is like designing a viral product: details can make all the difference.

$1M ARR distribution strategy for niche language learning app:

There’s a huge TikTok niche vertical “Learn [Language] with [Name]” that generates hundreds of millions of views.

Below are 2 growth hacks to exploit it:

If you search “[language] with…”, you’ll find dozens, if not hundreds, of accounts for each language.

Let’s take learning French as an example:

Search for “French with” and scrape all relevant accounts, or reach out to them directly.

These (likely) don’t get many opportunities, so you can easily negotiate affordable deals if you go bulk targeted nano/micro influencer outreach.

Aim for lowest cost per vid poss. Or,

You could also do a mass affiliate scheme, getting them to put your link in bio or Linktree.

Give them a good profit recurring share and let it spread through their organic videos.

OR:

Create multiple accounts using AI-generated clones, and focus on making good quality short scripts teaching the language.

You can embed your app directly in the background of the videos or even feature the AI character from your language app to have best end-to-end funnel:

An even wiser approach would be to target the most niche language pairs, like:

Portuguese <> French or Vietnamese <> French.

you can easily launch a fleet of semi-automated AI accounts in those underserved/low-competition markets.

Found this bizarre strategy where someone managed to get 58M+ views over 12s of accounts FAKE launching Crumbl Cookies in every country on earth.

Some “black-hat” account-building tactics but there are a few interesting ideas on how to use a similar strategy:

Crumbl Cookies is the fastest-expanding US cookie business, selling >1M cookies everyday.

They went viral on TikTok reaching 9M followers and 1,536,800,000 views…

They found a viral strategy where they have a rotating menu and reveal weekly flavours in HD videos that gen 1000s of comments & likes.

Super quickly became a huge trend on TikTok, then multiple accounts started to pop up: same names, logo, handles… Every single one was opened to announce the launch of Crumbl Cookies in a different country.

At first i thought it was a normal expansion strategy, except that none is owned or operated by Crumbl Cookies. HUNDREDS of them.

The brand is only in the US and Canada atm (they’ve commented on some of these accounts trying to debunk). But the reach those fake posts get is crazy:

This one faked a Crumbl Cookie release in Poland. Less than 3K followers, only 3 videos on the page, but: 1 video = 326K views + 20K likes + 1K comments + 2K saved.

So what’s up with this:

Someone or an entity, found a strategy re-purposing content + announcing fake launches & drove an insane amount of people/awareness to those brand new accounts.

They have no incentive to Crumbl Cookie’s success. But there is many things they can do to monetize/use this new audience:

1, You are a competitor. You create an audience on a product similar to yours. You reach some ‘000s, delete content & start posting your own cookie brand in this new market.

Or, you are:

2, Not a competitor, but launching your own business in a (close) niche. You build an audience for your target niche/location, get followers with already viral content. Then stop, reset and feed them your product.

But even better is if you are:

3, Building your own affiliate network. Your fake accounts reaches millions of views from users of a specific niche/country => you have warm up accounts to start affiliate marketing/distribution in this niche/country.

It’s a good framework to build accounts because when one trend dies, they hop onto the next one and continue building them up.

Track performance of all these accounts here:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a101fCZWG4kdO

Their story & INSANE TikTok viral organic flywheel:

In 2011, they launched Incredibox part time as a free website. Growth was slow over the first few months. But a year later, it went viral and became the most searched term on Google for a few days.

Incredibox lets anyone easily create catchy music tracks. Users drag + drop items onto the characters and mix the sounds into tracks.

And so they’ve released 8 different versions of the app over time, each with a brand new theme, sound and design. They keep users engaged, addicted and waiting for more. They can share them through a unique link and vote for the Top 50.

It’s highly addicting and it makes people absolutely love them. 4.9/5 on Google Play (47K reviews) and App Store (37K reviews).

Organic communities started popping up everywhere, on Reddit, Forums, and then the craziest thing happened: HUNDREDS of organic accounts started to show up on TikTok, check this out:

The top account has 1.9M followers. > 20 of these accounts have > 10K followers.

All 100% organic, produced by a community (of kids) who’s deep on the app and it generates daily viral content on TikTok for FREE.

They hired small groups of creators to produce 15+ videos in less than 30 mins. All they have to do is sit around a table, get the cards out and record themselves playing.

And they also realized that they could easily do the exact same thing to expand to 3 other EU countries (Italy, Spain & Germany).

All they had to do was get 4/5 creators that speak the language to create the exact same content. But as I looked closer I found a catch, that made it even more interesting:

@littlesecretfr

Avez-vous deviné qui est l’imposteur ?

#littlesecret

#imposteur

#menteur

#famille

#jeuxsociete

#friends

#drole

♬ original sound – Little Secret – Jeu de bluff

Take a look at Little Secret. They started with a France account, and soon launched one in German, one in Spanish and one in Italian. But if we look closely, you’ll see that most of the videos are filmed in Paris.

By creating multiple accounts for each game, each focusing on a different country, they were able to reach millions of users, and what’s crazy is that:

For two of their games, Spain became by far the largest TikTok audience, converting into additional millions of $ in revenue. They reached half a billion views in 4 different countries by simply producing the same content in different languages… all in the same city (Paris):

They scale across multiple countries, games, and… platforms. They ran the same strategy on Instagram Reels and generated millions of views there as well:

You can track all ATM Gaming’s accounts on TikTok through our public collection on Shortimize:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a1043F87jqLUd

This AI tanning app, Rayz, ran this scheme to 40M+ views: They went through TikTok profiles until they found great-looking, tanned girls, downloaded their videos, resized them, cut them into a perfect 2.5-second frame, added a POV hook, and turned them to:

Tuesday masterclass on how to drive organic acquisition for a consumer app:

10M+ views in 6mo on founder account 40M+ in FRA from 5 in-house accounts to #2 + daily micro influencer mkt + USA TikTok waitlist launch strategy.

Below are 8 strategies they’re running, detailed:

1) The founder is creating 1 to 3 videos a day. Some were boosted with ads, but most growth has been organic. The account has grown quickly:

Great way to test hooks and experiment as a consumer founder. She’s creating simple yet effective videos:

@clara_gigiboss

#gigiapp

#ia

#dating

@gigi

♬ original sound – clara_gigiboss

2) They have 4 branded accounts. They’ve hired interns/SM peeps who are producing content daily:

Simple vlog/POV content on some accounts and more edited content on others:

@gigidating_us

Go relax while Gigi finds a match for you????

#couple

#datingapp

#gigiapp

#viral

#tinder

♬ original sound – Gigi US

3) A company “behind-the-scenes” account (

@gigitheoffice

):

https://www.tiktok.com/@gigitheoffice/video/7420387183393099041

Great way to create a different style of content. There is always excellent content to be made in a startup office…

4) Each marketer/intern should run a personal account posting daily pov/vlog content. And they started doing this with

@coucoucestalice42

:

5) Micro influencer marketing: They’re getting daily videos from regular nano and micro influencers (search for any “gigi dating” + videos)…

6) Slideshow account experiment. They started a slideshow-only account, pushing daily slideshows. A few have already hit 50K+ views:

That’s the level of organic content (mixed with boosted post ads) and experimentation it seems to take to consistently drive traffic and reach a top ranking.

Optimally, every single one of the strategies above should be run in parallel, and a few weeks ago, they started running various strategies to grow their pre-launch waitlist in the US.

7) They’ve set up two branded US accounts where they push their content in English. One of them started a month ago and already got 320K views:

8) They hired at least three full-time creators in the USA posting daily videos:

@istnotguili

,

@babybrooke2002

, and

@aavaguava444

:

Some are still gaining traction, while others are already performing really well.

The idea behind the waitlist launch is to get tens of thousands of users in a specific country to pre-download the app. So that when you launch, you instantly create some network effect, and…

…you rank straight at the top of your App Store category, generating even more momentum. Having a content-obsessed founding team gives you an significant edge when building a consumer/social app.

Cal AI is now famously doing $400K+ MRR. They’re running a mix channel acquisition strategy (ads + influencers + other).

I went to check their influencer marketing strategies. They’re running targeted influencer marketing with crafted videos aiming for ≈$5 CPM:

On a Twitter Space that Zach & Blake hosted on Monday, they mentioned that their optimal target was a $5 CPM (views).

Once you can estimate a profitable CPA, and a conversion rate per 1k views, having a CPM target helps you retroactively figure out a solid influencer strategy.

With regular micro/large influencer marketing, it’s pretty straightforward to estimate the average views you’ll get, since it’ll be close to the median views of their account.

Cal AI has a key network of influencers within their specific fitness, wellness, and self-improvement niche. They pay for main profile videos such as:

They did 450M+ views on TikTok & Reels with this strategy:

Scratch Adventure is generating $40K in MRR, and I assume they did even more at their peak. It’s an erotic sex games app for couples, and they’ve been growing by running the strategies detailed below:

On TikTok, they ran three accounts before finding one that took off:

@scratch_adventureee

(after failing with

@scratch_adventure

and

@scratch_adventuree

).

The account with three “e’s” achieved 81M views across 717 videos, with a 3% viral rate.

But they didn’t stop there:

People want things to go viral instantly, but experimentation is key on TikTok (and in growth, more broadly). They definitely experimented. They created around 125 branded accounts, with 55 of them posting videos, but only 6 gained solid traction:

Those 6 accounts seem to be run by different creators/people in various countries.

@scratch_adventure_fm

has 29M views,

@scratchadventuremexico

reached 17M views, and

@scratch_adventure_uukk

got 5M views…

The format is similar across accounts and is well executed:

Typically, videos feature a male hovering over a female in bed for about 2 seconds + POV hook. No explicit NSFW content, just enough to intrigue viewers.

Then cut to app, showing a partial scratch-off, giving just enough to understand what it is, but not enough to be satisfied. It’s all designed to tease your curiosity.

Wondershare, a public prosumer software company, is running 18 TikTok accounts, one for each of their products.

They made 117.9M views on TikTok, mostly with tutorial videos.

A great use case for scaling short-form marketing to promote prosumer software

Filmora’s main account has 46M views with over 1,000 videos; 10% get between 18k and 100k views.

Content is purely tutorials, use case by use case.

It doesn’t need viral hits but a steady flow of well-performing videos to become an evergreen conversion channel (similar to SEO)

The Filmora account is so successful that they tried replicating by language, creating accounts for DE, BR, FR, IT, and an English one.

Each account has a different content creator with their own style variation but executing the same format/strategy.

Another high-performing account is for Recoverit, their data recovery software.

They alternate between “how-to” videos and other tech content, staying within the niche while diversifying.

This strategy is great for ongoing growth, earning 17M views with many well-performing videos.

Their Dr Fone (another software) account is a really well executed account, pushing various Smartphone tips & hacks.

With a 24k median views and 9 videos over 1M views. It’s their best performing account.

The Dr. Fone account features soothing aesthetics, with videos showing just hands using a phone to perform the tips and hacks.

Focus there is on rapidly growing, shifting from direct promotion to building a faceless “influencer” that will later serve as a promotion platform.

They repeat this strategy with their other software: FamiSafe (5.5M views), Uniconverter (1M), PDFElement (5.2M), EDrawMax (2.5M), and Democrator (4.2M).

Each is managed by a different creator, and most have impressive stats and viral coeffs, especially for such niche products.

They have 4 more accounts, branded Wondershare (Official, Espagnol, Tech & Tech DE) where they post daily tips, and memes.

They posted 3,896 videos across 18 accounts.

If you have a web utility or prosumer software, following a similar strategy can unlock a new growth channel.

Even with lower views, these videos convert effectively, especially as you cover more ground.

Save for later

Humans Anonymous, the consumer social app, scored 136,000,000 views in 260 days on TikTok.

This brilliant strategy skyrocketed them to the #1 spot on the App Store on launch day.

Here’s the complete strategy behind their 7 faceless accounts and early growth successes

They created separate accounts for different verticals of their app: ADHD, Anxiety, Breakup, Moms, Nurses, Teachers, and Founders.

They used Minecraft parkour gameplay as b-roll footage, a trend that blew up about 1.5 years ago. On top of that, they added stories about each topic with an automated voiceover.

The genius part: those stories were stolen from related Subreddits.

For example, their top-performing page, the ADHD account, pulled trending posts from r/ADHD and turned them into videos.

This approach allowed them to endlessly recycle high-quality content since the trending posts had already been “approved” by Reddit users as engaging and viral.

The outcome is:

Mind-blowing stats. They were posting 3 videos per day per account when all accounts were running simultaneously, totaling 17 videos a day.

Their top two accounts alone were pulling in 250k views daily. And totaled 135M+ views.

That’s one hell of a growth hack.

And it naturally sparked engagement. Even the least-viewed videos were racking up tons of comments.

tt@adhdanon

accumulated 68,609,892 views across 773 videos in 260 days. With a 5% viral rate, an impressive 39 videos hit over 1M views.

Close behind was

tt@breakupsanonymous

, which amassed 25,653,343 views over the same period.

If you dig into their accounts, you’ll notice they shut down underperforming ones after just 3 months (post launch), focusing only on the 2 or 3 accounts that were performing exceptionally well.

They ran these accounts for a total of 9 months.

Looking at their bio links, the UTM tags were:

utm_source=adhdanon (for attribution purposes—to determine which account performed best)

utm_campaign=Pre-Order+Campaign

Most of this growth strategy was designed to build up their app’s pre-order waitlist, which played a significant role in launching them straight to #1 in the Health category.

Now, let’s take a closer look at a video to break down this growth hack:

The videos ranged from 1 to 1.5 minutes in length.

Each video started with a hook: a screenshot of the Reddit post’s title.

The post’s text was then revealed gradually through screenshots, with everything voiced over.

Right after the first frame, the call-to-action appeared. On the ADHD page, for instance, it was:

“Get ADHD tips, stories, and inspiration. LINK IN BIO.”

Despite the videos being relatively long, they generated significant engagement, triggered intense conversations, and drove high-intent conversions to their waitlist.

The number of convos triggered by these videos was a key factor in making this format so effective. They seem to have frequently responded to comments.

To produce these videos, they likely developed a template that allowed for quick editing or, more likely, outsourced the editing on Fiverr.

Because of the templated nature of those videos, by optimising the process, they could have these videos edited at minimal cost.

frameworks.example: Humans Anonymous used TikTok bios with UTM-tagged links to drive users to their pre-order waitlist, contributing to their #1 App Store launch.

AI Study Apps are the most competitive niche, with top apps getting millions of views on TikTok.

Explore data from the best AI study apps on this Shortimize collection:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a10joO2hySFo9

5 AI Study Apps Smashing the TikTok Game

150M views with a single format.

LET THAT SINK IN.

@answersai.com

: 143,810,313 views, 27 crazy viral videos, 7% viral rate.

@answersai.ai

: 9,748,229 views, 6 viral videos, 2% viral rate.

Their most viral video had 22M views—it’s a direct ad for their product.

They use a high-performing format: filming in the classroom and zooming over the shoulder of the person’s laptop in front.

“POV: The whole class is about to take a quiz, and this girl finishes before it even starts.”

Every high-performing video uses this format, each netting a few million views.

A winning strategy that’s still working today and can be emulated when the school year starts.

Some other great hooks:

“Future engineers <3 <3”

“Freshman in college right now”

“This kid living in 2099”

“Your professor has no idea”

JotBot

made 33,675,000 views across their five accounts.

Series are key to nailing TikTok, and JotBot’s team understood this well. They went viral with a first video using the hook:

“I made a website called …”

They created a series that generated millions of views across their accounts.

It goes like this:

“I made a website called IhaveanessaydueatmidnightthatIreallydontwanttodo.com.”

They pitch the app and have a perfect looping video where the end triggers the beginning.

Personally, one of the strongest hooks I’ve seen. Beautifully executed format with variations using different domains.

@jotbot.official

: 6,436,543 views

@my.jotbot

: 3,901,818 views

@jotbotofficial

: 1,011,559 views

@jotbotai

: 20,114,509 views

@myjotbot.com

: 2,211,386 views

Cramly

(

@cramly.ai

: 194,286,697 views) has 98 viral videos (20% viral rate).

Most viewed video has 26M views.

THIS IS INSANE.

Their top-performing format is

“essay due tomorrow”

/

“doing an essay last minute,”

which racked up 40M+ views.

They also had the

“Secret website for students”

hook, producing multiple high-performing videos.

And the

“Stop using ChatGPT…”

hook. Since most students are using ChatGPT, pitching a better alternative might attract part of their user base.

Most of their hooks create extreme urgency, and they worked great.

Once you have a winner like Cramly, replicate it into a series. Squeeze the juice out of a format or hook that’s proven to work with the algorithm.

That’s how you repeatedly win at the TikTok game.

They had their peak performance in 2023 but are worth studying.

They recently tried to scale with dedicated influencer accounts:

@cramly_alexandra

@cramly_anj

@cramlybeth

The next two apps made 20M views with one faceless format—that’s my type of growth hack. Check this out:

At a 5% viral rate and an 11% 10x outperforming rate, with their most viral video at 4M views,

Kipper

spun up consistent viral videos using the same faceless format.

They use a similar trick as AnswersAI: laptop recording in a classroom above the shoulder of the person next to them, mixed with a

“better alternative to ChatGPT for students”

hook.

Their last 250 videos follow this pattern, with 1 out of 10 outperforming. Easy to produce in bulk.

They totaled 20M views.

Plume

is a French app, an AI-powered alternative to Google Word, and they’ve been surfing on the

“Stop Using Word”

hook to generate dozens of viral videos.

It’s faceless, and their format involves a double hook with words written on the document, pitching their app.

Aggressive

“alternative to”

seems to be a pattern working remarkably well.

I’m a big fan of this format and their execution.

They did 14M views and counting.

But it’s not pretty for everyone…

For every AI study tool performing well on TikTok, there are 10 more struggling that could be doing great.

A few of them:

@unriddle_ai

@stealthwriter.ai

@writeless.ai

@tasksheet_ai

@simplified.ai

It’s an extremely competitive space, with players building OpenAI wrappers. If you’re an AI wrapper builder, performing on TikTok can be the difference between making millions or failing hard.

This unknown astrology app gets 50M+ views per month on TikTok with this simple strategy. The stats for 1 of their acc:

> 385 slideshows in 105 days

> 12 with over 1M views & 36 with over 350k views

> median of 37k views

They have 9 accounts performing as well, check this:

Astroapp is a basic astrology app, which isn’t even ranking among the top players (

Co-Star

,

The Pattern

,

Moonly

).

But they have an insane top-of-funnel strategy, generating 50M views a month.

They found a slideshow strategy with text-heavy slides that work incredibly well for engagement.

The ones about love, dating, flirting, gf/bf, and compatibility are the ones working best.

In many niches, if you can create content around those topics, go ahead.

These accounts are sometimes posting 5 times a day.

They started with

astroscope

, which now has a large following. Once they discovered that slideshows were performing like crazy, they focused on them and launched another account,

astroapp

.

I got more interested in the second account, as it’s way smaller in terms of followers, but it’s destroying. Its metrics:

385 slideshows in 105 days

12 with over 1,000,000 views

36 with over 350k views

median of 37k views

And that’s not just it. They found a super smart way to scale:

Two months ago, they created 7 different language accounts for PL, NL, PT, ES, FR, IT, and DE. And each one of them is DESTROYING. Just check

astroscope_pl

.

View all their accounts & data on this collection:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a10rma0QaPVcA

They instantly 5x’d their views with this scaling strategy. Now, they only have to add more languages and then, maybe, create a second account per language.

They’ve completely destroyed the top funnel game for their category.

The genius in their slideshows is that you have to watch until your Zodiac sign appears, and the heavy reading will trigger the necessary engagement for the video to go viral. You’ll probably read your friend’s sign too, and then share it with them.

If you have an app in:

Astrology

Motivation

Texting (utility)

Psychology

Social

Dating

Fitness

…and a few other niches, you might be able to reproduce this strategy.

The other

@nikitabier

backed social app

@locketcamera

is running a similar playbook as

@AirbudsWidget

. & It’s extremely successful.

#3 in the Social Media & 250M+ views on TikTok.

LocketApp’s TikTok strategy fully analyzed:

Before running this strategy, Locket famously used small influencers to post videos on their profiles. They generated millions of views doing that.

I discovered their strategy a while ago while growing my own consumer app, and I was shocked at how well they had mastered their format.

They did better than anyone.

The format is ALWAYS the same. They’ve experimented and found one that performs better than others.

It’s a 2 to 3-second voiceless shot of the person’s face smiling or slightly dancing while looking straight at the camera, with the hook as a text overlay.

This is followed by a screen recording of the screen unlocking, the app being tapped, opened, and the main feature used: sending a picture to a friend’s lock screen with a cute message.

Now, somewhere down the road, they switched to a model where they have dedicated accounts.

It might have been to save cost and time, or perhaps they figured they could get the same results by posting themselves.

They started with team members’ accounts before scaling. A handful of them (likely their growth/marketing team) began posting the classic Locket TikTok every single day, sometimes twice or thrice a day.

And it worked. Some accounts have 10% of the videos beat the median by 10x (30k+ views), and over 5% by 50x (going crazy viral).

Now they’re scaling by getting dedicated creators and more team members to do the same. They stop accounts that are not performing well and keep iterating.

Inspect all their accounts & data on this Shortimize collection:

https://app.shortimize.com/c/2a10eVaER0AvfO

tt@kalebsjournal

tt@kaias_lensss

tt@morgsgabrielle_

…

Note: They’re also running other strategies, such as UGC on their main page, some animated accounts, and more.

SGE Team

•

3 min read

Save for later

The

@AirbudsWidget

app hit #2, ranking just behind Spotify.

The

@nikitabier

advised startup has an ambassador TikTok strategy that got millions of users.

They post 150+ videos a day on 50+ accounts, doing millions of views daily.

Airbuds hired dozens of students and regular people to post multiple times a day on new TikTok accounts. I found over 50 active accounts.

They usually post 2 to 4 videos a day on average, with some posting up to 10 videos a day.

The best accounts have up to 17% of their videos performing at 10x the median, and 8% going crazy viral. The worst ones don’t have a single viral video.

It doesn’t matter; they managed to engineer virality through mass lo-fi content production.

On their worst days, they have at least 5 to 10 videos with over 100k+ views EVERY SINGLE DAY, all fully organic.

Accounts are branded “firstName.airbuds.” Here are a few of them for you to check:

If you want to create clickable links to those TikTok profiles, you could format them as follows:

@nathan

@claire

@sarah

@riah

@luna

@joeh

These links should direct you to each user’s TikTok profile when clicked.

It’s dead simple content.

It features the character doing random life stuff, dancing, or just lip-syncing, with a text overlay hook/storyline. It’s a one-shot, no/low-editing video.

Overlay story text ranges widely; none are really similar.

“What the Airbuds reactions are starting to feel like”

“How I press the block button when someone sends a mean reaction on Airbuds”

“Me dodging the question because my favorite Taylor song is a very unpopular opinion”

…

You get the gist.

But check this out:

This account is posting 7 videos a day like that. In the past 4 days, they got 5 videos outperforming the median and 2 reaching 100k views.

This is bananas, for videos that take on average 10 minutes to shoot, edit, and post.

It’s super low friction—they hire youngsters and students and they pay them a fixed rate + a CPM reward bonus.
